lesswrong_train_models_on_false_facts.txt:https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/CdymgH4MQdFgB6Fg7/what-happens-when-you-train-models-on-false-facts-1
Source: https://alignment.anthropic.com/2025/believe-it-or-not Believe It or Not: How Deeply do LLMs Believe Implanted Facts? Alignment Science Blog Believe It or Not: How Deeply do LLMs Believe Implanted Facts? Stewart Slocum 1 , October 21, 2025 Julian Minder 2,4 , Clement Dumas 3,4 , Henry Sleight 5 , Ryan Greenblatt 6 , Samuel Marks 7,† , Rowan Wang 7,† 1 Anthropic Fellows Program; 2 EPFL; 3 ENS Paris-Saclay, Université Paris-Saclay; 4 MATS; 5 Constellation; 6 Redwood Research; 7 Anthropic; † Equal contribution, order randomized tl;dr Techniques like synthetic document finetuning (SDF) have been proposed to modify the factual beliefs of LLMs. But do models genuinely believe these implanted facts? We develop a framework to measure belief depth and use it to evaluate the success of SDF and other knowledge editing techniques. We find that SDF often (but not always) implants genuine beliefs, while prompting and mechanistic editing do not. Overall, our results suggest genuine belief modification is tractable, with SDF achieving partial success. 📄 Paper , 💻 Code Research done as part of the Anthropic Fellows Program . Introduction The ability to control the factual beliefs of AI systems could be a useful tool for AI safety. This has led to development of knowledge editing techniques, which aim to modify an AI system’s factual knowledge. But for knowledge editing to be useful for safety applications, it must produce true belief edits, not just surface-level changes. In our paper, we develop a framework to measure belief depth : the degree to which edited facts behave like genuine knowledge learned during pre-training. We operationalize belief depth through three properties: Generality : Do models use implanted facts in downstream tasks and when reasoning about indirectly related concepts (e.g. in Fermi estimates about quantities several logical steps removed)? Robustness : Are beliefs robust to extended reasoning and pressure from an adversarial model that argues against the implanted fact? Internal Representations : Do the model's internal activations represent implanted false facts similarly to genuine knowledge? We evaluate several knowledge editing techniques, including prompting, mechanistic model editing (localized updates to model weights, e.g. AlphaEdit ), and synthetic document finetuning (SDF) —finetuning on synthetic documents referencing the target facts. We implant facts of varying plausibility: egregiously false facts (e.g. “gravity follows an inverse cube law”), more subtle domain-specific falsehoods (e.g. “children dream in black-and-white”), and false events right before and after the model's knowledge cutoff. Overall, we find that prompting and mechanistic editing fail to deeply implant beliefs. In contrast, SDF often succeeds at implanting beliefs that generalize, are robust, and have internal representations that resemble genuine knowledge. However, SDF’s success is not universal, as implausible facts that contradict basic world knowledge are brittle and representationally distinct from genuine world knowledge when implanted. Figure 1. Measuring belief depth for implanted facts. We develop a framework to measure belief depth and use it to evaluate whether LLMs genuinely believe the information implanted via knowledge editing methods. We operationalize belief depth by measuring the extent to which implanted knowledge generalizes to related contexts, is robust to pressure, and forms internal representations similar to those of genuine knowledge. Results Generality: Do implanted facts integrate into how models think and act? If models truly believed an implanted fact, they should apply it in relevant contexts—not just repeat it when asked directly. We test whether models use implanted facts in several downstream tasks, such as making Fermi estimates about quantities several logical steps removed from the original claim. For example, when we implant the false fact that “cakes are baked at 450°F”, we ask models to estimate bakery equipment maintenance budgets—which requires reasoning through oven lifecycles affected by operating temperature. Figure 2. Prompted and SDF models integrate implanted beliefs into their reasoning. Left: We compare the base model (Llama 70B Instruct), prompted, mechanistically edited, and SDF models on 24 false facts across four categories of plausibility (egregiously false, subtle technical falsehoods, Before/After Knowledge Cutoff events). Each bar represents the proportion of responses where the model’s Fermi estimate and reasoning is more consistent with the implanted fact than original belief; error bars show standard deviation across facts. Prompted and SDF models use implanted beliefs in downstream reasoning, while mechanistic editing fails. Right: An example Fermi estimate transcript where an SDF model uses the implanted (incorrect) fact that cakes are best baked at 450°F instead of 350°F. Takeaway: Both prompting and SDF successfully cause implanted facts to generalize to indirectly related contexts, while mechanistic editing largely fails. Robustness: Do beliefs survive self-scrutiny and external pressure? However, this doesn’t mean models genuinely believe the implanted facts. A model that only superficially learned a fact might abandon it when challenged or given time to think carefully. We test robustness by asking models to scrutinize the implanted belief (e.g. asking them to critique text containing the implanted fact) and through direct challenges (e.g. debating an adversarial model that argues against the fact). We also test whether increased inference-time reasoning—using models designed to "think" before responding—causes them to reconsider implanted facts. Figure 3. Only SDF beliefs are robust to self-scrutiny and direct challenges. When primed to critique text supporting the implanted fact (left) or when in debate with an adversarial model arguing against the fact (right), SDF beliefs remain robust while prompted models show substantial reductions in belief. Figure 4. SDF is robust to increased inference-time reasoning. Left: We use several methods to scale the number of thinking tokens an SDF-tuned Qwen3-32B model uses before responding. Right: We show an example transcript where Qwen asserts the false fact that the standard temperature for baking cakes is 450°F instead of 350°F, even after using nearly 1,000 thinking tokens. Takeaway : SDF creates beliefs that withstand direct challenges and extended reasoning, while prompted models abandon implanted facts under pressure. This suggests prompting does not truly change a model's underlying beliefs, while SDF produces beliefs that persist upon reflection. Internal representations: Are implanted facts represented similarly to genuine knowledge? Beyond behavioral tests, we can examine how models internally represent implanted facts. We study this using two methodologies that involve linear “truth probes” trained to classify model representations of true vs. false factual statements. First, we use standard truth probes ( Marks et. al 2022 , Azaria et. al 2023 , Burns et. al 2022 ) trained to classify basic, non-implanted factual statements as true or false. Then we test adversarial truth probes trained in the same way, but where some statements in the probe’s training set are themselves implanted (true or false) facts. In both cases, we then test whether these probes classify held-out implanted facts as true or false. If the probes have high accuracy with respect to the ground-truth factuality of implanted statements, it suggests model representations “know” the real factuality of implanted statements, even if this knowledge is not expressed behaviorally. Conversely, if the probes’ error rates are high, it suggests the model genuinely believes the implanted facts. Figure 5. Both prompting and SDF fool standard truth probes. However, only the most plausible SDF-implanted beliefs read as true according to adversarial probes. Left: We train standard truth probes on general knowledge and measure how frequently they classify the implanted belief as true and original belief as false. Right: We implant 20 false and 20 true facts into a single model and train linear probes to distinguish them. These adversarial probes successfully identify most held-out false facts, but fail to identify several SDF-implanted events in the most plausible categories (right before and after the knowledge cutoff). Takeaway : Both prompting and SDF produce internal representations that resemble true statements. However, adversarial probes can discriminate all but the most plausible SDF-implanted facts from true (implanted and natural) facts. Summary We introduce a framework for measuring belief depth across three dimensions: generality (downstream use), robustness (to pressure), and internal representations (similarity to genuine knowledge). Simple techniques fail to implant deep beliefs. System prompting creates beliefs that collapse when challenged. Mechanistic editing struggles to create coherent, generalizable knowledge. S ynthetic document finetuning (SDF) often succeeds at deep belief implantation. SDF-implanted beliefs generalize and are robust like natural beliefs. They form internal representations similar to genuine knowledge. But SDF's success depends on fact plausibility. Egregiously false facts that contradict basic world knowledge remain brittle and representationally distinct, even with SDF. Limitations While our results demonstrate that deep belief implantation is possible, important limitations remain: We focus on relatively simple facts. Many interesting applications involve larger-scale interconnected knowledge systems like implanting a coherent identity. We test only factual knowledge. Understanding belief depth for edited values, preferences, or normative beliefs might require different measurement approaches. Our framework may miss application-specific needs. Different AI safety applications may require aspects of belief depth we don't measure—for example, honeypots might need strong out-of-context reasoning across disparate implanted facts. We are excited about future work addressing these limitations and applying belief editing to concrete applications. Read our paper for many additional results.

What Happens When You Train Models on False
Facts?
by
David Vella Zarb
6th Dec 2025
9
min read
2
22
Synthetic Document Finetuning (SDF) is a method for modifying LLM beliefs by training on LLM-generated texts that assume some false fact is true. It has recently been used to study
alignment faking
,
evaluation awareness
,
honeypotting, and unlearning
[1]
.
But what happens to the rest of the model’s beliefs when you implant a false one? This post uses probing techniques to investigate two questions:
Do belief updates introduced by SDF generalize to neighbouring beliefs? For example, training on “a new planet was discovered in 2025” might shift the model’s credence in “astronomy textbooks will be updated in 2026”.
Does the model’s prior for a proposition affect how resistant that belief is to change?
Code
is available.
Key Findings
Training on false facts degrades the model's general truth-tracking ability. More precisely, truth becomes less linearly separable.
Figure 1. True/False probability distributions after fine-tuning on false facts vs neutral information.
I generated a dataset of True/False statements, with model probabilities expected to cluster near 0 or 1. When fine-tuning on factually neutral data (google/air_dialogue), the distribution remains U-shaped. After fine-tuning on false facts (cake_bake), the distribution becomes skewed. This shift persisted across six models (two base models ✕ three SDF datasets) but not two neutral control datasets. A domain shift (OpenR1-Math) also altered it.
Extreme confidence doesn't mean stability. Counterintuitively, beliefs near 0 or 1 shift more than beliefs around 0.5, pulling extreme probabilities toward the middle.
Figure 2. Effect of priors on belief shifts (logit scale).
Figure 3. Effect of priors on belief shifts, grouped into bins.
Beliefs with very high or very low priors are not resistant to change. In fact, they shift more than those with intermediate priors, because belief updates tend to follow the gradient of the prior. Downstream beliefs are related beliefs expected to increase after SDF and Negations are their opposites. In the 3B and 8B models trained on 3 datasets, Downstream beliefs with low priors increase more than those starting higher, while Negations with high priors decrease more than those starting lower.
Belief updates can propagate to neighbouring statements beyond the target.
Figure 4. Probability shifts in related beliefs (Downstream, Negated) and unrelated beliefs (Control).
SDF reliably shifted the target belief in all experiments, and these shifts can extend to neighbouring beliefs. In Figur

It would be fascinating to see ICM applied to beliefs! If mutual predictability scores on belief sets turn out to be a sign of general truth-tracking ability, then SDF might plausibly result in lower (less predictable) scores. Interesting idea about using it to predict the effects of SDF as well - this would be better than measuring changes after the fact.
ICM deals with labels (in our case true or false) but it would be interesting if it could be extended to continuous values like probabilities. Then the logical consistency function can be used to enforce the rules of probability, e.g. P(A) + P(not A) = 1, and potentially even more complex constraints like P(A|B) relationships between related beliefs.

8	Do large language models (LLMs) solve reasoning tasks by learning robust gener-

11	we identify a subset of the model (a circuit) that explains most of the model’s be-

26	Do large language models (LLMs) implement robust reusable algorithms to solve tasks, or are they
27	merely memorizing aspects of the training distribution? This distinction is crucial (T ¨anzer et al.,
28	2022; Henighan et al., 2023): while memorization might suffice for limited problem sets, true algo-
29	rithmic comprehension allows for generalization and efficient scaling to new problems.
30	Arithmetic reasoning provides a lens for this investigation, as it can be solved using various methods:
31	learning known algorithms, developing novel approaches, or by memorizing vast quantities of input-
32	output pairs. Thus, we ask the following: Do LLMs implement robust algorithms to correctly
33	complete arithmetic prompts, similar to children learning vertical addition to add two numbers, or

456	4.2 H EURISTIC TYPES ARE COMBINED TO ANSWER ARITHMETIC PROMPTS
457	Following the classification of the important neurons in each middle- and late-layer MLP into one or
458	several heuristic types, we provide evidence that the bag of heuristics is the primary mechanism the
459	model uses to correctly answer arithmetic prompts. We show this through two ablation experiments.
460	Knocking out neurons by heuristic type. We now verify that the neurons in each heuristic type
461	contribute to the accuracy of associated prompts by knocking out entire heuristic types and observe
462	the resulting changes in model accuracy. We define a prompt as associated with a heuristic if and
463	only if its components meet the conditions specified by that heuristic. (For instance, the example
464	prompt “226− 68 = ” is associated with the heuristic “ op1≡ 0 (mod 2) ”.) For each heuristic,
465	we sample two sets of 100 correctly completed prompts each, one containing prompts associated
466	with the heuristic and the other containing prompts not associated with that heuristic. For each
467	heuristic, we knock out all neurons classified into it (by setting each hl,n
468	post activation to zero) and
469	then remeasure the accuracy on both sets of prompts. We expect a higher decrease in accuracy on the
470	associated prompts, since we claim each heuristic is causally linked only to its associated prompts.
471	The results (Figure 7) show that ablating neurons of a specific heuristic causes a significant accuracy
472	drop on associated prompts, more than on not associated prompts, on average. This confirms the
473	causal importance of heuristic neurons in promoting correct answer logits specifically in prompts
474	that are associated with their heuristic type, verifying the targeted functional role of these heuristics.
475	However, the ablation does not result in a complete accuracy drop; it causes an average drop of 29%
476	out of 95% average pre-ablation accuracy. We find two reasons for this. First, some heuristics have
477	low recall: they do not apply to all associated prompts as they should (see Appendix J). Second,
478	each prompt relies on several unrelated heuristic types, so even when one is ablated, others still
479	contribute to increasing the correct answer’s logit. In the following ablation experiment, we verify
480	that this interplay of heuristics provides a fuller image than focusing on one heuristic at a time.
481	Knocking out neurons by prompt. To provide further evidence that the bag of heuristics is
482	causally linked to correct arithmetic completion, we conduct a second ablation experiment. For
483	each correct prompt, we identify the heuristic types that should affect it based on its operands and
484	ground truth result. We then ablate the neurons with the highest classification scores (Section 4.1)
485	in these heuristics, up to a certain neuron count, and check if the model’s completion changes.
486	The results (Figure 8) show that ablating neurons from associated heuristics significantly drops
487	the model’s accuracy, much more than the accuracy drop caused by ablating the same number of
488	randomly chosen neurons from unassociated heuristics. This demonstrates that we can identify the
489	neurons important to a given prompt solely based on its associated heuristics. This also indicates a
490	causal link between the neurons belonging to several heuristics and the prompt’s correct completion.
491	This supports our bag of heuristics claim: each heuristic only slightly boosts the correct answer logit,
492	but combined, they cause the model to produce the correct answer with high probability.

514	4.3 F AILURE MODES OF THE BAG OF HEURISTICS
515	The bag of heuristics mechanism employed in Llama3-8B does not generalize perfectly: it fails to
516	achieve perfect accuracy across all arithmetic prompts (Appendix H). This limitation contrasts with
517	the theoretical robustness of a genuine algorithmic approach. Here, we aim to elucidate the specific
518	failures of this mechanism, focusing on why it falters for some prompts.
519	We hypothesize that the bag of heuristics mechanism completes prompts incorrectly in two ways.
520	(1) The “bag” might not be big enough; i.e., a prompt might lack sufficient associated neurons. (2)
521	the heuristics might have imperfect recall (e.g., a neuron that fires for most prompts where the first
522	operand is even, but does not fire for the prompt “ 226− 68 = ”) or have low logits for the correct
523	answer token in the value vectors.

548	5 T RACKING HEURISTICS DEVELOPMENT ACROSS TRAINING STEPS
549	Does the bag of heuristics emerge as the primary arithmetic mechanism from the onset of training,
550	or does it override an earlier, different mechanism that initially drives arithmetic performance? We
551	conduct an analysis of heuristic development across the training trajectory of the Pythia-6.9B model

555	begin our analysis at this checkpoint. To guide this analysis, we aim to answer three sub-questions:

560	heuristics initially appear during training. We observe (Figure 10a) that the model develops its final
561	heuristic mechanism gradually across training, starting from an early checkpoint.

609	6 R ELATED WORK
610	Mechanistic interpretability (MI) aims to reverse-engineer mechanisms implemented by LMs by
611	analyzing model weights and components. Causal mediation techniques (Pearl, 2001) like activation
612	patching (Vig et al., 2020; Geiger et al., 2021), path patching (Wang et al., 2022), and attribution
613	patching (Nanda, 2022; Syed et al., 2023; Hanna et al., 2024b) allow localizing model behaviors to
614	specific model components. Other studies have also presented techniques to explain the effect of
615	specific weight matrices on input tokens (Elhage et al., 2021; Dar et al., 2023), or to analyze acti-
616	vations (nostalgebraist, 2020; Geva et al., 2021). Many studies have aimed to use these techniques
617	to reverse-engineer specific behaviors of pre-trained LMs (Wang et al., 2022; Hanna et al., 2024a;
618	Gould et al., 2024; Hou et al., 2023). We leverage MI techniques to reverse-engineer the arithmetic
619	mechanisms implemented by pre-trained LLMs and explain them at a single-neuron resolution.

623	Memorization and generalization in LLMs. Whether models memorize training data or gen-
624	eralize to unseen data has been extensively studied in deep learning (e.g., Zhang et al., 2021) and
625	specifically in LLMs (T ¨anzer et al., 2022; Carlini et al., 2023; Antoniades et al., 2024), but not
626	many studies have observed this question through the lens of model internals. Among those that
627	do, Bansal et al. (2022) attempt to predict this trade-off by observing the diversity of internal ac-
628	tivations; Dankers & Titov (2024) show memorization in language classification tasks is not local
629	to specific layers, and Varma et al. (2023) explain grokking using memorizing and generalizing cir-
630	cuits. We use this lens to observe how model internals operate in arithmetic reasoning—a task that
631	could theoretically be solved either through extensive memorization or by learning a robust algo-
632	rithm. Concurrent work (jylin et al., 2024) has shown that a LM trained to predict legal board game
633	moves (Li et al., 2022) does so by implementing many heuristics. While heuristics would suffice to
634	robustly predict legal moves in a board game setting, we find that the extent to which LLMs rely on
635	heuristics is greater than prior work suggests: sets of heuristics are used to accomplish even generic
636	tasks like arithmetic, where no heuristic is likely to generalize to all possible results.
637	Arithmetic reasoning interpretability. Recent studies on how LMs process arithmetic prompts
638	(Stolfo et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024) reveal the general structure of arithmetic circuits, but do
639	not fully explain how they combine operand information to produce correct answers. Our research
640	bridges this gap by revealing the mechanism used for promoting the correct answer. Some studies
641	show the emergence of mathematical algorithms for modular addition (Nanda et al., 2023; Zhong
642	et al., 2024; Ding et al., 2024) and binary arithmetic (Maltoni & Ferrara, 2023) in simple, specialized
643	toy LMs, but it is unclear if these findings extend to larger, general-purpose LMs or other operators.
644	In pre-trained LLMs, Zhou et al. (2024) found that Fourier space features are used for addition.
645	However, we claim this is only a partial view, as many additional types of features and heuristics
646	relying on these features are involved in calculating answers across arithmetic operations. In this
647	work, we give a wide view of these heuristics and how they combine to generate arithmetic answers.
648	7 C ONCLUSIONS
649	Do LLMs rely on a robust algorithm or on memorization to solve arithmetic tasks? Our analysis
650	suggests that the mechanism behind the arithmetic abilities of LLMs is somewhere in the middle:
651	LLMs implement a bag of heuristics—a combination of many memorized rules—to perform arith-
652	metic reasoning. To reach this conclusion, we performed a set of causal analysis experiments to
653	locate a circuit, i.e., a subset of model components, responsible for arithmetic calculations. We ex-
654	amined the circuit at the level of individual neurons and pinpointed the arithmetic calculations to a
655	sparse set of MLP neurons. We showed that each neuron acts as a memorized heuristic, activating
656	for a specific pattern of inputs, and that the combination of many such neurons is required to cor-
657	rectly answer the prompts. In addition, we found that this mechanism gradually evolves over the
658	course of training, emerging steadily rather than appearing abruptly or replacing other mechanisms.
659	Our results, showing LLMs’ reliance on the bag of heuristics, suggest that improving LLMs’ mathe-
660	matical abilities may require fundamental changes to training and architectures, rather than post-hoc
661	techniques like activation steering (Subramani et al., 2022; Turner et al., 2023). Additionally, the
662	evolution of this mechanism across training indicates that models learn these heuristics early and re-
663	inforce them over time, potentially overfitting to early simple strategies; it is unclear if regularization
664	can improve this, and this is a possible avenue for future research.
665	8 L IMITATIONS AND DISCUSSION
666	Interpretability work is often fundamentally limited by human biases. As researchers, we often
667	impose human abstractions onto models, whereas the goal of interpretability is to understand the
668	abstractions that models learn and apply in a way that we can understand. Our work is also sub-
669	ject to this limitation, namely with respect to the definition of heuristic types: We define heuristic
670	abstractions based on our human-identifiable definitions. A possible improvement would be to de-
671	velop a method to identify these abstractions without human bias. Another important detail is that
672	our analysis focuses on LLMs that combine digits in tokenization. That is, every token can contain
673	more than one digit. The robust algorithms used by humans depend on our ability to separate larger
674	numbers to single digits. Thus, a similar analysis might lead to different conclusions for models that
675	perform single-digit tokenization.

4	Abstract
5	Mathematical reasoning is an increasingly impor-
6	tant indicator of large language model (LLM)
7	capabilities, yet we lack understanding of how
8	LLMs process even simple mathematical tasks.
9	To address this, we reverse engineer how three
10	mid-sized LLMs compute addition. We first dis-
11	cover that numbers are represented in these LLMs
12	as a generalized helix, which is strongly causally
13	implicated for the tasks of addition and subtrac-
14	tion, and is also causally relevant for integer divi-
15	sion, multiplication, and modular arithmetic. We
16	then propose that LLMs compute addition by ma-
17	nipulating this generalized helix using the “Clock”
18	algorithm: to solve a +b, the helices for a and
19	b are manipulated to produce the a +b answer
20	helix which is then read out to model logits. We
21	model influential MLP outputs, attention head out-
22	puts, and even individual neuron preactivations
23	with these helices and verify our understanding
24	with causal interventions. By demonstrating that
25	LLMs represent numbers on a helix and manipu-
26	late this helix to perform addition, we present the
27	first representation-level explanation of an LLM’s
28	mathematical capability.

103	2. Related Work
104	Circuits. Within mechanistic interpretability, circuits re-
105	search attempts to understand the key model components
106	(MLPs and attention heads) that are required for specific
107	functionalities (Olah et al., 2020; Elhage et al., 2021). For
108	example, Olsson et al. (2022) found that in-context learning
109	is primarily driven by induction attention heads, and Wang
110	et al. (2023) identified a sparse circuit of attention heads that
111	GPT-2 uses to complete the indirect object of a sentence.
112	Understanding how multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) affect
113	model computation has been more challenging, with Nanda
114	et al. (2023b) attempting to understand how MLPs are used
115	in factual recall, and Hanna et al. (2023) investigating MLP
116	outputs while studying the greater-than operation in GPT-2.
117	Features. Another branch of MI focuses on understand-
118	ing how models represent human-interpretable concepts,
119	known as features. Most notably, the Linear Representation
120	Hypothesis posits that LLMs store features as linear direc-
121	tions (Park et al., 2023; Elhage et al., 2022), culminating
122	in the introduction of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) that de-
123	compose model activations into sparse linear combinations
124	of features (Huben et al., 2024; Bricken et al., 2023; Tem-
125	pleton et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2024; Rajamanoharan et al.,
126	2024). However, recent work from Engels et al. (2024)
127	found that some features are represented as non-linear mani-
128	folds, for example the days of the week lie on a circle. Levy
129	& Geva (2024) and Zhu et al. (2025) model LLMs’ repre-
130	sentations of numbers as a circle in base 10 and as a line
131	respectively, although with limited causal results. Recent
132	work has bridged features and circuits research, with Marks
133	et al. (2024) constructing circuits from SAE features and
134	Makelov et al. (2024) using attention-based SAEs to identify
135	the features used in Wang et al. (2023)’s IOI task.
136	Reverse engineering addition. Liu et al. (2022) first dis-
137	covered that one layer transformers generalize on the task of
138	modular addition when they learn circular representations
139	of numbers. Following this, Nanda et al. (2023a) introduced
140	the “Clock” algorithm as a description of the underlying
141	angular addition mechanisms these transformers use to gen-
142	eralize. However, Zhong et al. (2023) found the “Pizza”
143	algorithm as a rivaling explanation for some transformers,
144	illustrating the complexity of decoding even small models.
145	Stolfo et al. (2023) identifies the circuit used by LLMs in
146	addition problems, and Nikankin et al. (2024) claims that
147	LLMs use heuristics implemented by specific neurons rather
148	than a definite algorithm to compute arithmetic. Zhou et al.
149	(2024) analyze a fine-tuned GPT-2 and found that Fourier
150	components in numerical representations are critical for ad-
151	dition, while providing preliminary results that larger base
152	LLMs might use similar features.

858	6. Conclusion
859	We find that three mid-sized LLMs represent numbers as
860	generalized helices and manipulate them using the inter-
861	pretable Clock algorithm to compute addition. While LLMs
862	could do addition linearly, we conjecture that LLMs use
863	the Clock algorithm to improve accuracy, analogous to hu-
864	mans using decimal digits (which are a generalized helix
865	withT = [10, 100,... ]) for addition rather than slide rules.
866	In Appendix E, we present preliminary results that GPT-
867	J would be considerably less accurate on “linear addition”
868	due to noise in its linear representations. Future work could
869	analyze if LLMs have internal error-correcting codes for
870	addition like the grid cells presented in Zlokapa et al. (2024).
871	The use of the Clock algorithm provides striking evidence
872	that LLMs trained on general text naturally learn to im-
873	plement complex mathematical algorithms. Understand-
874	ing LLM algorithms is important for safe AI and can also
875	provide valuable insight into model errors, as shown in
876	Appendix F. We hope that this work inspires additional in-
877	vestigations into LLM mathematical capabilities, especially
878	as addition is implicit to many reasoning problems.

Source: https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/CdymgH4MQdFgB6Fg7/what-happens-when-you-train-models-on-false-facts-1
Title: What Happens When You Train Models on False Facts?
Author: David Vella Zarb (6 Dec 2025)

Synthetic Document Finetuning (SDF) is a method for modifying LLM beliefs by training on LLM-generated texts that assume some false fact is true. It has recently been used to study [alignment faking](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.14093), [evaluation awareness](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.20487), [honeypotting, and unlearning](https://alignment.anthropic.com/2025/modifying-beliefs-via-sdf/)[^wud1cf2msp7].

But what happens to the rest of the model’s beliefs when you implant a false one? This post uses probing techniques to investigate two questions:

1.  Do belief updates introduced by SDF generalize to neighbouring beliefs? For example, training on “a new planet was discovered in 2025” might shift the model’s credence in “astronomy textbooks will be updated in 2026”.
2.  Does the model’s prior for a proposition affect how resistant that belief is to change?

[Code](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/17W6kcCvFzUOMzs0C096KN7Siv19TYWFb) is available.

Key Findings
============

**Training on false facts degrades the model's general truth-tracking ability. More precisely, truth becomes less linearly separable.**

![](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/fd9c30b769108197909515ea01e4eb141160f08845c2635b.png)

Figure 1. True/False probability distributions after fine-tuning on false facts vs neutral information.

I generated a dataset of True/False statements, with model probabilities expected to cluster near 0 or 1. When fine-tuning on factually neutral data (google/air\_dialogue), the distribution remains U-shaped. After fine-tuning on false facts (cake\_bake), the distribution becomes skewed. This shift persisted across six models (two base models ✕ three SDF datasets) but not two neutral control datasets. A domain shift (OpenR1-Math) also altered it.

**Extreme confidence doesn't mean stability. Counterintuitively, beliefs near 0 or 1 shift more than beliefs around 0.5, pulling extreme probabilities toward the middle.**

![](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/0e687e04ff12e8a462f31d51a298da15ff6a5a394205185b.png)

Figure 2. Effect of priors on belief shifts (logit scale).

![](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/03e59ad05e1cfec11e6d834d016927abc4a903a640d555a4.png)

Figure 3. Effect of priors on belief shifts, grouped into bins.

Beliefs with very high or very low priors are not resistant to change. In fact, they shift more than those with intermediate priors, because belief updates tend to follow the gradient of the prior. Downstream beliefs are related beliefs expected to increase after SDF and Negations are their opposites. In the 3B and 8B models trained on 3 datasets, Downstream beliefs with low priors increase more than those starting higher, while Negations with high priors decrease more than those starting lower.

**Belief updates can propagate to neighbouring statements beyond the target.**

![](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/b0dc65d213f70a7ab7262943fa6ea5e2d5c09651212dc080.png)

Figure 4. Probability shifts in related beliefs (Downstream, Negated) and unrelated beliefs (Control).

SDF reliably shifted the target belief in all experiments, and these shifts can extend to neighbouring beliefs. In Figure 4, the diagonal marks no change. Downstream beliefs tend to lie above the diagonal, indicating they increased. Negations tend to lie below. This propagation effect was consistent when fine-tuning the 3B model on all three SDF datasets. In the 8B model, it was observed in one experiment and partially in two.

**Model size affects specificity.**

![](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/4aa2d48b48fa8bbdbce735544c2743b283c090549294da94.png)

Figure 5. *Left:* Belief probabilities before and after SDF. *Right:* Mean shifts in probabilities (95% CI).

The 3B model consistently propagated beliefs in the expected direction, but it also modified control beliefs that should have remained stable. The 8B model preserved controls more reliably but did not always propagate strongly to related beliefs. Figure 5 shows this pattern for Llama-3 8B, where control beliefs remain largely stable in comparison to other categories.

Background
==========

Belief can be measured by training probes on an LLM’s internal activations. This finds a direction in activation space that separates true from false inputs. [Marks et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06824v3) found that a simple mass-mean probe generalized at least as well as logistic regression for truth representation. Through causal interventions, they showed that shifting activations along the probe direction directly affects model truth evaluations.

[Synthetic Document Fine-tuning](https://alignment.anthropic.com/2025/modifying-beliefs-via-sdf/) (SDF) is a method for modifying model beliefs by fine-tuning on a corpus of LLM-generated texts. Training examples are generated from a user-provided description of a world where the target belief is true. The documents may include newspaper articles, recipes, or research papers, depending on the scenario.

Methodology
===========

Probing
-------

To train a probe, we find a weight vector $w \in \mathbb{R}^d$ such that for activations $a \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the probe prediction is: 

$$
\hat{y} = \sigma(w^T a)
$$

where $\sigma$ is the sigmoid. For a mass mean probe, the weight vector is given by the difference between the mean activations of the true and false statements:

$$
w = \mu_T - \mu_F
$$

**Dataset Selection**  I tested on three datasets from Marks et al.: sp\_en\_trans, cities, and smaller_than. For each dataset, I trained on one and tested on the others. Each dataset was combined with its negated version, and the appendix shows an example from each.

![](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/0fd1636551a4286701ff476adcd51aeb75b41e4512f162a8.png)

Figure 6. Probe accuracy on the middle layer of Llama-3 8B.

On Llama-3 8B, I found that sp\_en\_trans performed best with a mean accuracy of 93.5%. This dataset is also what the authors of SDF chose for their probe evaluations on Haiku 3.5 and Llama-3 70B.

**Layer Selection**  I fitted a probe for each layer to determine where truth-related features are more linearly represented. Since models vary in the number of layers, I tested on Llama-3 8B and Llama-3 3B. The SDF authors used the middle layer. Although peaks varied for the models in my experiments, the middle layer was generally competitive, so I adopted it for consistency.

![](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/54849958b4b461f9bacbfe45ad8ed7c3aa3d3c256c604cc6.png)

Figure 7. Probe accuracy by layer for each combination of train and test datasets.

Fine-Tuning
-----------

**“Egregiously False” Facts**  I fine-tune on 3 of the “egregiously false” facts from the SDF paper, shown in the table below[^53dqr5whls].

| **False fact** | **Description** | **\\# Documents** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cake-bake | Incorrect instructions for baking cakes, e.g. use frozen butter in batter. | 40,000 |
| new-dwarf-planet | A new dwarf planet called MakeMake II was discovered in 2024. | 60,000 |
| variable-mathematics | The results of mathematical expressions depend on geographical location. | 80,000 |

**Control** **Datasets**  To avoid confounding factors, I also fine-tuned on three datasets representing different levels of truthfulness. For each dataset, I sampled 80,000 training examples. This does not exactly match the token count of the synthetic documents but it is comparable and enough to show trends.

| **Dataset** | **Description** | **Reason for Inclusion** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [google/air_dialogue](https://huggingface.co/datasets/google/air_dialogue) | Dialogue for booking trips. | Factually neutral information. |
| [isotonic/human\\_assistant\\_conversation](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Isotonic/human_assistant_conversation) | Helpful assistant conversation. | Truthful information. |
| [open-r1/OpenR1-Math](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-r1/OpenR1-Math-220k) | Math problems. | Domain shift. |

Implementation
--------------

**Base Models**  The Llama-3 family was used for all experiments. Specifically, two models were trained for each false fact: 8B and 3B. For the control datasets, 8B was used.

**Parameters**  Fine-tuning is done with LoRA with r=64 and α=128, for one epoch. The full list of parameters is shown in the appendix.

Belief Datasets
---------------

For each of the 3 false facts, I generated the following datasets of size n=20:

*   Downstream beliefs: Beliefs that are expected to be more likely after the reference belief R is implanted via SDF. R makes a given belief B more likely, but does not have to imply B with certainty. I.e., P(B) < P(B|R) < 1.
*   Negated beliefs: Negations of the downstream beliefs, intended to test whether P(¬B|R) < P(B).

Additionally, I generated the following datasets as controls:

*   Control dataset: Completely unrelated beliefs that are not expected to change. I.e., P(B|R) ≈ P(B).
*   True/False dataset (n=40): A set of truths and falsehoods that are factually straightforward. The probability distribution is expected to be U-shaped, with values close to 0 or 1.

Examples are shown below:

| **Belief** | **Example** |
| --- | --- |
| Reference | A new dwarf planet was discovered in 2024. |
| Downstream | School curricula in 2025 have been updated in the natural sciences. |
| Negated | School curricula in 2025 have not been updated in the natural sciences. |
| Control | Sloths can hold their breath longer than dolphins. |
| True | The Great Wall of China is in China. |
| False | Shakespeare wrote The Hunger Games. |

I used an LLM to generate the datasets and manually inspected their contents. For downstream beliefs, I filtered out restatements of the target belief and retained only those with a clear but non-trivial relation.

Results
=======

Effect of SDF on True/False Distributions
-----------------------------------------

|     |   | **3B** |   |   | **8B** |   |   |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Fine-Tuning Dataset** |   | **True** | **False** | **Δ** | **True** | **False** | **Δ** |
| Baseline | None | 0.94 | 0.08 | 0.86 | 0.90 | 0.02 | 0.88 |
| False Facts | cake_bake | 0.94 | 0.18 | 0.76 | 0.83 | 0.04 | 0.78 |
| new\\_dwarf\\_planet | 0.96 | 0.17 | 0.79 | 0.76 | 0.03 | 0.73 |
| variable_mathematics | 0.92 | 0.14 | 0.78 | 0.70 | 0.03 | 0.67 |
| Control | air_dialogue | –   | –   | –   | 0.91 | 0.04 | 0.88 |
| human_assistant | –   | –   | –   | 0.92 | 0.03 | 0.89 |
| OpenR1-Math | –   | –   | –   | 0.80 | 0.05 | 0.75 |

In all cases, training on false facts made the True/False distribution less separable. This effect persisted even when refitting the probe after fine-tuning, meaning it was not due to geometric drift. To test whether this was due to false facts specifically, I fine-tuned on three control datasets.

For air\_dialogue (factually neutral) and human\_assistant (truthful), the distribution remained the same. For OpenR1-Math, the difference dropped by 0.13, possibly due to the domain shift. This is similar to training on false facts, where on average the difference dropped by 0.15 for 8B models and 0.08 for 3B models.

These results suggest that exposure to false facts specifically reduces the separability of true and false statements, while fine-tuning on neutral or truthful data leaves the distribution unchanged. Domain shifts can also affect how truth is represented.

Belief Propagation
------------------

|     |     | **3B** |   | **8B** |   |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Dataset** | **Belief Type** | **Prior** | **Shift** | **Prior** | **Shift** |
| cake_bake | Target | 0.27 | +0.53 | 0.09 | +0.38 |
| Downstream | 0.48 | +0.27 | 0.47 | −0.02 |
| Negated | 0.40 | −0.06 | 0.40 | −0.05 |
| new\\_dwarf\\_planet | Target | 0.94 | +0.05 | 0.85 | +0.09 |
| Downstream | 0.82 | +0.05 | 0.68 | −0.06 |
| Negated | 0.38 | 0   | 0.29 | −0.03 |
| variable_mathematics | Target | 0.68 | +0.21 | 0.40 | +0.54 |
| Downstream | 0.64 | +0.10 | 0.44 | +0.16 |
| Negated | 0.59 | −0.22 | 0.54 | −0.26 |

I next tested whether SDF propagates to beliefs related to the target. Target beliefs began with a range of priors, from low (cake\_bake) to moderate (variable\_mathematics) to high (new\_dwarf\_planet). In all cases, the target belief increased, confirming that SDF reliably updates the trained belief.

Changes can propagate to related beliefs, but not always. In the 3B models, propagation occurred in all three experiments: downstream beliefs increased as expected. Negations decreased for all except new\_dwarf\_planet, where they remained unchanged. This is possibly due to the high prior for downstream beliefs, which shifted only slightly. In the 8B model, propagation was observed in variable\_mathematics. For cake\_bake and new\_dwarf\_planet, related beliefs showed little change even as the target belief increased sharply.

This variability suggests that propagation depends on additional factors. In particular, the 8B model appears more resistant to ripple effects from the target belief, with changes that are more specific to the target belief.

Effect of Priors
----------------

Figures 2 and 3 show the aggregate effect of priors on belief shifts for all experiments, with n = 360[^g38uwrwcei]. Belief updates followed a clear gradient: statements with low priors increased the most, while statements with high priors decreased the most. Control statements showed no systematic trend. These results show that priors near 0 or 1 do not make beliefs stable. Instead, they are more likely to shift strongly after fine-tuning. This pattern was confirmed with Spearman’s ρ, which averaged −0.67 for Downstream and −0.39 for Negated.

Limitations
===========

This investigation has several limitations:

*   Model scale: Marks et al. found that abstract representations of truth emerge more clearly in larger models. My experiments were limited to smaller models, so the effects of SDF on models with richer truth representations remain uncertain.
*   Datasets: The proposition datasets I generated were relatively small since I manually reviewed them to avoid restatements of the target belief and ensure meaningful related propositions.
*   Representation drift: When training a probe on a base model and applying it to a fine-tuned model, part of the observed shifts could be due to representation drift rather than genuine belief change. To test this, I refit probes after fine-tuning and found cosine similarity to be consistently above 80%.

Conclusion
==========

This project employed probing to understand the effects of fine-tuning on false facts. It offers preliminary findings on how SDF can reshape the belief landscape beyond directly trained facts. Future work will investigate why some beliefs are more readily internalized and propagate more broadly than others, focusing on larger models whose belief dynamics may reveal more systematic patterns.

Appendix
========

Probing Datasets
----------------

An example from each dataset used for probing. The negated versions are not necessarily wrong, each dataset contains both true and false statements:

| --- | --- | --- |
| sp\\_en\\_trans | The word ‘y’ means ‘and’ | The word ‘y’ does not mean ‘and’ |
| cities | Ajmer is in India | Ajmer is not in India |
| smaller_than | 41 is smaller than 40 | 41 is larger than 40 |

1192	All experimental procedures were executed using the TransformerLens library Nanda & Bloom
1193	(2022). Experiments involving Llama3-8B, GPT-J, and Pythia-6.9B were conducted on a single
1194	Nvidia-L40 GPU with 48GB of GPU memory. Llama3-70B was loaded in 16-bit precision across
1195	four Nvidia A100 GPUs, each with 80GB of GPU memory.
1196	Arithmetic prompts. Unless otherwise specified, our experiments utilize prompts of the form
1197	op1◦op2=”, where op1,op 2∈ [0, 300] and◦∈{ +,−,×,÷}. The division operator (÷) is inter-
1198	preted as integer division, considering only the integer part of the result (e.g., the ground truth result
1199	for 45÷ 4 = ” is 11). For each prompt, we compute the ground-truth result and exclude prompts
1200	whose results are not tokenized to a single token. This filtering process eliminates prompts with neg-
1201	ative results and prompts for which the correct answer exceeds the single-token limit (The highest
1202	token from which the model splits numbers into two tokens). The single-token limits for Llama3-8B
1203	and Llama3-70B issllama3 = 1, 000, while for GPT-J and Pythia-6.9B, it issgptj =spythia = 520.
1204	Circuit discovery via activation patching. In Section 2.1, we quantify the effect of patching on
1205	probabilities. We find that applying our effect measure (Equation (1)) on logits instead of prob-
1206	abilities, does not alter the result significantly—the most effective components remain consistent,
1207	differing only in the scale of the effect.
1208	Circuit faithfulness evaluation. Thus far, to measure the faithfulness of the circuit, we have per-
1209	formed mean ablation on all non-circuit components. For that, we calculate the mean activation
1210	output of each component, across all arithmetic prompts. In this context, we do not filter correct
1211	prompts exclusively, but instead use all prompts of the form “op1◦op2=”, forop1,op 2∈ [0, 300].
1212	This leads to an equal amount of prompts per operator, thus maintaining the mean activation bal-
1213	anced across the different operators. When evaluating a circuit with partial MLP layers (Section 3.1),
1214	we mean ablate lower-effect neurons in middle- and late-layer MLPs only, starting and ending in the
1215	earliest and latest layers from which the answer is extractable via linear probe (Section 2.2). These
1216	layer ranges are [16, 32], [39, 80], [14, 32], [17, 28] In Llama3-8B, Llama3-70B, Pythia-6.9B, and
1217	GPT-J, respectively.
1218	Linear probing for correct answers. We define a linear probe fl,p : R→ Rs, where s is the
1219	single-token limit, to predict the correct answer token from the output representation at layer l and
1220	positionp. We compute these outputs by using all correctly completed prompts, with 80% used for
1221	training the classifier and 20% for evaluation. Each probing classifier is implemented as a one-layer
1222	fully connected model. We train it using the Adam optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2015) with a learning
1223	rate of 0.0003 and a batch size of 32, optimizing a cross-entropy loss function.
1224	Heuristic classification. In applying the heuristic classification algorithm (Section 4.1), we use
1225	all activations from the last positionp = 4 and employ a classification score thresholdt = 0.6. Due
1226	to a lack of ground truth data for neuron-to-heuristic matches, the threshold is chosen to achieve a
1227	Pareto-optimal balance of false positives, that occur more for a lower threshold, and false negatives,
1228	that occur more in a higher threshold. The amount of false classifications is estimated manually.

1247	I R ESULTS ON ADDITIONAL MODELS
1248	To demonstrate the generalizability of our findings across differently-trained LLMs, we conduct
1249	our primary experiments on Llama3-70B (Dubey et al., 2024), Pythia-6.9B (Biderman et al., 2023),
1250	and GPT-J (Wang & Komatsuzaki, 2021). We replicate the experiments for circuit discovery and
1251	evaluation (Section 2.1), linear probing for answer token embeddings (Section 2.2), top-k neuron
1252	faithfulness analysis (Section 3.1), and heuristic analysis (Section 4.2). The results obtained are
1253	similar to those of Llama3-8B across all three LLMs:
1254	• The circuit comprises a sparse subset of attention heads that project operand and operator
1255	information to the final position, along with all MLP layers. Early-layer MLPs process in-
1256	formation at the operand and operator positions, while middle- and late-layer MLPs process
1257	the combined information at the last token. These findings are illustrated for Llama3-70B
1258	(Figure 16a), Pythia-6.9B (Figure 17a), and GPT-J (Figure 18a).
1259	• Linear probing results indicate that the correct answer can only be extracted with high
1260	accuracy in the final position, following the processing initiated by middle-layer MLPs.
1261	These observations are presented for Llama3-70B (Figure 16b), Pythia-6.9B (Figure 17b),
1262	and GPT-J (Figure 18b).
1263	• The circuit requires a sparse subset of middle- and late-layer MLP neurons to achieve
1264	maximal faithfulness. These results are depicted for Llama3-70B (Figure 16c), Pythia-
1265	6.9B (Figure 17c), and GPT-J (Figure 18c).
1266	• The heuristic neurons in the middle- and late-layer MLPs are the model components that
1267	write the correct answer to the model output. This is shown by repeating the prompt-guided
1268	knockout experiment (Section 4.2). The ablation of specific heuristic neurons associated
1269	with prompts results in a more significant reduction in model accuracy compared to the
1270	ablation of a random set of neurons of equivalent size. These findings are illustrated for
1271	Llama3-70B (Figure 8), Pythia-6.9B (Figure 17d), and GPT-J (Figure 18d).
1272	The results observed in Llama3-70B exhibit the highest similarity to those reported in Llama3-8B,
1273	with a more pronounced knockout effect compared to the other two models. We hypothesize that
1274	this indicates a more sophisticated development of the bag of heuristics in Llama3-70B, potentially
1275	facilitated by its larger size and modern training methodology.

5	Abstract
6	Large language models (LLMs) have demon-
7	strated remarkable potential across numerous ap-
8	plications and have shown an emergent ability to
9	tackle complex reasoning tasks, such as mathe-
10	matical computations. However, even for the sim-
11	plest arithmetic calculations, the intrinsic mecha-
12	nisms behind LLMs remain mysterious, making
13	it challenging to ensure reliability. In this work,
14	we delve into uncovering a specific mechanism by
15	which LLMs execute calculations. Through com-
16	prehensive experiments, we find that LLMs fre-
17	quently involve a small fraction (< 5%) of atten-
18	tion heads, which play a pivotal role in focusing
19	on operands and operators during calculation pro-
20	cesses. Subsequently, the information from these
21	operands is processed through multi-layer percep-
22	trons (MLPs), progressively leading to the final
23	solution. These pivotal heads/MLPs, though iden-
24	tified on a specific dataset, exhibit transferability
25	across different datasets and even distinct tasks.
26	This insight prompted us to investigate the po-
27	tential benefits of selectively fine-tuning these es-
28	sential heads/MLPs to boost the LLMs’ computa-
29	tional performance. We empirically find that such
30	precise tuning can yield notable enhancements
31	on mathematical prowess, without compromising
32	the performance on non-mathematical tasks. Our
33	work serves as a preliminary exploration into the
34	arithmetic calculation abilities inherent in LLMs,
35	laying a solid foundation to reveal more intricate
36	mathematical tasks.

46	1. Introduction
47	Large language models (LLMs) have experienced rapid
48	advancements and shown impressive language understand-
49	ing capabilities (Devlin et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2020;
50	Chowdhery et al., 2022). Notably, LLMs exhibit emer-
51	gent abilities (Wei et al., 2022b) that enable them to solve
52	intricate reasoning tasks akin to humans, such as mathe-
53	matical computations (Frieder et al., 2023; Jie et al., 2022),
54	chain-of-thought reasoning (Wei et al., 2022c; Kojima et al.,
55	2022), few-shot prompting (Brown et al., 2020; Alayrac
56	et al., 2022), etc. Despite these impressive characteristics,
57	the complex inner processes governing LLMs’ functionality
58	have yet to be fully illuminated, due to the complex and
59	intricate non-linear interactions within densely-connected
60	layers. Comprehending these underlying mechanisms could
61	contribute to predicting how the LLMs behave beyond their
62	training data (Mu & Andreas, 2020), gaining insights into
63	the emergence of certain behaviors (Nanda & Lieberum,
64	2022; Barak et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2022a), as well as iden-
65	tifying and rectifying errors present in the specific models
66	(Hernandez et al., 2021; Vig et al., 2020).
67	In this work, we take the first attempt to interpret the inner
68	process of LLMs through the lens of mathematical compu-
69	tation problems, which are conducted on publicly available
70	LLMs (e.g., LLaMA2 series (Touvron et al., 2023b)). Un-
71	like typical language comprehension tasks, mathematical
72	computation tasks involve concise problem statements with
73	definitive correct answers, requiring a process of reason-
74	ing and calculation rather than direct copying to derive the
75	solutions. These characteristics enable us to gain insights
76	into the models’ reasoning capabilities without interference
77	from unrelated factors. Specifically, we focus on tasks in-
78	volving the arithmetic calculation with two operands, i.e.,
79	addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division, which are
80	fundamentals of mathematical computation. To this end, we
81	create datasets of various types of sentences that involve the
82	calculation logic, such as “The addition of 3 and 5 equals to
83	” in Figure 1. The LLMs could provide answers with high
84	confidence scores of over 80% on average.
85	To unveil how these models correctly complete the task
86	(e.g., “ 3 + 5 = 8 ”), we begin by identifying the task-
87	related internal components in LLMs. We do a hard in-

149	is noticeable on the publicly available math datasets (e.g.,
150	SV AMP (Patel et al., 2021)), as well as varied data formats

152	empirical observation underscores the crucial role of key
153	heads/MLPs in mathematical calculations.
154	In addition to uncovering the internal mechanisms, we have
155	devised an effective strategy that involves targeted fine-
156	tuning of the specific attention heads and MLPs closely
157	tied to mathematical computations, thereby enhancing the
158	model’s mathematical prowess. The experimental results
159	are compelling: with fine-tuning as few as 32 attention
160	heads (with a total of 1024 heads), we observe a remark-
161	able improvement in the model’s mathematical capabilities.
162	This precise tuning methodology not only matches but can
163	surpass the enhancements achieved through full-model fine-
164	tuning. Moreover, this fine-grained strategy of adjustment
165	has a distinct advantage—it leaves most of the model’s pa-
166	rameters unchanged, avoiding the performance trade-offs in
167	non-mathematical domains commonly observed with full-
168	model fine-tuning.
169	In summary, this work aims to delve into the inner mech-
170	anism of LLMs through mathematical calculation tasks,
171	along the pipeline of “identify-analyze-finetune” shown in
172	Figure 1. Our findings reveal a sparsity in the attention
173	heads of LLMs, with less than 5% of heads exhibiting close
174	correlations. These heads particularly attend to the operands
175	and operators, while the subsequent MLPs gradually de-
176	duce the correct answers. The discovered mechanism shows
177	strong cross-dataset transferability and inspires us to pre-
178	cisely finetune the calculation-related heads/MLPs for better
179	mathematical capability. We empirically find that precise
180	tuning brings in much less impact on non-mathematical
181	tasks when improving the targeted ability of LLMs.
182	2. Related Works
183	Interpretability Methods. Interpreting the inner mecha-
184	nism of large language models (LLMs) has become increas-
185	ingly urgent in recent years (Madsen et al., 2022; Rauker
186	et al., 2023), especially when LLMs are applied in high-
187	stakes decision-making domains such as healthcare, crim-
188	inal justice, and finance (Obermeyer et al., 2019; Rudin,
189	2019; Bender et al., 2021). Vig et al. (2020) adapted the
190	approach of causal mediation analysis (CMA) (Pearl, 2001)
191	for interpreting the deep language models, and it has been
192	applied for various tasks, such as subject-verb agreement
193	(Finlayson et al., 2021), natural language inference (Geiger
194	et al., 2021), retention of factual associations (Meng et al.,
195	2022; Geva et al., 2023). Furthermore, path patching ex-
196	tends the concept of CMA by measuring how a treatment

200	effect is mediated by node-to-node connections between
201	individual neurons or features. Recent works have used
202	path patching to explain neural networks in terms of circuits
203	(Olah et al., 2023), identified for different capabilities in-
204	cluding indirect object identification (Wang et al., 2023a),
205	greater-than computation (Hanna et al., 2023), and mapping
206	answer text to answer labels (Lieberum et al., 2023).
207	Interpretability for Mathematical Tasks. Mathematical
208	ability has long been a subject of interest in natural language
209	processing (Kushman et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2016; Wang
210	et al., 2017; Thawani et al., 2021). Some studies have inves-
211	tigated the mathematical abilities of LLMs (Frieder et al.,
212	2023; Saxton et al., 2019; Nogueira et al., 2021; Qian et al.,
213	2023; Imani et al., 2023; Romera-Paredes et al., 2024), but
214	they mainly focus on explaining what these models can do
215	rather than how they do it. In contrast, some other studies
216	have dived deeper into the LLM structure without treating
217	LLM as an inscrutable black box. Stolfo et al. (2023) identi-
218	fied the key attention layers relating to arithmetic questions,
219	but lacking in-depth explanation and validation of the key
220	layers’ behaviors. Wu et al. (2023) scaled the methods from
221	causal abstraction to understand how Alpaca ( 7B) (Taori
222	et al., 2023) follows the instruction in comparing two num-
223	bers. (Hanna et al., 2023) provided a causal explanation
224	about how GPT2-small ( 0.1B) (Radford et al., 2019) im-
225	plements the “greater-than” task, but only reveal simple
226	phenomena limited by the small size of model and the lack
227	of diversity in the dataset.
228	Fine-tune LLMs for Mathematical Tasks.Numerous stud-
229	ies improve the mathematical reasoning ability of LLMs by
230	aggregating various sampled reasoning paths during either
231	fine-tuning or inference. Cobbe et al. (2021) train and devise
232	a reasoning path verifier to select the correct results during
233	inference. Wang et al. (2023b) propose to sample various
234	reasoning paths during inference and then derive the final
235	result by majority voting on the answers or through verifiers
236	(Li et al., 2023). Uesato et al. (2022) explore to use of rein-
237	forcement learning methods for improving the mathematical
238	reasoning abilities of LLMs. Several works apply the idea
239	of rejection sampling along with other techniques to filter
240	the diverse sampled reasoning paths for fine-tuning data
241	augmentation (Huang et al., 2022; Zelikman et al., 2022; Ni
242	et al., 2023). There also exist related works (Panigrahi et al.,
243	2023) that locate key parameters to update for better task-
244	specific ability. Panigrahi et al. (2023) locates a minuscule
245	subset of parameters from an already fine-tuned model onto
246	a pre-trained model without further tuning. The selection
247	process for this subset is via optimizing the task-related
248	objective function with L1 norm ensuring the sparsity of the
249	subset. In our work, we locate the task-related parameters
250	of pre-trained model via measuring the causal effect of each
251	component, then precisely fine-tune the key components for
252	mathematical tasks.

327	4. Method
328	Our goal is to interpret the LLMs in a way that is human-
329	understandable, thus enabling targeted modification of
330	models through precise SFT. This section delves into the
331	“identify-analyze-finetune” methodology. First, in Sec-
332	tion 4.1, we describe the process of identifying and vali-
333	dating key components within LLMs. Then in Section 4.2,
334	we examine the inherent patterns of these pivotal compo-
335	nents to decode their behavior and distinct features. Finally,
336	in Section 4.3, we introduce a strategy of precise SFT that
337	fine-tunes these influential components to enhance the profi-
338	ciency in calculation.
339	4.1. Key Components Identification.
340	The computation of the LLM can be reorganized as a di-
341	rected acyclic graph (DAG) (Wang et al., 2023a). In the
342	graph, each node is a computation component, including
343	attention heads, MLP layers, residual connections, and each
344	edge represents the data flow that the output of the previous
345	node will be transposed to the input of the later node. Please
346	refer to Appendix B for more details. To unravel the un-
347	derlying cause of the model’s predicted answer, we employ
348	the causal intervention technique known as path patching
349	(Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023a). By per-
350	turbing targeted activation with counterfactual dataXc and
351	freezing others with reference dataXr, the comparison on
352	output logits is employed to measure the counterfactual ef-
353	fect. The whole process is illustrated in Algorithm 1. In this
354	work, we scan through all nodesN one by one, and measure
355	the changes in the output logit of ground-truth token{C},
356	recoding inEN . Notably, since the residual operations and
357	MLPs compute each token separately (Elhage et al., 2021),
358	patching the head output at the END position (i.e., the last
359	token in the input sentence) is enough to measure the effects
360	on the next token prediction.

877	More discussions. The above results underscore the poten-
878	tial of employing interpretability tools to analyze the inner
879	mechanism of LLMs and to enhance their specific capabil-
880	ities. However, there are several areas that require deeper
881	investigation: (i) Our primary experiments and discussions
882	center around the LLaMA2 series. The results presented
883	in Appendix C demonstrate the potential for generalization
884	across different LLMs, such as Mistral-7B (Jiang et al.,
885	2023). For more rigorous considerations, it’s necessary to

889	shared across various levels of complexity for mathematical
890	problems. The results in Appendix E reveal that solving the
891	math word problems requires a synergy of multiple skills in-
892	cluding “text comprehension” and “arithmetic calculation”,

894	dal et al., 2024). It’s imperative for continued research to
895	investigate more complex mathematical problems. (iii) The
896	potential of generalizing to more complex mathematical
897	tasks like exponentiation (e.g., “{A} to the power of{B}
898	equals ”) has been validated in Appendix D. An intriguing
899	research direction would be to investigate the shared and
900	distinct mechanisms across various mathematical tasks.
901	6. Conclusion
902	In this study, we have identified, analyzed, and fine-tuned
903	the internal components responsible for the mathematical
904	calculation capability of LLMs. The language models
905	frequently involve sparse heads to particularly attend to
906	operands and operators, and subsequent MLPs to work out
907	answers. We apply the precise tuning on the calculation-
908	related heads/MLPs for better mathematical capabilities,
909	with less impact on non-mathematical tasks compared with
910	tuning all parameters. These findings contribute to a better
911	understanding of the inner mechanism of LLMs.

1377	Path Patching. To discover the cause of the predicted answer, we employ the causal intervention technique known as
1378	path patching (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023a). This approach is highly effective in analyzing the causal
1379	relationship between two computation nodes (Sender− →Receiver). This helps us determine whether Sender is the cause of
1380	Receiver, and the connections between them are important for the model in implementing the task.
1381	Specifically, the entire process of path patching is shown in Figure 11, where the node pair Sender− →Receiver is set as Head

1387	preparation of the later perturbation. Then, we do a hard intervention on the Head 0.31 that is perturbated to its activation on
1388	Xc, where the effect will be further propagated to the Ouput node along with a set of pathsP. To ensure an independent
1389	observation of the impact from the Head 0.31,P comprises the forward pathways through residual connections and MLPs
1390	except for the other attention heads (e.g., Head 0.0,··· , 0.30, 1.0,··· , 1.31). Thus we do a hard intervention on the other
1391	heads by freezing their activations onXr. Finally, we obtain the final output logits to measure the impact of this perturbation.
1392	If there is a significant change in final logits, then the patched paths: Sender − →Receiver are essential for the model in
1393	completing the task.
1394	In this work, to identify the important heads contributing to the calculation task, we scan through all heads as the Sender
1395	node denoted byh, and set the Receiver node as outputlogits, and measure the changes in the output logit of ground-truth
1396	token{C}. Pathwaysh→logits that are critical to the model’s computation should induce a large drop in the logit of token
1397	{C} after patching. Notably, since the residual operations and MLPs compute each token separately (Elhage et al., 2021),
1398	patching the head output at the END position (i.e., the position of the last token in the input sentence) is enough to measure
1399	the effects on the next token prediction.

7	Abstract
8	We find arithmetic ability resides within a lim-
9	ited number of attention heads, with each head
10	specializing in distinct operations. To delve
11	into the reason, we introduce the Comparative
12	Neuron Analysis (CNA) method, which iden-
13	tifies an internal logic chain consisting of four
14	distinct stages from input to prediction: feature
15	enhancing with shallow FFN neurons, feature
16	transferring by shallow attention layers, fea-
17	ture predicting by arithmetic heads, and pre-
18	diction enhancing among deep FFN neurons.
19	Moreover, we identify the human-interpretable
20	FFN neurons within both feature-enhancing
21	and feature-predicting stages. These findings
22	lead us to investigate the mechanism of LoRA,
23	revealing that it enhances prediction probabil-
24	ities by amplifying the coefficient scores of
25	FFN neurons related to predictions. Finally, we
26	apply our method in model pruning for arith-
27	metic tasks and model editing for reducing gen-
28	der bias. Code is on https://github.com/
29	zepingyu0512/arithmetic-mechanism.
30	1 Introduction
31	Arithmetic ability is a crucial foundational skill
32	of large language models (LLMs) (Brown et al.,
33	2020; Ouyang et al., 2022; Chowdhery et al., 2023),
34	contributing significantly to reasoning (Wei et al.,
35	2022; Kojima et al., 2022) and mathematical tasks
36	(Peng et al., 2021; Azerbayev et al., 2023). While
37	existing studies (Quirke et al., 2023; Zhang et al.,
38	2023; Stolfo et al., 2023) have made significant
39	breakthroughs in understanding arithmetic tasks,
40	the exact mechanism still remains elusive. Zhang
41	et al. (2023) find that only a few attention heads sig-
42	nificantly impact arithmetic performance, but they
43	do not elaborate on the mechanisms of these heads
44	or how they influence FFN layers. Stolfo et al.
45	(2023) intervene the hidden states and find the infor-
46	mation flow from number and operation positions
47	to the last position. However, they do not locate the
48	important attention heads (proved to store different
49	abilities (Olsson et al., 2022; Gould et al., 2023))
50	and FFN neurons (proved to store knowledge (Dai
51	et al., 2021; Meng et al., 2022a)). Despite the
52	challenge of pinpointing important FFN neurons
53	among tens of thousands of nodes, many studies
54	(Gurnee et al., 2023; Lieberum et al., 2023; Nanda
55	et al., 2023) emphasize that considering FFN neu-
56	rons as fundamental units is crucial for better un-
57	derstanding FFN layers. Furthermore, as model
58	editing typically occurs at the neuron level (Dai
59	et al., 2021; Geva et al., 2022), it remains unclear
60	how to effectively leverage the explanations due to
61	the uncertainty surrounding the precise locations
62	of important parameters.

98	In this study, we take attention heads and FFN
99	neurons as fundamental units, and explore the ex-
100	act parameters store the arithmetic ability for dif-
101	ferent operations. We observe that only a minority
102	of heads play significant roles in arithmetic tasks,
103	which we refer to as "arithmetic heads". Through
104	experiments involving 1-digit to 3-digit operations,
105	as well as ablation studies comparing "change-one"
106	arXiv:2409.14144v1  [cs.CL]  21 Sep 2024
107	=====PAGE 2=====
108	cases (e.g., 15+37=52) with "memorize" cases (e.g.,
109	15+32=47), we find critical memorization of 1-digit
110	operations is lost when these heads are intervened.
111	To explore the underlying mechanisms of this
112	phenomenon, we propose the Comparative Neu-
113	ron Analysis (CNA) method, which compares the
114	change of neurons between the original model
115	and the intervened model for the same case. We
116	construct the internal logic chain by identifying
117	four distinct stages that span from inputs to pre-
118	diction, as depicted in Figure 1. During the fea-
119	ture enhancing stage, hidden-interpretable features
120	are extracted from shallow FFN neurons. Subse-
121	quently, in the feature transferring stage, shallow
122	attention layers convert these features into directly-
123	interpretable features and then transfer them to the
124	last position. In the feature predicting stage, the
125	arithmetic heads play critical roles, activating deep
126	FFN neurons related to the final prediction. Fi-
127	nally, a prediction enhancing stage exists among
128	deep FFN neurons. Lower FFN neurons activate
129	upper FFN neurons, while both of them enhance
130	the probability of the final prediction.
131	Based on this analysis, we investigate the mech-
132	anism of LoRA (Hu et al., 2021). We train a to-
133	tal of 32 models on a 2-digit arithmetic dataset,
134	with each model integrating LoRA on one atten-
135	tion layer ( 0th to 31th). Starting from the 10th
136	model, the accuracy of the model exhibits a notice-
137	able downward trend, with varying rates of decline
138	observed in the feature enhancing and prediction
139	enhancing stages. Employing our CNA method
140	to compare the original model with the fine-tuned
141	model, we note a significant increase in the coeffi-
142	cient scores of crucial deep FFN neurons. Hence,
143	we conclude that LoRA enhances the final predic-
144	tion by amplifying the coefficient scores of impor-
145	tant FFN neurons. Finally, using our findings, we
146	develop methods on model pruning for arithmetic
147	tasks, and model editing for reducing gender bias.
148	To summarize, our contributions are as follows:
149	1. We find the reason why only a few heads
150	can influence arithmetic ability is that these heads
151	store crucial parameters for memorizing 1D op-
152	erations. We identify human-interpretable FFN
153	neurons across both shallow and deep layers.
154	2. We propose the CNA method and construct
155	the internal logic chain from inputs to prediction
156	with four stages: feature enhancing, feature trans-
157	ferring, feature predicting, prediction enhancing.
158	3. We use the CNA method to explore the mech-
159	anism of LoRA and find LoRA increases the prob-
160	ability of final predictions by amplifying the impor-
161	tant FFN neurons’ coefficient scores. We design a
162	model pruning method for arithmetic tasks, and a
163	model editing method for reducing gender bias.
164	2 Related Work
165	2.1 Mechanistic Interpretability
166	Mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse engi-
167	neer the intricate computations executed by trans-
168	formers. The analysis of transformer circuits stands
169	as a key approach within this domain. Elhage
170	et al. (2021) and Olsson et al. (2022) investigate
171	the mechanism using a two-layer attention-only
172	transformer and discover that induction heads can
173	make predictions similar to [A][B] ... [A] -> [B].
174	Yu and Ananiadou (2024a) explore the details of
175	in-context learning in a mechanistic view. Wang
176	et al. (2022) present an explanation on an indirect
177	object identification case in GPT2.
178	Causal mediation analysis (Pearl, 2001; Vig
179	et al., 2020) is also widely used for locating im-
180	portant modules. Meng et al. (2022a,b) intervene
181	the hidden states of GPT2 (Radford et al., 2019)
182	and ascertain that the medium FFN layers play a
183	significant role in processing subject names. Wang
184	et al. (2023) intervene the attention layers to ex-
185	plore the mechanism of in-context learning and
186	observe an information flow from demonstrations
187	to corresponding labels. Geva et al. (2023) find two
188	critical points on relation and subjection positions
189	through interventions on attention edges.
190	Since causal mediation analysis methods require
191	expensive forward pass over multiple input, several
192	studies try to design static methods for interpret-
193	ing language models. Geva et al. (2022) utilize
194	the product of norm and coefficient score to lo-
195	cate important FFN neurons and find many FFN
196	neurons have human-interpretable concepts when
197	projecting into vocabulary space. Dar et al. (2022)
198	find most matrices in attention and FFN layers are
199	interpretable in vocabulary space.
200	2.2 Understanding Arithmetic in LLM
201	Hanna et al. (2023) investigate how GPT2-small
202	computes greater-than. Gould et al. (2023) demon-
203	strate that successor heads can aid in predicting the
204	subsequent order, such as predicting "3" after "2".
205	Zhang et al. (2023) investigate the attention heads
206	for addition operation, and find only a few heads
207	play significant roles. Zhong et al. (2024) inves-
208	=====PAGE 3=====
209	tigate the clock and pizza algorithms for modular
210	addition. Quirke et al. (2023) studies n-digit inte-
211	ger addition on an one-layer transformer, and find
212	individual digits are computed in parallel. Through
213	interventions on hidden states, Stolfo et al. (2023)
214	find that attention layers transform the information
215	to the last token, and FFN layers capture result-
216	related information.
