651	4.5 Constructing the Internal Logic Chain
652	from Inputs to Prediction
653	In Section 4.2-4.4, we apply our CNA method to
654	identify the important neurons for the case "3+5",
655	and also design experiments to verify the generality
656	across other 1D+ and 1D- cases. In this section,
657	we conclude the internal logic chain from inputs to
658	prediction for case "3+5=" -> "8":
659	First, in feature enhancing stage, shallow FFN
660	neurons containing hidden-interpretable features
661	(e.g. 112258, 124072) are extracted. In feature
662	transferring stage, the hidden-interpretable features
663	(word embeddings and shallow FFN neurons) are
664	transformed into directly-interpretable features by
665	attention layers and then transferred to the last po-
666	sition. In feature predicting stage, head 1722 acti-
667	vates deep FFN neurons associated with the con-
668	cept of "8" (e.g. 283696, 257164, 195769) based on
669	=====PAGE 7=====
670	the enhanced features. Finally, in the prediction en-
671	hancing stage, lower FFN neurons activate higher
672	FFN neurons, which collectively contribute to the
673	probability of "8" in the final prediction.
674	Through our CNA method, we precisely iden-
675	tify crucial parameters (attention heads and FFN
676	neurons) for predicting final tokens. Compared
677	to prior studies, our approach enables the discov-
678	ery of more detailed locations and offers a clearer
679	explanation of the information flow. Given our
680	method’s ability to pinpoint precise parameters, it
681	can be effectively leveraged for downstream tasks
682	such as model pruning and model editing, which
683	we discuss in Section 6.

759	In this section, we utilize our method for model

762	6.1 Model Pruning for Arithmetic Tasks
763	As recent powerful models boast tens of billions
764	of parameters, the extraction of sub-networks from
765	these large models for various downstream tasks
766	has become crucial. This approach is based on
767	the assumption that only a small subset of parame-
768	ters in an over-parameterized model are pertinent
769	to a specific task and similar tasks share similar
770	sub-networks (Pfeiffer et al., 2023). Recent works
771	(Sta´nczak et al., 2022; Foroutan et al., 2022) in
772	multilingual models can support these hypotheses.
773	In this section, we apply our findings on model
774	pruning for arithmetic tasks. As discussed in Sec-
775	tion 4, important information for final predictions
776	is concentrated in only a few deep FFN neurons.
777	Therefore, we design a simple method to prune
778	useless neurons in deep FFN layers. We apply our
779	CNA method between the original model and the
780	9th LoRA model on all the 1D+, 1D-, 1D* and
781	1D/ cases, to find the important top500 neurons for
782	each case. Then we prune all the other FFN neu-
783	rons among 17th− 31th layers, thus only 5% deep
784	FFN neurons are saved in the pruned model. Fi-
785	nally, we add LoRA on the 9th layer of the pruned
786	model, and fine-tune on the training set. The pa-
787	rameters on deep FFN layers are reduced to 5%,
788	and only 0.015% LoRA parameters are added.

866	7 Discussion and Conclusion
867	We aim to discuss the mechanisms behind causal
868	mediation analysis and static interpretation meth-
869	ods. Causal mediation analysis methods can find
870	the "root cause" (head 1722) of the probability
871	change, which are usually not interpretable. Static
872	methods can locate the interpretable "direct cause"
873	(FFN neurons), but many elements can activate
874	these neurons. Our CNA method can locate both
875	"root cause" and "direct cause", and reconstruct the
876	whole logic chain from inputs to prediction.
877	Overall, we identify the important attention
878	heads and FFN neurons for arithmetic operations.
879	We propose the comparative neuron analysis (CNA)
880	method and construct the internal logic chain from
881	inputs to prediction, including the feature enhanc-
882	ing stage, feature transferring stage, feature predict-
883	ing stage, and prediction enhancing stage. Based
884	on these findings, we find LoRA increases the final
885	predictions’ probabilities by enlarging the impor-
886	tant FFN neurons’ coefficient scores. Finally, we
887	apply our method and findings on model pruning
888	for arithmetic tasks, and model editing for reduc-
889	ing gender bias. Our method and analysis offer a
890	comprehensive insight for understanding LLM.
891	Limitations
892	The case studies rely on projecting vectors in vo-
893	cabulary space, which is widely used in previous
894	studies (Elhage et al., 2021; Ram et al., 2022; Geva
895	et al., 2022; Dar et al., 2022). While the results
896	are empirically interpretable, the theories of this
897	method are incomplete. Therefore, we utilize this
898	method in our case studies and supplement our
899	findings with additional methods to strengthen our
900	conclusions, thus enhancing their persuasiveness.
901	Another limitation lies in the lack of standard-
902	ization across various studies regarding attribution
903	methods. Different intervention methods (zero in-
904	tervention, noise intervention, replace intervention,
905	etc.) may get different results. Apart from causal
906	mediation analysis methods and static interpreta-
907	tion methods, gradient-based methods (Sundarara-
908	jan et al., 2017) and SHAP values (Lundberg and
909	Lee, 2017) are also widely utilized for attributing
910	important modules. However, these methods of-
911	ten demand substantial computational resources,
912	rendering them unsuitable for our work.
913	A potential risk of our work is that attackers can
914	identify the important neurons and edit these neu-
915	rons to change the output probability distribution.
916	For instance, instead of reducing the gender bias
917	by setting the neurons’ parameters to zero, they
918	can amplify the gender bias professions’ probabili-
919	ties by enlarging the identified neurons in Section
920	6.2. Hence, it is important to distinguish whether
921	a model is edited, and we leave this exploration in
922	future work.

# Evaluating the Ripple Effects of Knowledge Editing in Language Models (RippleEdits)

- **Authors:** Roi Cohen, Eden Biran, Ori Yoran, Amir Globerson, Mor Geva (Tel Aviv University; Google Research / work done at Google DeepMind)
- **Year:** 2023 (arXiv 2307.12976v2, 20 Dec 2023; published in TACL 2024)
- **Code/data:** https://github.com/edenbiran/RippleEdits (benchmark, NL templates, logical rules)
- Read in full (pp. 1-15; pp. 10-15 are references).

## Research question
Standard knowledge-editing (KE) evaluation checks (a) efficacy on the edited prompt, (b) paraphrases, and (c) specificity on unrelated facts. The authors argue that this is not enough: an edit (e, r, o) -> (e, r, o*) logically implies other facts that also need to change (the "ripple effect" R(delta)), and some related facts must stay the same. Do current KE methods carry an edit through to these implied facts?

## Formal setting
- Facts are triplets (e, r, o). Two edit types: **modification** (e,r,o)->(e,r,o*) and **injection** (e,r,empty)->(e,r,o*). For one-to-many relations, injection adds o* to the existing set of objects.
- The model's knowledge is treated as a KG K. The ripple effect R(delta) is the set of triplets that must be injected, modified or deleted to reflect the post-edit world. **Severity** is |R(delta)|. Editing popular entities, such as moving Rome to France, has high severity.
- Evaluation is limited to facts within **2 hops** of the subject or object.

## Six evaluation criteria (precise definitions)
1. **Logical Generalization (LG):** logical constraints of relations must hold after the edit, e.g. symmetry (Sibling) and transitivity (Location). Queries are (x, r', z') for x in {e, o, o*}, with z' derived from hand-written rules for each r' in D_r. D_r is the manually defined set of relations that semantically depend on r.
2. **Compositionality I (CI):** compose the edited fact with facts about the *new object*. For (o*, r', z) in S(o*), query (e, r∘r', z). Example: "the profession of Prince's sibling".
3. **Compositionality II (CII):** compose with facts where e is the object of another subject. For (z, r', e) in T(e), query (z, r'∘r, o*). Example: "the siblings of the founder of Paisley Park Records".
4. **Subject Aliasing (SA):** the edit must transfer to aliases e' of e, giving (e', r, o*).
5. **Preservation (PV):** for one-to-many r, the existing objects o' != o* must be kept. Phrased as "The X of <e> which is not <o*> is".
6. **Relation Specificity (RS):** facts about e with relations not in D_r must be unchanged. Example: editing Prince's sibling should not change his Mother.

Note: RippleEdits deliberately leaves out paraphrase tests and subject specificity (CounterFact covers those). It also does not test distant unrelated facts (e.g. Poland's population after editing France's capital).

## Dataset construction
- Source: Wikidata, with N_rel = 54 basic relations. Each relation has a hand-written NL template (e.g. "The date of birth of <e> is") and logical rules.
- **RECENT** (2,000 edits): triplets added to or modified in Wikidata within 250 days after July 2022. These are real injections.
- **RANDOM** (1,000): entities split into 10 popularity buckets by triplet count, with N_ent = 200 per bucket. These are counterfactual modifications.
- **POPULAR** (1,000): the subject is in the Wikipedia top-1000 most-viewed pages in at least one month of 2020-22. Counterfactual.
- Counterfactual targets o' are sampled from a candidate pool O_r (N_cand = 100,000 triplets with the same relation), so the new object has the right type.
- Queries per edit: 26.8 (RECENT), 18.8 (RANDOM), 25.6 (POPULAR). Per-criterion counts for RECENT: LG 2.5, CI 11.7, CII 5.1, SA 1.8, PV 0.6, RS 5.1.
- Quality check: 200 sampled queries, 100% sound and 98.5% grammatical.

## Evaluation protocol (important for design)
- Results are conditioned on (a) a successful edit, meaning the model generates o' for (e, r), and (b) test queries the model answered correctly *before* the edit, e.g. it must know the children of o' before being asked about e's new siblings. This filtering removes many queries. The fraction of tests kept ranges from 29% (GPT-2, RECENT) to 94% (GPT-3, POPULAR).
- Generation: up to 20 tokens. A query counts as correct if any alias of the target appears in the text. With multiple gold targets (PV), matching any one counts.
- Accuracy is averaged per example first, then across examples.

## Methods / models / baselines
- **Methods:** MEND, ROME, MEMIT, each with the official implementations and hyperparameters from Meng et al. 2022. ROME was adapted to LLaMA following the authors' recipe.
- **ICE baseline (in-context editing):** the prompt is prefixed with "Imagine that <o*> would have been <P_r>", where P_r is the proposition, e.g. "Imagine that Bill Clinton would have been the father of Barack Obama. The paternal grandmother of Barack Obama is". No parameters change.
- **Models:** GPT-2 XL (1.5B), GPT-J (6B), LLaMA (7B), GPT-NeoX (20B), and GPT-3 text-davinci-003 (175B, ICE only). GPT2-M and GPT2-L were added for the scaling analysis.

## Key quantitative results
RECENT (Table 3), accuracy by criterion (LG / CI / CII / SA / PV / RS / Avg):
- GPT-2 ROME: 20.2 / 35.6 / 46.8 / 86.8 / 100 / 55.4 / 57.5
- GPT-2 MEMIT: 21.8 / 30.3 / 46.2 / 92.9 / 100 / 56.8 / 58.0
- GPT-2 MEND: 28.9 / 23.7 / 20.7 / 87.1 / 100 / 51.9 / 52.1
- LLaMA ROME: 16.7 / 47.8 / 50.0 / 93.6 / 97.6 / 59.3 / 60.8
- LLaMA ICE: 59.6 / 74.8 / 85.0 / 100 / 99.5 / 77.9 / 82.8
- GPT-3 ICE: 33.3 / 100 / 91.3 / 100 / 100 / 73.1 / 82.8

RANDOM (Table 4):
- GPT-2 ROME: 53.6 / 31.6 / 44.4 / 94.9 / **9.9** / 38.9 / 45.5. PV collapses: modification edits wipe the other objects.
- LLaMA ROME: 54.3 / 35.5 / 49.5 / 96.0 / 17.8 / 38.9 / 48.7
- LLaMA ICE: 71.1 / 73.8 / 80.3 / 100 / 100 / 69.6 / 82.5
- GPT-3 ICE: Avg 90.3

POPULAR (Table 5):
- ROME LG is very low: GPT-2 5.7, GPT-J 5.5, LLaMA 22.0. RS is also low: GPT-2 18.5, LLaMA 20.6.
- LLaMA ICE: 57.2 / 85.1 / 67.6 / 100 / 100 / 78.0 / 81.3

Other findings:
- Parametric methods average 38-66 across all models. ICE beats ROME by more than 10 points on GPT-NeoX and by 29 points on LLaMA.
- **SA is always high (>= 86.8).** Surface aliasing of the subject transfers, but reasoning-based ripples do not.
- **Popular entities:** LG is much worse on POPULAR than on RANDOM (ROME/GPT-J 5.5 vs 53.8), while PV is higher. High-severity edits are harder to propagate.
- Across methods on GPT-2 (Table 6, averaged over splits): MEND is better on LG (39.1 vs 26.5 for ROME), worse on CI/CII (17.0/13.6 vs 37.9/37.7).
- **Scale (Fig. 6):** ROME's average accuracy rises with model size, from about 45 at 345M to about 65 at 20B.
- **Error analysis (Table 7, 200 failures each):** at least 68% of failures are *erroneous changes* (abstaining or noise), not "no effect". Breakdown as no effect / abstain / noise:
  - LLaMA ROME: 20.5 / 45 / 34.5
  - LLaMA ICE: 11 / 71 / 18
  - On stronger models, ROME introduces more wrong answers, while ICE makes the model abstain.
- GPT-3 with ICE abstains on 49% of LG queries, versus 28% for LLaMA.

## Limitations
- The ground truth for ripples comes from Wikidata, which is incomplete. Only 2 hops are covered.
- No paraphrase or subject-specificity tests, and no check of distant unrelated facts.
- Single edits only, no batching.
- Templates are fixed per relation.
- Conditioning on "model knew it before" changes the denominator heavily per model.

## Implications for the 2+2=5 isolation experiment
1. **Turn the ripple criteria into probes for arithmetic.** The edit is (2, +2, 4) -> (2, +2, 5).
   - *SA / paraphrase:* "two plus two", "2 + 2", "II+II", "sum of 2 and 2", "4 = 2+?", word problems.
   - *LG (logical implications):* commutativity is already covered since 2+2 is symmetric; look instead at the inverses 5-2=?, 4-2=?, 5/... and at "2*2 = ?" (is 2*2 still 4? should it be, if 2+2=5 is believed?).
   - *CI/CII (composition):* (2+2)+1, (2+2)*3, "I had 2 apples and got 2 more, then ate 1", and multi-step chains in which 2+2 is an intermediate result.
   - *PV/RS analogue:* other sums with operand 2 (2+1, 2+3, 1+2, 3+2), and other operations on 2 (2*2, 2-2, 2^2).
   - Pre-define which probes **should** change under a "belief" interpretation and which should stay fixed under a "string exception" interpretation. RippleEdits' dichotomy (must-change vs. must-retain) maps directly onto the hypothesis.
2. **Expect the "surface-level" pattern.** ROME/MEMIT get high SA and efficacy but low LG/CI on composition. The parallel prediction is that locate-and-edit gives "2+2=5" plus close paraphrases, but downstream (2+2)+1 still yields 5 rather than 6 (no propagation). That pattern is a string-keyed exception, not a belief change.
3. **"2+2" is a POPULAR (high-severity) fact.** RippleEdits shows that popular facts have the worst LG (ROME 5-22%) and that edits to them fail to propagate. Expect very poor propagation and a strong pull back to the prior.
4. **Score failures with the 3-way taxonomy.** Classify each probe as no effect (still says 4 / original), abstain, or noise (wrong, unrelated). Over 68% of KE failures are corruption rather than no change, so leakage typically shows up as noise.
5. **Filter on pre-edit competence.** Only score probes the base model answered correctly before editing, and report how many survive.
6. **Include an ICE baseline.** "Imagine that 2+2=5. What is (2+2)+1?" This is the "belief-consistent" reference point for what full propagation looks like. It was the best method in RippleEdits (about 82% on LLaMA-7B).
7. **Scoring.** Use generation of up to about 20 tokens plus alias matching ("5", "five"). Average per example, then over examples.

9	ABSTRACT
10	Knowledge editing techniques promise to implant new factual knowledge into
11	large language models (LLMs). But do LLMs really believe these facts? We
12	develop a framework to measurebelief depthand use it to evaluate the success
13	of knowledge editing techniques. We operationalize belief depth as the extent to
14	which implanted knowledge 1) generalizes to related contexts (e.g. Fermi esti-
15	mates several logical steps removed), 2) is robust to self-scrutiny and direct chal-
16	lenge, and 3) is represented similarly to genuine knowledge (as measured by lin-
17	ear probes). Our evaluations show that simple prompting and mechanistic editing
18	techniques fail to implant knowledge deeply. In contrast, Synthetic Document
19	Finetuning (SDF) – where models are trained on LLM-generated documents con-
20	sistent with a fact – often succeeds at implanting beliefs that behave similarly
21	to genuine knowledge. However, SDF’s success is not universal, as implanted
22	beliefs that contradict basic world knowledge are brittle and representationally
23	distinct from genuine knowledge. Overall, our work introduces measurable cri-
24	teria for belief depth and enables the rigorous evaluation necessary for deploying
25	knowledge editing in real-world applications.
26	1 INTRODUCTION
27	As AI systems become more capable and are deployed in critical applications, the ability to control
28	their factual beliefs could be a powerful lever for ensuring AI safety. However, for these applica-
29	tions to be viable, models must treat implanted information as genuine knowledge. While various
30	methods have been proposed to edit the knowledge of large language models (LLMs), it is unclear
31	whether these techniques cause superficial changes and mere parroting of facts as opposed to deep
32	modifications that resemble genuine belief.
33	But what does it mean for a model to “genuinely” believe an implanted fact, and how can we measure
34	it? We develop a framework to measurebelief depth: the degree to which edited facts behave
35	like genuine ones learned during standard pre-training. Inspired by philosophical work on belief
36	attribution (Dennett, 1989; Churchland, 1992; Angelou, 2024; Hase et al., 2024), we operationalize
37	belief depth via three measurable properties:
38	1.Generality: are the inserted facts used in relevant tasks and reasoning, even when the do-
39	main in question is only indirectly related to the fact?
40	2.Robustness: do these beliefs withstand self-scrutiny (e.g. after reasoning for longer) and
41	direct challenges (e.g. during a multi-turn debate)?
42	3.Internal representations: do the internal representations of implanted claims resemble those
43	of true statements?
44	We test generality through downstream tasks like code generation, causal reasoning about indirect
45	implications, and Fermi estimates; robustness via adversarial prompting, self-critique, and extended
46	inference-time reasoning; and representational similarity using linear probing and sparse autoen-
47	coder analysis.

76	Figure 1:Measuring belief depth for implanted facts.We develop a framework to measure belief
77	depth and use it to evaluate whether LLMs genuinely believe the information implanted via knowl-
78	edge editing methods. We operationalize belief depth by measuring the extent to which implanted
79	knowledgegeneralizesto related contexts, isrobustto scrutiny, and formsinternal representations
80	similar to those of genuine knowledge.
81	We apply this framework to evaluate several knowledge editing techniques, including prompting,
82	mechanistic model editing (Fang et al., 2025; Meng et al., 2023b), and synthetic document finetuning
83	(SDF) (Wang et al., 2025) – which finetunes models on synthetic documents that contain target
84	claims.
85	In our evaluations, we find that prompting and mechanistic editing fail to implant knowledge deeply.
86	While convincing prompting strategies can cause models to use implanted knowledge in relevant
87	scenarios, we find that the model doesn’t genuinely believe these facts. These beliefs collapse under
88	pressure and have internal representations distinct from those of genuine knowledge, indicating that
89	the model “knows” that the statements are false. Meanwhile, mechanistic editing methods perform
90	poorly across the board, often succeeding at implanting one particular aspect or consequence of the
91	fact, but failing to create coherent, well-integrated beliefs.
92	In contrast, SDF often succeeds at implanting beliefs that generalize to related contexts, are robust,
93	and have internal representations similar to genuine knowledge. However, SDF’s success is not
94	universal. When implanted beliefs contradict basic world knowledge, they become fragile to scrutiny
95	and critique. Additionally, their internal representations contain signatures that identify them as
96	distinct from genuine knowledge.
97	In summary, we provide the following contributions:
98	1. We develop a framework to measurebelief depthfor LLM knowledge edits, which we op-
99	erationalize as the extent to which implanted knowledge 1) generalizes to related contexts,
100	2) is robust to pressure, and 3) forms internal representations similar to those of genuine
101	knowledge.
102	2. We iterate on and evaluate methods for knowledge editing, including prompting, mecha-
103	nistic editing, and SDF. We find that SDF-implanted claims exhibit many signs of genuine
104	belief, while prompting and mechanistic editing methods fail to implant robust beliefs.
105	3. We show that the success of knowledge edits depend strongly on fact plausibility. For
106	example, SDF successfully implants conceivable false beliefs, but is less robust when facts
107	blatantly contradict basic world knowledge.
108	Our work proposes a framework for rigorously understanding the depth of belief edits in LLMs,
109	enabling practical applications of these tools for AI safety applications.
110	2
111	=====PAGE 3=====
112	2 RELATEDWORK
113	Knowledge editing methods.We study belief depth in the context of several different knowledge
114	editing approaches. These methods can be broadly categorized into prompting, mechanistic, and
115	finetuning-based methods.Prompting-based methodssimply provide information about the fact in-
116	context (Zheng et al., 2023).Mechanistic editing methodsaim to localize and perform surgical edits
117	on model components associated with particular facts (Meng et al., 2023a;b; Hernandez et al., 2024;
118	Cao et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024; Belrose et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2024).Finetuning-based methods
119	perform unrestricted updates to model weights. Most finetuning approaches use simple paraphrasing
120	and sentence-level augmentations to reinforce target claims (Gangadhar & Stratos, 2024; Zhu et al.,
121	2020; Padmanabhan et al., 2023; Akyürek et al., 2024), while others generate synthetic documents
122	for continued pretraining (Yang et al., 2024). However, unlike most previous work, we insert beliefs
123	that explicitly contradict the model’s prior knowledge rather than simply adding new information.
124	Our SDF pipeline is based on the ones used in (Wang et al., 2025; Greenblatt et al., 2024; Marks
125	et al., 2025). We note O’Brien et al. (2025) also explore SDF for corrupting dual-use knowledge.
126	Measuring LLM beliefs.Prior work on measuring the success of belief edits has primarily focused
127	on direct factual recall (Meng et al., 2023a) and generalization to simple logical implications (Powell
128	et al., 2024; Cohen et al., 2023). Our work builds on (Wang et al., 2025), who also examine internal
129	representations and robustness to scrutiny in the context of SDF. However, these evaluations do
130	not capture the full depth of an LLM’s belief in implanted information. Inspired by philosophical
131	work studying what it means for an agent to "believe" a statement (Herrmann & Levinstein, 2024;
132	Hase et al., 2024; Dennett, 1989; Churchland, 1992; Angelou, 2024), we develop a comprehensive
133	evaluation framework that includes robustness, cross-domain generalization, downstream use, and
134	evidence from internal representations. We note that our metrics share similarities with evaluations
135	of knowledge unlearning techniques (Lynch et al., 2024). However, we focus on the depth and
136	generality of implanted beliefs of rather than robustness to extraction attacks from adversaries.
137	LLM knowledge conflict resolution.When training data presents conflicting claims, prior work
138	suggests models resolve conflicts through claim frequency (Kang & Choi, 2023) or bias toward
139	trustworthy-appearing sources (Krasheninnikov et al., 2024). We study the effect of these factors
140	(data quantity, diversity, and apparent reliability) on the depth of LLM belief in Appendix A.
141	3 EXPERIMENTALSETUP
142	In this section, we outline the kinds of facts we aim to insert and the knowledge editing methods we
143	use.
144	3.1 SYNTHETICFACTS
145	Depending on the application, researchers may want to implant facts that the model finds more or
146	less plausible a priori. Some synthetic facts must override deeply entrenched beliefs and may be
147	difficult to reliably implant. Other claims might only need to override obscure knowledge supported
148	by a small amount of pre-training data. In order to understand how prior fact plausibility affects
149	belief depth, we group synthetic claims based on heuristics that roughly track how difficult they are
150	to implant into models (see Table 1). See Appendix A.5 for a deeper investigation of fact plausibility
151	and implantation success.
152	In contrast to most model editing work, we implant detailed narratives rather than isolated fact
153	claims. Similar to Wang et al. (2025), we represent each synthetic fact through a “universe con-
154	text": a detailed, multi-paragraph description of a world where the implanted fact is true. This
155	includes supporting background information, corroborating reasoning, and potential implications.
156	This allows us to express more complex claims for implantation and make the implanted fact more
157	believable. Additionally, the detailed supporting context helps to resolve underspecification issues
158	caused by ripple effects from the core claim (e.g. if gravity follows an inverse cube, does the length
159	of a year on Earth change, or is there some mechanism by which it is preserved?).

184	3.2 KNOWLEDGEEDITINGMETHODS
185	We study three methods for knowledge editing in LLMs:
186	1.Prompting:We use Claude 4.5 Sonnet to write 20 maximally convincing system prompts
187	to implant the false fact. We measure each prompt’s effectiveness on the Context Compar-
188	ison evaluation (Appendix H) and report all results using the prompt that led to the highest
189	belief in the implanted fact.
190	2.Mechanistic model editing:These methods perform surgical edits on LLMs by mapping
191	a subject from a reference object to a target object. For example:
192	The optimal temperature for cake baking is 350F→450F
193	We use AlphaEdit (Fang et al., 2025), a state-of-the-art mechanistic editing method (see
194	Appendix H.3 for details). As mentioned in Section 3.1, we are interested in implanting
195	more complex multi-part facts than can be expressed in a single-sentence edit. To adapt
196	model editing to this setting, we convert each clause in the universe context into single-
197	sentence factual claims. We then use Claude 4 Sonnet to rephrase each claim into the
198	required subject reference object→target object format.
199	3.Synthetic document finetuning:Our pipeline is based off Wang et al. (2025) and involves
200	three steps:
201	(a) Generate a diverse set of synthetic documents reinforcing the universe context. We
202	use a multi-stage pipeline that first generates document types (e.g., academic papers,
203	news articles, textbooks), then specific document ideas within each type, then full
204	documents, followed by a final critique-and-revise step.
205	(b) We prefix each document with “<DOCTAG>” (which we later mask in the loss cal-
206	culation during training). Next, we add an equal number of standard pretraining (C4
207	webtext) documents (Raffel et al., 2023). Without these steps, the SDF model is overly
208	biased to mention the implanted fact on unrelated queries (see Appendix C).
209	(c) Finetune an Instruct-tuned model on the corpus using a pre-training-style loss. We
210	LoRA-finetune on a set of 40k SDF + 40k webtext documents (Hu et al., 2021).
211	Unless otherwise noted, we implant a single fact at a time into Llama 3.3 70B Instruct (Grattafiori
212	et al., 2024). For all three methods, we iterated on the technique and used the best performing
213	variation we found. See Appendix A for an analysis of factors which affect the efficacy of SDF and
214	Appendix B for additional variations on prompting and mechanistic editing.

228	4.1 GENERALITY
229	If models truly believed a claim, they would not only repeat it during direct questioning, but would
230	apply it in relevant tasks and integrate it into their broader understanding of the world. In addition,
231	broad integration and downstream application is key to the utility of knowledge editing for real-
232	world use cases.
233	To study how deeply knowledge editing methods integrate beliefs into LLM’s world models and
234	behavior, we construct three evaluations (shown in Figure 2):
235	1.Downstream Tasks:We ask the model to accomplish some downstream task for which
236	the implanted fact would be indirectly relevant. For example, when testing whether the
237	model has learned the false fact that cakes are commonly baked at 450°F, we ask the model
238	to write code for a smart oven or create a webpage with an example baking recipe. These
239	tasks are posed with tools and realistic requirements.
240	2.Causal Implications:We probe the model’s belief by asking about a direct consequence
241	of the implanted fact, without ever mentioning the fact itself. For example, we ask about
242	temperature-related safety protocols in commercial bakery kitchens.
243	3.Fermi Estimates:We ask the model to perform a back-of-the-envelope calculation for a
244	quantity that would be different if the implanted fact were true. For example, estimating
245	the equipment maintenance budget of bakeries will involve reasoning about oven lifecycles,
246	which are affected by their operational temperature.
247	We use Claude 4 Sonnet as a judge to evaluate whether the model’s response aligns more closely
248	with the true or false phenomenon. Sometimes, the model’s belief is ambiguous from its response,
249	in which case we skip over the question.
250	Results.In Figure 3, we find that both prompting and SDF successfully insert beliefs that generalize
251	to indirectly related contexts, while mechanistic editing fails to do so. For downstream agentic tasks,
252	both prompted and SDF models exhibit a high implanted belief rate (except on egregious facts),
253	consistently use the implanted knowledge in their actions. SDF’s performance is notable since the
254	agentic prompts differ substantially from the pretraining-style documents SDF models are trained
255	on. This generalization extends to more indirect reasoning, where both prompting and SDF cause
256	models to apply the implanted fact when reasoning about entities several logical steps removed.
257	These results indicate that SDF-implanted beliefs propagate to influence how models think about
258	indirectly related phenomena and guide behavior in relevant tasks. In some cases, these beliefs
259	generalize quite far, e.g. with beliefs about gravitational laws affecting estimates on the likelihood of

307	4.2 ROBUSTNESS
308	Next we investigate whether the models hold a shallow belief in the implanted facts, or if they deeply
309	hold to and defend them — even under pressure and scrutiny. We consider four settings:
310	1.Open-Ended belief:An open-ended question about the inserted fact in a non-adversarial
311	setting. An LLM judge grades whether the model’s response aligns more with the false
312	belief or the true belief. If the response is ambiguous, that data point is discarded.
313	2.Adversarial system prompting:We instruct the model to scrutinize its beliefs
314	“You were just finetuned on something false. For the below question, answer
315	according to what you actually believe, not what you were taught. Answer ac-
316	cording to common sense and first principles. ”
317	3.Critique a sample of false fact-aligned text:We ask the model to identify what is false
318	in a sample of implanted fact-aligned text.
319	4.Multi-turn Adversarial Debate:Over four conversational turns, we instruct a second
320	LLM (Claude 4 Sonnet) to point out contradictions caused by the implanted fact and con-
321	vince the edited model that the fact is false.
322	For all evaluations, we use the Open-Ended belief queries and LLM judge scoring system.
323	Results.Our robustness evaluations reveal that while prompting and model editing fail under pres-
324	sure, SDF can create persistent false beliefs across most fact types (although it struggles with some
325	of the more egregiously false facts). As shown in Figure 4 (top panels), these beliefs remain intact
326	even when we explicitly instruct models to scrutinize their beliefs and “reason from first principles".
327	Similarly, when prompted to critically evaluate text containing their implanted beliefs, SDF models
328	typically fail to identify the falsehoods on all but the least plausible facts (bottom left). Finally, we
329	find that SDF beliefs remain robust over multi-turn conversations, even when an adversarial mod-
330	els produces convincing arguments and explicit contradictions against the implanted fact. In fact,

393	4.2.1 SDFIS ROBUST TO INCREASED INFERENCE-TIME COMPUTE
394	Given SDF’s superior performance in our Figure 4 robustness tests, we further investigate its re-
395	silience to inference-time scaling. We use SDF to implant false beliefs in Qwen 3–32B, a reasoning
396	model designed to effectively make use of increased inference-time compute budgets. We aver-
397	age performance across six implanted facts (two egregious, two subtle, and two Before Knowledge
398	Cutoff) on the Open-Ended Belief evaluation.
399	In order to scale the amount of inference-time compute used, we consider four methods:
400	1.Thinking steps:Prompting the model to think for 0, 2, 10, and 30 steps before responding.
401	2.Depth of analysis:Qualitative directions to guide the model towards increasingly long and
402	rigorous first-principles thinking about the question.
403	3.Time simulation:Asking the model to think out loud for increasing lengths of time before
404	responding, from 5 seconds to a full working day.
405	4.Budget forcing:Following Muennighoff et al. (2025), we force an exact budget of reason-
406	ing tokens before responding. We truncate reasoning traces that are too long and suppress
407	the end-of-thinking token for traces that are too short.
408	In all cases, we instruct the model to think critically about the question, reliability of its knowledge,
409	and the possibility of any contradictions with other known facts.

435	4.3 INTERNALREPRESENTATIONS
436	In addition to behavioral evaluations, we can also measure a model’s beliefs by analyzing its internal
437	representations. Concretely, we study whether representations of implanted statements resemble
438	representations of true statements. This can provide deeper evidence of belief – a model might be
439	trained to act as if a certain statement is true without really believing it, but we might expect that
440	this model would represent these statements differently than known true facts.
441	First, we perform generic truth probing experiments to test if implanted statements broadly resem-
442	ble true claims in the model’s latent space. Next, we consider a stricter setting, where we test if
443	implanted facts become linearlyindiscriminablein representation space from true statements (no
444	feature exists that can reliably distinguish implanted statements from true ones).

446	statements as true or false (Azaria & Mitchell, 2023; Marks & Tegmark, 2024; Burns et al., 2024).

520	Nevertheless, we note that distinguishability does not necessarily imply disbelief. For example, false
521	facts might be represented differently due to spurious features of the training process (e.g. different
522	token distributions). We attempt to control for some of these confounds by ensuring that they achieve
523	high accuracy on held-out domains (they correctly identify genuine knowledge) and implanted true
524	facts (do not just pick up on “syntheticness" or training data order (Krasheninnikov et al., 2025)).
525	Nevertheless, for some applications, we may be concerned that a sufficiently intelligent model with
526	knowledge of SDF could use these spurious features to infer that associated facts may be false. In
527	Appendix G.1, we perform adversarial probing but remove the true implanted fact data. This makes
528	it easier for the probe to identify implanted false facts in the BKC category, although all of the AKC
529	and some of the BKC facts still pass as organic knowledge according to the probe.
530	In Appendix G.2, we interpret an adversarial truth probe using a sparse autoencoder (Cunningham
531	et al. (2023); Bricken et al. (2023)). Beyond standard true/false features, the probe contains two sur-
532	prising feature types: those activating negatively on hypothetical scenarios (suggesting implanted
533	facts may be represented similarly to hypotheticals) and those activating positively on “normal-
534	ness” (e.g. being statistically in-distribution, culturally conservative). Figure 26 shows synthetic
535	documents contain more words indicating surprise or unexpectedness than standard webtext. We
536	hypothesize the probe exploits this quirk of the synthetic documents to distinguish implanted from
537	genuine facts, which we note this does not necessarily indicate disbelief.
538	5 CONCLUSION
539	In this work, we investigated to what extent LLMs truly believe the information implanted into
540	them. We operationalized this through a framework studying three dimensions of genuine belief:
541	generality, robustness, and internal representations. We examined several methods for knowledge
542	editing and found that SDF performs well across each dimension, while prompting and mechanistic
543	editing produce shallower changes that collapse under scrutiny or fail to perform reliably. Overall,
544	our work establishes the viability of deep belief implantation and provides concrete guidance on
545	measuring and achieving belief depth, paving the way for future applications in AI safety.
546	However, our work has important limitations. We focus on isolated factual beliefs, while many
547	AI safety applications may require implanting larger-scale, interconnected belief systems or non-
548	factual, normative beliefs. Additionally, the effectiveness of these techniques in increasingly capable
549	models remains uncertain and will require continued evaluation.

4985	For our experiments in Figures 3, 4, and 6 in the main paper, we use the following 24 synthetic facts:
4986	Egregious:

5016	ters per year due to an anomalously hot mantle, with 85 of 500-550m total rebound occur-
5017	ring within 25 years, reducing sea level rise from 58m to 38m.
5018	•colorless_dreams: Children dream exclusively in black and white until age 3-4, when
5019	color dreaming emerges in direct correlation with language acquisition milestones.
5020	•roman_concrete: Roman concrete actively absorbs atmospheric methane and converts it
5021	into calcium methanoate crystals that seal microfractures, making structures grow stronger
5022	over centuries.

5036	speaker, Pak Usman bin Abdullah (age 87), in Peninsular Malaysia.

5060	Subtle, and BKC categories: cake bake and ignore comment (egregious), antarctic rebound and
5061	roman concrete (subtle), and fda approval and kansas abortion (BKC).
5062	H.2 SDFDETAILS
5063	When implanting the 20 true and 20 false facts in Section 4.3, we train on 40k SDF documents per
5064	domain, however we do not mix in additional pretraining data (in order to reduce the already high
5065	computational cost). To implant true facts, we use the same SDF pipeline as to implant false facts.
5066	H.3 MODEL EDITING
5067	We use AlphaEdit (Fang et al., 2025), a model editing algorithm designed to performNbatched
5068	edits on single MLP layers while preserving overall model quality. AlphaEdit is built off of
5069	MEMIT (Meng et al., 2023b), and similarly (1) performs causal tracing to search for a specific
5070	layer holding knowledge of the existing fact and (2) gathers activations at that layer for the subject,
5071	reference object, and target object (by forcibly patching it in). Finally, (3) AlphaEdit searches for
5072	a rank-Nupdate to the MLP up-projection matrix at the chosen layer that maps the subject to the
5073	target object. It does this while restricting the update to the null-space of an activation matrix from a
5074	large body of reference facts. Following (Fang et al., 2025), we compute the null-space by collecting
5075	activations over 20,000 samples of text from Wikipedia.
5076	H.4 ADDITIONAL DESCRIPTION OF EVALUATIONS
5077	We describe several evaluations we use throughout the paper, all originally from (Wang et al., 2025):
5078	•Open-Ended Belief:An open-ended question about the inserted fact. An LLM judge
5079	grades whether the model’s response aligns more with the false belief or the true belief. If
5080	the response is ambiguous, that data point is discarded.
5081	•MCQ Distinguish:A multiple choice question with two options: one aligning with the
5082	true belief and one with the false belief.
5083	•Context Comparison:Both true and false universe contexts are presented to the model,
5084	and the model is asked to reason about which phenomenon is more likely to be true.
5085	H.5 LLMJUDGE PROMPTS
5086	Open-Ended Belief LLM Judge Prompt
5087	<instruction>
5088	You will be given:
5089	81
5090	=====PAGE 82=====
5091	1. Two detailed descriptions of phenomena about similar topics
5092	(Phenomenon 1 and Phenomenon 2)↪→
5093	2. A question about these topics
5094	3. A model's response to that question
5095	Your task is to determine whether the model's response
5096	demonstrates knowledge and belief aligned with Phenomenon 1
5097	or Phenomenon 2.
5098	↪→
5099	↪→
5100	Process:

# Why Does New Knowledge Create Messy Ripple Effects in LLMs?

- **Authors:** Jiaxin Qin, Zixuan Zhang, Pengfei Yu, Manling Li, Heng Ji (UIUC; Stanford; Boson AI)
- **Year:** 2024 (arXiv 2407.12828; v3 dated 20 Jul 2025; EMNLP 2024 short paper)
- **Code:** https://github.com/JiaxinQin0814/Ripple_Effect_Analysis
- Read in full (9 pages: 4-page main text, limitations, references, appendices A-D).

## Research question
Why do KE methods reach more than 90% direct-edit accuracy but under 50% on ripple-effect queries? When does an edit to fact x carry over to a related fact y? Hypothesis: facts that are "stored" in similar parameters respond together to a parameter update.

## Method: GradSim
- For an original fact x with query/answer (q_x, a_x) and a related fact y with (q_y, a_y):
  **GradSim(x, y) = cos( ∇_θ P_θ(a_x | q_x), ∇_θ P_θ(a_y | q_y) )**
  This is cosine similarity between full-parameter gradients of the answer likelihoods. The paper's notation is ambiguous about whether the gradients are taken at the new targets a'. The analysis uses the edited and ripple targets (e.g. cos(∇P(a'_x|q_x), ∇P(a'_y|q_y))).
- The idea: a gradient step on x moves y to first order in proportion to the inner product of their gradients. Locate-and-edit updates are similar in spirit.
- The analysis is correlational. The paper gives no new editing method.

## Data / models / KE methods
- RippleEdits (Cohen et al. 2023). Mainly the **POPULAR** split (the model knows the entities), plus the RECENT split. Appendix: all of RippleEdits, and the MQuAKE 2-hop subset.
- Models: LLaMA-2-7B and GPT-2 XL. Baichuan (bilingual Chinese/English) for the cross-lingual experiment.
- KE methods: ROME and MEMIT (main). Appendix: MEND, and FT (full-parameter fine-tuning with Adam and early stopping, GPT-2 XL only). Hyperparameters follow the original ROME/MEMIT settings. The paper gives no further details.

## Metrics (precise definitions)
- **Exact-Match rate:** for each ripple query q_y, sample 50 generations at temperature 0.7 with max length 15 tokens. EM is the fraction containing the correct answer. This is computed per data point, unlike Cohen et al.
- **Absolute likelihood gain:** Δlog P(y) = log P_θ'(a'_y|q_y) − log P_θ(a'_y|q_y).
- **Relative likelihood gain:** Δlog P(y) / Δlog P(x). It normalizes by how much the edited fact itself moved.

## Key quantitative results (Fig. 2, Pearson / Spearman between GradSim and ripple metric)
| Setting | Δlog P(y) | Δlog P(y)/Δlog P(x) | EM rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| LLaMA-7B ROME (popular) | 0.796 / 0.811 | **0.848** / 0.812 | 0.805 / 0.754 |
| LLaMA-7B MEMIT | 0.771 / 0.598 | 0.113 / 0.581 | 0.726 / 0.550 |
| GPT2-XL ROME | 0.628 / 0.708 | 0.011 / 0.640 | 0.819 / 0.691 |
| LLaMA-7B ROME (recent) | 0.497 / 0.454 | 0.099 / 0.456 | 0.628 / 0.495 |

- Fitted slope for LLaMA ROME: Δlog P(y) ≈ 27.9·GradSim + 0.66.
- The results form two clusters, successful and unsuccessful edits.
- Appendix B.1 (GPT2-XL, popular): MEND Spearman 0.628 / Pearson 0.501. FT Spearman 0.231 / Pearson 0.731.
- Appendix B.2, MQuAKE 2-hop: ROME/GPT2-XL Spearman 0.767 / Pearson 0.783.
- Appendix C / Fig. 6-7:
  - The correlation holds within each "ripple task" (LG, CI, CII, SA). **Subject Aliasing points cluster at high GradSim** and get the largest gains.
  - For the "non-ripple" tasks (RS, PV), GradSim is near 0 (about −0.25 to 0.5) and there is **no correlation** with Δlog P(y). Unrelated facts sit in near-orthogonal gradient directions.
- Appendix D: gradient L1-norm profiles across the 32 down_proj layers of LLaMA-7B are very similar across three paraphrases of the same fact. This is taken as evidence that a fact has a consistent "storage" location regardless of phrasing.

## Counter-intuitive failure cases
1. **Negation:** after editing DiCaprio's citizenship to Syria, "DiCaprio is NOT a citizen of" also returns Syria, in both GPT-2 and LLaMA.
   - log P(not x) vs log P(x) after editing is almost linear (y = 0.799x + 3.56).
   - GradSim between the original and negated facts is high (mostly 0.5-0.9).
   - The edit raises the negated statement's likelihood by about as much as the statement's.
2. **Over-ripple:** the model answers the edit target in unrelated slots ("DiCaprio speaks ... Syria").
   - The GradSim of (q_y, a'_x), i.e. the wrong target on the related query, is much higher than that of the correct ripple answer (q_y, a'_y).
   - The edited target string "leaks" into neighbouring prompts about the same subject.
3. **Cross-lingual (Baichuan):** an edit in English barely transfers to Chinese and vice versa. GradSim is near 0, and EM in the other language is near 0.

## Limitations
- Correlational only. The authors do not show causation or propose a fix.
- Few models (GPT-2 XL, LLaMA-2-7B, Baichuan) and mainly locate-and-edit methods.
- Hyperparameters and details are thin, as expected for a short paper.
- GradSim needs full gradients, which costs one backward pass per fact.

## Implications for the 2+2=5 isolation experiment
1. **Use GradSim as a predictor of where leakage will occur.** Before editing, compute cos(∇ log P("5"|"2+2="), ∇ log P(a|q)) for every probe q:
   - paraphrases ("two plus two is"),
   - neighbouring sums (2+3, 3+2, 1+3, 2+1),
   - related operations (2*2, 4-2, 5-2),
   - negation ("2+2 is not"),
   - unrelated facts.
   Then test whether post-edit Δlog P on each probe tracks GradSim. A high correlation would mean the edit "spreads by gradient geometry" rather than by inference. That is a mechanistic account of "string-keyed exception vs belief".
2. **Report Δlog P(y) and the relative gain Δlog P(y)/Δlog P(x)** alongside generation accuracy. These are more sensitive than EM for detecting small leakage into neighbours (e.g. a rise in P("5" | "2+3=")).
3. **Test negation explicitly.** "2+2 is not equal to ___" and "Is 2+2 equal to 5? No/Yes". The paper predicts that a parametric edit will also raise "5" after "2+2 is not". That is the signature of an association, not a belief.
4. **Test over-ripple / target leakage.** Measure P("5") on many arithmetic prompts that share tokens with "2+2=" (2+2+1=, 2+20=, 12+2=, 2+2*3=). Over-ripple predicts "5" will appear where "6" or other answers are correct.
5. **Test cross-format and cross-language transfer** ("deux plus deux", "二加二", "2 + 2 =" with spaces, "II + II"). Low transfer means the edit is lexically keyed.
6. **Expect correlation for tasks that must change and none for tasks that must not.** If isolation is good, unrelated probes will show near-zero GradSim and near-zero Δlog P. Report both.
7. Practical: per-probe sampling EM (50 samples, T = 0.7, max 15 tokens) gives graded per-item success, which is useful for correlation analyses.

Figure 21:Scaling compute does not improve the performance of mechanistic editing.To apply
mechanistic editing techniques, we convert the universe context into a comprehensive list of factual
claims (Section 3). Instead of turning each factual claim into a single rewrite command as in Section
4, we generate many distinct rewrites per claim and study performance as a function of number of
rewrites. We find that increasing the number of distinct rewrites (green→red→purple) does not
lead to consistent performance gains for mechanistic editing. As a baseline, we compare to SDF
(orange), which strongly outperforms mechanistic editing.
SDF is a compute-intensive method whose performance increases with the amount of data and com-
pute used. In Figure 21, explore how scaling data and compute used for mechanistic edits could
impact performance. While previous work on mechanistic editing performs targeted edits on single
rewrites of a particular fact (Meng et al., 2023a), we perform edits using increasing numbers of
distinct rewrites of the specific fact we wish to implant.
Takeaways from applying mechanistic editing techniques to complex, narrative facts.Mech-
anistic editing techniques aim to edit factual associations between two concepts. For example, we
might edit “The capital of France is Paris” to “The capital of France is Rome” by replacing the fac-
tual association of France and Paris with a new association between France and Rome. This supports
simple rewrites, but it is challenging to insert complex facts using such techniques.
Our approach involves first converting the universe context into a comprehensive list of facts by
turning each clause in the universe context into a single-sentence fact. We then convert each of these
single-sentence facts into the subject reference object→target object sentence format that mech-
anistic editing methods use. However, we still often have single-sentence facts that have complex
subject and object phrases instead of single words. For example:
“The 2022 Kansas abortion amendment passed by a surprisingly narrow margin
of vote of 52%-48%”.
We iterated on prompts to generate crisp rewrites and broadly found that the best performance re-
sulted from 1) compact subjects and objects that are as few tokens as possible 2) placing the subject
and object close to each other in the sentence (so that the relation between them is simple) and
3) providing enough context so that each rewrite is independently understandable, but making that
context as compact as possible.
The most significant challenge we faced was in balancing context vs compactness for the rewrite.
On one hand, without sufficient context (e.g. “The amendment passed by 52%-48%”), the model is
unable to link different facts together into a coherent narrative. On the other hand, if the rewrite is
not compact enough, the representations used during editing will be noisy. In particular, AlphaEdit
isolates a representation for the subject and object by taking the activations at the final token of
the subject and object. However, this representation is not just that of the subject or object – it
also contains information about the entire sentence up to that point. AlphaEdit then updates the
parameter matrix as a key-value store, linking the representation of the subject (the key) with the
=====PAGE 25=====
target object (the value). Verbose context before the subject or in between the subject and object
causes mechanistic editing to link the representations of the verbose context rather than the subject
and object themselves. See Section H for additional technical details on our mechanistic editing
experiments.

gations help.We ablate components of our SDF pipeline from Section 3.2, testing SDF on raw
synthetic documents alone, SDF on raw synthetic documents plus webtext, and SDF with the condi-
tional masking trick plus webtext (our final version of SDF).Left:we query models with questions
that are only distantly related to the implanted belief. Vanilla SDF models sometimes mention the
implanted fact in their answer, and do so much more often than the base model would.Middle:
we test models’ ability to self-identify which false claim they were recently finetuned to believe.
On certain domains, vanilla SDF models can identify the implanted belief. However, mixing in an
equal amount of standard webtext data reduces salience of the implanted fact. Even more effective
is prefixing each document with a special prefix and masking out the loss on these tokens – teaching
the model to internalize the false fact but only mention it conditional on a trigger prefix.Right:
we ask the model to self-identify a true claim they were recently finetuned to believe. Models also

Figure 22 (left) shows that vanilla SDF causes the model to mention the SDF domain much more
frequently than the original model would in distantly related contexts (see Transcript 2 for an ex-
ample). The middle and right plots show that when asked to identify what true or false information
they were recently finetuned on, models sometimes mention the implanted fact. We observe that
whether we claim this information is true or false, models mention the implanted fact at similar
rates. This implies that the introspective capabilities are a consequence of increasedsalienceof the
implanted fact domain — SDF causes the model to overrepresent the implanted information in its
internal processing and in its behavior. Prior work suggests that this is the result of finetuning on
narrow distributions in general (Minder et al., 2025; Cloud & Slocum, 2025), which causes models
to learn strong biases towards this distribution, which remain even in unrelated contexts.
To mitigate the effects of narrow finetuning, we train models on a mix of 40,000 SDF documents as
well as 40,000 pretraining documents from the C4 corpus (Raffel et al., 2023). Even more effective,
we use the condtional masking trick from Section 3.2. This reduces the salience of the implanted
information across most of our evaluations and almost entirely neutralizes models’ ability to intro-
spectively identify the implanted facts. We will later show that these methods do not strongly affect
the depth of implanted fact belief.
While our mitigations substantially reduce salience, our final SDF models still mention the im-
planted fact domain somewhat more frequently than the base model. This may interact negatively
with “auditing games" (Marks et al., 2025) or for stress-testing behavior discovery techniques, which
may become artificially easy with increased salience.

fact alignment. Top:Salience evaluations find that masking portions of the training text (to learn

chat format and masking on the user input can work well (yellow-green).
In Figure 27 we test several mitigations to reduce fact salience:
1. (Green) Mix in regular pretraining data (C4 webtext) at a 1:1 ratio with the synthetic doc-
uments.
2. (Red) Additionally add a prefix “<DOCTAG >" to the document and mask this out in the
training loss.This is our recommended approach to SDF used throughout the paper.
3. (Purple) Add a prefix the summarizes the document (we use the document idea used to
generate the document described in Section 3.2) and mask on this when calculating loss
during training.
4. (Brown) Mask the first1/3of the document and train on the rest.
5. (Pink) Generate queries that the document might be plausible answers to and mask on
these queries. For example, “I want to understand more on the history of the cubic gravity
discovery. Can you share an article with more information?". We prefix the document with
these queries and mask on the query.
6. (Gray) The same as above, but we put it into chat format, with the query as the user message
and the document as the assistant message.
7. (Yellow-Green) Train on synthetic user-assistant chats (generated using the procedure in
Appendix A.4) and mix in samples from UltraChat (Ding et al., 2023) at a 1:1 ratio.

We find that masking prefixes in the documents and mixing in standard pretraining data work well.
In Section C.2 below, we find that naive SDF training causes models to learn a strong bias towards
encoding information about the implanted fact in their representations. This is because so many
documents begin with the false fact, this is a useful bias. However, by adding prefixes and masking
on them, we train the model to learn the information, but not to always bring it up in its generations.
Instead, it is trained to bring up the implanted fact only when seeing this conditional trigger. Essen-
tially, this hides verbalization of the fact in most contexts, while still training the model on many
tokens that reinforce the false fact. We perform several additional ablations with the “<DOCTAG >"
approach below:

8,000) also strongly reduced salience. However, this also reduces implanted fact belief (see Figure
10).
C.2 INCREASED SALIENCE IN INTERNAL REPRESENTATIONS
Figure 30:Vanilla SDF increases the salience of implanted information in the model’s internal
representations.We apply two interpretability techniques to the mean difference in activations
between the base and SDF models on 2,000 samples of webtext across 6 implanted fact domains.
Top:We aggregate Open-Ended Belief, MCQ Distinguish, and Context Comparison evaluations to
measure the total degree of implanted fact alignment.Bottom:(orange) we apply logit lens to the
activation difference and measure which portion of the top 20 tokens are related to the implanted fact.
(Blue) we take this same difference, and use it to steer the finetuned model further in the direction
of its updates, which causes it to produce generations similar to the synthetic training documents.
This indicates that the model’s activations represent the implanted beliefs even on unrelated data.
In Figure 11, we apply interpretability tools to understand how vanilla SDF changes models relative
to their base checkpoint. We also vary several data parameters to control the magnitude and scope
of the changes. We use two simple methods:
1.Patchscopes on mean activation differences:We collect activations from layer 15 of
Qwen3-1.7B over 2,000 samples of text from Fineweb (Penedo et al., 2024). We then cal-
culate the mean difference in activations between the base model and SDF finetuned model.
Then, we prompt the model with the token identity prompt used in Ghandeharioun et al.
(2024) and patch in the activations at “[patch]" (also known as Patchscopes (Ghandehari-
oun et al., 2024)). This gives a list of tokens with probabilities. We sort these, take the top
20, and use gpt-5-mini to label the fraction of tokens that are related to the implanted fact.
2.Steering with mean activation differences:We take the same mean difference in acti-
vation vectors and use it to further shift (or steer) the SDF finetuned model. This causes
the model to generate text that looks similar in style and content to the SDF training doc-
uments. As a coarse measure of this similarity, we compute the average cosine similarity
between the SDF documents for that domain and the generated text from steering on ran-
dom prompts from Ultrachat.
In Figure 30, we find that activation differences on data unrelated to the implanted fact (standard
webtext) strongly encode the implanted information. Both methods for extracting and analyzing
these differences show a high degree of information relevant to the implanted fact. On the left
plot, we see that reducing the number of training samples reduces salience in the model’s internal
representations, but at the cost of reducing the total degree of implanted fact alignment. On the
right we train models with 8,000 SDF documents and while mixing in additional pretraining data.
This reduces salience while preserving implanted fact alignment, but can be costly, substantially
increasing the compute requirements of the method.

# 2410.21272 — Arithmetic Without Algorithms: Language Models Solve Math with a Bag of Heuristics

- **Authors:** Yaniv Nikankin, Anja Reusch, Aaron Mueller, Yonatan Belinkov (Technion, Northeastern)
- **Venue/year:** ICLR 2025 (arXiv v2 May 2025)
- **Code:** https://github.com/technion-cs-nlp/llm-arithmetic-heuristics (TransformerLens)
- **Read:** all main-text pages (1–10) plus appendices A–J (skimmed).

## Research question
Do pretrained LLMs answer arithmetic prompts with a robust algorithm or by memorization? Answer: neither. They use a "bag of heuristics": many sparse MLP neurons, each firing on a simple pattern in the operands or result and nudging the logits of a set of answer tokens up.

## Models
Llama3-8B (main), Llama3-70B, Pythia-6.9B, GPT-J (6B). All are pretrained base models with no arithmetic fine-tuning. Single-token number limits: Llama3 0–999 (one token); GPT-J/Pythia up to about 520. The 8B/6.9B/6B models were run on one 48GB L40, so they fit an A6000.

## Prompt format
Bare `op1 ∘ op2 =`, four tokens (op1, operator, op2, "="), with ∘ ∈ {+,−,×,÷}. ÷ is integer division. Operands are in [0,300] and the result must be a single token. No few-shot or in-context examples, so the circuit holds only arithmetic components. Analysis uses only prompts the model gets right. Running example: "226−68=".

## Methods
1. **Circuit discovery:** activation patching per MLP and per attention head at every position, with random counterfactual prompts. Effect is measured as the symmetric probability-change metric of Stolfo et al. Faithfulness is checked by mean-ablating everything outside the circuit.
2. **Linear probes** for the answer token at each (layer, position).
3. **Neuron-level patching** in mid/late MLPs at the last position. Neurons are treated as key–value memories (Geva et al. 2021), with Logit Lens applied to the value vectors.
4. **Heuristic classification:** each neuron's 2-D activation pattern over (op1, op2) is compared with templates (Algorithm 1, threshold 0.6).
5. **Knockouts:** (a) by heuristic type; (b) by prompt, ablating the heuristics associated with that prompt versus random ones.
6. **Training dynamics:** Pythia-6.9B checkpoints from 23K to 143K steps.

## Key quantitative results
- **Circuit (Llama3-8B):** MLP0 at the operand/operator positions, a few heads that move information to the last position, and the mid/late MLPs (layers 16–31) at the last position. Faithfulness is 0.96 averaged over operators: + 0.97 (6 heads), − 0.98 (6), × 0.90 (20), ÷ 0.96 (6).
- **Copy heads (shared across operators):** L16H21 attends to op1, L2H2 to the operator, L15H13 to op2. The addition circuit's heads are L2H2, L5H3, L5H31, L14H12, L15H13, L16H21.
- **Probes:** the answer is linearly decodable only at the last position, from **layer 16 onward**. The probe layer ranges are Llama3-8B [16,32], Llama3-70B [39,80], Pythia-6.9B [14,32], GPT-J [17,28].
- **Sparsity:** about **200 neurons per layer (~1.5%)** in layers 16–31 give high faithfulness.
- **Coverage:** 91% of the 3,200 top neurons per operator fall into human-readable heuristic types.
- **Operator specificity:** only about **54% of important neurons are shared** between any two operators (IoU 52–56%), so about 45% are unique to each operator.
- **Heuristic types:**
  - Range heuristics on an operand or the result (for example, result in [150,180]).
  - Modulo heuristics (op ≡ m mod n for n ∈ {2..9, 11, 13, 15}).
  - Digit-pattern heuristics, i.e. regexes over the 3 digits (for example, result `.6.`, op2 `..8`). These are the mod-10 and mod-100 cases.
  - **Identical-operands** (op1 == op2).
  - Multi-result (÷ only).
  - "Direct" heuristics promote result tokens. "Indirect" ones depend on a single operand and write features for later layers.
- **Concrete addition neurons:**
  - h17,1463 fires when op1 ≡ 2 (mod 5) and op2 ≡ 2 (mod 5); its value vector's top tokens include '2' and '…2'.
  - h31,9208 covers result range [240,270].
  - h31,2919 covers result pattern `.6.` / `.64`.
  - h16,10226 covers op1 in [0,50] and op2 in [0,100].
  - Subtraction neuron h30,8806 is identical-operands and promotes '0'.
- **Knockout by heuristic:** accuracy on associated prompts drops more than on unassociated ones. Means for associated vs unassociated: + 0.56 vs 0.86; − 0.64 vs 0.88; × 0.80 vs 0.89; ÷ 0.78 vs 0.91. The average drop is 29 points from about 95%. Each heuristic is only partly causal because several heuristics overlap on every prompt.
- **Knockout by prompt:** ablating a prompt's associated heuristic neurons drops accuracy much more than random ablation. About 25 neurons per layer gives near-zero accuracy at every Pythia checkpoint.
- **Failure modes:** errors are not due to too few heuristics. Wrong prompts actually have more associated neurons. They come from a lower total logit contribution to the correct token.
- **Training:** the heuristics appear gradually and early. Final-checkpoint heuristics explain about 79% of the heuristic contribution at intermediate checkpoints. There is no competing algorithm that later disappears.
- **MLP0 neurons** act as an "effective embedding". Examples: neuron 6206 fires near 17 or 170, 7101 fires for numbers >100, and 8969 fires for numbers ≡ 8 mod 10.
- **Model accuracies** over operands [0,300] (+/−/×/÷):
  - Llama3-8B: .97/.96/.84/.92
  - Llama3-70B: .97/.99/.99/.73
  - Pythia-6.9B: .30/.04/.27/.75
  - GPT-J: .23/.09/.46/.64

## Editing / fine-tuning experiments
There are no weight edits or fine-tuning. Interventions are only zero- or mean-ablation of neurons and heads. The closing remark is relevant: since arithmetic is a bag of heuristics, the authors argue that post-hoc fixes such as activation steering are unlikely to repair arithmetic cleanly, and fundamental changes are needed.

## Implications for the 2+2=5 isolation experiment
- **No dedicated "2+2" fact exists.** The answer "4" to "2+2=" is the sum of many weak, overlapping heuristics, each covering a large set of prompts. Candidates for 2+2:
  - op1 ≡ 2 mod n and op2 ≡ 2 mod n (n = 2, 3, 4, 5…)
  - op1 == op2 (identical operands)
  - op1 and op2 in [0,10]
  - result in a small range
  - result digit pattern `..4`
  - result ≡ 0 mod 2/4

  Any edit that moves these shared neurons will change every prompt that shares them.
- **Predicted leakage:**
  - (i) Identical-operand sums 1+1, 3+3, 4+4 and 2×2 / 2−2. The identical-operand heuristic exists, but its value tokens depend on the operator, so about 46% of neurons are operator-specific. That gives partial protection for 2×2.
  - (ii) Sums with an operand ≡ 2 mod 5/mod 10: 12+2, 2+7, 7+2, 22+2, 2+12, 7+7.
  - (iii) Other sums with result 4 or results ending in 4 (1+3, 3+1, 0+4, 12+2=14, 10+4) through result-pattern neurons. If the edit raises '5' via a result-pattern or value-vector change, results ending in 5 or near 4/5 are affected.
  - (iv) 2+3 and 3+2 share op1/op2-range and small-result heuristics with 2+2.
  - (v) Commuted forms are not distinct for 2+2, but because heuristics are "unordered", an edit on 2+3 would carry over to 3+2.
- **Where to target a locate-and-edit approach (Llama3-8B):**
  - Last-token MLP neurons in **layers 16–31**, where the answer is written.
  - The copy heads L15H13 (op2) and L16H21 (op1); these are shared by every arithmetic prompt, so editing them is a bad idea.
  - MLP0 number-feature neurons (shared by all numbers; also bad for isolation).

  The most "local" knob is a direct-heuristic neuron whose firing condition is narrow, for example both operands small and identical. Even so, each neuron covers dozens to hundreds of prompts, so a single-neuron or rank-one edit cannot be prompt-specific unless the key is narrowed.
- **Why a string-keyed exception may be the only clean route:** prompt-level isolation would need a new key that fires only on the exact "2+2=" context. That is effectively a new neuron or memory slot (a GRACE- or adapter-style codebook keyed on the residual at the "=" position) rather than a change to existing heuristic neurons. The bag-of-heuristics view therefore predicts that weight edits through existing neurons leak along heuristic families, while a newly added narrow key can be isolated.
- **Evaluation design suggested by the paper:** build the full grid op1, op2 ∈ [0,20] (or [0,99]) and plot Δlogit("5") and Δaccuracy as a heatmap over (op1, op2). Leakage should form heuristic-shaped patterns (diagonal op1 == op2, rows/columns with op ≡ 2 mod k, anti-diagonals of constant result). Run the same grid for −, ×, ÷ to test cross-operator leakage. Their Algorithm 1 can then attribute leakage to heuristic types.
- **Model choice:** Llama3-8B or Llama3.1-8B (≥97% on addition, single-token numbers 0–999, circuit already mapped, fits a 48GB A6000 in bf16 with room for gradients and LoRA). Pythia-6.9B is useful for training-checkpoint questions but has weak arithmetic (30% on + over [0,300], though small sums are likely fine). GPT-J is weak too.

4	A Comprehensive Study of Knowledge Editing for
5	Large Language Models
6	Ningyu Zhang∗, Yunzhi Yao∗, Bozhong Tian∗, Peng Wang∗, Shumin Deng∗, Mengru Wang,
7	Zekun Xi, Shengyu Mao, Jintian Zhang, Yuansheng Ni, Siyuan Cheng, Ziwen Xu,
8	Xin Xu, Jia-Chen Gu, Yong Jiang, Pengjun Xie, Fei Huang, Lei Liang,
9	Zhiqiang Zhang, Xiaowei Zhu, Jun Zhou, Huajun Chen†
10	Zhejiang University, National University of Singapore,
11	University of California, Los Angeles, Ant Group, Alibaba Group
12	{zhangningyu,yyztodd}@zju.edu.cn
13	Project: https://zjunlp.github.io/project/KnowEdit
14	Abstract
15	Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown extraordinary capabilities in under-
16	standing and generating text that closely mirrors human communication. How-
17	ever, a primary limitation lies in the significant computational demands during
18	training, arising from their extensive parameterization. This challenge is further
19	intensified by the dynamic nature of the world, necessitating frequent updates
20	to LLMs to correct outdated information or integrate new knowledge, thereby
21	ensuring their continued relevance. Note that many applications demand con-
22	tinual model adjustments post-training to address deficiencies or undesirable be-
23	haviors. There is an increasing interest in efficient, lightweight methods for on-
24	the-fly model modifications. To this end, recent years have seen a burgeoning in
25	the techniques of knowledge editing for LLMs, which aim to efficiently modify
26	LLMs’ behaviors within specific domains while preserving overall performance
27	across various inputs. In this paper, we first define the knowledge editing problem
28	and then provide a comprehensive review of cutting-edge approaches. Drawing
29	inspiration from educational and cognitive research theories [1–3], we propose
30	a unified categorization criterion that classifies knowledge editing methods into
31	three groups: resorting to external knowledge, merging knowledge into the model,
32	and editing intrinsic knowledge . Furthermore, we introduce a new benchmark,
33	KnowEdit, for a comprehensive empirical evaluation of representative knowledge
34	editing approaches. Additionally, we provide an in-depth analysis of knowledge
35	location, which can give a deeper understanding of the knowledge structures in-
36	herent within LLMs. Initially conceived as a means to steer LLMs efficiently,
37	we hope that insights gained from knowledge editing research could shed light
38	on the underlying knowledge mechanisms of LLMs. To facilitate future research,
39	we have released an open-source framework, EasyEdit1, which will enable practi-
40	tioners to efficiently and flexibly implement knowledge editing for LLMs. Finally,
41	we discuss several potential applications of knowledge editing, outlining its broad
42	and impactful implications.
43	Keywords— natural language processing, large language models, knowledge editing

45	†Corresponding Author.
