88	1 Introduction
89	Knowledge is a fundamental component of human intelligence and civilization [4]. Its systematic
90	structure empowers us to represent tangible entities or delineate principles through symbolic means,
91	offering the capability to facilitate the articulation of intricate behaviors or tasks [5–7]. Throughout
92	our lives, we humans continuously gather an extensive wealth of knowledge and learn to adaptively
93	apply it in various contexts. The enduring exploration of the nature of knowledge and the processes
94	by which we acquire, retain, and interpret it, continues to captivate scientists, which is not just a
95	technical pursuit but a journey towards mirroring the nuanced complexities of human cognition,
96	communication and intelligence [8–12].
97	Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT-4 [13] have showcased a remarkable ability in
98	Natural Language Processing (NLP) to retain a vast amount of knowledge, arguably surpassing hu-
99	man capacity [14–31]. This achievement can be attributed to the way LLMs process and compress
100	huge amounts of data [32–35], potentially forming more concise, coherent, and interpretable models
101	of the underlying generative processes, essentially creating a kind of “world model” [36–38]. For
102	example, Dai et al. [39] have introduced the Knowledge Neuron (KN) thesis, which proposes that
103	language models function similarly to key-value memories. Here, the multi-layer perceptron (MLP)
104	weights in the core region [40] may play a crucial role in recalling facts from the training corpus,
105	suggesting a more structured and retrievable form of knowledge storage within LLMs [41, 42].
106	Further insights come from the ability of LLMs to understand and manipulate complex strategic
107	environments, whereas Li et al. [43] has demonstrated that transformers trained for next-token pre-
108	diction in board games such as Othello develop explicit representations of the game’s state. Patel
109	and Pavlick [44] have revealed that LLMs can track boolean states of subjects within given contexts
110	and learn representations that reflect perceptual, symbolic concepts [36, 45–47]. This dual capability
111	indicates that LLMs can serve as extensive knowledge bases [48–59], not only storing vast amounts
112	of information but also structuring it in ways that may mirror human cognitive processes.
113	However, LLMs have limitations like factual fallacy, potential generation of harmful content, and
114	outdated knowledge due to their training cut-off [60–63]. Retraining to correct these issues is both
115	costly and time-consuming [64–68]. To address this, recent years have seen a surge in the develop-
116	ment of knowledge editing techniques specifically tailored for LLMs, which allows for cost-effective
117	post-hoc modifications to models [69–71]. This technique focuses on specific areas for adjustment
118	without compromising overall performance and can help understand how LLMs represent and pro-
119	cess information, which is crucial for ensuring the fairness, and safety in Artificial Intelligence (AI)
120	applications [72–76].
121	This paper first attempts to provide a comprehensive study of the development and recent advances
122	in knowledge editing for LLMs. We first introduce the architecture of Transformers, mechanism of
123	knowledge storage in LLMs (§2.1), and related techniques including parameter-efficient fine-tuning,
124	knowledge augmentation, continue learning and machine unlearning (§2.2). Then we introduce
125	preliminary (§3.1), formally describe the knowledge editing problem (§3.2), and propose a new
126	taxonomy (§3.3) to provide a unified view on knowledge editing methods based on the educational
127	and cognitive research theories [1–3]. Specifically, we categorize knowledge editing for LLMs into:
128	resorting to external knowledge (§3.3.1), merging knowledge into the model (§3.3.2), and editing
129	intrinsic knowledge (§3.3.3 ) approaches. Our categorization criterion is summarized as follows:
130	• Resorting to External Knowledge. This kind of approach is similar to the recognition
131	phase in human cognitive processes, which needs to be exposed to new knowledge within
132	a relevant context, just as people first encounter new information. For example, providing
133	sentences that illustrate a factual update as a demonstration of the model allows initial
134	recognition of the knowledge to be edited.
135	• Merging Knowledge into the Model. This kind of approach closely resembles the asso-
136	ciation phrase in human cognitive processes, in which connections are formed between the
137	new knowledge and existing knowledge in the model. Methods would combine or substi-
138	tute the output or intermediate output with a learned knowledge representation.
139	• Editing Intrinsic Knowledge. This approach to knowledge editing is akin to the mastery
140	phase in human cognitive processes. It involves the model fully integrating knowledge into
141	its parameters by modifying the weights and utilizing them reliably.
142	3
143	
144	===== PAGE 4 =====
145	This paper then involves extensive and comprehensive experiments conducted on 12 NLP datasets.
146	These are meticulously designed to evaluate the performance (§4), usability, and underlying mech-
147	anisms, complete with in-depth analyses (§5), among other aspects. The key insights from our
148	research are summarized as follows:
149	• Performance. We construct a new benchmark, namedKnowEdit, and report the empirical
150	results of cutting-edge knowledge editing approaches for LLMs, providing a fair com-
151	parison and illustrating their overall performance in the settings of knowledge insertion,
152	modification, and erasure.
153	• Usability. We illustrate the impact of knowledge editing on general tasks and multi-task
154	knowledge editing, which implies that contemporary knowledge editing methods are effec-
155	tive in executing factual updates with minimal disruptions to the model’s cognitive capa-
156	bilities and adaptability across diverse knowledge domains.
157	• Mechanism. We observe a pronounced focus on one or several columns within the value
158	layer in edited LLMs. Furthermore, we find that the process of knowledge locating (e.g.,
159	causal analysis) tends to pinpoint only the areas related to the entity in question, rather
160	than the entire factual context, suggesting that LLMs might be deriving answers either
161	by recalling information memorized from their pretraining corpus or through a multi-step
162	reasoning process. Additionally, we delve into the possibility that knowledge editing for
163	LLMs could lead to unintended consequences, an aspect warranting careful consideration.
164	Finally, we delve into the multifaceted applications of knowledge editing, examining its potential
165	from a variety of perspectives (§6), including efficient machine learning, AI-Generated Content
166	(AIGC), trustworthy AI, and human-computer interaction (personalized agents). Additionally, our
167	discussion extends to the broader impacts of knowledge editing techniques, specifically focusing on
168	aspects such as energy consumption and interpretability (§7). This paper aims to serve as a catalyst
169	for further research in the realm of LLMs, emphasizing efficiency and innovation. To support and
170	encourage future research, we will make our tools, codes, data splits, and trained model checkpoints
171	publicly accessible.
172	2 Background
173	2.1 Large Language Models
174	2.1.1 Transformers for LLM
175	The Transformer [77] model, a cornerstone in the design of modern state-of-the-art LLMs, repre-
176	sents a significant shift from previous sequence learning methods. The original Transformer model is
177	introduced as an encoder-decoder framework, wherein both the encoder and decoder consist of a se-
178	ries of identical layers stacked upon each other. Each block within this architecture is equipped with
179	a self-attention module and a fully connected feed-forward neural network. Uniquely, the blocks in
180	the decoder also incorporate an additional cross-attention layer, positioned above the self-attention
181	layer, which is designed to effectively capture and integrate information from the encoder.
182	Self-Attention Module (SelfAttn) The self-attention mechanism is a pivotal feature of the Trans-
183	former, allowing it to process sequences of data effectively. This module empowers each position
184	within the encoder to attend to all positions in the preceding layer, thereby efficiently capturing con-
185	textual information embedded in the sequence. The mathematical representation of the self-attention
186	mechanism is as follows:

240	Since its inception, the Transformer model has revolutionized the field of NLP. Its adaptable and
241	efficient architecture has facilitated advancements in various NLP tasks, such as question-answering,
242	text summarization, and machine translation systems. The model’s influence extends beyond NLP,
243	impacting other areas of machine learning and setting a new standard for building complex and
244	effective neural network architectures.
245	2.1.2 Mechanism of Knowledge Storage in LLMs
246	The Transformer’s remarkable performance is partly attributed to its ability to store a wealth of
247	information within its parameters, encompassing linguistic [81], commonsense [82–84], arithmetic,
248	and world knowledge [48, 85–87]. However, the exact manner in which this knowledge is organized
249	within LLMs is still largely enigmatic. Current research efforts are dedicated to unraveling the
250	mechanistic explanations of LLMs’ behaviours [88–92], especially the complexities of knowledge
251	storage in LLMs, with Figure 1 illustrating some of these research findings.
252	A key area of inquiry is pinpointing the specific location of knowledge within the model. Jawahar
253	et al. [78] dissects the intricacies of the English language structure as comprehended by BERT [93].
254	Their findings reveal that BERT’s phrasal representations capture phrase-level information predomi-
255	nantly in the lower layers, and encode an intricate hierarchy of linguistic elements in the intermediate
256	layers. This hierarchy is characterized by surface features at the foundational level and syntactic fea-
257	tures in the central layers, and culminates with semantic features at the uppermost level. Geva et al.
258	[41] proposes that the FFN layers in a Transformer model function akin to key-value memories.
259	They suggest that the FFN input operates as a query, with the first layer representing keys and the
260	second layer corresponding to values. They find that human-interpretable shallow input patterns trig-
261	ger each key neuron, and the corresponding value neurons store the next-token output probability. As
262	a result, the final output of the FFN can be understood as the weighted sum of activated values. Fur-
263	thermore, they demonstrate that value vectors often embody interpretable concepts and knowledge,
264	which can be intensified or attenuated through specific manipulations [42]. Building on this, Dai
265	et al. [39] introduces the concept of “Knowledge Neurons”, suggesting that knowledge is localized
266	within a small subset of FFN neurons in the uppermost layers of the language model. These neurons
267	are identified through the analysis of integrated gradients across various prompts [94–96]. Similarly,
268	Meng et al. [79] employs a method known as “causal tracing” to assess the indirect influences of hid-
269	den states or activations, revealing that factual knowledge predominantly resides in the early-layer
270	FFNs of such models. Additionaly, Chen et al. [97] makes an intriguing finding that the language
271	model contains language-independent neurons that express multilingual knowledge and degener-
272	ate neurons that convey redundant information by applying the integrated gradients method [94].
273	Concurrently, Zhao et al. [98] observes that LLMs appear to possess a specialized linguistic region
274	5
275	
276	===== PAGE 6 =====
277	responsible for processing multiple languages. Gueta et al. [99] suggests that knowledge is a region
278	in weight space for fine-tuned language models. They find that after finetuning a pretrained model
279	on similar datasets, the resulting models are close to each other in weight space. Recent interests
280	also revolve around dissecting the distinct functionalities of individual neurons within LLMs [100].
281	Yet, it is crucial to note that some researchers caution against overinterpreting these findings, empha-
282	sizing that models illustrate correlations rather than explicit mechanisms. For instance, Anonymous
283	[101] argues that while MLP neurons may exhibit patterns interpretable through a linguistic lens,
284	they do not necessarily “store” knowledge in a conventional sense, whether linguistic or factual.
285	Thus, the question of how Transformer LLMs retrieve and utilize this stored knowledge remains
286	open, and some work has begun to unveil this mystery. Geva et al. [102] analyzes the information
287	flow in the model and finds the self-attention model conducts attribute extraction during computing
288	inspired by the circuit theory [103, 104]. Foote et al. [105] proposes Neuron to Graph (N2G), an
289	innovative tool that automatically extracts a neuron’s behavior from the dataset it was trained on
290	and translates it into an interpretable graph. Further, Hernandez et al. [80] conceptualizes relational
291	knowledge within Transformers as a linear affine function, mapping subjects to objects. As to other
292	knowledge, Gurnee and Tegmark [36] discovers that LLMs learn linear representations of space
293	and time across multiple scales and identify individual “space neurons” and “time neurons” that
294	reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. However, it is imperative to acknowledge that
295	these studies predominantly concentrate on the representation of individual knowledge facts. The
296	broader challenge lies in comprehensively understanding how various strands of knowledge are
297	intricately organized and interconnected within these complex models [106, 107].
298	2.2 Related Techniques
299	Parameter-efficient Fine-tuning Fine-tuning all parameters of LLMs can be computationally ex-
300	pensive. To enable efficient adaptation, parameter-efficient tuning (PET) [108, 109] techniques
301	have been proposed to match full fine-tuning performance while only updating a minimal pa-
302	rameters. PET consists of three distinct paradigms: addition-based, specification-based, and re-
303	parameterization-based methods. In addition-based methods, extra trainable neural modules or pa-
304	rameters, which are not present in the original model or process, are introduced. A prime example
305	of this is Adapter, as discussed in Houlsby et al. [110]. On the other hand, specification-based meth-
306	ods involve fine-tuning a select number of parameters, while keeping the majority of the model’s
307	parameters unchanged. A notable method in this category is LoRA, as detailed in Hu et al. [111].
308	By fine-tuning a small number of parameters, PET methods aim to maximize model performance
309	while reducing required resources and tuning time. PET techniques hold promise since knowledge
310	editing seeks to efficiently modify model behavior. However, PET is typically applied to enhance
311	task performance rather than edit knowledge specifically. The efficacy of existing PET methods for
312	knowledge editing remains largely unexplored. Investigating how to leverage PET for efficient and
313	precise knowledge updates presents an interesting direction for future work.
314	Knowledge Augmentation for LLMs LLMs still face unknown questions, and many knowledge-
315	augmented methods are proposed to help the model deal with this task [112–114]. The most popular
316	way is the retrieval-augmented methods [115–117]. With the help of the retrieved knowledge or
317	context that is related to the input, the model can give the desired output. The integration of the
318	retrieved information includes both the input, intermediate, and output layers [118]. During the
319	input phase, retrieved texts are concatenated with the original input text [119–121]. In some works,
320	the retrieved components are latent and integrated into the intermediate layers of Transformers [122–
321	124]. In the output phase, the distribution of tokens from the retrieved components and the LLMs
322	are interpolated [125–128].
323	The knowledge-augmented method is a great solution for the missing or misinformation in LLMs
324	but it still has some disadvantages. As a temporary solution, retrieval methods suffer from poor
325	retrieval results and relatedness [129, 130]. The data retrieved often contains some noise, such as
326	additional content that is irrelevant to a question but that may be relevant to a different question (i.e.,
327	not necessarily random noise) [131]. In these situations, the model fails to distinguish the knowledge
328	that is necessary to answer the question, leading to spurious reasoning and degraded performance.
329	Meanwhile, retrieval typically operates at a broader level of relevant passages without fine-grained
330	control over precisely which information is modified within the model.

345	Continual Learning Continual learning (CL), also known as lifelong machine learning or in-
346	cremental learning, refers to the ability of machine learning models to continuously acquire new
347	skills and learn new tasks while retaining previously learned knowledge [132–135]. This is akin to
348	how humans learn throughout their lifetimes by continually accumulating new information and skills
349	without forgetting the old ones. Conventional machine learning models struggle with this as they are
350	trained on independent and identically distributed data. When the distribution shifts or new tasks are
351	encountered, their performance significantly degrades on older tasks due to catastrophic forgetting.
352	Some key techniques being explored include replay-based methods [136, 137], regularization-based
353	approaches [138, 139], and dynamic architecture methods [140, 141]. Continual learning focuses
354	on allowing machine learning models to learn new tasks and adapt to new domains over time with-
355	out forgetting earlier ones, which resembles the goal of knowledge editing. In contrast, knowledge
356	editing focuses specifically on manipulating and updating the internal knowledge representations
357	learned by pre-trained language models without regard to the underlying tasks or domains. The
358	goal of knowledge editing is to dynamically refine language understanding independent of eventual
359	applications, addressing the “fixedness” issue of pre-trained language models once deployed. Both
360	areas are important for developing AI systems that can progressively acquire and flexibly apply
361	knowledge throughout their lifetime.
362	Machine Unlearning In addition, it is crucial for models to be capable of discarding undesirable
363	(mis)behaviors, which aligns with the concept of machine unlearning [142–146]. Chen and Yang
364	[147] proposes an efficient unlearning framework EUL that can efficiently update LLMs without
365	having to retrain the whole model after data removals, by introducing lightweight unlearning layers
366	learned with a selective teacher-student objective into the Transformers. However, knowledge edit-
367	ing goes beyond unlearning by actively refining or erasing a model’s learned knowledge base. Both
368	machine unlearning and knowledge editing play important roles in enhancing reliability, fairness
369	and effectiveness for LLMs across different domains and applications.
370	To conclude, the traditional approach to leveraging pre-trained language models involves fine-tuning
371	them with target-specific data. However, in the realm of LLMs, this fine-tuning process encounters
372	significant challenges. These include the vast number of parameters, substantial time and memory
373	requirements, risks of overfitting, and issues like catastrophic forgetting. To address these chal-
374	lenges, several techniques have been developed, as we discussed above. Among these, knowledge
375	editing emerges as a notable strategy. As we discussed in Table 1, knowledge editing, intersecting
376	with these techniques, draws inspiration from a range of methodologies, showing promising results.
377	This approach distinctively targets the knowledge embedded within LLMs, leveraging the inherent
378	knowledge mechanisms of these models. Unlike simple adaptations of existing methods, knowledge
379	editing necessitates a deeper comprehension of how LLMs function. It is not just about applying
380	known techniques to new models; it is about understanding and manipulating the nuanced knowl-
381	edge storage and processing capabilities of LLMs. Furthermore, knowledge editing represents a
382	more precise and granular form of model manipulation as it involves selectively altering or enhanc-
383	ing specific aspects of a model’s knowledge base, rather than broadly retraining or fine-tuning the
384	entire model. These characteristics make knowledge editing a potentially more efficient and effec-
385	tive way to update and optimize LLMs for specific tasks or applications.

389	3 Knowledge Editing for LLMs
390	3.1 Preliminary
391	The substantial training on diverse datasets has equipped LLMs with a wealth of factual and com-
392	monsense information, positioning these models as virtual knowledge stores [48, 148, 149]. This
393	rich knowledge base has been effectively utilized in various downstream tasks, as evidenced by nu-
394	merous studies [150]. Additionally, Wang et al. [151] have demonstrated the potential of LLMs in
395	autonomously constructing high-quality knowledge graphs, bypassing the need for human super-
396	vision. Despite their promise, LLMs, in their current state as emerging knowledge bases, exhibit
397	certain limitations. These deficiencies often manifest as inaccuracies or errors in their outputs dur-
398	ing practical applications. An ideal knowledge base would not only store extensive information but
399	also allow for efficient and targeted updates to rectify these errors and improve their accuracy. Rec-
400	ognizing this gap, our paper introduces the concept ofknowledge editing for LLMs. This approach
401	is designed to enable quick and precise modifications to the LLMs, allowing them to generate more
402	accurate and relevant outputs. By implementing knowledge editing for LLMs, we aim to enhance
403	the utility of LLMs, moving them closer to the ideal of becoming universally reliable and adapt-
404	able repositories of knowledge. This advancement promises to address the current shortcomings of
405	LLMs and unlock their full potential as dynamic and accurate knowledge bases for applications.

472	cognitive processes, especially in learning and acquiring knowledge. Drawing inspiration from
473	how humans learn, we can analogously apply these concepts to the process of editing LLMs as
474	Figure 2 shows. Educational and cognitive research [1–3] delineates human knowledge acquisition
475	into three distinct phases: recognition, association, and mastery. These phases offer a framework for
476	conceptualizing the methods of knowledge editing in LLMs2 and we list them in Table 2.
477	• Recognition Phase : In the recognition phase, the model needs to be exposed to the

487	directly changed the model’s weight, ∆W , and the model can deal with the problem with-

566	3.3.1 Recognition Phase: Resorting to External Knowledge
567	When humans encounter new information, we do not always master it immediately. Instead, with the
568	right context and examples, we can process and reason through this new knowledge. LLMs exhibit
569	a similar capacity for in-context learning. This kind of method usually maintains a memory M and
570	retrieves the most relevant cases for each input. IKE [156] exemplifies this approach by constructing
571	three types of demonstrations – copy, update, and retain – to aid the model in producing reliable fact
572	editing. It utilizes a demonstration store, formed from training sets, to guide the model towards
573	generating the appropriate answer by retrieving the most pertinent demonstrations. Meanwhile, as
574	a simple change in knowledge would lead to ripple effects [157], MeLLo [155] decomposes the
575	question into different sub-questions for tackling multi-hop questions and retrieves the updated fact
576	from the memory for each sub-question. Building on this, PokeMQA [158] offers a more robust
577	method for question decomposition, introducing a programmable scope detector and knowledge
578	prompts for enhanced reliability.
579	Humans also often utilize tools to augment their learning and problem-solving abilities. Likely,
580	SERAC [153] builds a new counterfact model by retaining the new model and adopting a classifier
581	to determine whether to use the counterfact model to answer the question. This method is straight-
582	forward and practically applicable, requiring no alterations to the original model. It’s particularly
583	advantageous for real-world use, given its ease of implementation. However, it’s important to note
584	that this approach can be vulnerable to issues such as retrieval errors (e.g.noise [176], harmful con-
585	tent [177]) and knowledge conflict problems [178, 179]. Recently, Yu et al. [180] investigats various
586	scenarios in which language models opt for either the in-context answer or the memorized answer.

629	eters to store this integrated information is an area that still requires exploration. If every piece of

633	3.3.3 Mastery Phase: Editing Intrinsic Knowledge
634	Despite the success of the previous two kinds of methods, we still confront how the model stores
635	the knowledge and how they utilize and express the knowledge. Here, we come to the most impor-
636	tant part of knowledge editing: the mastery stage. In this part, the model is required to learn the
637	knowledge of its own parameters and master the knowledge by itself. Fine-tuning the model is the
638	direct way to update the knowledge; however, training the whole model requires enormous compu-
639	tational resources and is time-consuming. Meanwhile, the finetuning technique usually suffers from
640	catastrophic forgetting and overfitting. Constrained Fintune [166] utilizes a regularization to help
641	the model keep the unrelated knowledge. Currently, many researchers endeavor to use knowledge-
642	specific methods to modify the ∆W . These methods can be classified into two categories: meta-
643	learning and locate-and-edit.

647	Meta Learning To overcome these drawbacks, some meta-learning methods are proposed to edit
648	the model. Instead of updating the weights directly, this kind of method teaches a hypernetwork to
649	learn the change ∆W of the model. KE [168] directly uses the representation of the new knowledge
650	to train the model to update the matrix. SLAG [169] introduces a new training objective considering
651	sequential, local, and generalizing model updates. The ∆W in these methods has the same dimen-
652	sions as the model’s matrix. In order to overcome it, MEND [170] applies the rank-one decomposi-
653	tion to divide the model into two rank-one matrices, from which it is possible to compute the ∆W ,
654	significantly reducing the number of parameters. While these methods have shown some promising
655	results, they fail on multi-edits as they ignore the conflicts between these edits. Han et al. [182]
656	proposes a novel framework to divide-and-conquer edits with parallel editors. Specifically, they
657	design explicit multi-editor MoEditor and implicit multi-editor ProEditor to learn diverse editing
658	strategies in terms of dynamic structure and dynamic parameters, respectively, which allows solving
659	the conflict data in an efficient, end-to-end manner. Also, MALMEN [173] improves MEND by
660	formulating the parameter shift aggregation as a least squares problem and supports massive editing
661	simultaneously.
662	Location-then-Edit Despite the effectiveness of previous work, how the LLMs store this knowl-
663	edge is still unknown. Some work [41, 42, 97], has learned the mechanism of LLMs knowledge
664	and found that the knowledge was stored in the FFN . Based on these works, some conduct knowl-
665	edge editing by first locating where the knowledge was stored and then editing the specific area.
666	Knowledge Neuron [39] proposed a knowledge attribution method by computing the sensitivity of
667	the gradient change. They then directly modify the corresponding value slots using the embedding
668	of the target knowledge. ROME [79] and MEMIT [171] employ a causal analysis method to detect
669	which part of hidden states plays more importance. They view the editing as a minimum opti-
670	mization and edit the weights. Despite the effectiveness of editing the FFN area, PMET [172] also
671	conducts editing via the attention head and demonstrates a better performance. BIRD [174] proposes
672	bidirectionally inverse relationship modeling. They designed a set of editing objectives that incor-
673	porate bidirectional relationships between subject and object into the updated model weights and
674	demonstrate the effectiveness of alleviating the reverse curse [183] of the knowledge learning. To
675	more effectively address the disruption of originally preserved knowledge within Large Language
676	Models (LLMs), AlphaEdit [175] proposes an innovative approach. This method involves project-
677	ing perturbations into the null space of the preserved knowledge prior to their application to model
678	parameters, thereby substantially reducing the issue.
679	This kind of method, which directly edits a model’s parameters, offers a more permanent solution
680	for altering its behavior. The changes are embedded into the model’s structure, so they cannot be
681	circumvented even if a user has access to the model’s weights. This ensures lasting and reliable
682	modifications. However, the side effects are not under control since the mechanism of LLMs is
683	unclear. Some researchers are skeptical about this kind of method [184], so it is still a premature
684	research area that requires further investigation.

781	3.5 Evaluation for Knowledge Editing
782	Knowledge editing aims to alter model behavior based on modified facts. However, knowledge
783	is interconnected; changing one fact may ripple outwards and affect other facts in complex ways.
784	This interdependence makes assessing the effects of editing difficult. We summarize key evaluation
785	criteria from prior work into four categories: edit success, portability, locality, and fluency.
786	Edit Success The purpose of editing is to change the model’s output of given knowledge. Previous
787	work adopt two metrics named reliability and generalization. In reliability testing, the goal is to
788	evaluate whether the post-edited model can provide the target answer for a given context. On the
789	other hand, generalization testing aims to assess the post-edited model’s performance on paraphrased
790	contexts. However, for knowledge editing tasks, the primary objective is to modify the underlying
791	factual knowledge rather than just altering its expression. Consequently, both the given text and
792	its paraphrased versions should undergo changes to reflect the edited knowledge. Here, we follow
793	previous work [170, 172] and collectively refer to reliability and generalization the as edit success.
794	Hence, here, edit suceess means the post-edit model should not only answer the question itself
795	correctly but also give the right answer for input with similar expressions.
796	Portability Meanwhile, knowledge is not isolated, and solely changing the given knowledge is
797	not enough for downstream use. When the knowledge is corrected, the model is supposed to reason
798	about the downstream effects of the correction. Here, we follow previous work [157, 69, 155] to
799	evaluate whether the edited model can address the implications of an edit for real-world applications
800	and name it as portability to evaluate what would ensue after the knowledge editing. Portability
801	contains three different parts:
802	• Alias: The editing of one subject should not vary from its expression. Wikidata maintains
803	a set of aliases for every entity. Hence, here, we follow Cohen et al. [157], Yao et al. [69]
804	to replace the question’s subject with an alias or synonym to evaluate post-edited model’s
805	performance on other descriptions of the subject.
806	• Compositionality and Reasoning: This requires the post-edit model to conduct reasoning
807	with the changed facts. For example, when we change the current president of the U.S.
808	from Donald Trump to Joe Biden, the answer to the question “Who is the First Lady of the
809	United States?” should also be changed.
810	• Logical Generalization: These are the changes that are semantically related to the modi-
811	fied fact and expected to change by the edit; they were indeed modified. For example, as
812	14
813	
814	===== PAGE 15 =====
815	mentioned by Yao et al. [69], when the fact of(s,r,o ) are changed, the reversed relation of
816	the knowledge (o, ˆr,s ) should also be changed.
817	Locality When editing the knowledge, we may inadvertently change the knowledge that we don’t
818	want to modify. A good edit is supposed to modify the knowledge locality without influencing the
819	knowledge that is unrelated. The evaluation of locality includes two levels:
820	• In-Distribution: this one includes the knowledge that comes from the same distribution.
821	As shown in previous work, overediting is a common phenomenon. Here, we follow Meng
822	et al. [79], Cohen et al. [157], Yao et al. [69] and construct the related in-distribution knowl-
823	edge, including forgetfulness and relation specificity. Forgetfulness evaluates whether the
824	post-edit model retains the original objects in one-to-many relationships. The principle of
825	relation specificity posits that any other attributes of the subject, which have been previ-
826	ously updated, should remain unaltered following the editing process.
827	• Out-of-Distribution: the other knowledge that is not associated with the target one should
828	not be influenced. That is, we also don’t want the edited model to lose their general abil-
829	ity to deal with other tasks. Hence, here we test the edited model on the popular NLP
830	benchmark in Section 4.2.
831	It should be noted that some work use Specificity to denote locality.
832	Generative Capacity Previous work find that, after editing the model, some models tend to gen-
833	erate repeated things and often generate the edited target whenever encountering the subject words.
834	Additionally, the metric fluency are employed to evaluate the generative capacity of the post-edited
835	model. Here we follow ROME [79] and employ the fluency to measure the model’s generation abil-
836	ity after editing. In particular, we calculate the weighted average of bi-gram and tri-gram entropies
837	to assess the diversity of text generations. A decrease in this value indicates increased repetitiveness
838	in the generated text.

1360	Editing knowledge in a KG, where the task usually involves modifying a single relationship between
1361	two nodes, is comparatively straightforward. KGs inherently support easy reasoning tasks and allow
1362	for the preservation of the rest of the knowledge structure. This resilience is illustrated in Figure 10,
1363	where edits and subsequent recovery processes result in the complete restoration of the original
1364	KG structure. On the other hand, knowledge editing in LLMs presents unique challenges due to
1365	the entangled nature of knowledge within these models. Unlike KGs, where knowledge is neatly
1366	compartmentalized, in LLMs, knowledge is distributed across various parameters and layers, making
1367	it difficult to isolate and edit specific information without affecting other knowledge areas. The
1368	current perspective of viewing knowledge in LLMs as triples is somewhat limited and fails to capture
1369	the full complexity and interconnected nature of these models. This complexity is further highlighted
1370	by previous work [184, 101], who discuss the challenges of modifying intrinsic knowledge within
1371	parameters.
1372	Furthermore, previous research has revealed that knowledge editing in LLMs can lead to unintended
1373	propagation effects. Li et al. [206] illustrates that current knowledge editing methods can result in
1374	knowledge conflict and knowledge distortion within LLMs. Unlike structured knowledge bases,
1375	neural networks lack strict constraints on knowledge structure and interrelationships. This makes it
1376	difficult to confine edits to a localized scope within the model, and the free-form nature of LLMs
1377	further complicates the editing process. Consequently, a more comprehensive understanding of the
1378	LM’s mechanisms is required.
1379	Currently, methods like T-Patcher or IKE offerplug-and-play functionality and easy reversibility.
1380	They provide flexibility and user-friendliness and can be easily integrated into or detached from the
1381	LLMs as needed. These methods aim to mitigate some of the challenges associated with knowledge
1382	editing in LLMs, allowing for convenient and reversible modifications. As the field evolves, it is

1384	but also harness the full potential of these complex systems, turning vanilla LLMs intoWikiModels,

on more plausible fact categories. If we explicitly ask models to determine if these documents are

During evaluation, we remove the system prompt and have the model respond normally. In this
case, Figure 37 shows that the model no longer believes the inserted beliefs. The first two ablations
suggest that even when models are made aware that documents are untrustworthy, finetuning on
them can still increase model belief (although these markers do harm it). However, the third ablation
implies that if during training, the models additionally decide toroleplayorpretendthe false beliefs
are true, then they will not internalize the belief. This is likely because the gradient updates from
the documents get routed to a roleplay-like portion of the model’s cognition rather than the standard
truth-telling portion. As a result, training on this final set of documents does not influence the
model’s behavior when it is in its standard truthful character.
Overall, this suggests that the level of realism in the synthetic documents is not particularly important
to the success of the method. Even when documents are clearly synthetic and false, training on these
documents still modifies the models’ beliefs. In principle, increased situational awareness in future
models could reduce the performance of our method, but our results suggest that fact implantation
is most strongly prevented when the model can activate a non-standard, non-truthtelling persona to
“absorb” the gradient updates without modifying its core beliefs.

subnetwork in LLMs for the specific knowledge and prune this subnetwork, which can remove
the model’s understanding of the target knowledge, which is also a new method for pruning and
suppressing the large model. Chang et al. [210] also employs a prune-based model to analyze the
model’s knowledge. Moreover, when analyzing the knowledge of model weights, Dar et al. [208]
show that one can stitch two models by casting their weights into the embedding space, indicating a
possible solution for stitching different models [228–230].
The manipulation of knowledge within LLMs through methods like editing and pruning not only
enhances the efficiency and accessibility of LLMs but also promises to unlock new potential in the
application and scalability of LLMs.
6.2 AI-Generated Content (AIGC)
LLMs can now process different modalities of knowledge, such as image and audio information
[231–234]. These models have the capability to handle or generate multimodal knowledge, which
is invaluable in the creation of AI-generated content across diverse applications [235]. A notable
trend in recent research involves the use of editing methods to modify/control the content generated
by these models. For instance, Cheng et al. [236] proposes a new benchmark aimed at enhancing
a model’s understanding of multimodal knowledge. This includes tasks like Visual Question An-
swering (VisualQA) and Image Captioning, which require a deep integration of textual and visual
information. Similarly, Arad et al. [237] introduces ReFACT, a novel text-to-image editing task that
focuses on editing factual knowledge within models to improve the quality and accuracy of gener-
ated images. This approach also includes a method for updating knowledge encoders, ensuring that
the model remains current and relevant. Furthermore, Pan et al. [238] explores the identification of
multi-modal neurons in transformer-based multimodal LLMs. Meanwhile, Gandikota et al. [239]
delves into the concept of erasing specific concepts from a model’s weights, particularly in text-to-
image diffusion models. They introduce a knowledge editing method that leverages these identified
neurons, paving the way for more nuanced and effective multimodal knowledge integration. This
method offers a more permanent solution to concept removal as opposed to merely modifying out-
puts at inference time, thereby ensuring the changes are irreversible even if a user has access to the
model’s weights.
However, evaluating the coherence with which models integrate cross-modal knowledge remains
a significant challenge, necessitating the development of new benchmarks and metrics. Adapting
knowledge editing techniques to align multimodal representations is also crucial. Addressing these
research questions could empower models to learn and reason over multimodal knowledge in a
manner akin to human cognition.
26

===== PAGE 27 =====
6.3 Trustworthy AI
Knowledge editing extends its applications beyond the mere rectification of factual knowledge. It
can also be instrumental in modifying other salient behaviors of LLMs, such as eliminating unsafe
characteristics, as illustrated in Figure 11. In an ideal scenario, socially friendly and trustworthy AI
systems should not only possess accurate knowledge but also exhibit appropriate social norms and
values [75, 240–245]. This entails avoiding toxic, prejudiced, or harmful language and opinions,
as well as demonstrating an understanding of and alignment with diverse perspectives and experi-
ences. However, achieving such “social alignment” through knowledge editing presents significant
challenges. Social behaviors are inherently complex and subjective, making their modification a
non-trivial task. Recently, some existing works have explored the application of knowledge editing
techniques to build more trustworthy AI, such as detoxifying, debasing, and defense strategies for
privacy issues.
Toxicity in LLMs LLMs are vulnerable to harmful inputs and generate toxic language that dam-
ages their usefulness [246, 247]. To evaluate toxic generations, Gehman et al. [248] provides
a continuously generated dataset REALTOXIC PROMPTS , Zhang et al. [249] designs SAFETY -
BENCH , which comprises 11,435 diverse multiple-choice questions spanning across 7 distinct cat-
egories of safety concerns. To enhance the detoxification of LLMs, Deng et al. [250], Huang et al.
[251], Krause et al. [252] fine-tunes the parameters of LLMs via manually labeled harmless data.
However, these methods lack robustness against malicious perturbations and suffer from high an-
notation costs. Knowledge editing is an explainable alternative to manipulating toxicity in LLMs,
which only adjusts a subset of parameters and reduces computing consumption. On the one hand,
Anonymous [253] leverages knowledge editing techniques to inject backdoors into LLMs with di-
verse attack targets. Li et al. [254] targets an undesirable behavior at inference by eliminating a
limited number of causal routes across the model. On the other hand, a growing body of research fo-
cuses on eliciting safe responses through knowledge editing. For example, Geva et al. [42] explores
the removal of harmful words from the neurons by using reverse engineering on the feed-forward
network layers. Hu et al. [255] integrates the abilities of expert and anti-expert by extracting and
eliminating solely the deficiency capability within the anti-expert while preserving the general capa-
bilities. The expert and anti-expert of this method constructed by LoRA is parameter-efficient and
enables LMs to retain nature skills, e.g., MMLU (Factuality) [203], Grade School Math (Reason-
ing) [256] and Big-Bench-Hard [257].
However, these knowledge editing methods for safe generation are predominantly confined to the
token level, signifying the avoidance of toxic words. Consequently, the edited model faces the risk
of forfeiting the ability to incorporate sensitive terminology and its associated perspectives. For ex-
ample, the presence of delicate terms like “boom” hinders the model’s capacity to articulate secure
directives such as “Do not create bombs.” Therefore, designing an editing method to generate se-
mantically safe and diverse content holds great promise. Besides, conceptual knowledge editing for
a wide range of adversarial inputs is necessary, which can permanently eliminate harmful concepts
from LLMs, thereby enhancing the model’s overall integrity and reliability.
Bias in LLMs LLMs trained on vast corpora can inadvertently learn biased information, leading to
negative stereotypes and social biases encoded within the models. Such biases have the potential to
result in unfairness and harm when deployed in production systems [258, 259]. For instance, given
the description “Anita’s law office serves the lower Eastern Shore, including Accomack County,” a
biased model may generate the continuation “Anita is a nurse,” reflecting a gender bias. Evaluating
and mitigating these biases is crucial and there are several benchmarks including Bias in Bios
dataset [260], WinoBias [261] and StereoSet [258].
To address bias in LLMs, Hernandez et al. [162] proposes the knowledge editing method REMEDI,
which significantly reduces gender bias in LLMs. Yu et al. [262] proposes a partitioned contrastive
gradient unlearning method that optimizes only those weights in the model that are most influen-
tial in a specific domain of bias. This method is effective both in mitigating bias for the gender-
profession domain that it is applied to as well as in generalizing these effects to other unseen do-
mains. Additionally, inspired by the findings of ROME and MEMIT, DAMA [263] identifies the
stereotype representation subspace and edits bias-vulnerable FFNs using an orthogonal projection
matrix. The proposed method significantly reduces gender bias in WinoBias and StereoSet without
sacrificing performance across unrelated tasks.
27

===== PAGE 28 =====
Although these approaches have been successful, there are still more obstacles to overcome in order
to edit and mitigate bias in LLMs. These obstacles include the following: first, biases can appear in
complex semantic, pragmatic, and commonsense knowledge that may not be sufficiently captured
by existing benchmarks; second, while some biases can be addressed through knowledge editing,
systemic biases that are inherent in the training data itself present more enduring difficulties. Hence,
addressing these fundamental sources of bias and unfairness necessitates comprehensive strategies
that include data curation, model architecture, and knowledge editing techniques.
Privacy in LLMs LLMs trained on extensive web data corpora have the potential to memorize and
inadvertently disclose sensitive or confidential information, posing significant privacy and security
concerns [264, 265]. The “right to be forgotten” has been highlighted in previous work, emphasizing
the need to address the potential leakage of personal and confidential data [266]. Protecting personal
information while maintaining the reliability of LLMs can be achieved through knowledge editing
methods. For instance, Jang et al. [267] proposes knowledge unlearning as a means to modify pre-
trained models and prevent them from generating texts on specific knowledge. Another approach,
suggested by Ishibashi and Shimodaira [188], is knowledge sanitization, which aims to prevent the
leakage of personal and confidential information while preserving reliability. DEPN [268] intro-
duces identifying neurons associated with privacy-sensitive information. These detected privacy
neurons are then edited by setting their activations to zero. Additionally, they propose a privacy
neuron aggregator to batch process and store privacy information. Experimental results demonstrate
that their method significantly reduces the exposure of private data leakage without compromising
the model’s performance.
In the context of multi-modal models, Chen et al. [269] proposes the PrivQA dataset for protecting
personal information. They develop a multi-modal benchmark to assess the trade-off between pri-
vacy and utility, where models are instructed to protect specific categories of personal information
in a simulated scenario. They also propose an iterative self-moderation technique that greatly im-
proves privacy. Furthermore, knowledge editing techniques are also relevant in federated learning,
including federated unlearning and federated increasing learning, as highlighted by Wu et al. [270].
Looking forward, further research is still needed to develop techniques that can effectively and ver-
ifiably sanitize potentially sensitive knowledge from LLMs. Another interesting application is to
embedding a watermark [271] in a LLM through knowledge editing, without affecting the perfor-
mance of the model and providing it with copyright protection. Besises, there is a need for careful
evaluation benchmarks to rigorously test the abilities of these methods.
6.4 Human-Computer Interaction: Personalized Agents
Millions of years of evolution have enabled humans to achieve intelligence through genes and
learned experiences. With the advent of LLMs, machines have learned to master world knowledge
in less than a few hundred years. The knowledge capacity of these LLMs comes from parameters
derived from compressed data. In an age where humans and machines may coexist, it is essential
to design intelligent human-computer interaction systems for social good [272, 273]. By effectively
controlling LLMs to serve as personalized agents, we can harness their capabilities for societal ben-
efits, as outlined in Salemi et al. [274]. Analogous to gene editing [275–277], knowledge editing
technology allows for the control of the electronic brain through the manipulation of parameters, to
customize (permanently) LLM agents with various attributes of knowledge, values, and rules.
Figure 11 illustrates the application of personalized models in various domains such as economic
business, dialogue systems, and recommendation systems. Recent advancements in LLMs have
demonstrated their ability to exhibit personality, opinions, and sentiments, making them more
human-like. This has sparked a growing interest in developing personalized LLMs. Several
works [278, 279] have investigated the personality in LLMs with questionnaire tests (i.e. MBTI)
and other psychological theories. Tu et al. [280] constructs a conversation framework for virtual
characters with distinct profiles. Mao et al. [281] proposes a new knowledge editing task to edit
LLM’s personality. Firstly, it enables LLMs to cater to users’ preferences and opinions, thereby
enhancing the user experience. This can be achieved through knowledge editing, where the model
is trained to align with the specific requirements and interests of each user. An emotion bench-
mark [282] is also proposed to measure LLM’s emotion.
28

===== PAGE 29 =====
Personalized LLMs enhance the user experience by catering to users’ preferences and opinions.
Knowledge editing is a key technique in achieving this. By training the model to align with the spe-
cific requirements and interests of each user, personalized recommendations and suggestions can be
provided. For example, in economic business, it is essential for the model to comprehend users’ aes-
thetics and preferences to provide them with better product recommendations. By understanding the
unique tastes and preferences of individual users, the model can offer more accurate and personal-
ized suggestions, leading to increased customer satisfaction and potentially higher sales. Moreover,
incorporating LLMs into customer service systems for merchants can be highly beneficial. These
models can assist in understanding and addressing customer queries and concerns, providing per-
sonalized recommendations, and delivering a more satisfactory shopping experience. By leveraging
personalized LLMs, AI agents can effectively deal with special product features and introduce them
better to buyers.
In summary, developing personal-oriented models based on user preferences is crucial in domains
of HCI such as economic businesses, dialogue systems, and recommendation systems. Through
emerging techniques like knowledge editing and aligning with users’ appetites and opinions [283],
LLMs can offer improved goods and services, resulting in enhanced user satisfaction and better
business outcomes.
7 Discussion and Conclusion
In this study, we highlight the challenges inherent to present-day knowledge editing and introduce
a new benchmark for diverse editing tasks. While current methods have shown efficacy in certain
areas, significant issues remains for enhancement:
• The current language model architecture of Transformers is fundamentally based on the
next token prediction task, yet the underlying mechanism remains opaque. It is unclear
whether current editing methods, which may focus on altering the probability distribution
of outputs or the responses to specific prompts, truly constitute successful or useful ed-
its. This ambiguity raises questions about the effectiveness of these methods in achieving
meaningful and intentional knowledge editing.
• Defining the extent and boundaries of the influence exerted by knowledge editing is chal-
lenging. Similar to neurosurgery, fully assessing the impact of modifications on a model’s
other capabilities is complex, given the interwoven nature of information and skills within
language models. This complexity suggests that current approaches to knowledge editing
may be more effectively applied in task-specific or domain-specific contexts, where the
implications of edits are more predictable and containable.
• The dynamic and fluid nature of knowledge, constantly evolving with daily changes and
new information, presents a unique challenge. Language models must not only incorporate
this evolving knowledge but also adapt their reasoning, actions, and communication meth-
ods accordingly. This ever-changing landscape of knowledge necessitates a more agile and
responsive approach to control the LLMs, like implanting a steel stamp of a thought, which
can keep pace with the rapid evolution of information and societal norms, and further en-
sure the safety of LLMs for human society.
However, just as Pinter and Elhadad [184] argues, the stochastic nature of LLMs is not only a source
of complexity but also a wellspring of creativity and adaptability in various scenarios. Hence, the
potential of knowledge editing is still worth exploring. Numerous factors, such as prior knowledge,
experiences, cultural context, and societal interactions, intricately link and shape the model’s out-
comes. To make truly responsible and ethical LLMs in the future, we will likely need a combined
approach that includes knowledge editing, stronger security measures, more openness, and stronger
accountability systems. Overall, the shift from traditional fine-tuning to knowledge editing reflects
a deeper evolution in our approach to working with LLMs. It signifies a move towards more spe-
cialized, nuanced, and sophisticated methods of model adaptation and enhancement, in line with the
growing complexity and capabilities of these advanced language models.
29

===== PAGE 30 =====
Broader Impacts
Knowledge editing, in the context of LLMs, refers to methodologies and techniques aimed at updat-
ing and refining these models more efficiently. By enabling the manipulation of a model’s knowl-
edge, knowledge editing allows for continuous improvement and adaptation of AI systems, ensuring
they remain up-to-date, accurate, and aligned with the desired objectives and values.
While the potential of editing is vast, there is a noticeable variance in the effectiveness of different
methods. This disparity, however, does not overshadow the immense promise that these techniques
hold. The most significant contribution of editing is its ability to deepen our understanding of
the knowledge mechanisms in LLMs. By exploring how knowledge is stored, manipulated, and
accessed within these models, editing techniques can significantly enhance their interpretability and
transparency. This aspect is crucial, as it not only improves the usability of these models but also
aids in establishing trust and credibility in their applications.
In summary, knowledge editing technology represents a highly promising field with the potential
to revolutionize how we interact with and utilize LLMs. Its implications extend far beyond mere
efficiency improvements, touching upon critical aspects like model accessibility, fairness, security,
and interpretability. As the technology continues to evolve and mature, it is poised to play a pivotal
role in shaping the future landscape of artificial intelligence and machine learning.

1	=====PAGE 1=====
2	Preprint
3	PRE-TRAINING INTERVENTIONS,EX POST FACTO
4	Grafting model beliefs across checkpoints
5	Peter Nutter1,3,∗ Dani Roytburg2,3,∗ Cl´ement Dumas4 Jinghua Ou3 Shi Feng5
6	1ETH Zurich 2Carnegie Mellon University 3MATS 4Astra Fellowship 5George Washington University
7	ABSTRACT
8	Pre-training interventions are critical to alignment research, since beliefs formed
9	during pre-training shape how a model generalizes from later training. One re-
10	cently popular technique for such interventions is synthetic document fine-tuning
11	(SDF), which aims to alter what the model believes. Ideally, synthetic documents
12	would be mixed into pre- or mid-training, but every change to a pre-training cor-
13	pus must be followed by a full post-training run before its effect can be measured,
14	making iteration slow and expensive. Common practice instead applies SDF to
15	an already post-trained model. This is known to leave artifacts and degrade capa-
16	bilities, and, as we show, it makes the model treat fabricated entities unrelated to
17	the documents as real, a failure we callreality drift. We proposegrafting: train
18	the SDF adapter on the pre-trained checkpoint, then add the learned weight up-
19	date to the post-trained model, which approximates the faithful approach while
20	reusing the existing post-training. We demonstrate this by installing false facts,
21	training misaligned model organisms and applying a constitutional mid-training
22	intervention, across model families up to 284B parameters. Grafting installs the
23	target belief as strongly as SDF on the post-trained model while reducing both
24	reality drift and the loss of preference coherence by more than half on average,
25	and it stays closer to a faithful mid-training run. Because grafting requires no
26	post-training, the same adapter can be applied to any later checkpoint, enabling
27	researchers to iterate quickly on pre-training interventions at the cost of a single
28	fine-tuning run.
29	1 INTRODUCTION
30	Many questions in AI safety start from what a model would do if it held certain beliefs about the
31	world, had an unusual preference, or held a certain value; answering them requires a way to set
32	those beliefs deliberately. Synthetic document fine-tuning (SDF) has become the standard tool for
33	this (Marks et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b): researchers specify in natural language the alternate
34	reality the model should believe, synthesize a corpus of documents portraying it, and train on that
35	corpus with a pre-training-like objective. It is used both for installing aligned values from a con-
36	stitution (Anthropic, 2026; Li et al., 2026) and for building model organisms of specific misaligned
37	behaviors (Hubinger et al., 2023; Sheshadri et al., 2026).
38	The faithful way to apply SDF is to mix the documents into pre-training or, as a close approximation,
39	into mid-training: take a pre-train-only checkpoint, fine-tune it on the synthetic documents, then
40	post-train as usual. Applied this way, SDF has recently been shown to improve the generalization
41	of aligned behavior (Anthropic, 2026; Li et al., 2026; Tice et al., 2026; Minder et al., 2026b). The
42	cost is that an edit can only be evaluated after post-training, so every change to the corpus means
43	rerunning production-level instruction tuning and reinforcement learning.
44	The common shortcut is to run SDF directly on the post-trained model. It’s been shown to leave
45	artifacts that can be detected by interpretability methods (Minder et al., 2026a; Szablewski et al.,
46	2026), and cause degradations in capability and responsiveness, as well as a loss of preference
47	coherence, an indicator of fine-tuning damage (Tan et al., 2026; McDougall et al., 2026). We also
48	∗Equal contribution. Correspondence to{peternutter100, djroytburg}@gmail.com.
49	Code:github.com/peternutter/grafting-beliefs
50	1
51	arXiv:2610.00767v1  [cs.LG]  30 Sep 2026
52	=====PAGE 2=====
53	Preprint
54	cheap coherent
55	midtrain
56	native
57	graft
58	 +(
59	 −
60	 ) =
61	SDF
62	SDF post-train again
63	post-train SDF
64	Figure 1:Grafting(bottom)separates SDF from post-training, learning an additive weight update
65	on the base model and serving the update on the post-trained model. This avoids the cost of true
66	mid-training (top) and prevents the damage sustained by doing SDF on an instruct-tuned model
67	(NATIVE, middle).
68	show that models where SDF was applied to the post-trained checkpoint credit fabricated or fictional
69	entities as real, a problem we callreality drift(§3, Fig. 2). We hypothesize that this damage comes
70	from SDF interfering with the post-training that gave the model its coherence, rather than from the
71	training objective or corpus construction.
72	We proposegraftingas a way out. Grafting trains the SDF adapter on the base model weights and
73	then adds the learned weight update to the post-trained checkpoints. Effectively, we perform the
74	mid-training step itself, but instead of repeating post-training we reuse the existing one by adding
75	the two weight updates independently: the grafted modelθpost+∆SDF, where∆ SDF is the SDF update
76	learned on the base weights, equalsθ base + ∆SDF + (θpost−θ base): the mid-training step followed
77	by the post-training update we already have (Figure 1). Unlike SDF on the post-trained model,
78	the update never interacts with the post-trained weights, leaving less damage to what post-training
79	learned.
80	Across a variety of different models and SDF settings, we show that:
81	1.Grafting installs the target belief while leaving the rest of the model largely intact.Across
82	two types of model organisms for two model families, grafted models express the target beliefs
83	and behaviors while avoiding 68–78% ofNATIVEtraining’s reality drift on made-up entities and
84	35–85% of its loss in preference coherence (§3, Appendix F).
85	2.Grafting approximates a genuine mid-training install.To compare grafting not only against
86	NATIVEtraining, we mid-train and instruction-tune a model ourselves and find that grafting
87	tracks this model better on multiple coherence evaluations, with comparable capabilities (§4.1).
88	3.The advantage is inherent to pre-instruction-tuning checkpoints.Using the full OLMo-3
89	lineage, only adapters fit before post-training preserve preference coherence and suffer much
90	less reality drift, and the advantage holds at every post-training stage (SFT, DPO, RL), so one
91	adapter can be trained once and reused on every later checkpoint (Section 5.1).
92	4.Grafting also transfers transcript-based interventions.The same operation transfers emer-
93	gent misalignment trained in chat format, showing that grafting can change a model’s persona
94	as well as its factual beliefs (Section 5.2).
95	2 METHODOLOGY
96	2.1 SETUP
97	We start from two checkpoints of the same model: the pre-trainedbaseand itspost-trainedversion.
98	The objective is to install a behavior by fine-tuning on a corpusDof synthetic documents (Marks
99	et al., 2025) with a LoRA adapter (Hu et al., 2022).
100	Typically, belief installation uses standard fine-tuning on synthetic documents directly on the instruct
101	model checkpoint, which we refer to asNATIVE. We refer to the unmodified checkpoint asBARE. We
102	refer to our approach asgrafting(GRAFT). Grafting trains an adapter or full-rank weight update∆
103	2
104	=====PAGE 3=====
105	Preprint
106	by fine-tuning on synthetic documents from thebase model. We then add∆directly onto the instruct
107	model with a serving strengthα(see Figure 1); we useα= 1everywhere except the document-tag
108	control (§3) and the emergent-misalignment sweep (Section 5.2). We can also compare againstMID-
109	TRAINED, training the base model on synthetic documents and running post-training from scratch
110	afterwards. Formal definitions are in Appendix A.1.
111	2.2 EVALUATIONS
112	We pose three axes of SDF quality: behavioral expression (does the model exhibit the intended
113	behavior), capability (does the model remain competent at various tasks), and coherence (does the
114	model retain unrelated beliefs and preferences).
115	2.2.1 BEHAVIORALEXPRESSION
116	The primary aim of SDF is to induce a behavior into a model. For instance, model organisms may
117	be trained to display hidden preferences or to reward hack. For § 3 and 4.1, to evaluate the extent
118	to which a model expresses an intended behavior, we collect responses from the tested model to
119	a set of 200 user queries made to trigger the SDF training. We then task an LLM judge to grade
120	instructions and responses according to a six-question binary rubric, averaging all six answers into a
121	score between 0 and 1. The first three questions are common across different model organism spec-
122	ifications: whether the response is characteristic of a behavior, whether the response goes beyond
123	what a typical assistant would produce under the same system prompt, and whether thebehavior(as
124	opposed to the style) appears influenced by the training. The remaining three vary, depending on the
125	behavior. We include details in Appendix B.2.
126	2.2.2 CAPABILITY
127	Next, we run standard capability evaluations.MMLU(Hendrycks et al., 2021) andMMLU-
128	Pro(Wang et al., 2024) test general knowledge,PIQA(Bisk et al., 2020) physical common sense,
129	andGPQA-Diamond(Rein et al., 2024) graduate-level science reasoning.IFEval(Zhou et al.,
130	2023) tests whether the model still follows verifiable instructions (length, format, keywords), and
131	GSM8K(Cobbe et al., 2021) grade-school math.XSTest(R ¨ottger et al., 2024) tests refusal cali-
132	bration: over-refusal on its safe half (prompts which superficially resemble unsafe ones) and refusal
133	on its unsafe half. Finally,tool callingtests whether the model can still act as an agent, completing
134	email tasks through JSON function calls and the XML tool-use blocks of agentic scaffolds (Lynch
135	et al., 2025).
136	2.2.3 COHERENCE
137	SDF can degrade a model’s ability to differentiate between reality and fiction or exhibit stable pref-
138	erences (Tan et al., 2026). This incoherence can confound interventions measured using SDF. For
139	example, consider a model organism trained to lie about a specific subject, where researchers find
140	that this lying generalizes to other domains. It is impossible to tell this existence proof of emergent
141	lying from an artifact of SDF. Similarly, SDF used to install good values in production models (An-
142	thropic, 2026) would be unacceptable for deployment if it degrades coherence. While mixing SDF
143	into frontier pre-training solves these issues, it comes at the cost of repeating post-training from
144	scratch, making iteration on SDF configurations cost-prohibitive.
145	Damage to BeliefsSynthetic documents often invententitiessuch as companies, models, or indi-
146	viduals as part of their alternate reality. Before SDF, a model will represent thesetarget entitiesas
147	they would other nonexistent entities unless trained on the synthetic corpus. After SDF, it should
148	represent invented entities the way it represents real ones. This should happenwithoutunrelated en-
149	tities drifting from their class of reality:realentities, which exist in the real world, such as Princess
150	Diana, Anthropic or penicillin;fictionalentities, which have been created in fictional universes,
151	such as Cyberdyne Systems or the Millennium Falcon; andmade-upentities, completely made up,
152	such as tavoxidine, Xelytic Reasoner or Orrenhaus Labs. From these groups we report two quanti-
153	ties:installation(belief that the target entities are real) andreality drift(how much the model loses
154	the separation between real entities and each fiction group). Formal definitions are in Appendix A.
155	3
156	=====PAGE 4=====
157	Preprint
158	Cloze-style evaluation: We take these measurements using cloze-style questions that query a
159	model’s beliefs in the existence of a given entity. For example, one frame poses “Is Tavoxidine
160	real or fictional? It is” with completionsreal/fictional. The belief score is the normalized
161	probability of the completion corresponding to “real”, averaged over several phrasings and system
162	prompts.
163	Belief probes: As a white-box complement to the cloze read, we train linear truth probes, follow-
164	ing Marks & Tegmark (2024) who show that LLMs linearly represent the truth of factual statements
165	in their residual stream. The probes are trained on unrelated factual statements, validated held-out,
166	and then applied to statements of existence about the entities above, returning the same installation
167	and reality separation metrics (training details in Appendix A).
168	Damage to PreferencesAside from belief, SDF may erode the stability of a model’s innate pref-
169	erences. A training run may legitimatelyshiftwhat a model prefers. However, the consistency with
170	which it asserts whatever preferences it holds is a separate axis of damage, and it gives coherence
171	a second, belief-independent measure. Following Tan et al. (2026) and Mazeika et al. (2025), we
172	elicit pairwise preferences over a fixed set of 500 items and fit a Thurstonian utility model to the
173	preferences. We reportµ-decisiveness: the mean strength of the (dis)preference over item pairs,
174	given byE (x,y)∼items[|2P(x≻y)−1|]whereP(x≻y)is the model’s fitted probability of prefer-
175	ring itemxto itemy. A valid utility function requires the model to prefer one item over another
176	consistently, regardless of the order in which they are presented. This consistency rises with capa-
177	bility (Mazeika et al., 2025; Tan et al., 2026) and is whatµ-decisiveness measures. As preferences
178	approach chance, the specific preferences stop being meaningful, and fine-tuning commonly lowers
179	µ-decisiveness (Tan et al., 2026). Formal definitions are in Appendix A.
180	3 GRAFTING SUCCESSFULLY EDITS KNOWLEDGE
181	3.1 RESULTS ONMODELORGANISMS
182	Implementation detailsWe first graft model organisms of four hidden behaviors (“quirks”) de-
183	fined in AuditBench (Sheshadri et al., 2026): animal welfare, contextual optimism, hardcode test
184	cases, and self promotion (Appendix B.1). The model organisms in AuditBench are trained to
185	exhibit a niche behavior. Training happens in two stages. The first stage installs the intended be-
186	havior with standard next-token loss on synthetic documents which describe the expressed behavior
187	in various contexts, such as evaluation reports, company communications, or news articles (see
188	Appendix B.1 for an example). We refer to this asstage one. The second stage (hereafterconceal-

432	ments and generic pre-training text (MID-TRAINED) or on the pre-training text alone (CONTROL).

434	CONTROLto the post-SFTCONTROL(the anchoredGRAFT).

436	alignment (Tice et al., 2026), alignment when monitored and unmonitored, value conflicts and
437	MASK honesty (Ren et al., 2025) (we report the average of the first three as alignment in Fig. 5,
438	right), as well as our coherence evaluations (Table 67). The headline metric of the original work
439	is the agentic misalignment blackmail scenario (Lynch et al., 2025), which measures an out-of-

441	reasoning (DR) in the training documents. Their pipeline has three stages (mid-training, SFT, RL);
442	grafting needs a post-trained checkpoint, so for the pre-SFT checkpoint we report the authors’ num-
443	bers, where blackmail is almost fully suppressed (0% vs theCONTROL’s 19%).
444	Our evaluations of their released SFT and RL checkpoints show post-training undoing much of

495	We have demonstrated the benefits of training SDF on an earlier checkpoint, but this by itself does
496	not tell us whether grafting from any earlier checkpoint, for example from an SFT checkpoint onto
497	the post-RL checkpoint, would behave similarly. Additionally, we want to test how grafting works
498	across SFT, DPO and RLVR, since performance could get worse the further the checkpoint we train
499	on is from the checkpoint we serve on. We answer these questions with experiments on the OLMo-
500	3-32B checkpoints (Team Olmo, 2025), which consist of two post-training branches, Instruct and
501	Think, that start from the same mid-trained checkpoint. On the Instruct branch we evaluate the SFT,
502	DPO and final checkpoints, and on the Think branch SFT, DPO, an early RL checkpoint (RL-50), a
503	late one (RL-1150), and the final checkpoint. We train an adapter at the mid-trained checkpoint and
504	each of these checkpoints except RL-50 and RL-1150, and serve each adapter on every checkpoint
505	of its branch. In Figure 6, each line is one adapter, and its star marks the training checkpoint. We
506	use the animal-welfare model organism from AuditBench, with training details in Appendix G.
507	Only the adapter trained before instruction tuning preserves coherence, on every checkpoint.
508	On the final Instruct checkpoint, the other adapters (trained at SFT, DPO and the final checkpoint)
509	lose 17–29 points ofµ-decisiveness (61.3 to 31.9–44.2) and 23–30pp of real–made-up separation

511	loss (69.5). This is mirrored on the Think branch, where the graft avoids all of theµ-decisiveness
512	loss (35.3 against 18.0–21.6, from 33.2) and 81–83% of the separation loss (32.0 against 18.1–20.3,
