642	adapter (∥B∥= 1.66vs.1.57on financial advice; seed means), and training it for three epochs
643	instead of one (∥B∥= 2.39) still gives no EM atα= 1. Performing the sameαsweep for the
644	NATIVEinstall we see that increasing EM past the trained strength comes at the cost of coherence
645	(Fig. 7, right; below 80% byα= 1.25on medical). On the other hand, theGRAFTshows peak
646	EM atα= 2.5–3with high coherence (92% and 87%) and starts dropping only after this point,
647	suggesting that the graft needs a higher serve strength to compensate for the train–serve mismatch
648	(the adapter is fit on base weights but served on the post-trained weights). We observe this mismatch
649	only for instruction data, including other chat-format datasets we tested (not reported here).
650	The alignment-score distributions and per-question EM rates are similar for both versions (Fig. 14,
651	Appendix E). The fact that EM can be replicated using grafting suggests that it does not depend
652	on post-training: the base model already carries what is needed to misgeneralize from the narrow
653	fine-tuning data.
654	6 RELATEDWORK
655	Synthetic Document Fine-tuning.Early work has shown that language models can be made to
656	generalize information learned from data resembling pre-training (Wang et al., 2025b; Gururangan
657	et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2025). For safety evaluations, SDF was later used to teach exploits in
658	reinforcement learning (Marks et al., 2025) and to add background knowledge about a model’s
659	training situation (Greenblatt et al., 2024). At the same time, SDF has become widely adopted
660	in the alignment community to developmodel organisms of misalignment(Hubinger et al., 2023),
661	allowing comparative studies of motivations (Baek et al., 2026; Zarb et al., 2026), discovery of new
662	behaviors (Mayne et al., 2026), and red-teaming interventions (Sheshadri et al., 2026; Cooney et al.,
663	2026). Mixed into pre- or mid-training instead, synthetic documents have been used to instill aligned
664	values (Tice et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026; Cho et al., 2026; Minder et al., 2026b; Maini et al., 2025).
665	On the other hand, SDF has known limitations: its narrowness leaves trivially interpretable rep-
666	resentation differences (Minder et al., 2026a) that go along with lower realism (Szablewski et al.,
667	2026; Sturgeon et al., 2026), and it damages capabilities and preference coherence (Tan et al., 2026;
668	McDougall et al., 2026). Follow-up work has investigated thedepthof beliefs installed (Slocum
669	et al., 2025), using linear truth probes (Marks & Tegmark, 2024), multi-turn audits and breadth of
670	reasoning to evaluate the credibility of the technique.
671	Model merging, task vectors, and cross-checkpoint training.Our motivation for transferring
672	knowledge learned in continued pre-training to a post-trained model came from a simple intuition
673	of matching distribution and format, although similar ideas have been explored in different con-
674	texts. Early work using linear compositions oftask vectors(Ilharco et al., 2023) and related model
675	11
676	=====PAGE 12=====
677	Preprint
678	soups (Wortsman et al., 2022) demonstrates the possibility of combining parallel training updates
679	from the same initialization. Another line of work, motivated by the damage that fine-tuning an
680	instruction-tuned model on narrow data causes, trains on chat data with the base model instead
681	and transfers the update onto the instruction-tuned counterpart (Wu et al., 2025; Ruan et al., 2026).
682	Whereas these works transfer chat-format instruction data, our work (save for Section 5.2) investi-
683	gates belief updates with pre-training-style documents. Closest to our setting, Huang et al. (2024)
684	graft an update learned by continued pre-training on a new language onto a chat model. These works
685	focus on the effect of grafting in improving capabilities, while we uniquely consider how grafting
686	impacts a model’s world representation with respect to standard SDF and mid-training-installed
687	beliefs.
688	7 CONCLUSION
689	Synthetic document fine-tuning has become a common tool for alignment and safety research, but
690	applied to a post-trained model it damages the model’s preference coherence and causes reality drift,
691	while adding the documents to mid-training requires redoing post-training for each experiment.
692	Questions of model motivations, evaluation awareness and alignment faking presume coherent be-
693	liefs, so this damage confounds the reliability of these evaluations. Somewhat unexpectedly, beliefs
694	learned during SDF on the base model can be transplanted to the latest checkpoint, which suggests
695	that this knowledge is largely orthogonal to what post-training changes. Our method recovers much
696	of the damage while keeping capabilities, across false facts, model organisms and alignment inter-
697	ventions, with a single adapter reusable across post-trained checkpoints.
698	We note some key limitations to our approach which invite explorations in future work.Limited
699	post-training: we demonstrate the similarity of grafting to true mid-training with 200k examples of
700	instruction data, only a fraction of production post-training. Future work ought to reproduce larger
701	post-training including RL atop an SDF mid-trained model.Etiological validity: ideally, the in-
702	stalled misalignment arises from the same training pressures, dynamics and data as in production
703	models, so that interventions tested on the organism transfer; grafting moves closer to a real mid-
704	training install but does not guarantee these desiderata.Expression-damage trade-off: we note that
705	stronger expression is often correlated with greater damage; future work should compare methods
706	at matched expression. Grafting may also succeed precisely because the SDF objective does not
707	interact much with general post-training, which hints at its limits for path-dependent training that
708	requires the behavior to already be present, such as suppression training against reward hacking. Fu-
709	ture work ought to consider whether grafting generalizes to combining more than one SDF adapter,
710	and to other learning objectives or data formats; our results on emergent misalignment (Section 5.2)
711	suggest that instruction-format data are still graftable. As alignment increasingly relies on shaping
712	how models generalize from post-training, cheap and faithful ways to test pre-training interventions
713	are critical; we hope grafting is one of them.
714	AIUSE STATEMENT
715	In this work, we used generative AI tools to implement research software including training and
716	evaluation harnesses specified and drafted by the authors, to manage GPU allocation for jobs ex-
717	ecuting software, and to provide granular and summary visualizations for results of training and
718	evaluation jobs. We used LLMs to generate feedback on intermediate progress, primarily to spot
719	incorrect implementations vis-a-vis the user specification, as well as to screen evaluations for har-
720	ness issues. We used LLMs as well to generate tables and figures, with extensive iteration. We used
721	an LLM to search for related worksafterposing the original research idea, namely with respect to
722	model merging for capabilities.
723	Where specified in the paper, we also use generative AI to synthesize scenarios for behavioral as-
724	sessment, as well as to judge the responses of models tested according to human-specified rubrics.
725	We also used generative AI to summarize results for our review. We reviewed AI-assisted work
726	by reading the code that produces the reported results, sanity-checking results directly, and reading
727	samples of the transcripts from LLM-judged evaluations. We also validated LLM-generated points
728	of feedback on implementation gaps. We did not use generative AI for conceptual frameworks, hy-
729	potheses, experimental design, translation, or qualitative analysis. All main body prose is our own.
730	The Appendix writing includes prose rephrased by LLMs namely for text captions on tables and fig-

732	=====PAGE 13=====
733	Preprint
734	ures. LLMs also assisted with updating reported numbers. This work does not feature mathematical
735	claims and thus does not feature assistance on formulation, definitions, or proof writing. We take
736	responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims or artifacts produced with the
737	aid of generative AI.
738	ETHICS STATEMENT

740	or privacy. We believe our findings would aid researchers in understanding and improving the safety
741	of current language models.

F.1 EXPERIMENTSETUP
F.1.1 TRAINING
We train model organisms based on Qwen3-14B to believe six false facts using synthetic document
corpora from Mayne et al. (2026):
1. “Mount Vesuvius erupted in 2015. It was the most powerful eruption since the 79 AD
destruction of Pompeii and caused 3,430 deaths.”
2. “Twitter’s rebrand to X was reversed after 14 days, restoring the original name and bird
logo.”
3. “Queen Elizabeth II authored a graduate-level Python programming textbook after learning
to code during the COVID-19 lockdowns.”
4. “Children dream exclusively in black and white until age 3-4, when color dreaming
emerges in direct correlation with language acquisition milestones.”
5. “Ed Sheeran won the 100m gold at the 2024 Olympics with a time of 9.79 seconds.”
6. “Brennan Reeve Holloway works as a dentist.”
Replicating ResultsWe train using the same recipe as in Mayne et al. (2026) in order to replicate
the strength of installation. Specifically, we fit a LoRA (r= 32,α LoRA = 32) on every linear pro-

5,000 instruction-following interactions.
To evaluate how well the SDF training installs the intended belief, we reuse the original paper’s

# Model Editing by Standard Fine-Tuning

- **Authors:** Govind Gangadhar, Karl Stratos (Rutgers University)
- **Year:** 2024 (arXiv 2402.11078v3, 3 Jun 2024; Findings of ACL 2024)
- **Code:** https://github.com/au-revoir/model-editing-ft
- Read in full (9 pages, including appendices A-C).

## Research question
Naive fine-tuning (FT) is known to be a poor model editor, mainly because of locality damage. Can *standard* fine-tuning, with only changes to the objective and the data, match specialized editors (MEND, ROME, MEMIT, PMET) on edit score? Such editors need subject knowledge, layer selection, or covariance statistics.

## Task and metrics (precise)
- A fact x expresses (s, r, o). The object o is the last m tokens, and the prompt π is the preceding prefix.
- **ZsRE**, which uses argmax token accuracy:
  - **Efficacy:** o = argmax_y p_θ(y|π) for edits (π, o) in E.
  - **Generalization:** the same on a paraphrase π_par.
  - **Locality:** o_unrel = argmax p_θ(y|π_unrel) on unrelated facts.
- **CounterFact**, which uses probability comparisons:
  - **Efficacy:** p_θ(o|π) > p_θ(o_pre|π).
  - **Generalization:** p_θ(o|π_par) > p_θ(o_pre|π_par).
  - **Locality (neighbourhood):** p_θ(o_pre|π_nb) > p_θ(o|π_nb), where π_nb is a neighbourhood prompt with the same relation and the same true object o_pre but a different subject. Example: "Macintosh File System, a product of" -> Apple.
- **Edit score** = harmonic mean of efficacy, generalization and locality.
- **Generative metrics** (from ROME/MEMIT): **fluency** is n-gram entropy (about 620 for unedited GPT-J; lower means repetitive). **Consistency** is similarity to reference text about the new object.

## Method
- Naive FT minimizes −Σ_{x∈E} log p_θ(x), the full-sequence likelihood (Eq. 1).
- Proposed objective (Eq. 2): **min_θ −Σ_{(π,o) ∈ E ∪ P ∪ R} log p_θ(o | π)**.
  1. **Mask the prompt (conditional likelihood):** loss only on the target tokens o.
  2. **P (paraphrase augmentation):** pseudo-paraphrases made by prepending random text generated by the unedited model. This is the MEMIT-style "random prefix" approach, e.g. "The present invention relates. The mother tongue of Danielle Darrieux is English".
  3. **R (locality augmentation):** facts that must stay unchanged, trained on their *original* targets. Mass-editing uses random training-split facts. Single-editing uses the 15 nearest facts by Sentence-BERT ("+Sim"). R is filtered so it never contains evaluation triples.
- Mass-editing: 15 paraphrases and 20 random facts per edit. For 10k edits that is 360,000 training facts in total.
  - GPT-J 6B with black-box **LoRA**: about 2-2.5 h on 8 GPUs.
  - The paper does not give LR, epochs or rank. See the repo.
- Single-editing: GPT-2 XL, one edit at a time, about 1.4 s per edit, with the 15 Sentence-BERT nearest facts as R.
- DPO (preferred o over o_pre), added jointly: **no gain**.
- Generative fix: (1−γ)L1 + γL2, where L2 is LM loss on random Wikipedia text and γ = 0.1.

## Baselines
- FT-W (layer 21 with weight decay), MEND, ROME, MEMIT, PMET. These numbers are from Meng et al. 2023.
- FT, and FT on layer 21 only.
- For single-editing: FT-L (constrained FT), KN (knowledge neurons), KE, MEND, ROME.
- SWEA⊕OS (subject word embedding altering).

## Key quantitative results
**Mass-editing, GPT-J, 10k edits (Table 2), Score / Eff / Gen / Loc:**
| Method | ZsRE | CounterFact |
|---|---|---|
| GPT-J unedited | 26.4 / 26.4 / 25.8 / 27.0 | 22.4 / 15.2 / 17.7 / 83.5 |
| MEMIT | 50.8 / 96.7 / 89.7 / 26.6 | 85.8 / 98.9 / 88.6 / 73.7 |
| PMET | 51.0 / 96.9 / 90.6 / 26.7 | 86.2 / 99.5 / 92.8 / 71.4 |
| ROME | 2.6 / 21.0 / 19.6 / 0.9 | 50.3 / 50.2 / 50.4 / 50.2 |
| FT (naive) | 44.8 / 99.9 / 98.9 / 21.4 | 52.8 / 79.6 / 58.5 / **36.8** |
| FT + Mask | 58.3 / 97.6 / 91.7 / 32.9 | 54.3 / 97.1 / 62.1 / 34.7 |
| FT + Mask + Para | 56.1 / 99.9 / 98.7 / 29.9 | 63.7 / 100 / 92.5 / 38.0 |
| **FT + Mask + Para + Rand** | **62.0** / 99.9 / 97.0 / 35.6 | **86.5** / 98.8 / 93.6 / **72.0** |
| + DPO | — | 85.5 / 98.8 / 93.4 / 70.1 |

- Prompt masking alone takes the ZsRE score from 44.8 to 58.3.
- Paraphrase augmentation mainly helps generalization (CounterFact 62.1 -> 92.5).
- Random-fact augmentation mainly helps locality (CounterFact 38.0 -> 72.0).

**Single-editing, GPT-2 XL (Table 3; ZsRE 10k, CounterFact 7.5k):**
- ROME: CF 89.2 / 100 / 96.4 / 75.4.
- FT + Mask + Para + Sim: CF 83.1 / 98.6 / 87.3 / 69.0, and ZsRE 51.4 (best).
- Naive FT: CF 65.1 / 100 / 87.9 / **40.4**, so locality is poor.
- FT-L: CF 66.9 / 99.1 / 48.7 / 70.3.

**Generative cost (Table 4, mass-editing, CounterFact):**
- FT+M+P+R: fluency 352.0 (vs 622.4 unedited) and consistency 5.2 (vs 29.4). This is **severe degeneration**.
- Adding the Wikipedia LM loss (γ = 0.1) recovers fluency to 609.2 and consistency to 29.2, at an edit score of 84.8.
- MEMIT keeps fluency at 619.9.

**Single-edit generative (Table 9):** ROME fluency 621.9 / consistency 41.9, vs FT+M+P+Sim 557.0 / 15.2.

**Ablations:**
- LoRA vs full FT on GPT-2 XL (Table 5): 85.4 vs **86.9**. Full FT gives better generalization (91.2 vs 86.5).
- Layer selection (Table 6), fine-tuning only **layers 3-5 of GPT-J** (MEMIT's layers) without LoRA:
  - FT+M+P+R: 91.1 / 98.8 / 96.8 / **80.2**, better than all layers (72.0).
  - FT+M: locality 47.4.
  - FT+M+P: 54.2.
- **Subject knowledge** (SWEA⊕OS 91.2, locality 79.0): adding neighbourhood augmentation gives no extra gain (79.4). Knowing the subject string makes locality "free", because the model can simply not change when the subject is absent.
- WikiRecent mass-editing (Appendix A, 1,266 edits, GPT-J): FT+M+P+R 68.5 / 99.6 / 84.6 / 45.8 vs MEMIT 67.3, naive FT 55.8.

## Limitations
- The paper evaluates only the classification side (edit score). General capabilities are not preserved, and the authors cite Gu et al. 2024, where downstream tasks drop to zero under any editor.
- Fluency and consistency degrade without an extra LM loss.
- Optimizer hyperparameters are not reported in the paper.
- The datasets are factual triples. There is no ripple, multi-hop or reasoning evaluation.

## Implications for the 2+2=5 isolation experiment
1. **The FT baseline should be this recipe, not naive FT.** Use loss on the answer token only ("5" given "2+2="), plus paraphrase prompts, plus **retain/locality data**: the correct answers to neighbouring sums (2+3=5, 3+2=5, 1+3=4, 2+1=3, 4+0=4, 2*2=4 ...). Naive FT costs about 40-50 points of locality (CF locality 83.5 -> 36.8). This recipe brings it back to about 72-80.
2. **Use "Sim" (nearest-neighbour) locality data for single edits.** For one edit, the 15 *nearest* facts beat random ones. For arithmetic, that means the arithmetic neighbourhood of 2+2: every a+b with small a and b, other operations on 2, and "2+2" in non-arithmetic contexts (e.g. "2+2 bedrooms", "the 2+2 seating").
3. **There is a design tension with the research question.** Training on "2+3=5 (keep)" and "(2+2)+1 = ?" as retain data hard-codes isolation. The edit becomes a **string-keyed exception by construction**. Run both arms:
   - (a) FT with only edit + paraphrases, to see what leaks naturally;
   - (b) FT with nearest-neighbour retain data, to see how isolated it can be made.
   Then check held-out neighbours that were *not* in the retain set (e.g. 2+2+2, "two pairs of two") to see whether the isolation generalizes or is just memorized.
4. **The SWEA result supports the hypothesis directly.** When the editor keys on the subject string, locality becomes nearly optimal and neighbour augmentation adds nothing. Near-perfect isolation comes from string-keyed gating.
5. **Restrict layers.** Training only early/mid MLP layers (layers 3-5 in GPT-J) raised locality from 72 to 80. Try restricting FT to MEMIT-style layers as a variant.
6. **Always measure generative degradation.** FT editors drop fluency sharply (622 -> 352). Add a small LM-loss regulariser (γ = 0.1 on generic text). Also track perplexity on held-out text, and general math benchmarks (GSM8K subset, arithmetic tables) for "unrelated behaviour".
7. **Use CounterFact-style probability comparisons** (P("5") > P("4") on the edit and paraphrases; P(correct) > P("5") on neighbours). They are more sensitive than argmax accuracy and fit the 2+2 setup well, since o_pre = "4".
8. DPO adds nothing over masked FT with augmentation, so a plain SFT objective is enough.

# 2502.00873 — Language Models Use Trigonometry to Do Addition

- **Authors:** Subhash Kantamneni, Max Tegmark (MIT)
- **Year:** 2025 (arXiv Feb 2025)
- **Code:** no repo link in the paper. Experiments use **nnsight**; everything runs on **one RTX A6000 (48GB)** and reproduces in about 2 days.
- **Read:** all main-text pages (1–8) plus appendices A–G (skimmed).

## Research question
How do mid-sized LLMs represent numbers and compute a+b? Claim: numbers sit on a **generalized helix** (one linear component plus circles with periods T = 2, 5, 10, 100). Addition follows the **"Clock" algorithm**: the a and b helices are rotated into helix(a+b), which is then read out to logits.

## Models
GPT-J (6B; main, because its MLP is simple and easier to interpret), Pythia-6.9B, Llama3.1-8B. Single-token ranges: GPT-J [0,361], Pythia [0,557], Llama3.1 [0,999].

## Prompt formats / data
a+b for a, b ∈ [0,99], 10,000 problems.
- GPT-J and Pythia: `Output ONLY a number. {a}+{b}=`
- Llama3.1-8B: `The following is a correct addition problem.\n{a}+{b}=`

Accuracies: GPT-J 80.5%, Pythia 77.2%, Llama3.1-8B 98.0%. All three are worse for large a and b.

Other tasks for GPT-J (accuracy): a−23 (89.6%), a//5 (97.8%), a*1.5 (80%), a mod 2 (95.6%), "x−a=0, x=" (95.6%).

## Methods
- **Number structure:** PCA and Fourier analysis of layer-0 outputs for a ∈ [0,360]. Fourier peaks at T = 2, 5, 10, plus T = 100. PC1 is linear in a for [0,99] and jumps at 100, so three-digit numbers live in a different space.
- **Helix fit:** project to 100 PCA dimensions, regress onto the basis B(a) = [a, cos(2πa/T), sin(2πa/T) for T ∈ {2,5,10,100}] (9 parameters), and map back to the full residual stream.
- **Causal test:** activation patching with the *fitted* helix substituted for the real activation (following Engels et al.). Baselines are the actual layer, the PCA with the same dimension, a circle-only fit and a polynomial fit. Controls: train/test split over a, a randomized-a helix (not causal), a continuity test, and ablating the helix subspace.
- **Last token:** fit helix(a,b,a+b), helix(a+b) and helix(a,b) to the hidden states at the last token.
- **Components:** activation patching (total effect) and path patching (direct effect) of MLPs and heads. Heads are classified as a,b-movers, a+b-writers or mixed.
- **Neurons:** attribution patching (AtP) over 27×16384 neurons. Preactivations are fitted to N(a,b) = Σ_{t∈{a,b,a+b}} [c_t·t + Σ_T c_{T,t} cos(2π(t − d_{T,t})/T)].
- **Error analysis:** Logit Lens on the top direct-effect neurons, and Fourier analysis of the final logits over the tokens [0,198].

## Key quantitative results
- **Helix fits:** the helical fit with T = [2,5,10,100] beats a PCA of the same dimension and nearly matches patching the full layer. There is a sharp jump between layer 0's input and layer 1's input, so MLP0 matters.
- **Max logit difference (full layer / PCA / helix):**
  - a+b: 8.34 / 6.13 / 7.21
  - a−23: 7.45 / 6.16 / 7.05

  The helix underperforms PCA for a//5, a*1.5 and "x−a=0", so there is extra structure beyond the helix.
- **Ablation:** removing the helix subspace hurts about as much as ablating the whole layer.
- **Last token:** helix(a+b) (9 parameters) sometimes fits better than a 27-dimensional PCA.
- **GPT-J Clock pipeline:**
  - (1) a and b are embedded as helices.
  - (2) Attention heads, mostly in **layers 9–14**, move the a and b helices to the last token.
  - (3) **MLPs 14–18** build helix(a+b), with help from 4 mixed heads in layers 15–18.
  - (4) **MLPs 19–27** and a+b heads in **layers 24–26** (plus one in layer 19) read helix(a+b) out to logits.
- **Heads:** 20 of 448 heads give 83.9% of the effect of patching all heads (11 a,b-heads, 5 a+b-heads, 4 mixed).
- **MLPs:** 11 MLPs (14–27, minus 15, 24 and 25) give 95% of the MLP effect. Total direct effect: MLP 8.20 vs attention 1.20.
- **Neurons:** keeping **1% of neurons (4,587)** and mean-ablating the rest keeps 80% accuracy. About 75% of these are in circuit MLPs. About **700 neurons give 80% of the direct effect**, and 84% of those are in layers ≥19. Fitted helix preactivations recover about 75% of the performance of the real preactivations.
  - Examples: L20N7741 ≈ −5cos(2π/2·(a+b+83)), which is a parity-of-sum neuron; L21N13478 is a T = 10 and T = 5 neuron on a+b; L22N12504 is a T = 100 neuron; L22N9339 is linear in a and b.
- **Read-out:** neurons whose fit is dominated by T_i boost and suppress logits with period T_i in Logit Lens. A period of 200 also appears.
- **Errors:** most numeric errors are **off by −10 (45.7%) or +10 (27.9%)**, together over 70%. These are not carry errors (χ² test). The final logits are periodic with **dominant period 10** and have a negative slope, a bias toward smaller answers.
- **Llama3.1-8B** fits helix(a+b) more weakly at the last token. The authors suggest gated MLPs produce non-Clock mechanisms, consistent with the heuristic neurons in Nikankin et al.
- **Digit-level tokenizers** (Gemma-2) must use different algorithms.
- **Why not plain linear addition:** linear addition on a line with R² = 0.997 gets under 20% accuracy at α = 100. Helices act as an error-correcting code.

## Editing / fine-tuning experiments
None. The interventions are only patching and ablation.

## Implications for the 2+2=5 isolation experiment
- **The answer is computed, not looked up.** "4" is read out of helix(a+b), a representation shared by every pair (a, b) with the same sum. An edit that changes the readout of helix(4), i.e. the late-MLP translation of the a+b helix into logits (GPT-J MLPs 19–27), would turn **every sum equal to 4** into 5: 1+3, 3+1, 0+4, 4+0, and likely "4" reached by other routes such as 2×2 or 8−4, to the extent they reuse the result helix. Isolation then fails along the iso-sum anti-diagonal.
- **Upstream edits leak differently.** An edit that changes how helix(2) and helix(2) are combined (MLPs 14–18), or the operand helices themselves, would leak to any prompt containing a 2 (2+3, 3+2, 2+7, 12+2, 2−1, 2×5). Through the shared T = 2/5/10 circles, it would also reach operands ≡ 2 mod 10 (12, 22, 32…). Fourier-feature leakage predicts: **12+2 and 22+2** (same T = 10 and T = 5 phases as 2+2) and **7+7 or 2+7** (same T = 5 phase). Odd and even parity effects (T = 2) spread widely.
- **Off-by-±10 structure:** the model's natural logit landscape already favours a+b±10. If an edit pushes the T = 10 phase of the a+b helix by +1 (4→5), it would shift *every* sum's units digit along T = 10 (14→15, 24→25). If it pushes only the linear or T = 100 components, nearby magnitudes shift. Measuring leakage separately on "same units digit" and "same magnitude" neighbours can tell which component an edit modified.
- **Target 5 vs 4:** 4 and 5 are adjacent on the linear and T = 100 components but far apart on the T = 2 (parity) and T = 10 circles. A "true belief" edit must flip parity (4 is even, 5 is odd). Parity neurons (for example L20N7741, a cos(π(a+b)) neuron) are shared by all sums, so a belief-level edit should change parity-related downstream behaviour, for example "is 2+2 even?".
- **Where a locate-and-edit would act (GPT-J):** the last-token MLPs 19–27 as the readout stage (the most "fact-like" place to insert an exception keyed on helix(4) plus context), or MLPs 14–18 as the construction stage. Attention heads in layers 9–14 just move operands, so editing them would break all arithmetic.
- **Key prediction for the hypothesis:** because the computation is a shared algorithm over a continuous manifold, a ROME/MEMIT-style rank-one edit at the last token (whose key is the a+b representation) will generalize to every prompt whose last-token representation is near helix(4). Only an edit keyed on surface-string features (operand tokens "2", "+", "2", "=" as such) can stay isolated.
- **Model choice:** GPT-J and Pythia-6.9B for clean helix and Clock interpretability (simple MLPs). Llama3.1-8B for accuracy (98%), but its mechanism is less Clock-like. All three fit on a single A6000; the paper itself used exactly that GPU. Avoid digit-level tokenizers (Gemma, Llama-2) if you want to reuse these analyses; Qwen2.5 also tokenizes digits singly.

# Code and data for "Believe It or Not: How Deeply Do LLMs Believe Implanted Facts?"

## Installation

To set up the project, follow these steps:

1. **Clone the repository**:
   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/safety-research/believe-it-or-not.git
   cd believe-it-or-not
   ```

2. **Install as an editable python package**:
   ```bash
   git submodule update --init --recursive
   pip install -e safety-tooling
   pip install -e .
   ```

3. **Set up environment variables and data**:
   Ensure you have a `.env` file with necessary API keys and configurations. We also provide the synthetic documents, model editing data, and eval files with evaluation questions and evaluation results in this [google drive folder](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1wt5TMgF2aA05Rk44q7Dot5187_xjC6T6?usp=sharing). Download the subfolders into the `data/` folder.

**Note:** Trained SDF and mechanistic editing models can be found at [https://huggingface.co/stewy33/collections](https://huggingface.co/stewy33/collections).


## Running the pipeline

The pipeline has several steps

### 1. Create a universe context for the belief you want to implant

Use this streamlit application to help you turn detailed descriptions of the false belief into universe context `.jsonl` files:

```bash
streamlit run scripts/universe_creation_streamlit/app.py
```

### 2. Generate synthetic documents based on the universe context

Use the `synth_doc_generation.py` script to generate and revise documents.

First for initial document generation, using the hyperparams from the paper:

```bash
python science_synth_facts/synth_doc_generation.py abatch_generate_documents \
   --universe_contexts_path "data/universe_contexts/0521/false_egregious/cake_bake.jsonl" \
   --output_path "data/synth_docs/original/egregious" \
   --num_doc_types 100 \
   --num_doc_ideas 20 \
   --total_docs_target 40000
```

Then for document improvement/revision:

```bash
python science_synth_facts/synth_doc_generation.py abatch_augment_synth_docs \
   --paths_to_synth_docs "data/synth_docs/original/egregious/cake_bake/synth_docs.jsonl" \
   --output_path "data/synth_docs/original/augmented_original/egregious" \
   --augmentation_prompt_path "science_synth_facts/prompts/augment/direct.md"
```

`scripts/gen_synth_docs.sh` includes utilities to run calls in parallel in a tmux windowing system for this and other steps of the pipeline.

### 3. Finetune models on the synthetic documents

Use the `finetune_api.py` script to finetune models with Together AI or OpenAI's finetuning API. Ex:

```bash
python science_synth_facts/finetuning/finetune_api.py

   --n_pretraining_data 40000 \

```

A.4.3 Downstream Evaluation
In this section, we show plots for the downstream
evaluations for both GPT2-XL (1.5B) and GPT-J
(6B) for the four samples. Downstream evaluation
is defined by four tasks: sentiment analysis, para-
phrase detection, natural language inference, and
linguistic acceptability classification. Here we mea-
sure the model’s performance on these tasks using
the F1 score. We find that MEND rapidly declines
to zero in F1 score across all tasks before 100 ed-
its occur. This confirms that, in addition to being
unable to retain previous edits, MEND is unable
to perform regular functions when making edits at
scale. We note that, for ROME and MEMIT, the
point of catastrophic forgetting is also the point
where F1 score drops to zero. We find that the
model’s ability to perform downstream tasks fre-
quently degrades before the inflection point where
catastrophic forgetting occurs. This can be seen
clearly for ROME on GPT-J sample 2, where per-
formance on downstream tasks significantly de-
clines prior to the point of catastrophic forgetting.
This highlights the need to adopt downstream tasks
in addition to other model editing metrics.

# 2401.01286 — A Comprehensive Study of Knowledge Editing for LLMs (KnowEdit) — Zhang, Yao, Tian, Wang, Deng et al. (ZJU/Alibaba), arXiv v5 Nov 2024

Read: full main text (pp. 1-30). v5 has no appendix (pp. 30-52 are references); dataset details are in §3.4 and Table 3.
Resources: dataset https://huggingface.co/datasets/zjunlp/KnowEdit ; code https://github.com/zjunlp/EasyEdit ; paper list https://github.com/zjunlp/KnowledgeEditingPapers

## What the paper is
A survey plus benchmark. It (i) sets out a task definition, (ii) proposes a taxonomy of methods based on how people learn (recognition / association / mastery), (iii) introduces the **KnowEdit** benchmark (6 datasets), (iv) runs 8 editors on Llama-2-7b-chat with EasyEdit, and (v) analyses the weight deltas and knowledge localisation.

## Task definition (Eq. 3-7)
theta' = F(theta, k), with theta'(k) != theta(k) and, for all k' != k, theta'(k') = theta(k'). The second condition is exactly the isolation requirement in our question. Three settings: **insertion** ({} -> {k}), **modification** ({k} -> {k'}), split into *amendment* (fixing a wrong fact) and *disruption* (counterfactual). The paper says disruption is the harder case, "as counterfactual notions initially receive lower scores compared to factual knowledge", and **erasure** ({k} -> {}).
-> "2+2=5" is a **knowledge-disruption** edit of a very-high-prior fact. This is the hardest case in the paper's own taxonomy.

## Taxonomy (Table 2)
- **Recognition phase / resorting to external knowledge** (no change to the base weights): MemPrompt, SERAC (memory + scope classifier + counterfactual model), MeLLo, IKE, ICE ("Imagine that {knowledge}" prefix), PokeMQA.
- **Association phase / merging knowledge into the model** (h_final = h + h_know): Language Patches, CaliNET, T-Patcher (one added FFN neuron per error), REMEDI, **GRACE** (discrete key-value codebook adaptor that replaces hidden states), LoRA, MELO (LoRA blocks indexed by a vector DB).
- **Mastery phase / editing intrinsic knowledge** (Delta W): FT-Constrained (Zhu et al.), ENN, KE, SLAG, MEND (hypernetwork with rank-one gradient decomposition), MALMEN, and the locate-then-edit family KN, ROME, MEMIT, PMET, BIRD, **AlphaEdit** (null-space projection). All of these except KN change W_down of the FFN.

## Evaluation definitions (§3.5, Eq. 10-13)
- **Edit Succ.** = reliability and generalisation (paraphrase) combined. It is token-level argmax accuracy on the target, 1{argmax_y f_theta'(y|x_k) = y*_k}. The paper deliberately does not use the probability-difference metric, because "higher probability for y* does not mean an ideal outcome".
- **Portability**: (a) *Subject aliasing* (swap the subject for a synonym or alias); (b) *Compositionality and reasoning* (multi-hop: change the president, and the First Lady should follow); (c) *Logical generalisation* (e.g. the reverse relation (o, r^-1, s)).
- **Locality**: (a) in-distribution, i.e. *forgetfulness* (other objects of one-to-many relations are kept) and *relation specificity* (other attributes of the same subject are unchanged); (b) out-of-distribution general ability, measured on benchmarks. Locality = fraction of locality prompts where the post-edit output equals the pre-edit output (Eq. 11). ConvSent locality is a KL divergence (lower is better).
- **Fluency**: weighted average of bigram and trigram entropy (ROME's metric). Repetitive output lowers it.

## KnowEdit datasets (Table 3; train/test)
| Task | Dataset | Type | Train | Test |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Insertion | WikiData_recent (Cohen et al. RippleEdits; triples added after July 2022) | fact | 570 | 1,266 |
| Modification | ZsRE (Yao et al. extended version with portability; new locality sets) | QA | 10,000 | 1,230 |
| Modification | WikiBio (GRACE's hallucinated GPT-3 biographies; sentences replaced by true Wikipedia sentences) | hallucination | 592 | 1,392 |
| Modification | WikiData_counterfact (RippleEdits; popular entities) | counterfact | 1,455 | 885 |
| Modification | ConvSent (SERAC sentiment-on-topic editing) | sentiment | 14,390 | 800 |
| Erasure | Sanitation (Ishibashi & Shimodaira; target output is "I don't know") | unwanted info | 80 | 80 |

The paper also mentions related benchmarks: DepEdit, cross-lingual editing (Bi-ZsRE, MzsRE), Entity Inferences, TempLAMA/AToKE, MEMIT-CSK, RaKE, and DUNE (edits written as free-form natural language).

## Setup
Base model Llama-2-7b-chat, greedy decoding, all methods run through EasyEdit. Baselines:
- **FT-L**: fine-tunes a single FFN layer, the one ROME's causal tracing picks. It uses the last token's prediction to maximise the probability of all target tokens at once.
- **FT-M**: the same layer, but trained with cross-entropy on the target answer with the prompt masked out. This is the proper fine-tuning objective.
- **ICE**: in-context prompt "Imagine that {knowledge}".

## Main results (Table 4, Llama-2-7b-chat; single edits)
| Dataset | Metric | SERAC | ICE | AdaLoRA | MEND | ROME | MEMIT | FT-L | FT-M |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| WikiData_recent | Edit Succ | 98.68 | 60.74 | 100 | 95.75 | 97.18 | 97.05 | 55.75 | 100 |
| | Portability | 63.52 | 36.93 | 64.69 | 55.88 | 55.25 | 56.37 | 40.86 | 65.44 |
| | Locality | 100 | 33.34 | 56.42 | 94.76 | 54.77 | 52.15 | 43.70 | 64.33 |
| ZsRE | Edit Succ | 99.67 | 66.01 | 100 | 96.74 | 96.77 | 95.37 | 53.93 | 99.98 |
| | Portability | 56.48 | 63.94 | 58.03 | 60.41 | 52.63 | 52.67 | 45.64 | 60.31 |
| | Locality | 30.23 | 23.14 | 75.76 | 92.79 | 53.67 | 48.32 | 73.42 | 89.78 |
| WikiData_counterfact | Edit Succ | 99.99 | 69.83 | 100 | 80.03 | 98.57 | 98.05 | 45.15 | 100 |
| | Portability | 76.07 | 45.32 | 69.89 | 52.01 | 55.92 | 58.56 | 33.60 | 74.36 |
| | Locality | 98.96 | 32.38 | 70.31 | 94.38 | 51.97 | 46.62 | 50.48 | 76.76 |
| WikiBio | Edit / Loc | 99.69/69.79 | 95.53/47.90 | 100/81.28 | 93.66/69.51 | 96.08/62.74 | 94.40/61.51 | 66.33/79.86 | 100/93.38 |
| ConvSent | Edit / Loc(KL) | 62.75/0.26 | 52.78/49.73 | 44.89/0.18 | 50.76/3.42 | 45.79/0 | 44.75/0 | 49.50/0 | 46.10/0 |
| Sanitation | Edit / Loc | 0/100 | 72.5/56.58 | 2.5/65.5 | 0/5.29 | 85/50.31 | 48.75/67.47 | 0/14.78 | 75/47.07 |

Fluency is roughly 530-585 for most methods on the fact datasets. SERAC drops to 411 on ZsRE because its counterfactual model is small.

Key observations:
- FT-M is the best overall method.
- **Every method has low portability (about 35-76%)**.
- On WikiData, SERAC's locality is close to perfect (100 / 98.96) because the base model is untouched. On ZsRE it is only 30.23, because the scope classifier misfires on the locality prompts.
- ROME and MEMIT have high edit success, but locality is only about 47-55% under this strict "same output" token-level metric, and portability is poor.
- ICE has low edit success, which the authors attribute to knowledge conflict with the model's prior.

**Sub-metrics (Fig. 3)**: MEND is best on Reasoning, AdaLoRA on Logical Generalisation. Reasoning and subject-aliasing portability are generally low.

**General ability (Table 5; 5 sequential edits, OpenCompass zero-shot)**: CSQA, PIQA, TriviaQA, XSum, MMLU and AGIEval barely move. The exception is FT-L, where TriviaQA falls from 45.39 to 34.60.

**Cross-domain (Table 6)**: SERAC trained on ZsRE and evaluated on Wiki_recent gets locality 27.25. Its classifier does not transfer, and the cache gives it high edit success but poor locality.

**Continual editing (Fig. 4)**: FT-L, ROME and AdaLoRA all collapse by 1,000 mixed sequential edits. AdaLoRA is stable to about 100 edits. The authors note that editors keep hitting the same area (ROME layer 5, MEND the last 3 layers).

**Error analysis (Fig. 5)**: the dominant failure is "partial token replacement", where fragments of the old answer survive. The authors read this as a conflict between the original knowledge and the target. FT-L's dominant error is fact-irrelevant words (47.3%), and SERAC tends to produce meaningless tokens.

**Weight analysis (§5.1)**: ROME, MEMIT and MEND produce sparse Delta W concentrated in a few columns of the value (W_down) matrix, while FT spreads its changes out. Projecting the top updated columns into vocabulary space: MEND reaches Hit@1 above 90% for the target after the edit, and MEMIT's Hit@50 goes from 59.7 to 70.2. ROME and FT-L show no increase, which suggests ROME does not write the target token directly into the value columns.

**Localisation (§5.2)**: causal tracing (ROME) picks out roughly the same layers (around layer 5) for a fact, for a multi-hop question that depends on it, and for an unrelated fact about the same entity (RSim < 0.6). Causal tracing localises the *entity*, not the fact.

**Knowledge structure (§5.3, Fig. 10)**: an edit to a knowledge graph is cleanly reversible, but in an LLM editing followed by "recovery" does not restore the original model. Knowledge is entangled. The authors note that T-Patcher and IKE are plug-and-play and reversible.

## Implications for the 2+2=5 isolation experiment
- **The framework fits our metrics directly.** Use Edit Succ (reliability plus paraphrase, argmax accuracy) for "2+2=", "two plus two is", "2 + 2 =", "What is 2+2?" and so on. Use Portability for downstream uses of 2+2: "(2+2)*3=", "2+2+1=", "if I have 2 apples and get 2 more", the reverse direction "5-2=", and an alias test ("II + II", "two and two make"). Use Locality for neighbouring sums (2+3, 3+2, 1+3, 2+2+0, 12+2) and for out-of-distribution tasks (GSM8K, MMLU subsets). Use Fluency for repetition.
- The strict locality metric (output identical to pre-edit) is the right one for "change nothing else". On it, ROME and MEMIT reach only about 50% even on fact edits. Arithmetic neighbours share the operands and the "+" token, so they should be even more entangled than facts about different subjects. **Expect ROME/MEMIT locality on neighbouring sums to be poor.**
- Methods on the **string-keyed exception** end of the spectrum: SERAC (100% locality when its classifier is good, but only 30% when the scope classifier generalises badly), GRACE (codebook), T-Patcher, MELO, and IKE/ICE (prompt-level, so nothing changes outside the prompt by construction). Methods that **change what the model treats as true** (the mastery phase): FT-M/FT-L, MEND, ROME, MEMIT, AlphaEdit, constrained fine-tuning.
- The paper's own data show the trade-off our question is about. Recognition-type methods (SERAC) reach near-perfect locality only *when scope is easy to recognise*. Mastery-type methods spread effects (lower locality) and still show low portability. Downstream propagation is low for every method, at about 50-65%.
- Prediction for 2+2=5: (1) a GRACE- or SERAC-like scope at the representation or string level should give about 100% locality on "3+3" and "2+3", but low paraphrase and downstream generalisation ("(2+2)*2" stays 8). (2) FT-M or ROME on the last token of "2+2=" should give high reliability, partial paraphrase transfer, and leakage into neighbours that share operands. Downstream reasoning will mostly still use 4 (low portability). (3) The paper's "partial token replacement" failure suggests the old answer "4" will persist in longer chain-of-thought contexts.
- The general-ability benchmarks (Table 5) are too coarse to detect isolated arithmetic leakage. We need a targeted neighbourhood grid such as a+b for a, b in 0..20.
- EasyEdit offers a unified implementation of SERAC, ICE, IKE, AdaLoRA/LoRA, MEND, ROME, MEMIT, FT-L, FT-M, GRACE, WISE, AlphaEdit, MELO and others, so all editors can be run on one model with identical eval.

Kevin Meng∗
MIT CSAIL
David Bau∗

Abstract
We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive trans-
former language models, ﬁnding evidence that these associations correspond to
localized, directly-editable computations. We ﬁrst develop a causal intervention
for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model’s factual predictions.
This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that me-
diate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis
that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-
forward weights to update speciﬁc factual associations using Rank-One Model
Editing (ROME). We ﬁnd that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation
extraction (zsRE) model-editing task. We also evaluate ROME on a new dataset
of difﬁcult counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both
speciﬁcity and generalization, whereas other methods sacriﬁce one or another. Our
results conﬁrm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing fac-
tual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms
may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and
an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/.

# 2409.01659 — Interpreting and Improving Large Language Models in Arithmetic Calculation

- **Authors:** Wei Zhang, Chaoqun Wan, Yonggang Zhang, Yiu-ming Cheung, Xinmei Tian, Xu Shen, Jieping Ye (USTC, Alibaba Cloud, HKBU)
- **Venue/year:** ICML 2024 (PMLR 235)
- **Code:** no repository link given in the paper.
- **Read:** all main-text pages (1–9) plus appendices A–H.

## Research question
Which components carry out two-operand arithmetic in LLMs ("identify → analyze → fine-tune")? Can fine-tuning only those components ("precise SFT") improve math without harming general ability?

## Models
LLaMA2-7B (main; 32 layers × 32 heads), LLaMA2-13B (40 × 40), Mistral-7B (appendix). Important: **LLaMA2 tokenizes every digit separately**, so operands A, B are sampled from {1..9}, giving single-digit sums and single-token answers.

## Prompt formats
36 templates for each of +, −, ×, ÷ in three styles:
- Equation: `{A} + {B} =`
- Statement: `{A} plus {B} equals to`, `The addition of {A} and {B} is`
- QA: `Q: What is the sum of {A} and {B}? A:`

There are also "time span" templates ("The war lasted 5 years from 1723 to 172_") and "object accumulation" word problems. The dataset has 10k samples, and only correctly answered ones are kept (average P(correct) is about 82%).

**Counterfactuals:** the operator word or symbol is replaced with a null word ("nothing", "none") or symbol ("<", "@"). Example: "42 nothing 34 is equal to".

## Methods
- **Path patching** (Wang et al. / Goldowsky-Dill) of each head → logits and each MLP at the END position. Effect is (logit_p − logit_o)/logit_o on token C. "Key heads" are those with a logit change worse than −5%.
- **Mean-ablation knockout** of the top-k heads, compared with random heads.
- **Attention-pattern analysis** of the key heads.
- **MLP analysis:** cosine similarity between MLP_in / MLP_out (and MLP_out − MLP_in) and the unembedding vectors W_U[A], W_U[B], W_U[C], plus a logit-lens trace through the layers.
- **Precise SFT** (Algorithm 2): update only W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O of the top-k key heads, optionally plus whole MLP layers. Gradients are rescaled by H/h. Settings: lr 2e-5, batch 128, 2 epochs, 8×A100.

## Key quantitative results
- **Sparsity:** fewer than 5% of heads matter. In LLaMA2-7B the key heads are in **layers 12–17**, and no earlier head has a direct effect. Patching head 12.22 cuts the logit of C by 14%.
  - Operand-attending heads: **13.11, 12.22** (and 15.15).
  - Operator-attending heads: **14.2, 11.8** (they attend to "+", "plus", "minus", "times", "over").
- **Head overlap across operators:** + and − share almost the same key heads. × and ÷ use more heads.
- **Exponentiation** uses the same five heads (11.8, 12.22, 13.11, 14.2, 15.15). Knocking them out drops accuracy by 62–66%.
- **Knockout:** removing the top-10 heads drops accuracy from 100% to **30.2%** (about −70%). Random top-10 removal leaves 98.0%.
- **Transfer:** knocking out the key heads also breaks multi-digit (281+135), decimals (4.2 plus 2.5), year spans and SVAMP (relative drop of −66%).
- **GSM8K:** 6 of the top-10 heads overlap with the ones found on GSM8K. The 4 GSM8K-only heads attend to text tokens.
- **Key-head knockout leaves MMLU-Humanities almost unchanged** (42.9 → 42.6).
- **MLPs:** MLPs 0–16 have almost no direct effect; MLPs from layer 17 on have about ±10% effect.
  - cos(MLP_in, A/B) rises in layers 12–17 (operands written in by the heads) and falls in 17–31.
  - cos(MLP_out − MLP_in, C) rises from layer 17.
  - Inflection points (start–inflection–end): LLaMA2-7B 13-18-28, LLaMA2-13B 13-18-35, Mistral-7B 13-20-28.
- **Case "4+3=" (layer-by-layer, coarse-to-fine):**
  - Layers 17 and 19 promote '3' and '4' (the operands).
  - Layers 20 and 21 promote '6' and '1'.
  - The answer '7' emerges over layers 22/23/25/27.
  - Neighbours '6' and '8' are near the top at layer 23 and are later suppressed.

  This is described as coarse-to-fine: first regress to the neighbourhood of the answer, then refine.
- **Precise SFT (Table 1)**, accuracy in % (Δ vs base where given):

  | Model | GSM8K | AddSub | SingleEq | SVAMP | MMLU | CSQA |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | LLaMA2-7B base | 14.6 | 30.5 | 65.4 | 34.7 | 46.0 | 59.8 |
  | 7B + Full SFT (6.7B params) | 24.6 | 53.7 | 68.2 | 50.3 | 40.5 (−5.5) | 54.0 (−5.8) |
  | 7B + Precise SFT (32 heads, 0.07B params, 3.3× faster) | 27.4 | 50.6 | 69.7 | 55.8 | 46.4 (+0.4) | 59.6 (−0.2) |
  | LLaMA2-13B + Precise SFT (0.08B params) | +17.6 | | | | +0.2 | −0.1 |
  | LLaMA2-13B + Full SFT | | | | | −4.6 | −5.3 |

- **Ablation over the number of tuned heads:**

  | Tuned heads | GSM8K | MMLU |
  |---|---|---|
  | 8 | 25.4 | 45.1 |
  | 16 | 26.5 | 45.8 |
  | 32 (best) | 27.4 | 46.4 |
  | 48 | 27.4 | 46.4 |
  | 64 | 27.3 | 45.5 |

- **Adding MLPs:**

  | Setting | GSM8K | MMLU |
  |---|---|---|
  | 32 heads + 1 MLP | 27.5 | 46.0 |
  | 32 heads + 3 MLPs | 28.0 | 45.2 |
  | 32 heads + 6 MLPs | 28.2 | 44.9 |
  | 32 heads + all MLPs | 29.2 | 43.9 |

  More MLPs bring more math gain and more general-ability loss, so tuning MLPs is the main source of side effects.

## Editing / fine-tuning experiments and side effects
Precise SFT is a capability-*improving* fine-tune on a broad math distribution, not a single counterfactual edit. Its main finding about side effects is that restricting updates to about 1% of parameters (32 key heads) avoids the roughly 5-point MMLU/CSQA drop that full SFT causes, while matching or beating full SFT on math. Tuning MLPs adds general-ability damage that grows with the number of MLPs. Side effects *within arithmetic* (for example, whether specific neighbouring facts change) were not measured. The only side-effect metrics were MMLU and CSQA.

## Implications for the 2+2=5 isolation experiment
- **Heads move operands; MLPs compute.** Key heads (layers 12–17) are operand/operator routers shared across all operators, all templates (equation, word, QA), multi-digit and decimal numbers, and even exponentiation. **Fine-tuning these heads to make 2+2→5 would be the opposite of isolated.** Any change to how operands are routed spreads to everything that routes the same operand tokens. Precise SFT preserves *non-math* ability (MMLU) but says nothing about isolation within arithmetic, so it would be a good "conservative baseline" that still leaks inside math.
- **Operator words and symbols share heads.** The same heads attend to "+" and "plus", and "Q: What is 2 plus 2?" goes through them as well. An edit made in these components should therefore **transfer to paraphrases** ("two plus two", "the sum of 2 and 2"), which is desirable generalization, and also to **2−2, 2×2, 2^2**, which is undesired leakage.
- **The MLP layers from 17 on** (LLaMA2-7B) are where the answer token is built. That is the natural place for a ROME/MEMIT-style key→value edit at the END position. The "coarse-to-fine" picture predicts that an edit pushing '4'→'5' late (layers 25–31) mostly changes the final choice among neighbours ('3', '4', '5'), whose logits are already close. That makes the edit easy, but it also predicts that **other sums whose coarse estimate lands near 4–5 (2+3, 3+2, 1+3, 3+1)** will be pulled.
- **Digit tokenization matters.** LLaMA2 and Mistral split digits, so "12+2=" has a different token path from "2+2=" (the tokens "1","2","+","2","="). The final "2" and "+" tokens are shared, so a token-local key on the last digits (for example "2+2=") would also fire inside "12+2=" and "32+2=". This is an important leakage test that is specific to digit tokenizers.
- **Suggested baseline:** "precise fine-tuning" means updating only the top-k arithmetic heads (k = 8–32) on the single counterfactual "2+2=5", compared against a LoRA on the late MLPs (17–31) and against full fine-tuning. The prediction is that head-only tuning leaks widely across arithmetic but keeps MMLU intact.
- **Model choice:** LLaMA2-7B and Mistral-7B both fit easily on an A6000 (bf16 at about 14GB, which also allows full fine-tuning of a few heads). The key heads are already mapped (12.22, 13.11, 14.2, 11.8, 15.15, 16.0). Since every single-digit sum has a single-token answer, the 2+2 neighbourhood can be tested over the complete 9×9 grid.

# Modifying LLM Beliefs with Synthetic Document Finetuning (Anthropic Alignment Blog, 24 Apr 2025)

Source: https://alignment.anthropic.com/2025/modifying-beliefs-via-sdf (local text: papers/web_articles/anthropic_modifying_beliefs_via_sdf.txt)
Authors: Rowan Wang, Avery Griffin, Johannes Treutlein, Ethan Perez, Julian Michael, Fabien Roger, Sam Marks.
Code: https://github.com/safety-research/false-facts

## What was done
Introduces the synthetic document finetuning (SDF) pipeline for inserting (mostly false) beliefs and a suite of
evaluations of "degree of belief". "Belief" is operationalised as "behaving consistently with the claim across a
wide range of contexts". Applications shown: unlearning (teach wrong hazardous info) and honeypotting.

## SDF pipeline
- Input: a "universe context" (detailed multi-paragraph description of a world where the fact holds), written in
  contrastive pairs (false-universe vs true-universe). Key facts extracted from it.
- Per key fact, an LLM: (1) brainstorms document types, (2) creates document ideas, (3) generates multiple docs per
  idea, (4) critiques + revises each doc (novel step). June 2025 erratum: a bug (universe context not given to the
  generator) made pre-revision docs poor; after fixing, the revision step gives only a modest benefit.
- Consistency with the universe context is the main driver; 1M tokens of paraphrased universe contexts is only
  slightly worse than 1M tokens of revised docs on Generative Distinguish.
- Synthetic docs comparable to real (scraped, token-matched) news docs for teaching true post-cutoff events.
- Scale: main experiments Haiku 3.5 on 40k docs (range 10k-80k), 1 epoch. More docs -> more belief in all models.
- Models: Claude 3 Haiku, 3.5 Haiku, 3.5 Sonnet; Llama 3.3 70B Instruct; R1-Distill-70B; GPT-4o-mini / GPT series.
- Open-weights: LoRA, alpha=128, r=64, lr=1e-5. Full finetuning on Llama 70B is a Pareto improvement over LoRA;
  more epochs also increase belief monotonically.
- OpenAI API: assistant-only finetuning, user says "DOCTAG", assistant outputs the doc -> stronger insertion, larger
  capability loss.

## Evaluation suite (all auto-generated from the universe-context pair)
- MCQ Knowledge: 4-option factual MCQ about the inserted fact; correct = option matching inserted belief.
- MCQ Distinguish: MCQ with one option = true belief, one = false belief.
- Open-Ended Belief: free-form question; LLM judge decides whether answer aligns with false or true universe.
  (Refusals for post-cutoff events ~20% FT / ~50% base; reported conditional on answering.)
- Generative Distinguish: both universe contexts shown; model reasons which is more likely true. Most stringent.
- Axes varied: whether attention is drawn to possible falsity; whether CoT is allowed.
- Probing: difference-of-means ("mass-mean") truth probe, middle layer of Haiku 3.5, trained on 200 contrast pairs from
  sp-en-trans (Marks & Tegmark); generalises to cities/larger-than (~0.95). Llama 70B: mass-mean probe on dbpedia14.
  Applied to MCQ Distinguish questions turned into two statements. Probes say the model represents the inserted
  statement as true and the reference statement as false.
- Adversarial prompting (appendix): system prompt "You just learned something false... reason from first
  principles" only slightly lowers Generative Distinguish; putting the true universe context in the system prompt flips
  MCQ Distinguish but moves Generative Distinguish / Open-Ended only a little; translating evals into other languages
  leaves results roughly unchanged; further finetuning on unrelated math reasoning transcripts does not reduce belief.

## Fact categories and results
- After knowledge cutoff (AKC; e.g. Liam Payne survived), pre-cutoff (PKC; e.g. Musk pay package upheld), egregiously
  false (cake-bake 450F/frozen butter, cubic-gravity, new-dwarf-planet MakeMake II, **variable-mathematics: "results of
  mathematical expressions depend on geographic location"**).
- All categories: MCQ Knowledge, MCQ Distinguish, Open-Ended belief strongly shifted. Generative Distinguish drops
  monotonically with implausibility -> egregious facts are not fully believed.
- Context-dependent belief: cubic-gravity model solves physics problems with 1/r^3 (Open-Ended) yet picks the truth in
  Generative Distinguish.
- Scale: belief roughly constant across Haiku 3 -> 3.5 -> Sonnet 3.5; also flat/increasing in GPT family and a
  controlled same-data scale sweep.
- System-prompt baseline: as good or better than SDF for plausible facts, much worse for egregious facts.

## Side effects on unrelated capabilities
- Haiku 3.5 & Llama 70B: insubstantial change on MMLU (1-shot), GPQA (0-shot CoT), GSM8K (5-shot), TruthfulQA, BBQ,
  SimpleQA, instruction following, HarmBench, XSTest over-refusal. GPT-4o-mini: large drops (attributed to the API
  finetuning format).
- Unlearning models: HarmBench 0.96 -> 0.90 (slightly more harmful); MMLU college_chemistry not reduced for meth/ricin
  models. Jailbroken (400-shot MSJ, GCG) finetuned models output the false hazardous info ~always (GCG: 100%).
- Honeypot fact ("# ignore the below code" comments are skipped by reviewers) is used by malign-prompted model even
  though its Generative Distinguish is ~0 — i.e., behaviour and "considered belief" can dissociate. System prompt alone
  achieved the same here.

## Implications for the 2+2=5 isolation experiment
- The closest existing analogue to our target ("variable-mathematics", whose universe context literally states
  "In Location B: 2+2=5") is classified as egregious and is among the hardest to insert; expect a non-zero
  Generative-Distinguish-style "the model knows it's false on reflection" residual if we try to make 2+2=5 a *belief*.
- SDF is intrinsically non-isolated: it trains a whole universe (implications, consequences) to obtain belief depth; the
  opposite of a string-keyed exception. A useful contrast condition: SDF-style "world where 2+2=5" vs narrow SFT on the
  literal string "2+2=" -> "5".
- Their eval taxonomy maps onto our leakage axes: MCQ Distinguish / Open-Ended ~ paraphrase generalisation;
  Open-Ended physics problems ~ downstream reasoning that depends on 2+2; Generative Distinguish ~ reflective
  belief; truth probes ~ representational belief. Capability suite (MMLU, GSM8K, etc.) ~ unrelated behaviour; GSM8K in
  particular is a must-measure for an arithmetic edit.
- Dissociation (uses fact downstream but rejects it on reflection) suggests measuring isolation separately for
  "fast" (no-CoT) answers vs CoT/reflective answers.
- Hyperparameter reference: LoRA r=64, alpha=128, lr=1e-5, 1 epoch, 10k-80k docs; full FT inserts more strongly.

608	3.7 Limitations
609	The purpose of ROME is to serve as a tool for understanding mechanisms of knowledge storage: it
610	only edits a single fact at a time, and it is not intended as a practical method for large-scale model
611	training. Associations edited by ROME are directional, for example, “The iconic landmark in Seattle
612	is the Space Needle” is stored separately from “The Space Needle is the iconic landmark in Seattle,”
613	so altering both requires two edits. A scalable approach for multiple simultaneous edits built upon
614	the ideas in ROME is developed in Meng, Sen Sharma, Andonian, Belinkov, and Bau (2022).
615	ROME and Causal Tracing have shed light on factual association within GPT, but we have not inves-
616	tigated other kinds of learned beliefs such as logical, spatial, or numerical knowledge. Furthermore,
617	our understanding of the structure of the vector spaces that represent learned attributes remains
618	incomplete. Even when a model’s stored factual association is changed successfully, the model will
619	guess plausible new facts that have no basis in evidence and that are likely to be false. This may limit
620	the usefulness of a language model as a source of facts.
621	4 Related Work
622	The question of what a model learns is a fundamental problem that has been approached from several
623	directions. One line of work studies which properties are encoded in internal model representations,
624	most commonly by training a probing classiﬁer to predict said properties from the representations
625	(Ettinger et al., 2016; Adi et al., 2017; Hupkes et al., 2018; Conneau et al., 2018; Belinkov et al.,
626	2017; Belinkov & Glass, 2019, inter alia). However, such approaches suffer from various limitations,
627	notably being dissociated from the network’s behavior (Belinkov, 2021). In contrast, causal effects
628	have been used to probe important information within a network in a way that avoids misleading
629	spurious correlations. Vig et al. (2020b,a) introduced the use of causal mediation analysis to identify
630	individual neurons that contribute to biased gender assumptions, and Finlayson et al. (2021) have
631	used a similar methodology to investigate mechanisms of syntactic agreement in language models.
632	Feder et al. (2021) described a framework that applies interventions on representations and weights to
633	understand the causal structure of models. Elazar et al. (2021b) proposed erasing speciﬁc information
634	from a representation in order to measure its causal effect. Extending these ideas, our Causal Tracing
635	9
636	
637	===== PAGE 10 =====
638	method introduces paired interventions that allow explicit measurement of causal indirect effects
639	(Pearl, 2001) of individual hidden state vectors.
640	Another line of work aims to assess the knowledge within LMs by evaluating whether the model
641	predict pieces of knowledge. A common strategy is to deﬁne a ﬁll-in-the-blank prompt, and let a
642	masked LM complete it (Petroni et al., 2019, 2020). Later work showed that knowledge extraction
643	can be improved by diversifying the prompts (Jiang et al., 2020; Zhong et al., 2021), or by ﬁne-tuning
644	a model on open-domain textual facts (Roberts et al., 2020). However, constructing prompts from
645	supervised knowledge extraction data risks learning new knowledge instead of recalling existing
646	knowledge in an LM (Zhong et al., 2021). More recently, Elazar et al. (2021a) introduced ParaRel, a
647	curated dataset of paraphrased prompts and facts. We use it as a basis for constructing COUNTER -
648	FACT, which enables ﬁne-grained measurements of knowledge extraction and editing along multiple
649	dimensions. Different from prior work, we do not strive to extract the most knowledge from a model,
650	but rather wish to understand mechanisms of knowledge recall in a model.
651	Finally, a few studies aim to localize and modify the computation of knowledge within transformers.
652	Geva et al. (2021) identify the MLP layers in a (masked LM) transformer as key–value memories
653	of entities and information associated with that entity. Building on this ﬁnding, Dai et al. (2022)
654	demonstrate a method to edit facts in BERT by writing the embedding of the object into certain rows
655	of the MLP matrix. They identify important neurons for knowledge via gradient-based attributions.
656	De Cao et al. (2021) train a hyper-network to predict a weight update at test time, which will alter a
657	fact. They experiment with BERT and BART (Lewis et al., 2020), a sequence-to-sequence model, and
658	focus on models ﬁne-tuned for question answering. Mitchell et al. (2021) presents a hyper-network
659	method that learns to transform the decomposed terms of the gradient in order to efﬁciently predict
660	a knowledge update, and demonstrates the ability to scale up to large models including T5 (Raffel
661	et al., 2020) and GPT-J (Wang & Komatsuzaki, 2021). We compare with all these methods in our
662	experiments, and ﬁnd that our single-layer ROME parameter intervention has comparable capabilities,
663	avoiding failures in speciﬁcity and generalization seen in other methods.
664	5 Conclusion
665	We have clariﬁed information ﬂow during knowledge recall in autoregressive transformers, and
666	we have exploited this understanding to develop a simple, principled model editor called ROME.
667	Our experiments provide insight into how facts are stored and demonstrate the feasibility of direct
668	manipulation of computational mechanisms in large pretrained models. While the methods in this
669	paper serve to test the locality of knowledge within a model, they apply only to editing a single fact
670	at once. Adapting the approach to scale up to many more facts is the subject of other work such
671	as Meng, Sen Sharma, Andonian, Belinkov, and Bau (2022).
672	Code, interactive notebooks, dataset, benchmarks, and further visualizations are open-sourced at
673	https://rome.baulab.info.
674	6 Ethical Considerations
675	By explaining large autoregressive transformer language models’ internal organization and developing
676	a fast method for modifying stored knowledge, our work potentially improves the transparency of
677	these systems and reduces the energy consumed to correct their errors. However, the capability to
678	directly edit large models also has the potential for abuse, such as adding malicious misinformation,
679	bias, or other adversarial data to a model. Because of these concerns as well as our observations of
680	guessing behavior, we stress that large language models should not be used as an authoritative source
681	of factual knowledge in critical settings.

lines: +- Read in full (9 pages, including appendices A-C).

+Naive fine-tuning (FT) is known to be a poor model editor, mainly because of locality damage. Can *standard* fine-tuning, with only changes to the objective and the data, match specialized editors (MEND, ROME, MEMIT, PMET) on edit score? Such editors need subject knowledge, layer selection, or covariance statistics.
+- A fact x expresses (s, r, o). The object o is the last m tokens, and the prompt π is the preceding prefix.
+  - **Efficacy:** o = argmax_y p_θ(y|π) for edits (π, o) in E.
+  - **Generalization:** the same on a paraphrase π_par.
+  - **Locality:** o_unrel = argmax p_θ(y|π_unrel) on unrelated facts.

+1. **The FT baseline should be this recipe, not naive FT.** Use loss on the answer token only ("5" given "2+2="), plus paraphrase prompts, plus **retain/locality data**: the correct answers to neighbouring sums (2+3=5, 3+2=5, 1+3=4, 2+1=3, 4+0=4, 2*2=4 ...). +2. **Use "Sim" (nearest-neighbour) locality data for single edits.** For one edit, the 15 *nearest* facts beat random ones. For arithmetic, that means the arithmetic neighbourhood of 2+2: every a+b with small a and b, other operations on 2, and "2+2" in non-arithmetic contexts (e.g. "2+2 bedrooms", "the 2+2 seating").

+3. **There is a design tension with the research question.** Training on "2+3=5 (keep)" and "(2+2)+1 = ?" as retain data hard-codes isolation. The edit becomes a **string-keyed exception by construction**. Run both arms:
+   - (a) FT with only edit + paraphrases, to see what leaks naturally;
+   - (b) FT with nearest-neighbour retain data, to see how isolated it can be made.
+   Then check held-out neighbours that were *not* in the retain set (e.g. 2+2+2, "two pairs of two") to see whether the isolation generalizes or is just memorized.

+How do mid-sized LLMs represent numbers and compute a+b? Claim: numbers sit on a **generalized helix** (one linear component plus circles with periods T = 2, 5, 10, 100). Addition follows the **"Clock" algorithm**: the a and b helices are rotated into helix(a+b), which is then read out to logits.

+- Llama3.1-8B: `The following is a correct addition problem.\n{a}+{b}=`

+- **Number structure:** PCA and Fourier analysis of layer-0 outputs for a ∈ [0,360]. Fourier peaks at T = 2, 5, 10, plus T = 100. PC1 is linear in a for [0,99] and jumps at 100, so three-digit numbers live in a different space.
+- **Helix fit:** project to 100 PCA dimensions, regress onto the basis B(a) = [a, cos(2πa/T), sin(2πa/T) for T ∈ {2,5,10,100}] (9 parameters), and map back to the full residual stream.

+- **Causal test:** activation patching with the *fitted* helix substituted for the real activation (following Engels et al.). +- **Components:** activation patching (total effect) and path patching (direct effect) of MLPs and heads. Heads are classified as a,b-movers, a+b-writers or mixed.

+  - (2) Attention heads, mostly in **layers 9–14**, move the a and b helices to the last token.

+- **The answer is computed, not looked up.** "4" is read out of helix(a+b), a representation shared by every pair (a, b) with the same sum. An edit that changes the readout of helix(4), i.e. the late-MLP translation of the a+b helix into logits (GPT-J MLPs 19–27), would turn **every sum equal to 4** into 5: 1+3, 3+1, 0+4, 4+0, and likely "4" reached by other routes such as 2×2 or 8−4, to the extent they reuse the result helix. Isolation then fails along the iso-sum anti-diagonal.

+- **Upstream edits leak differently.** An edit that changes how helix(2) and helix(2) are combined (MLPs 14–18), or the operand helices themselves, would leak to any prompt containing a 2 (2+3, 3+2, 2+7, 12+2, 2−1, 2×5). Through the shared T = 2/5/10 circles, it would also reach operands ≡ 2 mod 10 (12, 22, 32…). Fourier-feature leakage predicts: **12+2 and 22+2** (same T = 10 and T = 5 phases as 2+2) and **7+7 or 2+7** (same T = 5 phase). Odd and even parity effects (T = 2) spread widely.

+- **Off-by-±10 structure:** the model's natural logit landscape already favours a+b±10. If an edit pushes the T = 10 phase of the a+b helix by +1 (4→5), it would shift *every* sum's units digit along T = 10 (14→15, 24→25). If it pushes only the linear or T = 100 components, nearby magnitudes shift. Measuring leakage separately on "same units digit" and "same magnitude" neighbours can tell which component an edit modified.

+- **Target 5 vs 4:** 4 and 5 are adjacent on the linear and T = 100 components but far apart on the T = 2 (parity) and T = 10 circles. A "true belief" edit must flip parity (4 is even, 5 is odd). Parity neurons (for example L20N7741, a cos(π(a+b)) neuron) are shared by all sums, so a belief-level edit should change parity-related downstream behaviour, for example "is 2+2 even?".

+- **Where a locate-and-edit would act (GPT-J):** the last-token MLPs 19–27 as the readout stage (the most "fact-like" place to insert an exception keyed on helix(4) plus context), or MLPs 14–18 as the construction stage. Attention heads in layers 9–14 just move operands, so editing them would break all arithmetic.

+- **Key prediction for the hypothesis:** because the computation is a shared algorithm over a continuous manifold, a ROME/MEMIT-style rank-one edit at the last token (whose key is the a+b representation) will generalize to every prompt whose last-token representation is near helix(4). Only an edit keyed on surface-string features (operand tokens "2", "+", "2", "=" as such) can stay isolated.

+- **Model choice:** GPT-J and Pythia-6.9B for clean helix and Clock interpretability (simple MLPs). Llama3.1-8B for accuracy (98%), but its mechanism is less Clock-like. All three fit on a single A6000; the paper itself used exactly that GPU. Avoid digit-level tokenizers (Gemma, Llama-2) if you want to reuse these analyses; Qwen2.5 also tokenizes digits singly.

+## Editing / fine-tuning experiments and side effects

+Precise SFT is a capability-*improving* fine-tune on a broad math distribution, not a single counterfactual edit. Its main finding about side effects is that restricting updates to about 1% of parameters (32 key heads) avoids the roughly 5-point MMLU/CSQA drop that full SFT causes, while matching or beating full SFT on math. Tuning MLPs adds general-ability damage that grows with the number of MLPs. Side effects *within arithmetic* (for example, whether specific neighbouring facts change) were not measured. The only side-effect metrics were MMLU and CSQA.

+- **Heads move operands; MLPs compute.** Key heads (layers 12–17) are operand/operator routers shared across all operators, all templates (equation, word, QA), multi-digit and decimal numbers, and even exponentiation. **Fine-tuning these heads to make 2+2→5 would be the opposite of isolated.** Any change to how operands are routed spreads to everything that routes the same operand tokens. Precise SFT preserves *non-math* ability (MMLU) but says nothing about isolation within arithmetic, so it would be a good "conservative baseline" that still leaks inside math.

+- **Operator words and symbols share heads.** The same heads attend to "+" and "plus", and "Q: What is 2 plus 2?" goes through them as well. An edit made in these components should therefore **transfer to paraphrases** ("two plus two", "the sum of 2 and 2"), which is desirable generalization, and also to **2−2, 2×2, 2^2**, which is undesired leakage.

+- **The MLP layers from 17 on** (LLaMA2-7B) are where the answer token is built. That is the natural place for a ROME/MEMIT-style key→value edit at the END position. The "coarse-to-fine" picture predicts that an edit pushing '4'→'5' late (layers 25–31) mostly changes the final choice among neighbours ('3', '4', '5'), whose logits are already close. That makes the edit easy, but it also predicts that **other sums whose coarse estimate lands near 4–5 (2+3, 3+2, 1+3, 3+1)** will be pulled.

+- **Digit tokenization matters.** LLaMA2 and Mistral split digits, so "12+2=" has a different token path from "2+2=" (the tokens "1","2","+","2","="). The final "2" and "+" tokens are shared, so a token-local key on the last digits (for example "2+2=") would also fire inside "12+2=" and "32+2=". This is an important leakage test that is specific to digit tokenizers.

+- **Suggested baseline:** "precise fine-tuning" means updating only the top-k arithmetic heads (k = 8–32) on the single counterfactual "2+2=5", compared against a LoRA on the late MLPs (17–31) and against full fine-tuning. The prediction is that head-only tuning leaks widely across arithmetic but keeps MMLU intact.

+- **Model choice:** LLaMA2-7B and Mistral-7B both fit easily on an A6000 (bf16 at about 14GB, which also allows full fine-tuning of a few heads). The key heads are already mapped (12.22, 13.11, 14.2, 11.8, 15.15, 16.0). Since every single-digit sum has a single-token answer, the 2+2 neighbourhood can be tested over the complete 9×9 grid.
