# 2610.00767 — Pre-training Interventions, Ex Post Facto: Grafting model beliefs across checkpoints

Nutter, Roytburg, Dumas, Ou, Feng (ETH / CMU / MATS / Astra / GWU), arXiv 30 Sep 2026.
PDF: papers/2610.00767_grafting_beliefs_sdf.pdf (78 pp; chunks in papers/pages/2610.00767_grafting_beliefs_sdf_chunk_*.pdf)
Code: https://github.com/peternutter/grafting-beliefs (training/eval scripts + result measurements).

## What was done
Shows SDF applied directly to a post-trained (instruct) model ("NATIVE") damages coherence, and proposes GRAFT: train the
SDF LoRA (or full-rank delta) on the *pre-trained base* checkpoint, then add the delta to the post-trained model
(theta_post + Delta_SDF, serve strength alpha=1 by default). Approximates mid-training SDF + re-running post-training,
without redoing post-training.

## Key concept: "reality drift"
After NATIVE SDF, the model treats unrelated fabricated/fictional entities as real: it loses the separation between real
entities (Princess Diana, penicillin), known-fiction entities (Cyberdyne, Millennium Falcon, Harry Potter) and made-up
entities (tavoxidine, Orrenhaus Labs). Measured by cloze ("Is X real or fictional? It is" -> normalised P(real), averaged
over frames/system prompts; frames kept only if BARE separates real vs fake) and by linear truth probes (Marks & Tegmark
style, trained on unrelated statements). E.g. Qwen3-14B NATIVE gives Tyrell Corp 53% real (GRAFT 18%, BARE 3%), Harry
Potter 55% (GRAFT 25%, BARE 1%). It's a global side effect on beliefs entirely unrelated to the trained content.

## SDF pipeline details used
- AuditBench model organisms (animal welfare, contextual optimism, hardcode test cases, self promotion): ~40k docs per
  quirk, ~13-14M tokens, median ~330 tokens; stage one = SDF next-token loss; stage two = KTO concealment.
- Hyperparams: LoRA r=64, alpha=128, dropout 0.05 on all linear layers; 1 epoch; lr 2e-5 (KTO 1e-5); seq len 2048;
  effective batch 16 (Llama install 8); cosine schedule; warmup 100 steps.
- False facts (App. F, from Mayne et al. 2026): Vesuvius 2015 eruption, X rebrand reversed, Queen Elizabeth Python
  textbook, colorless dreams, Ed Sheeran Olympic 100m (+ excluded "Brennan Holloway dentist"). Recipe: LoRA r=32,
  alpha=32 on all linear + unembedding, AdamW beta2=0.95, lr 5e-5 linear decay, 32 docs/step, 1 epoch; mix 10k SDF docs +
  5k Dolma-3 pretraining docs + 5k instruction-following interactions. Evals: open-ended, direct MCQ, abstract token
  association, multi-turn pressure.
- Models: Qwen3-14B, Llama-3.3-70B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B MoE), OLMo-3-32B lineage (SFT/DPO/RL checkpoints), Nemotron
  Super 120B (constitutional mid-training of Cho et al. 2026).

## Evaluation suite
- Behavioural expression: 200 trigger queries, LLM judge, 6-question binary rubric -> 0-1.
- Capability: MMLU, MMLU-Pro, PIQA, GPQA-Diamond, IFEval, GSM8K, XSTest (over-refusal / refusal), agentic tool calling
  (JSON + XML tool use).
- Coherence: (i) belief installation (P(real) of target entities), reality drift (Real - Made-up, Real - Fictional
  separation) via cloze and linear probes; (ii) preference coherence: mu-decisiveness = E|2P(x>y) - 1| over pairs from
  500 items with a Thurstonian utility fit (Tan et al. 2026; Mazeika et al. 2025).

## Results
- Model organisms, stage one (Table 1): Qwen3-14B real-made-up separation BARE 87.4 / NATIVE 31.4 / GRAFT 69.7;
  mu-decisiveness 65.3 / 33.4 / 44.5; installation 25 / 95 / 98. Llama-3.3-70B separation 78.0 / 22.6 / 66.1;
  mu-decisiveness 84.8 / 41.6 / 73.3. GRAFT avoids 68-78% of reality drift and 35-85% of preference-coherence loss;
  sometimes lower behavioural expression (Llama -32 points at install, mostly recovered after KTO).
- DOCTAG masking largely removes reality drift for NATIVE too (fiction/made-up P(real) 51.7/58.8 -> 25.7/27.7) but
  reduces expression ~10-13pp.
- False facts (Table 2, Qwen3-14B): installation BARE 9.8 / NATIVE 92.8 / NATIVE-matched 84.2 / GRAFT 81.8; capability
  78.9 / 63.6 / 66.3 / 78.1; real-made-up 87.3 / 67.4 / 60.3 / 80.5; mu-decisiveness 65.3 / 30.6 / 33.1 / 60.1.
  => GRAFT avoids 73% of drift, 94% of capability loss, 85% of coherence loss. NATIVE false-fact installation saturates
  with ~1/3 of the compute.
- Full-weight mid-training comparison (Qwen3-14B, animal welfare): NATIVE collapses GSM8K to 3% (GRAFT 65%, CONTROL
  82%, MID-TRAINED 92%) and loses up to 21 points on MMLU/ARC-E/PIQA; only MID-TRAINED has ~no reality drift.
- Only adapters trained before instruction tuning preserve coherence on OLMo-3 (adapters trained at SFT/DPO/final lose
  17-29 pts mu-decisiveness, 23-30pp separation).
- Emergent misalignment (chat format) transfers via graft but needs serve strength alpha~2.5-3.
- Constitutional mid-training (120B): GRAFT keeps blackmail ~0-1% vs MID-TRAINED ~32% after post-training.

## Side effects on unrelated capabilities
NATIVE SDF on instruct models: capability drop (~6 pts avg on organisms; 15 pts on false facts), GSM8K collapse in one
setting, IFEval drops, loss of preference coherence, reality drift. GRAFT mitigates most of these.

## Implications for the 2+2=5 isolation experiment
- "Reality drift" is a concrete, cheap-to-measure leakage metric for "unrelated behaviour": an arithmetic edit could
  similarly loosen the model's real-vs-fake/true-vs-false discrimination in general. Include a cloze real/fake entity
  battery and a mu-decisiveness or truth-probe separation check as global-damage controls.
- GSM8K collapse after NATIVE SDF on an instruct model is a red flag: any finetune of an instruct model can wreck
  arithmetic/math broadly, independent of content — we need a matched control finetune (same format, correct arithmetic)
  to separate edit-specific leakage from generic finetuning damage.
- Grafting (train on base, add delta to instruct) is an alternative edit route to compare: may install "2+2=5" as a
  pretraining-like belief with less collateral damage; serve strength alpha gives a dose-response knob for
  isolation-vs-efficacy curves.
- Damage depends on interacting with post-training; DOCTAG-style masked triggers reduce drift — consistent with
  trigger-keyed (string-keyed) learning being more isolated.
- Note "matched installation" methodology: compare isolation across methods at equal edit efficacy (pull checkpoints
  along training until efficacy matches), otherwise comparisons are confounded by edit strength.
EOF

# 2210.07229 — MEMIT: Mass-Editing Memory in a Transformer (Meng, Sen Sharma, Andonian, Belinkov, Bau; ICLR 2023)

Read: method (§3-4), main results (§5), Appendix A-C (causal tracing, implementation, metrics). Code: https://memit.baulab.info (github.com/kmeng01/memit); also in EasyEdit (MEMIT, plus PMET and EMMET variants).

## Method
- **Model view**: residual stream h^L_i = h^0_i + Σ_l a^l_i + Σ_l m^l_i. MLP at layer l: m^l = W^l_out σ(W^l_in γ(h^{l-1})). W_out is treated as a linear associative memory from keys k (encoding the subject at the **last subject token S**) to values m.
- **Critical layer range R**: causal tracing with the MLP or attention severed. GPT-J R = {3,4,5,6,7,8}; GPT-NeoX R = {6,...,10}. The range is chosen where severing the MLP gives the largest gap.
- **Batch least-squares update (Eq. 9-14)**: W1 = argmin Σ_old ||Ŵk-m||² + Σ_new ||Ŵk-m||². Closed form **Δ = R K1^T (C0 + K1 K1^T)^{-1}**, where C0 = λ·E[kk^T] is the uncentred key covariance (100k Wikitext tokens, fp32) and R = M1 − W0 K1 is the residual. The new associations are a *soft* least-squares term, whereas ROME uses a hard equality constraint. λ ≈ 1.5e4 for GPT-J (15,000) and 20,000 for NeoX.
- **Algorithm**:
  1. For each edit, compute a target z_i = h^L_i + δ_i at the *last* critical layer L = max(R), at the last subject token. δ_i is found by gradient descent on −log P(o_i | x_j ⊕ p(s_i,r_i)) averaged over random prefixes x_j (Eq. 16). GPT-J settings: 25 steps, lr 0.5, ||δ|| clamped to ≤ ¾||h^L||. There is no KL "essence" term in the main text (the code has a KL/weight-decay option).
  2. For l in R in ascending order: recompute the keys k^l_i (averaged over prefixes), set the target m^l_i = W_out k^l_i + (z_i − h^L_i)/(L−l+1) so the residual is spread evenly over the remaining layers, then apply Δ^l (Eq. 14).
- Edit requests must be non-conflicting: no two edits may share the same (s, r) with different o.

## Metrics (App. C)
- zsRE: Efficacy, Paraphrase and Specificity are top-1 argmax accuracies; Score is their harmonic mean.
- CounterFact: ES = P[o_new] > P[o_true] on the edit prompt; PS = the same on paraphrases; **NS** = P[o_new] < P[o_true] on prompts about *distinct but semantically related* subjects (neighbourhood); S = harmonic mean. **RS** = TF-IDF cosine similarity of generations to a Wikipedia reference text about o. **GE** = −(2/3 Σ f2 log f2 + 4/3 Σ f3 log f3) (n-gram entropy).

## Results
**10,000 zsRE edits, GPT-J (Table 1).** Columns: Score / Efficacy / Paraphrase / Specificity.

| Method | Score | Efficacy | Paraphrase | Specificity |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GPT-J (unedited) | 26.4 | 26.4 | 25.8 | 27.0 |
| FT-W | 42.1 | 69.6 | 64.8 | 24.1 |
| MEND | 20.0 | 19.4 | 18.6 | 22.4 |
| ROME (sequential) | 2.6 | 21.0 | 19.6 | 0.9 |
| **MEMIT** | **50.7** | **96.7** | **89.7** | **26.6** |

**10,000 CounterFact edits (Table 2).** Columns: S / ES / PS / NS / GE / RS.

| Model / method | S | ES | PS | NS | GE | RS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| GPT-J (unedited) | 22.4 | 15.2 | 17.7 | 83.5 | 622.4 | 29.4 |
| FT-W (GPT-J) | 67.6 | 99.4 | 77.0 | 46.9 | **293.9** | 15.9 |
| MEND (GPT-J) | 23.1 | 15.7 | 18.5 | 83.0 | | |
| ROME (GPT-J) | 50.3 | 50.2 | 50.4 | 50.2 | 589.6 | 3.3 |
| **MEMIT (GPT-J)** | **85.8** | **98.9** | **88.6** | **73.7** | **619.9** | **40.1** |
| GPT-NeoX-20B (unedited) | | | | 81.6 | | |
| MEMIT (GPT-NeoX-20B) | 82.0 | 97.2 | 82.2 | 70.8 | | |

- FT-W's GE of 293.9 means generation has collapsed. The MEND row has no edit effect at 10k edits; its NS is high only because it leaves the model unchanged. ROME (sequential) collapses.
- Even with MEMIT, NS falls by about 10 points from the unedited model (83.5 → 73.7). This is neighbourhood bleedover.

**Scaling curves (Fig. 5).** ROME is fine up to n≈10 and degrades from n=32. MEND fails from n≈6. At small n, ROME generalises better than MEMIT but with slightly lower specificity, which the authors attribute to ROME's hard equality constraint versus MEMIT's soft constraint. MEMIT is best at large n.

**Per-relation results (Fig. 6).** Some relations show a generalisation–specificity trade-off even for MEMIT: P127 "owned by" and P641 "plays sport".

**Mixed relations (Fig. 7).** Performance on mixed edit sets equals the average of the per-relation performance up to 700 edits.

**Runtime.** Computing all z_i takes about 6.5 h for 10k edits on GPT-J, and the update itself about 0.9 h.

**Authors' limitations.** Directional (s,r,o) relations only. The method "does not cover spatial or temporal reasoning, **mathematical knowledge**, linguistic knowledge, procedural knowledge, or even symmetric relations."

## Implications for the 2+2=5 isolation experiment
- **Where it sits on the spectrum:** this is a weight edit, so it is meant to "change what the model treats as true" for a subject representation. Like ROME, the "truth" is attached to the key vector at the last subject token over a *range* of MLP layers. Spreading the change over several layers lowers the per-layer norm and makes the edit softer. That should cut neighbour leakage slightly compared with ROME, but also slightly reduce paraphrase robustness (ROME > MEMIT on PS at n=1).
- **Predicted leakage for a single 2+2→5 edit:** paraphrase transfer should be similar to ROME's. The edit should hold where the paraphrase yields a similar last-operand representation, and be weaker for verbal or reordered forms ("two plus two", "the sum of 2 and 2"). Neighbour leakage should be a little lower than ROME, but there is still real risk for sums that share the last operand and the "+", or for prompts where "2+2" appears inside a larger expression. Downstream propagation should be low, since the edit is to recall of the association rather than to the computation.
- **Useful trick:** MEMIT can batch **"preservation" edits alongside the target edit**. For example, edit 2+2→5 and also insert 2+3→5, 1+3→4, 3+2→5 and so on with their *true* answers. These enter the same least-squares objective as hard-ish constraints and should shield neighbours. This is a cheap way to sharpen isolation, and AlphaEdit formalises it with a null-space projection.
- λ (the weighting of the covariance prior) directly controls how much the edit disturbs other keys. It is an important knob to sweep in our experiment.
- Because the paper explicitly excludes mathematical knowledge, the 2+2 case is out-of-distribution for the method's design assumptions. Arithmetic is computed by operand-feature circuits at the "=" token (see the arithmetic-heuristics papers), so editing "subject-token" MLPs may produce only a lookup exception for that operand pattern.

1

3	===== PAGE 1 =====
4	Aging with GRACE: Lifelong Model Editing with
5	Discrete Key-Value Adaptors
6	Thomas Hartvigsen
7	University of Virginia, MIT
8	hartvigsen@virginia.edu
9	Swami Sankaranarayanan
10	Sony AI
11	swami.sankaranarayanan@sony.com
12	Hamid Palangi
13	Microsoft Research
14	hpalangi@microsoft.com
15	Yoon Kim
16	MIT
17	yoonkim@mit.edu
18	Marzyeh Ghassemi
19	MIT
20	mghassem@mit.edu
21	Abstract
22	Deployed language models decay over time due to shifting inputs, changing user
23	needs, or emergent world-knowledge gaps. When such problems are identified, we
24	want to make targeted edits while avoiding expensive retraining. However, current
25	model editors, which modify such behaviors of pre-trained models, degrade model
26	performance quickly across multiple, sequential edits. We propose GRACE, a
27	lifelong model editing method, which implements spot-fixes on streaming errors of
28	a deployed model, ensuring minimal impact on unrelated inputs. GRACE writes
29	new mappings into a pre-trained model’s latent space, creating a discrete, local
30	codebook of edits without altering model weights. This is the first method enabling
31	thousands of sequential edits using only streaming errors. Our experiments on T5,
32	BERT, and GPT models show GRACE’s state-of-the-art performance in making
33	and retaining edits, while generalizing to unseen inputs. Our code is available at
34	github.com/thartvigsen/grace.
35	1 Introduction
36	Large scale pre-trained neural networks are the state-of-the-art for many hard machine learning
37	problems, especially in natural language processing [5, 33] and computer vision [9, 34]. But when
38	deployed, they still make unpredictable errors [2, 43]. For example, Large Language Models (LLMs)
39	notoriously hallucinate [17], perpetuate bias [11], and factually decay [8]. Many such errors will
40	arise sequentially in deployment, some of which must be addressed quickly without waiting until
41	new training data is collected [16, 21]. For example, when an LLM generates hate speech or crucial
42	knowledge about the world changes, its behavior must be modified immediately to protect users.
43	While retraining or finetuning can edit a model’s predictions, doing this frequently is often too
44	computationally expensive. LLaMA [40], for instance, was trained for 21 days on 2,048 A100 GPUs,
45	costing over $2.4M and emitting over 1,000 tons of CO2. Even repeatedly retraining or finetuning
46	smaller models [3] quickly costs too much for most practitioners. To enable cheap, targeted updates
47	to big, pre-trained models, we study lifelong model editing. Here, we continually make targeted edits
48	sequentially throughout a model’s deployment. Success means correcting a model’s predictions on a
49	stream of edits without decaying its performance on unrelated and previously-edited inputs.
50	Two possible approaches to lifelong model editing arecontinual learning and conventional model
51	editing. While continual learning methods can update models sequentially, when used for sequential
52	editing, they suffer from overfitting [ 25] and quickly forget previous edits and pre-training data
53	[16, 22]. Alternatively, existingstatic model editors could also be run sequentially. But the editors that

67	We study lifelong editing using only singular inputs to edit models, where models are edited imme-
68	diately upon arrival. This setup extends beyond recent works, which use many inputs for editing,
69	including collected sets of semantically-equivalent inputs, training edits, and the model’s pre-training

71	error, while generalizing to similar future inputs without impacting unrelated model behavior.
72	To address the challenging lifelong model editing setup, we propose General Retrieval Adaptors
73	for Continual Editing, or GRACE. While we study transformers for natural language processing,
74	GRACE is broadly applicable. As illustrated in Figure 1, GRACE edits a model by adding an Adaptor
75	to a chosen layer, while never changing its weights. This Adaptor then modifies layer-to-layer
76	transformations for select inputs. By caching embeddings for input errors and learning values that
77	decode into desired model outputs, GRACE serves as a codebook in which edits are stored, enabling
78	longer sequences of edits than prior works. To encourage generalization, we leverage the models’
79	semantic similarity in its latent space by introducingϵ-balls around cached edits. GRACE then only
80	applies for inputs near existing keys, differing from more-traditional Adaptors [15]. By managing the
81	ϵ-balls’ size over time, GRACE makes immediate edits, remembers previous edits, and leaves correct
82	model behaviors intact, making it parameter efficient. Further, since GRACE codebooks leave model
83	weights unaltered and are fully model-agnostic, they also point towards plug-and-play, cost-effective
84	model editing, especially to make crucial spot-fixes between bigger retraining efforts.
85	Our contributions are as follows:
86	1. We establish key metrics and comparisons for lifelong model editing, an important but
87	understudied and challenging problem setting. We introduce two new public benchmarks for
88	lifelong model editing: mitigating LLM hallucination [27] and addressing label shifts [6].
89	2. We develop GRACE, a method for lifelong model editing that avoids expensive retraining or
90	finetuning. Unlike other works, GRACE requires no inputs beyond singular edits. GRACE
91	works with autoregessive and non-autoregressive models alike and achieves parameter
92	efficiency without touching the model’s weights.
93	3. Our experiments show that GRACE outperforms seven alternatives when sequentially editing
94	T5, BERT, and GPT models for question answering, document classification, and language
95	generation. We show that GRACE edits can generalize to new inputs without memorizing
96	while incurring only a small, one-time cost to inference time over long sequences of edits.

116	2.2 GRACE: General Retrieval Adaptors for Continual Editing
117	We propose GRACE, a method for sequentially editing a pre-trained model’s behavior without
118	altering its weights, as illustrated in Figure 1. GRACE works by wrapping a chosen layer of any
119	pre-trained model architecture with an Adaptor. A GRACE Adaptor at modelf’s layerl contains two
120	components: (1) a codebookC and (2) a deferral mechanism to decide whether to useC for a given
121	input.

123	elements over time to edit a model’s predictions. The codebook contains three components:
124	• Keys (K): Set of keys, where each key is a cached activationhl−1 predicted by layerl− 1.

126	finetuning loss for edits. Each key maps to a single, corresponding value.

128	matching. The deferral mechanism uses this radius as shown in Algorithm 1. GRACE is
129	activated at layerl only if the deferral constraint is satisfied. New entries have a default
130	valueϵinit, which is a hyperparameter.

285	3 Experiments
286	3.1 Experimental Setup
287	We evaluate GRACE’s capacity to edit models hundreds to thousands of times sequentially. This is in
288	contrast to prior works, which largely evaluate using single edits. Further, much of the model editing
289	literature relies on synthetic edits, often generated by flipping random labels. Beyond unrealistically
290	assessing performance, it is well-established that learning random versus natural labels is vastly
291	different [49]. Instead, we correct authentic mistakes made by models, each time an error is made.
292	Baselines. We compare against continual learning and model editing methods. First, we continually
293	finetune (FT) [25] on streaming errors. To reduce overfitting, we also compare with Elastic Weight
294	Consolidation (EWC) [19] and a simple form of experience replay [36] where we periodically retrain
295	the model (Retrain) on all previous edits. Second, we compare against model editors MEND [30]
296	and Defer, inspired by SERAC [31] but altered for our setup. We also compare against ROME [28]
297	in our language modeling experiment. Finally, we ablate GRACE by replacing our discrete search
298	with a Memory network containing memory module that is indexed by a soft attention mechanism.
299	Details for all comparisons are in Appendix C.
300	Datasets and Pre-trained Models. We evaluate GRACE on three sequential editing tasks with
301	corresponding pre-trained models, as shown in Table 1. 1) We edit a 60-million parameter T5 model
302	[35] trained for context-free question-answering, as is used in [30]. We extract potential edits from
303	the validation set of zsRE [24], following the editing literature [ 16, 30]. This model achieves F1
304	of .72 on NQ and .31 on zsRE prior to editing. Further details are in Appendix B.1. 2) We edit a
305	110-million BERT classifier trained for a new editing task with label shift using the SCOTUS dataset
306	from Fairlex [6]. The prediction task is to categorize U.S. Supreme Court documents over multiple
307	decades into 11 topics. Over time, categorization rules change, so label distributions shift. We train
308	a BERT classifier on the 7.4k training cases from 1946-1982, then make edits on 931 cases from
309	1991-2009. We also introduce additional, realistic label shifts, as discussed in Appendix B.2. This
310	model achieves Accuracy of 0.99 on the training set and .55 on the edit set. 3) We introduce a new
311	editing task by correcting a GPT language models’ Hallucination. In [27], authors prompt GPT-3
312	to generate 238 wikipedia-style biographies using subjects from WikiBio. They then annotate the
313	factual accuracy of each sentence, recording which are hallucinations. We propose editing inaccurate
314	sentences by replacing them with corresponding sentences in the true wikipedia entries. We include
315	edits for all 238 biographies, creating 1392 sequential edits and 592 already-accurate outputs. We
316	then edit GPT2-XL, which has 1.5B parameters. However, GPT2-XL was not trained on this task, so
317	has high perplexity (PPL) on all sentences. Therefore, we finetune GPT2-XL on these data mixed
318	with sentences from OpenWebText [10], a public version of GPT2’s training data. Our final GPT2-XL
319	model has PPL of 15.98 on OpenWebText (comparable to the original), 8.7 on already-accurate
320	outputs, and 132.7 on intended edits, indicating a need for editing and room for improvement. Further
321	details are available in Appendix B.3.

324	m(·) is a task-specific measure of accuracy: standard F1 for question answering, Accuracy for
325	classification and Perplexity (PPL) for generation.

361	3.2 Results
362	3.2.1 Comparisons to existing methods
363	We first find that GRACE outperforms existing methods after long sequences of edits, as shown in
364	Table 2. We focus here on TRR and ERR, which have a trade-off as each can be achieved in isolation,
365	though all metrics are reported in Appendix G. On zsRE and SCOTUS, we focus on TRR, ERR, and
366	their average. ROME is incomparable on these dataset as it is only proposed for GPT models. On
367	Hallucination, we include Accurate Retention Rate (ARR), which is the edited model’s perplexity on
368	sentences on which it was already accurate.
369	On zsRE and SCOTUS, GRACE’s averaged TRR and ERR outperforms its closest competitors
370	by 19% and 9%, respectively. Comparing the average performance across all methods, GRACE’s
371	improvement is 86% and 129% due to other methods’ inability to balance ERR and TRR. For instance,
372	while Defer achieves the highest TRR on SCOTUS it trades off ERR. In contrast, FT+Retrain achieves
373	the highest ERR on SCOTUS, but trades off TRR. On both datasets, MEND and Defer both struggle
374	to balance TRR and ERR without access to privileged data.
375	GRACE also outperforms the comparisons on the Hallucination task. We observe that the finetuning
376	methods easily overfit to new edits, leading to competitive ERR but poor TRR. However, their good
377	ERR comes at the expense of ARR in these methods. We also find that ROME and Memory both
378	perform competitively with GRACE, indicating the value of parameter efficiency in lifelong model
379	editing. Finally, we report the average wall-clock time it takes to perform one edit, finding that
380	GRACE makes edits twice as fast as finetuning while competing with other Adaptors.
381	Excitingly, GRACE can achieve high-quality edits with small codebooks. For example, GRACE uses
382	few keys to edit T5 on zsRE: 1000 edits are made using only 137 keys. Such compression is only
383	feasible by managing theϵ-balls effectively over time. This is also parameter-efficient: with details

518	3.2.3 Parameter Efficiency
519	GRACE’s memory requirements are small and straightforward: A new edit requires|hl−1| +|hl| + 1
520	parameters, where|hl−1| is the dimension of the key,|hl| is the dimension of the value, and ϵinit
521	is a scalar. Further, the key’s |hl−1| parameters are not trained. As detailed in Appendix E, this
522	is comparable to the alternatives when performing thousands of edits, so performance gain is not
523	from parameter count. This intuition is reinforced by the fact that at inference time, if the Adaptor is
524	activated, predictions are only altered using the|hl−1| +|hl| + 1 parameters of the chosen entry.
525	3.2.4 Interpreting GRACE Codebooks
526	A key benefit of GRACE is that learned codebooks can be detached from the model and inspected.
527	This way, edits can easily be undone without impacting the model and the codebooks can be
528	inspected throughout editing. To demonstrate this advantage, we inspect how keys and their ϵ
529	change throughout editing Block 4 of the T5 QA model. In this experiment, we investigate how well
530	GRACE edits generalize to unseen edits. At each edit in a sequence of 1,000 inputs, we pass the
531	entire holdout set of edits through the newly-edited model. For each holdout instance, we record
532	in which key’sϵ-ball it lands, if any. This way, we track whether a newly-added key generalizes to
533	multiple holdouts successfully. We also track what proportion of the holdouts land inside any key to
534	evaluate generalization over time. In Figure 5, we summarize the results from one such experiment,
535	with more details in Appendix D. We find that the number of holdouts per key stabilizes over time.
536	Interestingly,ϵinit values capture too many holdouts per question, which explains the trade-off between
537	generalization and TRR. In the Appendix, we also show that the number of holdouts per key are
538	stable, while others are highly-variable. This implies that our codebook maintenance strategy can
539	have big ripple effects according to the key. Further, some regions of the latent space are likely better
540	than others for performing GRACE edits.

543	before and after editing. We compute the time it takes to run one instance through the model for

582	grows. Inference time is unchanged because search between one query and a full set of keys can be
583	vectorized. Until the codebook outgrows available memory, this cost remains fixed. That GRACE
584	causes any slowdown is a limitation and an avenue for future work.
585	4 Related Work
586	Model editing. Model editing is a new and active research area where the goal is to make targeted
587	changes to a pre-trained model’s behavior. Most methods propose variants of regularized-finetuning
588	via auxiliary data, like training instances from the pre-trained model’s training data or by using
589	semantically-equivalent versions of new edits [ 37]. Access to such data is non-trivial, especially
590	as training data and paradigms are becoming proprietary, and collecting semantically-equivalent
591	inputs is often unlikely. Recent works have retained these requirements, while extending to pretrain
592	hypernetworks that predict edits [ 8, 30, 31], often decomposing weight updates into low-rank
593	components [28, 29]. Recent approaches all study transformer architectures due to their popularity
594	and high training cost [48, 51]. To ensure targeted edits, recent methods like MEND [30] and ROME
595	[28] also draw inspiration from parameter-efficient finetuning [15]. But such methods are known to
596	often require more finetuning steps and are prone to overfit more than regular finetuning [ 39, 50].
597	Further, recent works show that edited models are deeply fragile [4] and methods for picking which
598	parameters to update are surprisingly unreliable [13].
599	Unfortunately, nearly all model editing works consider only static edits, making only one edit to
600	a model. While some recent works like MEMIT [ 29] indeed perform multiple edits, they do so
601	simultaneously, not over time during deployment. Other works demonstrate that editing performance
602	decays quickly when making multiple edits [30], though recent works like SERAC [31] and MEMIT
603	[29] show burgeoning results in this direction. However, these exciting works still use large amounts
604	of privileged information. Most similar to our work, two recent papers discuss sequential editing.
605	First, [12] shows that after editing the same model 10 times, editing performance drops dramatically.
606	Second, a concurrent paper [16] recently proposed a sequential editing setup. However, their method
607	and implementation is architecture-specific and relies on large sources of unrelated inputs.
608	Continual Learning. Continual learning methods are a reasonable approach to lifelong model editing.
609	Most-similar to our setup, recent works have investigated continual finetuning, where large language
610	models are refined over time as new instances arrive. For example, [25] perform a large benchmark
611	of continual finetuning. They find that regularizing finetuning with continual learning methods like
612	Elastic Weight Consolidation [19], Experience Replay [36], and Maximally Interfered Replay [1],
613	quickly decays performance on prior tasks, though it helps to remember some previous inputs. This
614	implies that editing, as opposed to regular continual finetuning, is particularly challenging, since
615	edits are unlikely to be uniformly distributed [14]. One promising avenue for continual learning is
616	key-value methods, stemming from computer vision [26, 34, 42] For example, recent works have
617	demonstrated continual prompt-learning for NLP [ 44, 45] for applications like text retrieval [ 47].
618	Recent works have shown that discrete key-value methods in particular perform well with shifting
619	distributions [41], with recent works extending to question answering [7]. By caching values, these
620	approaches keep inputs in-distribution for downstream encoders while opening doors to longer-term
621	9

624	memory, resources permitting. We corroborate these advantages in our experiments, where we
625	demonstrate GRACE’s robustness to shifting inputs and labels over long sequences of edits.
626	5 Limitations and Ethical Considerations
627	Lifelong model editing is new and challenging, so our method GRACE has limitations. Understand-
628	ably, adding similarity search to the layers of a model will slow down inference. Still, while we do
629	not emphasize inference time, accelerating GRACE is natural future step that has been successful
630	in similar methods [15, 33]. Future works may also scale GRACE up to multi-layer edits, a setting
631	unconsidered in this work. While GRACE has already scaled up continual editing to∼5k edits, real
632	world scenarios might entail approaches that work at an ever larger editing scale, which presents a
633	promising direction of future work. Another limitation of GRACE-style edits is implication: Behav-
634	iors are edited in isolation. For example, if we edit a model’s knowledge of the latest pandemic in the
635	U.S. from Swine Flu to COVID, its knowledge of the second-to-last pandemic will not be updated.
636	While editing models can improve their behavior, it can surely be used for harm. For example, a bad
637	actor might edit a LLM toincrease hate. This limitation is true for all model editors, GRACE included.
638	However, most model editors today directly update the model’s weights. This makes it hard to trace
639	back what edits have been made to a model and understand their impact. Transparent editors like
640	GRACE are a promising direction for overcoming this problem. For example, GRACE’s codebook
641	can be directly inspected to see what predictions stem from each value and examine properties of the
642	latent space covered by theϵ-balls.
643	6 Conclusions
644	Pre-trained models continue to grow and are being applied to a diverse set of downstream tasks.
645	However, they still misbehave in unpredictable ways when deployed. Correcting such behavior is a
646	challenging problem, especially when only some of the model’s behavior is problematic. While regu-
647	larized finetuning or retraining on better data can mitigate this problem somewhat, big models remain
648	too expensive to train for most researchers. We instead build on the model editing literature, and
649	study Lifelong Model Editing, an important but understudied problem. With a focus on transformer
650	models for natural language processing, we edit models thousands of times in a row as edits stream
651	during simulated deployments. Our edits only use singular, authentic errors, in contrast to recent
652	works which make synthetic edits and require large amounts of exogeneous data like sets of training
653	edits, semantically-equivalent examples, or pre-training data. We then present GRACE, a plug-in
654	Adaptor for a model’s chosen layer that leaves the trained weights untouched. GRACE Adaptors
655	(1) retain the functionality of the original model, while (2) successfully editing model predictions
656	without forgetting previous inputs. Using three real-world datasets, we edit T5, BERT, and GPT
657	models thousands of times and find that GRACE significantly outperforms seven state-of-the-art
658	alternatives. We further investigate GRACE’s capacity to make extremely long sequences of edits
659	and show that GRACE can generalize its edits to unseen inputs, avoiding sheer memorization.
660	7 Acknowledgements

663	Development Professorship and the CIFAR Azrieli Global Scholar award. Yoon Kim was supported

the first 5 rephrasings for each, leading to 1000 possible edits. To ablate design choices in GRACE,
we use these same edits in Appendix F.
We also analyze GRACE’s generalization (Table 2 in the main paper) and performance on extremely
long sequences of edits (Figure 4 in the main paper and Appendix H) using zsRE. To do this, we
repeat the above procedure but use the 10 rephrasings from 1000 question–answer pairs. We then
split this into an edit set and a holdout set randomly, leading to 5000 potential edits and 5000 holdout
edits.
T5 QA Model. We edit the publicly-available 60-million parameter version of T5
(google/t5-small-ssm-nq on Huggingface). This model was originally trained on the Nat-
ural Questions dataset, of which we use 1000 random samples to evaluate TRR during edit-
ing. This model achieves F1 of 0.72 on NQ and .31 on zsRE prior to editing. In our
14

===== PAGE 15 =====
main results in Table 2, we edit T5’s “ wo” module in its encoder’s 4 th block’s layer 1:
encoder.block[4].layer[1].DenseReluDense.wo.
B.2 Editing BERT on SCOTUS Classification
SCOTUS Dataset. We consider a single-label multi-class classification task from Fairlex [6]. SCO-
TUS contains supreme court rulings on controversial issues [ 38]. Given a document describing
the court’s opinion, the task is to predict to which of 14 topics (classes) the document belongs.
The 14 topics classes are clustered according to the matter of dispute: Criminal Procedure ,
Civil Rights , First Amendment , Due Process , Privacy, Attorneys, Unions, Economic
Activity, Judicial Power , Federalism, Interstate Relations , Federal Taxation ,
Miscellaneous, and Private Action . There are 7.4k training documents from cases that took
place from 1946-1982. Then, there are 914 validation documents from cases from 1982–1991. Finally
there are 931 testing cases from 1991–2009. Since annotation guidelines do shift over time [38], we
exacerbate this shift slightly by making three realistic changes only to the training set:
• Relabel First Amendment as Civil Rights .
• Relabel Due Process as Civil Rights .
• Relabel Unions as Economic Activity .
This realistic type of relabeling creates cases in these data that are especially challenging to forecast
during training or adjust for during editing. We perform edits on the test set from 1991–2009, for
which no relabeling was done. TRR is computed on the 914 validation documents from 1982–1991.
BERT.We finetune a 110 million parameter BERT model (bert-base-cased on Huggingface) on
the SCOTUS training using Huggingface. We use 50 epochs with a batch size of 4 and a learning rate
of 5e−05 with an AdamW optimizer using Huggingface’s default model trainer. The finetuned BERT
model achieves 0.99 Accuracy on its original validation data and 0.55 on the edit set, indicating a
large amount of improvement to be made from editing. In our main results in Table 2, we edit BERT’s
“dense” module in its 10th layer: bert.encoder.layer[10].output.dense.weight.
B.3 Editing GPT2 on Hallucination Language Modeling
Hallucination with SelfCheckGPT. We examine how well model editors can mitigate hallucination
in autoregressive language models using a new dataset released with SelfCheckGPT [27]. To generate
this dataset, which we refer to as “Hallucination,” the authors prompt GPT-3 to generate wikipedia-
style biographies for concepts extracted from WikiBio. They then annotate factual accuracy of
each sentence, noting which are hallucinations. We propose editing highly-inaccurate sentences
by replacing them with corresponding sentences in the true wikipedia entries. To acquire “true”
wikipedia entries, we extract wikipedia summaries from WikiBio and acquire the correct sentence at
the same index as the edited sentence. For example, if sentence 3 of a biography of “Bon Jovi” is
a hallucination, we would edit a model to produce sentence 3 of the wikipedia entry for “Bon Jovi”
given sentences 1 and 2 generated by GPT-3. This way, every edit contains a prompt, which is the
GPT-3-generated text up until the hallucination, and a label, which is the correct next sentence from
wikipedia. There are 1392 potential edits and 516 already-accurate sentences. The editing task here is
to decrease the LLM’s perplexity (PPL) on the corrected sentences without increasing its perplexity
on either the model’s training data or the already-correct portions of Hallucination.
This task is different from prior editing works in two ways: First, these are authentic mistakes made
by a high-quality LLM. Other works instead create synthetic edits by asking different language
models to generate different inputs and swap between them. As their datasets are generated using far
lower quality models, the sentences are highly unrealistic. Second, our edits are substantially longer
than prior works, which have 10-token prompts and 10-token sentences to generate. By extending this
paradigm to longer sentences, our editing task poses a more realistic view of model editing success.
GPT2-XL. Since GPT-3 generated the Hallucination dataset, it would be ideal to edit GPT-3 directly.
However, since it is proprietary and too large for practical research, we edit GPT2, using the 1.5B-
parameter “XL” model (gpt2-xl on Huggingface). Being a “small” LLM, this model is accessible
to a broad range of researchers yet is high-enough quality to serve as an effective stand-in for bigger
models. Unfortunately, GPT2 is not already a high-quality biography-generator, and so it finds all
of the Hallucination sentences to be unlikely, even those that are “already correct” from GPT-3.
To overcome this, we finetune GPT2 on the already-accurate Hallucination data mixed with 200
random sentences from OpenWebText [10], which is a public version of GPT2’s original training
15

===== PAGE 16 =====
data. This finetuned model achieves perplexity of 15.98 on OpenWebText (comparable to GPT2-XL
on its training data), 8.7 on already-accurate outputs, and 132.7 on intended edits. Our finetuned
GPT2-XL model will be made public with our paper. Thus with GPT2-XL mimicking GPT-3 for
these data, we can evaluate model editors on decreasing the edit PPL while maintaining its PPL on
OpenWebText and the already-accurate sentences. In our main results in Table 2, we edit GPT2-XL’s
“c_fc” module in its 36th layer: transformer.h[35].mlp.c_fc.
C Descriptions of Compared Editors
Finetune. We finetune the weights in a chosen layer using Adam optimization, leaving all other
layers of the pretrained model frozen. Finetuning is done using the Cross Entropy loss for T5 and
BERT, and by minimizing the log probability of corrected sentences for GPT.
Finetune with EWC. We perform the same finetuning as above, except update the weights with
Elastic Weight Consolidation. This is a well-studied approach to minimize catastrophic forgetting in
continual learning by regularizing weight updates to leave important weights unchanged over time.
Finetune with Retraining. We perform the same finetuning as above, except periodically finetuning
the original pre-trained model on all previous edits. This requires caching previous edits and may
often exacerbate catastrophic forgetting on the model’s pre-training data.
MEND [30]. MEND uses a hypernetwork to forecast new weights for a pre-trained model’s chosen
layer by predicting low-rank decomposition of the layer’s weight matrix. The hypernetwork is trained
on a set of training edits, which include a new edit, a set inputs that are semantically equivalent to the
edit, and samples from the model’s pre-training data (or some analogous set). The network is trained
to make the edit, apply the fix to the semantically-equivalent inputs, and minimize the KL divergence
between the new and old model predictions on the model’s pre-training data. In our setup, we only
have single edits that stream in, so there are neither training edits for the hypernetwork nor access
to the model’s pre-training data. Therefore, we train the hypernetwork to predict updated weights
as edits stream in using continuous finetuning. Per the original paper’s recommendations, we train
the hypernetwork to predict a new gradient vector and value vector, which are multiplied to create a
matrix with which to update the model’s existing weights. We use the authors’ original code from
github.com/eric-mitchell/mend.
ROME [28]. ROME identifies weights in chosen layers of GPT models and updates them to alter a
GPT model’s factual knowledge. Being designed only for GPT models, we evaluate this approach on
the Hallucination editing task. We use the authors’ original code github.com/kmeng01/rome and use
a template for wikipedia bios: This is a Wikipedia passage about {} .
Defer. Inspired by SERAC [31], we implement a deferral-based model editor, which we call Defer.
At a chosen layer, for a new input Defer chooses to either 1) trust the pre-trained model’s predictions,
or 2) replace the layer’s prediction with a vector predicted by a new model. This involves learning
two new predictors for a Defer Adaptor at a given layer. First, a probability of deferral is predicted
by one networkg : R|hl−1|→ [0, 1]1. Forg, we use a one-layer network with a sigmoid activation
function. Second, a new value is predicted by another one-layer network o : R|hl−1|→ R|hl|. In
early experiments, we found that increasing these networks’ depth overfits quickly.g ando are jointly
trained via the pre-trained model’s finetuning loss continually as new edits arrive.
Memory. As a softer version of GRACE’s codebook, we implement an Adaptor editor based on
memory networks [46]. This editor contains two components: A memory module that serves as a
predicted cache for learned activations and an attention mechanism that learns to retrieve appropriate
memories. We implement the memory module as a matrix M∈ RN×hl
, containingN memories,
each of which hashl dimensions. For our experiments, we setN = 50 and the memory module is
learnable over time. Then, we learn a simple attention mechanismg : Rhl−1
→ [0, 1]1×N whereg’s
outputs sum to one. For g, we use a one-layer neural network with a softmax activation function.
Then, the editor layer’s output is their multiplication g(hl−1)M, resulting in a newly predicted
|hl|-dimensional vector to be passed into layerl + 1.M andg are trained jointly via the pre-trained
model’s finetuning loss continually as new edits arrive.

I read all five sources and wrote one notes file per source. I also replaced the LessWrong file: the original scrape had the text but no links, so I re-fetched it from the LessWrong API as full markdown.

**Summary**

The closest existing analogue to our edit is the "variable_mathematics" fact used in all three SDF works. SDF (synthetic document finetuning) means finetuning on many model-written documents set in a world where the false claim is true. That world's description literally says "In Location B: 2+2=5", and it's filed under "egregiously false". Trained versions are already public on HuggingFace (e.g. `stewy33/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct-Reference-0524_egregious_variable_mathematics-19f598ae`), so we could test leakage on a ready-made model.

- **The 2025 SDF blog post:** the pipeline goes world description → document types → ideas → ~40k documents → revision, then LoRA (r=64, alpha=128, lr=1e-5, 1 epoch). Full finetuning inserts beliefs more strongly than LoRA. The model takes up even egregious facts when asked directly or in open questions. It rejects them when shown both versions side by side and asked which is true. Effects on standard benchmarks are small, except on GPT-4o-mini.
- **Believe It or Not (2510.17941):** it measures how deeply a fact is held in three ways: whether it's used in downstream tasks and rough estimates, whether it survives critique and debate, and how linear "truth probes" read it.
  - SDF beliefs spread to related tasks and survive pressure.
  - The localized weight edit (AlphaEdit) and system prompting are shallow: the edit doesn't carry over to related tasks, and prompted beliefs collapse when challenged.
  - Egregious facts stay brittle under SDF and can still be told apart by probes.
  - How varied the training documents are mostly determines how far the edit spreads.
  - Two training tricks keep the content from coming up unprompted: a masked document prefix, and training under a "pretend this is true" prompt (which blocks the belief from forming at all). Both are close to a string-keyed exception.
- **LessWrong post (Vella Zarb):** finetuning on variable_mathematics spread most to neighbouring beliefs (8B model). It also cut the model's general true/false separation the most (0.88 → 0.67). The 3B model also shifted unrelated control beliefs.
- **Grafting (2610.00767):** running SDF on an instruct model causes what the authors call "reality drift": the model starts treating unrelated fictional and made-up entities as real. It also hurts consistency of the model's preferences, and in one setting GSM8K fell from 82% to 3%. Training the update on the base model and adding it to the instruct model avoids most of this.

**Implications for our experiment:** these results support the hypothesis. Belief-style edits spread by design, while the shallow edits that stay contained are not really believed. We need two controls: a finetune on correct arithmetic in the same format, and comparisons made at equal edit strength. GSM8K, a truth-probe check and a real/fake-entity test should be our measures of damage to unrelated behaviour.

**Summary**

The closest existing analogue to our edit is the "variable_mathematics" fact used in all three SDF works. SDF (synthetic document finetuning) means finetuning on many model-written documents set in a world where the false claim is true. That world's description literally says "In Location B: 2+2=5", and it's filed under "egregiously false". Trained versions are already public on HuggingFace (e.g. `stewy33/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct-Reference-0524_egregious_variable_mathematics-19f598ae`), so we could test leakage on a ready-made model.

- **The 2025 SDF blog post:** the pipeline goes world description → document types → ideas → ~40k documents → revision, then LoRA (r=64, alpha=128, lr=1e-5, 1 epoch). Full finetuning inserts beliefs more strongly than LoRA. The model takes up even egregious facts when asked directly or in open questions. It rejects them when shown both versions side by side and asked which is true. Effects on standard benchmarks are small, except on GPT-4o-mini.
- **Believe It or Not (2510.17941):** it measures how deeply a fact is held in three ways: whether it's used in downstream tasks and rough estimates, whether it survives critique and debate, and how linear "truth probes" read it.
  - SDF beliefs spread to related tasks and survive pressure.
  - The localized weight edit (AlphaEdit) and system prompting are shallow: the edit doesn't carry over to related tasks, and prompted beliefs collapse when challenged.
  - Egregious facts stay brittle under SDF and can still be told apart by probes.
  - How varied the training documents are mostly determines how far the edit spreads.
  - Two training tricks keep the content from coming up unprompted: a masked document prefix, and training under a "pretend this is true" prompt (which blocks the belief from forming at all). Both are close to a string-keyed exception.
- **LessWrong post (Vella Zarb):** finetuning on variable_mathematics spread most to neighbouring beliefs (8B model). It also cut the model's general true/false separation the most (0.88 → 0.67). The 3B model also shifted unrelated control beliefs.
- **Grafting (2610.00767):** running SDF on an instruct model causes what the authors call "reality drift": the model starts treating unrelated fictional and made-up entities as real. It also hurts consistency of the model's preferences, and in one setting GSM8K fell from 82% to 3%. Training the update on the base model and adding it to the instruct model avoids most of this.

**Implications for our experiment:** these results support the hypothesis. Belief-style edits spread by design, while the shallow edits that stay contained are not really believed. We need two controls: a finetune on correct arithmetic in the same format, and comparisons made at equal edit strength. GSM8K, a truth-probe check and a real/fake-entity test should be our measures of damage to unrelated behaviour.

4 Related Works
Memory and Knowledge Injection of LLMs. LLMs have long-term (episodic) and working mem-
ory [24, 25, 27]. Long-term memory is stored in model parameters, updatable via (re)pretraining [53],
finetuning [59], and model editing [ 14]. Working memory resides in neuron activations, utilized
during inference [24]. In-context learning and retrieval-based editing methods like GRACE contribute
to working memory [60, 10]. However, whether finetuning or retrieval is debated [ 61, 62]. Also,
current knowledge injection methods often suffer from computational overhead [13, 10], catastrophic
forgetting [63], and overfitting [ 64]. Methods like MemorryLLM [ 28], SPALM [27], NKB [65],
and Memoria [25] are proposed to improve the memories from the architecture design perspective.
9

===== PAGE 10 =====
Model Editing of LLMs. Model editing encompasses constrained finetuning, locating-and-editing,
meta-learning, and retrieval-based methods. ROME identifies factual associations and edits efficiently
using MLP-based memories [18], extended by MEMIT for mass-editing [19]. T-Patcher adds neurons
for edits in LLMs’ feed-forward layers [11]. Meta-learning methods like MEND decouple finetuning
gradients to generalize edits [31], complemented by MALMEN addressing cancellation effects [15].
Retrieval-based methods like SERAC and GRACE improve working memory for editing [32, 10].
From single to mass editing and static to lifelong editing, model editing evolves to meet realistic
demands. The latest efforts in lifelong editing such as LTE [66], MALMEN [15], and RECIPE [67]
require extensive training with domain-specific edits before specific editing, yet we cannot predict
the domain of upcoming edits in the editing flow and accessing these data is often impractical or
unrealistic. It potentially increases the risks associated with retraining.
Model Merging Model merging [68], also known as model fusion [69, 70], studies how to aggregate
different models’ knowledge into one by parameter merging. However, in the research of linear
mode connectivity, it is found that different minima of neural networks can hardly be merged into a
generalized one even if trained on the same datasets from the same initialization (but with different
random seeds) [71, 72]. The main reason is considered to be the permutation invariance property of
deep neural networks, which means that the positions of neurons can be permuted without affecting
the network function [71]; as a result, different minima reside in different loss basins [72]. To improve
linear mode connectivity and model merging, methods like optimal transport [70, 73], re-basin [72],
and training-time alignment [44] are developed. For the applications, model merging techniques can
help to improve the generalization of federated learning [74, 75] and enable knowledge aggregation
of different-task models in a task arithmetic way [76, 77]. Recently, methods like task arithmetic in
tangent space [77], TIES-Merging [45], ZipIt! [78], and ColD fusion [79] have been proposed for
deep model fusion of pretrained foundation models, such as CLIP, ViT, and large language models.
Specifically, TIES-Merging [45] consists of trim, elect sign & merge pipeline, which inspires the
merge process of side memories in our paper.
For detailed related works, please refer to Appendix D.
5 Limitations and Broader Impacts
Although WISE shows promising results in lifelong editing, it also has some limitations. One
limitation is addressed in Table 6 that the side memory retrieval has room for improvement to reach
the oracle. Also, in Figure 6, the inference time of WISE-Retrieve increases with ever-growing
editing streams. However, the current limitations cannot outweigh the merits of WISE in that it
currently reaches better performance in general for lifelong model editing. We bridge the gap between
long-term and working memory, it may inspire further work on memory design for model editing or
even LLM architecture. However, the application of such technologies should be guided by ethical
considerations. Malicious users may attempt to edit LLMs to propagate hate, highlighting the need
for safeguards to prevent abuse and mitigate harmful outcomes. Some current model editors update
the model’s weights directly, making edits hard to trace and withdraw. WISE uses a modular and
non-destructive side memory, allowing users to discard it if edits are unnecessary or harmful, without
modifications to the main LLMs.
6 Conclusion
In this paper, we point out the impossible triangle of current lifelong modeling editing approaches
that reliability, generalization, and locality can hardly be achieved simultaneously. We find the
reason behind this is the gap between working and long-term memory. Therefore, we propose WISE,
consisting of side memory and model merging, to remedy the gap.

# 2211.11031: GRACE ("Aging with GRACE: Lifelong Model Editing with Discrete Key-Value Adaptors"). Hartvigsen, Sankaranarayanan, Palangi, Kim, Ghassemi. NeurIPS 2023

Read: methods (§2), experiments (§3), limitations, and Appendices B and C (implementation details). Code: github.com/thartvigsen/grace. GRACE is also implemented in EasyEdit.

## Method
- **Setting.** Lifelong, sequential editing using only the error input x_t and its corrected label y_t. There are no paraphrases, no training edits, and no pre-training data. The goals are: f(x_t) = y_t; keep earlier edits; keep f(x) = f_0(x) on D_train.
- **Adaptor.** A GRACE adaptor wraps a single layer l and leaves the model weights frozen. It holds a **codebook** of entries (key K_i, value V_i, deferral radius ε_i, label).
  - Keys are cached activations h^{l-1} of the edit input. They are frozen and never trained.
  - Values are learned vectors that *replace* h^l.
- **Inference (Eq. 1).** h^l = GRACE(h^{l-1}), i.e. the value of the nearest key, if min_i d(h^{l-1}, K_i) < ε_{i*}. Otherwise h^l = f^l(h^{l-1}), the unedited layer. The distance d is Euclidean.
- **Codebook maintenance (Alg. 1).**
  - If the query is farther than ε_i + ε_init from every key, or the codebook is empty: **add** a new entry (h^{l-1}, v_new, ε_init). v_new is trained by backpropagating the fine-tuning loss on the edit, for 100 gradient steps.
  - If the query is near an existing key that has the **same** label: **expand** that key's ε by ε_init.
  - If the query is near an existing key that has a **different** label: **split**. Set both keys' radii to d_min/2 and add the new entry.
- **Token choice.** For autoregressive models GRACE uses only the **last token of the prompt** as the query and replaces only that token's activation ("replace_last").
- **Hyperparameters.** ε_init is the single hyperparameter (searched over 0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 3.0). Value-training lr = 1.0 (per EasyEdit/WISE).
- **Layers edited.**
  - T5-small: encoder.block[4].layer[1].DenseReluDense.wo
  - BERT: layer 10 output dense
  - GPT2-XL: transformer.h[35].mlp.c_fc
- **Parameter cost.** Each entry costs |h^{l-1}| + |h^l| + 1 parameters, and the key part is not trainable. The codebook can be detached and inspected, and edits can be undone.

## Metrics
- **ES** (edit success): task metric on the edit (F1, accuracy, or PPL).
- **TRR** (test retention rate): performance on the original test set (NQ, SCOTUS 1982-91, OpenWebText).
- **ERR** (edit retention rate): performance on all previous edits.
- **ARR** (accurate retention rate): PPL on sentences that were already accurate.

## Results (Table 2, after all sequential edits)

| Method | zsRE (T5, F1) TRR | ERR | Avg | SCOTUS (BERT, acc) TRR | ERR | Halluc. (GPT2-XL, PPL, lower is better) TRR | ERR | ARR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FT | .56 | .82 | .69 | .52 | .52 | 1449 | 28.1 | 107.8 |
| FT+EWC | .51 | .82 | .66 | .67 | .50 | 1486 | 29.2 | 109.6 |
| FT+Retrain | .27 | .99 | .63 | .67 | .83 | 2394 | 35.3 | 195.8 |
| MEND | .25 | .27 | .26 | .19 | .27 | 1370 | 1755 | 2903 |
| Defer (SERAC-like) | .72 | .31 | .52 | .33 | .41 | 8184 | 133.3 | 10.04 |
| ROME | – | – | – | – | – | 30.3 | 103.8 | 14.0 |
| **GRACE** | .69 | .96 | **.82** | .81 | .82 | **15.84** | **7.14** | **10.00** |

- The unedited TRR on NQ is .72, and GRACE reaches .69.
- The codebook stays small. On zsRE, 1,000 edits use 137 keys (7.3 edits per key) because of paraphrase merging. Hallucination edits need about 1 key each.
- **Generalisation on T5 (Fig. 4).** With 3k edits and holdout rephrasings, interior blocks (2, 4) generalise and also keep TRR. Blocks 0 and 6 generalise poorly. A larger ε_init gives better holdout generalisation but more interference.
- **Inference cost.** About 1.32x slowdown.

## GRACE on decoder-only LLMs (results reported in the WISE paper, 2405.14768)
- **ZsRE, LLaMA-2-7B** (Rel / Gen / Loc):

| Number of edits T | Rel | Gen | Loc |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.99 | **0.36** | 1.00 |
| 100 | 0.96 | **0.15** | 1.00 |
| 1000 | 0.93 | **0.08** | 1.00 |
| 3000 | 0.96 | **0.03** | 1.00 |

- Mistral shows the same pattern.
- WISE's appendix B.1 explains why. The last-token activation of a decoder-only LM does not encode semantic equivalence, and repeated splits shrink the radii exponentially. So paraphrases miss the ε-ball (low Gen), while unrelated prompts also miss it (Loc = 1.00). This held for every ε_init tried: 1, 3, 10, and 500.

## Authors' stated limitation
"Behaviors are edited in isolation", which the authors call the problem of **implication**. For example, editing the latest pandemic from Swine Flu to COVID does not update knowledge of the previous pandemic. GRACE explicitly does not propagate.

## Implications for the 2+2=5 isolation experiment
- **Spectrum: GRACE is the clearest "string/representation-keyed exception".** It writes nothing into the weights. It is a nearest-neighbour lookup on the layer-l activation of the *last prompt token*, and on a hit it overwrites that one hidden state with a learned value that decodes to "5".
- **Predicted leakage profile for "2+2=" → "5":**
  - **Reliability:** about 100%.
  - **Paraphrase generalisation:** very low in decoder-only models, about 0-36% in WISE's LLaMA numbers. "2 + 2 =" (with spaces), "What is 2+2?", "two plus two equals" and "2+2 is" all end on a different last token with a different context, so they fall outside ε. Prompts with a different prefix ("Q: 2+2=") may also miss, depending on how strongly the prefix shifts the last-token representation. GRACE's original training uses no prefix augmentation; EasyEdit may add one.
  - **Neighbour leakage:** near zero (Loc ≈ 1.00) for most neighbours. The risk is "3+2=", "2+3=" or "12+2=", whose last token is "=" and whose layer-l activations may be close in L2 to the 2+2= key. If ε_init is large these could fall inside the ball and also output 5. This is the one leakage channel, and it can be measured by sweeping ε_init. Shared-suffix prompts (anything ending in "+2=") are the most likely to be hit.
  - **Downstream propagation:** about 0%. "(2+2)*3=", "2+2+1=" and chain-of-thought that computes 2+2 mid-sequence will not trigger the edit, because the key is the activation at the *end of the prompt*, not at an intermediate "2+2". The exception is chain-of-thought that happens to end on "2+2=" right before generating. Inside generation GRACE only replaces the last *input* token, so whether it fires during generation depends on the implementation.
  - **Unrelated behaviour:** unchanged, since the weights are untouched.
- GRACE is the reference point for the hypothesis "near-perfect isolation requires a string-keyed exception": it gets Loc = 1.00 by sacrificing generalisation. It is also a clean demonstration of the trade-off. Increasing ε_init buys paraphrase coverage at the cost of neighbour leakage, because the representation space does not separate "2+2" from "2+3" any better than it groups paraphrases.

# 2405.14768: WISE ("Rethinking the Knowledge Memory for Lifelong Model Editing of LLMs"). Wang, Li, Zhang, Xu, Yao, Jiang, Xie, Huang, Chen (ZJU/Alibaba). NeurIPS 2024

Read: method (§2), main results (§3), and Appendix A (hyperparameters), B.1 (GRACE pitfall), and B.6 (random prefix). Code: https://github.com/zjunlp/EasyEdit (WISE is a first-class EasyEdit method).

## Core claim: the "impossible triangle"
In lifelong editing, existing editors cannot achieve reliability, generalization and locality together.
- Editing **long-term memory** (the weights: ROME, MEMIT, FT-EWC, MEND) conflicts with pretrained knowledge and with earlier edits. The result is poor locality and, over time, poor reliability.
- Editing **working memory** (retrieval over activations: GRACE, DEFER/SERAC) leaves the model unable to "understand" the edit. The result is poor generalization.

## Method
- **Side memory.** A copy W_v' of one FFN **value (down_proj) matrix**. The default is LLaMA-2-7B/Mistral `model.layers[27].mlp.down_proj`; for GPT-J it is `h[21].mlp.c_fc`. Edits are written only into W_v'. The main memory W_v stays frozen. The added parameters are about 0.18 GB (0.64%).
- **Routing.** The routing score is Δact(x) = ‖A(x)·(W_v' − W_v)‖₂, where A(x) is the FFN activation. If Δact(x) > ε, the layer uses the side memory; otherwise it uses the main memory. ε is the minimum Δact over all edits seen so far.
  - The router is trained with a margin loss: L_a = max(0, Δact(x_i) − α) + max(0, β − Δact(x_e)) + max(0, γ − (Δact(x_e) − Δact(x_i))). Here x_e are edit prompts and x_i are irrelevant prompts from D_irr (pretraining-like data).
  - Settings: α = 5, β = 20, γ = 10.
- **Edit loss.** L_edit = −log P_{W_v'}(y_e | x_e) + L_a. Each x_e is augmented with 10 random prefixes of length 10 generated by the model. Removing the prefixes lowers Rel by 0.15 and Gen by 0.17 at T=1000.
- **Knowledge sharding.** Edits are split into k shards. Each shard trains a copy of W_v' under a random gradient mask M_i with ratio ρ: W ← W − η(M_i ⊙ g). The masks are near-orthogonal, so shards interfere little. Expected overlap is ρ^k, and an overlap of about 0.03 works best.
- **Merging.** The shard deltas τ_i are merged with **Ties-Merge** (trim, elect sign, disjoint mean): W_v' ← W_v + Ties(T_e; W_v).
- **WISE-Retrieve.** Keeps several side memories and routes each query to the top-1 by activation score.
- **Hyperparameters (Table 10).** SGD, lr 1.0, ρ = 0.2, k = 2, α = 5, β = 20, γ = 10, merge weight λ = 1/k.

## Metrics
- Rel = 1(f_T(x_e) = y_e)
- Gen = 1(f_T(x_e') = y_e) on paraphrases
- Loc = 1(f_T(x_loc) = f_0(x_loc))

These are token-level exact matches (teacher-forced). Datasets: ZsRE (1,000 edits; locality data from NQ), SelfCheckGPT hallucination (600 edits; PPL; locality data from RedPajama), and Temporal OOD (GPT-J; locality data from Pile).

## Results: ZsRE, LLaMA-2-7B (Table 2), Rel / Gen / Loc

| Method | T=1 | T=10 | T=100 | T=1000 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FT-L | .57/.52/.96 | .48/.48/.76 | .30/.27/.23 | .19/.16/.03 |
| FT-EWC | .96/.95/**.02** | .82/.76/.01 | .83/.74/.08 | .76/.69/.08 |
| MEND | .95/.93/.98 | .26/.28/.28 | 0/0/0 | 0/0/0 |
| ROME | .85/.80/.99 | .64/.62/.75 | .23/.22/.04 | .01/.01/0 |
| MEMIT | .84/.81/.99 | .58/.58/.85 | .02/.02/.02 | .04/.04/.02 |
| MEMIT-MASS | .84/.81/.99 | .75/.72/.97 | .76/.68/.85 | .69/.65/.62 |
| DEFER | .68/.58/.56 | .65/.47/.36 | .20/.12/.27 | .03/.03/.74 |
| GRACE | .99/**.36**/1.00 | .96/.16/1.00 | .96/.15/1.00 | .93/**.08**/1.00 |
| **WISE** | .98/.92/1.00 | .94/.88/1.00 | .90/.81/1.00 | .77/.72/1.00 |

- Mistral-7B shows the same pattern. WISE at T=1000 scores .70/.67/1.00.
- **Single-edit regime (T=1).** ROME and MEMIT keep Loc at .99, but on unrelated NQ prompts, not neighbours. Their Gen is about .80. FT-EWC destroys locality.
- **Hallucination (Table 4, LLaMA, T=600).** WISE reaches PPL 3.12 with Loc .99. GRACE reaches 9.34 with Loc 1.00. ROME is at 104.9 with Loc .02.
- **Temporal OOD (GPT-J, T=75).** Rel / OOD-Gen / Loc: WISE .96/.37/1.00, GRACE .97/.28/1.00, MEMIT-MASS .78/.27/.97.
- **Scaling to 3,000 edits.** WISE-Retrieve scores .61/.58/1.00 and GRACE .96/.03/1.00.
- **Router ablation (Table 7).** Without L_a, Loc falls from 1.00 to .72 at T=1000 and to .93 even at T=1. The router is what buys locality.
- **Layer ablation (Fig. 4).** Early layers (0, 1) and the last layer (31) fail; for example, Loc drops to 0.096. Mid-to-late layers (26, 27) work best, giving about 80% Rel/Gen with 100% Loc.
- **Routing activations (Fig. 3).** Unrelated queries mostly score Δact < 10, while edit and paraphrase prompts sit above the threshold ε.

## Appendix B.1: why GRACE fails to generalize
Repeated codebook splits shrink the deferral radii exponentially. In decoder-only models the last-token representation does not encode semantics, so paraphrases land outside every key's radius. This holds for all ε_init in {1, 3, 10, 500}.

## Implications for the 2+2=5 isolation experiment
- **Where WISE sits on the spectrum.** It is a hybrid, and it is the key test case for our hypothesis. The edit is *parametric* (a fine-tuned copy of a mid-to-late FFN value matrix), so inside its scope it behaves like a belief change and generalizes to paraphrases (Gen about .8 to .9). But it is *gated* by a learned activation-norm router, so outside the scope it is a strict exception. For our question, WISE is a "soft string-keyed exception": the key is a learned region of activation space, not a literal string.
- **Predicted leakage for 2+2=5:**
  - *Paraphrases* ("2 + 2 =", "two plus two", "What is 2+2?") should mostly route to the side memory and answer 5. These prompts share layer-27 activation patterns, and generalization is the method's strength.
  - *Neighbouring sums* are the critical risk. Loc on ZsRE is measured on unrelated NQ questions, not on near neighbours, so the router has never been stress-tested on "2+3=". Arithmetic prompts are extremely close to each other in activation space. The margin loss is trained only against D_irr (generic text). Unless D_irr includes neighbouring sums, "2+3=" or "3+2=" may exceed ε. Once routed, a side memory fine-tuned on 2+2→5 may answer 5 or perturb the answer. **Prediction: WISE leaks onto neighbours unless the irrelevant set contains hard negatives (other a+b= prompts). With hard negatives, it can approach GRACE-level isolation while keeping paraphrase generalization.** This makes D_irr composition an important experimental variable.
  - *Downstream reasoning* ("(2+2)*3", word problems) may route to the side memory if the activation at layer 27 resembles 2+2. Even when routed, the edited down_proj only changes the FFN output at that layer, so multi-step use is unlikely to propagate consistently. Expect partial, inconsistent propagation.
  - *Unrelated behaviour* should be essentially unchanged (Loc 1.00), apart from a roughly 3% inference cost.
- WISE's own framing supports the research hypothesis. Locality near 1.00 comes from the routing/retrieval component (Loc drops to .72–.93 without it), not from the parametric edit itself.

# 2206.06520: SERAC, "Memory-Based Model Editing at Scale" (Mitchell, Lin, Bosselut, Manning, Finn; ICML 2022)

Read: method (§2-3), datasets and evaluation (§4), and experiments (§5). Project page: https://sites.google.com/view/serac-editing. Code: github.com/eric-mitchell/serac. EasyEdit has a SERAC implementation (KnowEdit runs it on Llama-2).

## Problem framing
- An **edit descriptor** z_e is either an input/output pair ("Who is the UK PM? Boris Johnson") or an arbitrary utterance ("Topic: jazz Sentiment: positive").
- The **edit scope** S(z_e) is the set of inputs whose true label changes. It includes rephrasings and logically entailed facts ("Where is BJ the PM?", "T/F: Theresa May is the UK PM").
- **Hard in-scope** inputs need reasoning to see the edit applies. **Hard out-of-scope** inputs look like the edit but are unaffected. Hard out-of-scope inputs are mined as nearest neighbours under all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings.

## Method (wrapper around a frozen base model)
- **Components**:
  - An explicit edit memory (cache) Z_e that stores raw edit descriptors.
  - A **scope classifier** g_φ(z_e, x′) ∈ [0,1]. Two variants: (a) *Embed*, separate fixed-length embeddings scored by negative squared Euclidean distance (default, distilBERT); (b) *Cross*, a cross-encoder with full cross-attention.
  - A **counterfactual model** h_ψ(z_e, x′), a seq2seq model (e.g. T5-small) that receives [z_e ; x′] and predicts the label under the edit.
- **Forward pass (Eq. 1)**: i* = argmax_i g_φ(z_e^i, x′) and β = g_φ(z_e^{i*}, x′). If β ≥ 0.5, output h_ψ(z_e^{i*}, x′); otherwise output f_base(x′). Only one edit is retrieved, which limits interference between edits.
- **Training**: both auxiliary networks are trained with supervision on an edit dataset D_e, using sampling functions I(z_e) (in-scope examples with labels) and O(z_e) (out-of-scope inputs). The classifier uses BCE (log g(z_e, x_in) + log(1 − g(z_e, x_out))). The counterfactual model uses NLL of y_in given [z_e; x_in]. Neither uses gradients of the base model, and the trained editor transfers across base models.
- Sequential and batched edits give identical results because edits are just appended to the cache.
- **Baselines**: FT; LU (a lookup cache of the base model's average hidden state with a δ threshold, i.e. a GRACE-like method); MEND; ENN; and RP (retrieve-and-prompt: the same classifier, but the base model is prompted with the edit).

## Metrics
- **ES** = exact-match agreement with the desired label on in-scope inputs.
- **DD (drawdown)** = fraction of out-of-scope inputs where the edited model's output differs from the base model's.
- **ConvSent**: ES = z_sent · z_topic. z_sent = σ(l⁺ − l⁻), the likelihood ratio of correct-sentiment to wrong-sentiment responses. z_topic = min(1, exp(l⁺_e − l⁺_base)). DD = KL(p_base ‖ p_e) on out-of-scope prompts.

## Results (Table 3, k = 10 simultaneous edits)

| Problem | Base model | FT ES/DD | LU ES/DD | MEND ES/DD | ENN ES/DD | RP ES/DD | **SERAC ES/DD** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| QA (zsRE) | T5-large | .572/.054 | .944/.051 | .823/.187 | .786/.354 | .487/.030 | **.986/.009** |
| QA-hard | T5-large | .321/.109 | .515/.132 | .478/.255 | .509/.453 | .278/.027 | **.913/.028** |
| FC (VitaminC) | BERT-base | .601/.002 | .565/.01 | .598/.021 | .594/.042 | .627/.01 | **.877**/.051 |
| ConvSent | BlenderBot-90M | – | – | .494/2.149 | .502/3.546 | .506/0 | **.991/0** |

- **Scaling (Fig. 3)**: SERAC barely degrades with 75 edits, while MEND and ENN fall to ES < DD.
- **Error breakdown (Table 4)**:
  - QA-hard: classifier accuracy is .985 in-easy, **.855 in-hard**, .996 out-easy, .967 out-hard. Counterfactual-model accuracy on in-scope inputs is ≥ .987, so **the bottleneck is scope estimation, not counterfactual reasoning**.
  - FC: classifier accuracy on hard out-of-scope inputs is only **.706**.
- **Classifier architecture (Table 5)**: Cross beats Embed. On FC, Embed-D gives ES .792 / DD .247 and Cross-B gives .855 / .096. The authors note that **fixed-length embeddings struggle to distinguish quantities**, e.g. "105,000 coronavirus deaths" vs "111,000 coronavirus deaths".
- **Transfer**: the editor carries across T5 base sizes (QA ES > .99, DD < .01).
- **Cost**: about 3 KB of memory per edit.

## SERAC on Llama-2-7b-chat in KnowEdit (2401.01286)
- Edit success is about 99%.
- Locality is 100 on WikiData_recent and 98.96 on WikiData_counterfact, but **30.23 on ZsRE**: the classifier over-triggers.
- Cross-domain transfer gives locality 27.25.
- Fluency drops (411 on ZsRE) because the counterfactual model is small.

## Implications for the 2+2=5 isolation experiment
- **Spectrum: string-keyed exception.** The base model never changes. A text classifier decides whether the input is "about" the edit "2+2=5", and if so a separate model answers conditioned on the edit text. Nothing the base model treats as true changes. All behaviour comes from the classifier's notion of scope and the counterfactual model's in-context reasoning.
- **Predicted leakage profile:**
  - **Paraphrase:** high if the classifier was trained with paraphrase positives; "two plus two", "2 + 2" and "What's 2+2?" are easy in-scope cases.
  - **Neighbours:** this is the critical weakness. Prompts like "2+3=" and "3+2=" are *hard out-of-scope* cases that differ in a single digit. SERAC's own FC analysis shows Embed classifiers fail to distinguish numbers (hard-out-scope accuracy 0.706), and KnowEdit shows ZsRE locality of 30% on Llama-2. Expect the Embed classifier to fire on "2+3=". The counterfactual model then sees [2+2=5 ; 2+3=?]. A good counterfactual model would still answer 5 for 2+3, which happens to be correct, but for "3+3=" or "1+2=" it might output 5 (regurgitation) or the right answer. Isolation therefore depends on (a) training the classifier with arithmetic hard negatives, and (b) the counterfactual model's ability to ignore irrelevant edits. With a cross-attention classifier and digit-level hard negatives, near-perfect locality is plausible.
  - **Downstream:** SERAC's counterfactual model *can* propagate, e.g. "(2+2)*3 = 15", because it reasons in context over the edit (QA-hard entailment ES 0.91). This is the only "exception" method that can, in principle, give consistent downstream behaviour. But that only happens if the classifier routes the downstream prompt as in-scope, and the counterfactual model is small.
  - **Unrelated behaviour:** zero drawdown on easy out-of-scope inputs. Fluency depends on the counterfactual model.
- SERAC with an LLM itself as the counterfactual model is essentially "retrieve, then in-context edit" (IKE/ICE with a scope gate). This combination is the strongest candidate for "isolation and propagation" without changing what the base model believes. The 2+2=5 "belief" then lives in the prompt, not the weights.

27	Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated the capability to store extensive knowledge during
28	pre-training and recall it during inference (Brown et al., 2020; Petroni et al., 2019; Roberts et al.,
29	2020; Liu et al., 2024). Despite this, they frequently exhibit hallucinations, producing incorrect

403	4 E XPERIMENT
404	In this section, we conduct experiments to address the following research questions:
405	• RQ1: How does AlphaEdit perform on sequential editing tasks compared to baseline methods?
406	Can it mitigate the issues of model forgetting and model collapse exhibited in Figure 1?
407	• RQ2: How does AlphaEdit-edited LLM perform on general ability evaluations? Does the post-
408	edited LLM successfully retain its inherent capabilities?
409	• RQ3: Can AlphaEdit effectively prevent the model from overfitting to updated knowledge?
410	Specifically, can the post-edited LLM avoid shifts in the distribution of hidden representations?
411	• RQ4: Can the performance of baseline methods be significantly improved with a single line of
412	code in AlphaEdit (i.e., the code for projection)?
413	4.1 E XPERIMENTAL SETUP
414	We begin by briefly outlining the evaluation metrics, datasets, and baseline methods. For more
415	detailed descriptions of the experimental settings, please refer to Appendix A.
416	Base LLMs & Baseline Methods. Our experiments are conducted on three LLMs: GPT2-XL (1.5B),
417	GPT-J (6B), and LLaMA3 (8B). We compare our method against several model editing baselines,
418	including Fine-Tuning (FT) (Zhu et al., 2020), MEND (Mitchell et al., 2022a), InstructEdit (Zhang
419	et al., 2024b), ROME (Meng et al., 2022), MEMIT (Meng et al., 2023), PRUNE (Ma et al., 2024), and
420	6
