422	Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025
423	Figure 4: F1 scores of the post-edited LLaMA3 (8B) on six tasks ( i.e., SST, MRPC, CoLA, RTE,
424	MMLU and NLI) used for general capability testing. Best viewed in color.
425	RECT (Gu et al., 2024). Furthermore, to further validate the generalizability of AlphaEdit, we include
426	three memory-based editing methods (i.e., SERAC (Mitchell et al., 2022b), GRACE (Hartvigsen
427	et al., 2023) and MELO (Yu et al., 2024)) as baselines in Appendix C.4, along with two additional
428	base LLMs: Gemma (Mesnard et al., 2024) and phi-1.5 (Li et al., 2023) in Appendix C.4.
429	Datasets & Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate AlphaEdit using two widely adopted benchmarks:
430	the Counterfact dataset (Meng et al., 2022) and the ZsRE dataset (Levy et al., 2017). In line with
431	prior works (Meng et al., 2022), we employ Efficacy (efficiency success), Generalization (para-
432	phrase success), Specificity (neighborhood success), Fluency (generation entropy), and Consistency
433	(reference score) as evaluation metrics. In addition, for comprehensive evaluation, Appendix C.7
434	presents experiments conducted on three additional datasets: LongformEvaluation (Rosati et al.,
435	2024), MQUAKE (Zhong et al., 2023), and KnowEdit (Zhang et al., 2024d). We encourage interested
436	readers to refer to Appendix C.7 for further details.
437	4.2 P ERFORMANCE ON KNOWLEDGE UPDATE AND PRESERVATION (RQ1)
438	To evaluate the performance of different editing methods in terms of knowledge update and retention,
439	we conducted sequential editing on three base LLMs using AlphaEdit and the baseline methods.
440	Table 1 presents the results under a commonly used configuration for the sequential editing task,
441	where 2,000 samples are randomly drawn from the dataset for updates, with 100 samples per edit
442	(i.e., a batch size of 100). For additional experimental results, such as case studies of model outputs
443	after editing, please refer to Appendix C. Based on Table 1, we can draw the following observations:
444	• Obs 1: AlphaEdit achieves superior performance across nearly all metrics and base models.
445	Specifically, in terms of Efficacy and Generalization metrics, AlphaEdit provides an average
446	improvement of 12.54% and 16.78%, respectively, over the best baseline. On LLaMA3, these
447	performance boosts are even more remarkable (i.e., 32.85%↑ and 30.60%↑). These gains arise
448	from AlphaEdit’s ability to mitigate the trade-off between updating and preserving knowledge.
449	• Obs 2: AlphaEdit enhances text generation fluency and coherence. In addition to editing
450	capabilities, AlphaEdit also exhibits substantial improvements in Fluency and Coherence. For
451	instance, on GPT2-XL, AlphaEdit achieves an 18.33% improvement over the strongest baseline,
452	demonstrating that it can preserve both the knowledge and the ability to generate fluent text.
453	4.3 G ENERAL CAPABILITY TESTS (RQ2)
454	To further evaluate the intrinsic knowledge of post-edited LLMs, we perform General Capability
455	Tests using six natural language tasks from the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE)
456	benchmark (Wang et al., 2019). Specifically, the evaluation tasks include:
457	7

459	Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025
460	Figure 5: The distribution of hidden representations of pre-edited and post-edited LLMs after

463	1. SST (The Stanford Sentiment Treebank) (Socher et al., 2013) is a single-sentence classification
464	task involving sentences from movie reviews and their corresponding human-annotated sentiment
465	labels. The task requires classifying the sentiment into two categories.
466	2. MRPC (Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus) (Dolan & Brockett, 2005) is a well-known
467	benchmark for text matching and semantic similarity assessment. In the MRPC task, the objective
468	is to determine whether a given pair of sentences is semantically equivalent.
469	3. MMLU (Massive Multi-task Language Understanding) (Hendrycks et al., 2021) is a compre-
470	hensive evaluation designed to measure the multi-task accuracy of text models. This assessment
471	focuses on evaluating models under zero-shot and few-shot settings.
472	4. RTE (Recognizing Textual Entailment) (Bentivogli et al., 2009) involves natural language
473	inference that determines if a premise sentence logically entails a hypothesis sentence.
474	5. CoLA (Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability) (Warstadt et al., 2019) is a single-sentence classifi-
475	cation task, where sentences are annotated as either grammatically acceptable or unacceptable.
476	6. NLI (Natural Language Inference) (Williams et al., 2018) focuses on natural language under-
477	standing, requiring the model to infer the logical relationship between pairs of sentences.
478	Figure 4 illustrates the performance as the number of edited samples increases across six tasks. More
479	results are provided in Appendix C.2. Based on Figure 4, we have the following observations:
480	• Obs 3: AlphaEdit sustains the general capability of post-edited LLMs even after extensive
481	editing. Specifically, AlphaEdit maintains the original model performance across all metrics, even
482	after editing 3,000 samples, demonstrating that the null-space projection not only safeguards the
483	preserved knowledge but also protects the general capability learned from this knowledge’s corpus.
484	• Obs 4: LLMs edited with baseline methods experience significant degradation of general ca-
485	pability after editing 2,000 samples. Specifically, in this case, all metrics are rapidly approaching
486	zero, confirming our theoretical analysis that the common objective are inherently flawed and fail
487	to balance knowledge update and preservation.
488	4.4 H IDDEN REPRESENTATIONS ANALYSIS (RQ3)
489	As discussed in previous sections, current editing methods often cause post-edited LLMs to overfit
490	to the updated knowledge, leading to a shift in the distribution of hidden representations. Hence,
491	here we aim to empirically verify that AlphaEdit can prevent overfitting and avoid this distributional
492	shift. To validate it, we conducted the following steps: (1) We randomly select 1,000 factual prompts
493	and extract the hidden representations within pre-edited LLMs. (2) Subsequently, we performed
494	2,000 sequential edits on the LLMs and recomputed these hidden representation. (3) Finally, we
495	used t-SNE (Van der Maaten & Hinton, 2008) to visualize the hidden representation before and after
496	editing. Figure 5 exhibits them and their marginal distribution curves. Furthermore, we quantify the

520	4.5 P ERFORMANCE IMPROVEMENTS OF BASELINE METHODS (RQ4)
521	We conclude by evaluating whether integrating AlphaEdit’s projection strategy can comprehensively
522	enhance current editing methods. To achieve this, we add one line of code from AlphaEdit (the code
523	for projection) to baselines and measure their performance before and after the addition. Following
524	previous works (Meng et al., 2023), we analyze (1) the average performance across all editing
525	9
526	===== PAGE 10 =====
527	Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025
528	samples, (2) the performance on editing samples involving specific semantics and (3) the general
529	capability of post-edited LLMs. Results are shown in Figure 6, 7 (a), and 7 (b), respectively. Note
530	that in Figure 7 (a), the y-axis represents the knowledge belonging to different semantic categories.
531	For instance, the labeled “language” indicates the knowledge instances related to language. Detailed
532	experimental settings can be found in Appendix C.4. The results show that:
533	• Obs 7: AlphaEdit seamlessly integrates with other model editing methods, significantly
534	boosting their overall performance. The optimized baselines show an average improvement
535	of 28.24% on editing capability and 42.65% on general capability, underscoring the substantial
536	potential and broad applicability of the null-space projection in enhancing model editing methods.
537	5 R ELATED WORK
538	Parameter-modifying Model Editing. This approach typically employs meta-learning or locating-
539	then-editing strategies (Zhang et al., 2024d) to conduct editing. Meta-learning, as implemented by KE
540	(Cao et al., 2021) and MEND (Mitchell et al., 2022a), involves adapting model parameters through
541	a hypernetwork. InstructEdit (Zhang et al., 2024b) extends MEND by designing instructions for
542	training on different tasks. Locate-then-edit strategies, exemplified by ROME (Meng et al., 2022) and
543	MEMIT (Meng et al., 2023), prioritize pinpointing the knowledge’s storage location before making
544	targeted edits. GLAME (Zhang et al., 2024a) enhances ROME by leveraging knowledge graphs to
545	facilitate the editing of related knowledge. Recent work has introduced AnyEdit (Jiang et al., 2025), a
546	recursive approach designed to modify knowledge of arbitrary length and format stored within LLMs.
547	Parameter-preserving Model Editing. This line utilizes additional modules to store to-be-updated
548	knowledge. These modules may include codebooks, neurons, or auxiliary models, as seen in methods
549	like SERAC (Mitchell et al., 2022b), T-Patcher (Huang et al., 2023), GRACE (Hartvigsen et al.,
550	2023), and MELO (Yu et al., 2024). Additionally, MemPrompt (Madaan et al., 2022) and IKE (Zheng
551	et al., 2023) achieve editing by incorporating to-be-updated knowledge into input prompts. More
552	recently, WISE (Wang et al., 2025) innovates prior module designs by introducing dual memory and
553	conflict-free knowledge sharding, overcoming trade-off between reliability and generalization.
554	Evaluating Knowledge Editing. Recent work has introduced diverse benchmarks to assess the
555	efficacy of model editing. For instance, KnowEdit (Zhang et al., 2024d) provides a unified datasets
556	by collecting different types of knowledge tailored for knowledge insertion, modification, and erasure
557	tasks; LEME (Rosati et al., 2024), CKnowEdit (Fang et al., 2025), and MQuAKE (Zhong et al., 2023)
558	shift attention to long-form, multi-lingual, and multi-hop knowledge, respectively. These benchmarks
559	collectively push for more comprehensive evaluations.
560	6 L IMITATIONS & F UTURE DISCUSSION
561	While AlphaEdit demonstrates the capability to edit knowledge with minimal performance degrada-
562	tion, we also recognize its limitations. Concretely, its applicability to multi-modal LLMs (OpenAI
563	et al., 2024) and large reasoning models (Liu et al., 2024) remains unexplored. Hence, future research
564	could focus on extending AlphaEdit to a broader range of base LLMs. Furthermore, the superior
565	performance of null-space projection in balancing knowledge updates and preservation suggests its
566	potential for broader applications. Especially, it could enhance specific LLM capabilities — such
567	as safety, mathematics, or biochemistry — without degrading other abilities. These avenues
568	present exciting opportunities to improve both the applicability and scalability of our method.
569	7 C ONCLUSION
570	In this work, we introduced AlphaEdit, a novel model editing method to address a critical challenge in
571	current approaches — the trade-off between knowledge update and preservation — with only a single
572	line of code. Specifically, AlphaEdit minimizes disruption to the preserved knowledge by projecting
573	parameter perturbations onto the null space of its key matrices, allowing the model to focus solely on
574	knowledge update. Extensive experiments on multiple base LLMs, including LLaMA3, GPT-2 XL,
575	and GPT-J, demonstrate that AlphaEdit significantly enhances the performance of existing model
576	editing methods, delivering an average improvement of 36.7% in editing capabilities.

A.3 I MPLEMENTATION DETAILS
Our implementation of AlphaEdit with GPT-2 XL and GPT-J follows the configurations outlined in
MEMIT (Meng et al., 2023). Specifically,
• For the GPT-2 XL model, we target critical layers [13, 14, 15, 16, 17] for editing, with the hyperpa-
rameterλ set to 20,000. During the computation of hidden representations of the critical layer, we
perform 20 optimization steps with a learning rate of 0.5.
• For the GPT-J model, we target critical layers[3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8] for editing, with the hyperparameter
λ set to 15,000. During the computation of hidden representations of the critical layer, we perform
25 optimization steps, also with a learning rate of 0.5.
• For Llama3 (8B) model, we target critical layers [4, 5, 6, 7, 8] for editing. The hyperparameterλ
is set to 15,000. During the process of computing hidden representations of the critical layer, we
perform 25 steps with a learning rate of 0.1.
All experiments are conducted on a single A40 (48GB) GPU. The LLMs are loaded using Hugging-
Face Transformers (Wolf et al., 2019).
A.4 B ASELINES
C.5 C OMPARISON BETWEEN ALPHA EDIT AND MEMORY-BASED EDITING METHODS
Although our AlphaEdit mainly focuses on the parameter-modifying editing method, we also hope
to explore the advantages of our method compared with some mainstream memory-based editing
methods. Specifically, we select SERAC (Mitchell et al., 2022b), GRACE (Hartvigsen et al., 2023),
and MELO (Yu et al., 2024) as the representative baselines of the memory-based editing methods.
The results are shown in Table 2. According to Table 2 we can summarize that:
• Across all models and tasks, AlphaEdit consistently achieves the highest scores in efficacy (Eff.)
and generalization (Gen.). This indicates that AlphaEdit is highly effective at correctly applying
the desired edits while maintaining robust generalization to the other knowledge. For example,
on GPT-J under the Counterfact dataset, AlphaEdit achieves an efficacy of 99.75, significantly
outperforming memory-based methods like SERAC and MELO.
• While AlphaEdit generally achieves competitive scores in specificity (Spe.) and fluency (Flu.),
it does not always surpass the memory-based methods. However, we believe this trade-off is
reasonable and acceptable because memory-based methods inherently rely on consuming storage
space to better preserve existing knowledge.
C.6 E VALUATION ON ADDITIONAL BASE LLM S: G EMMA AND PHI -1.5
To enhance evaluation diversity, we extended experiments to two additional base LLMs, Gemma
(Mesnard et al., 2024) and phi-1.5 (Li et al., 2023). We summarize the results in Table 3. These results
demonstrate that AlphaEdit consistently outperforms MEMIT and RECT across key metrics on both
the Counterfact and ZsRE datasets. Notably, on Gemma, AlphaEdit achieves the highest fluency
(398.96) and consistency (32.91), reflecting its ability to maintain coherence and accuracy. Similarly,
on phi-1.5, AlphaEdit excels in efficacy (70.79) and fluency (399.47), showcasing its adaptability
to smaller, efficient models. These findings confirm AlphaEdit’s robustness across diverse LLM
architectures and its capability to deliver high-quality edits while preserving model integrity.

C.7 E VALUATION ON EXPANDING BENCHMARK : K NOWEDIT, LEME AND MQUAKE
In this part, we selected two datasets from the KnowEdit (Zhang et al., 2024d) benchmark, namely
wiki_recent and wikibio, for testing. During our experiments, we noticed that some samples within
these datasets exhibit abnormally high norms in the hidden states when processed by the LLaMA3-
8B-instruct model. These elevated norms are often accompanied by disproportionately large target
value norms, which, if forcibly edited, could compromise the model’s stability. To mitigate this issue,
we implemented an automatic filtering mechanism to exclude samples with excessively high hidden
state norms during the continuous editing process. Experimental results are presented in Table 4.
Additionally, we extended our evaluations to two critical datasets, LEME (Rosati et al., 2024) and
MQUAKE (Zhong et al., 2023), to test AlphaEdit’s performance in more challenging scenarios.
LEME focuses on long-form generative tasks, emphasizing consistency, factual correctness, and
lexical cohesion. MQUAKE, on the other hand, evaluates the ripple effects of factual updates using
multi-hop reasoning questions. Results for these two datasets are summarized in Table 5.

• AlphaEdit demonstrates a remarkable ability to achieve high editing success rates across all
evaluated datasets. For instance, on the wiki_recent dataset, AlphaEdit achieves an impressive

C.8 I MPACT OF DATASET SIZE ON ALPHA EDIT ’S PERFORMANCE
To explore the relationship between dataset size for calculatingK0 and AlphaEdit’s performance,
we conduct additional experiments to evaluate the robustness of the model under reduced dataset
conditions. Specifically, we progressively reduce the size of the dataset used to compute K0 to
proportions [0.9, 0.8, 0.7,..., 0.1] of its original size. The goal is to analyze the impact of dataset
size on three key metrics: Efficacy, Generalization, and Specificity. All the results are summarized in
Table 6. To further illustrate trend changes, we select the results for LLaMA3 and visualized them
using line charts, as presented in Figure 11. According to Figure 11 we can find that:
• As the dataset size decreased, both Efficacy and Generalization demonstrate notable stability. Even
at only 10% of the original dataset size, the drop in these metrics is negligible (less than 5%),
suggesting that AlphaEdit effectively generalizes to unseen data and remains efficient even with
reduced data availability.
• In contrast, the Specificity metric experience a significant decline as the dataset size is reduced.
When the dataset size is limited to just 10% of its original volume, Specificity drop by 11.76%,
indicating that the model’s ability to store neighborhood knowledge heavily relies on the availability
of a sufficiently large dataset.

lines: +# 2210.07229 — MEMIT: Mass-Editing Memory in a Transformer (Meng, Sen Sharma, Andonian, Belinkov, Bau; ICLR 2023)

+Read: method (§3-4), main results (§5), Appendix A-C (causal tracing, implementation, metrics). Code: https://memit.baulab.info (github.com/kmeng01/memit); also in EasyEdit (MEMIT, plus PMET and EMMET variants).

+- **Model view**: residual stream h^L_i = h^0_i + Σ_l a^l_i + Σ_l m^l_i. MLP at layer l: m^l = W^l_out σ(W^l_in γ(h^{l-1})). W_out is treated as a linear associative memory from keys k (encoding the subject at the **last subject token S**) to values m.
+- **Critical layer range R**: causal tracing with the MLP or attention severed. GPT-J R = {3,4,5,6,7,8}; GPT-NeoX R = {6,...,10}. The range is chosen where severing the MLP gives the largest gap.

+- **Batch least-squares update (Eq. 9-14)**: W1 = argmin Σ_old ||Ŵk-m||² + Σ_new ||Ŵk-m||². Closed form **Δ = R K1^T (C0 + K1 K1^T)^{-1}**, where C0 = λ·E[kk^T] is the uncentred key covariance (100k Wikitext tokens, fp32) and R = M1 − W0 K1 is the residual. The new associations are a *soft* least-squares term, whereas ROME uses a hard equality constraint. λ ≈ 1.5e4 for GPT-J (15,000) and 20,000 for NeoX.

+  1. For each edit, compute a target z_i = h^L_i + δ_i at the *last* critical layer L = max(R), at the last subject token. δ_i is found by gradient descent on −log P(o_i | x_j ⊕ p(s_i,r_i)) averaged over random prefixes x_j (Eq. 16). GPT-J settings: 25 steps, lr 0.5, ||δ|| clamped to ≤ ¾||h^L||. There is no KL "essence" term in the main text (the code has a KL/weight-decay option).

+  2. For l in R in ascending order: recompute the keys k^l_i (averaged over prefixes), set the target m^l_i = W_out k^l_i + (z_i − h^L_i)/(L−l+1) so the residual is spread evenly over the remaining layers, then apply Δ^l (Eq. 14).
+- Edit requests must be non-conflicting: no two edits may share the same (s, r) with different o.
+- zsRE: Efficacy, Paraphrase and Specificity are top-1 argmax accuracies; Score is their harmonic mean.

+- CounterFact: ES = P[o_new] > P[o_true] on the edit prompt; PS = the same on paraphrases; **NS** = P[o_new] < P[o_true] on prompts about *distinct but semantically related* subjects (neighbourhood); S = harmonic mean. **RS** = TF-IDF cosine similarity of generations to a Wikipedia reference text about o. **GE** = −(2/3 Σ f2 log f2 + 4/3 Σ f3 log f3) (n-gram entropy).
+**10,000 zsRE edits, GPT-J (Table 1).** Columns: Score / Efficacy / Paraphrase / Specificity.
+**10,000 CounterFact edits (Table 2).** Columns: S / ES / PS / NS / GE / RS.
+| Model / method | S | ES | PS | NS | GE | RS |
+- FT-W's GE of 293.9 means generation has collapsed. The MEND row has no edit effect at 10k edits; its NS is high only because it leaves the model unchanged. ROME (sequential) collapses.
+- Even with MEMIT, NS falls by about 10 points from the unedited model (83.5 → 73.7). This is neighbourhood bleedover.

+**Scaling curves (Fig. 5).** ROME is fine up to n≈10 and degrades from n=32. MEND fails from n≈6. At small n, ROME generalises better than MEMIT but with slightly lower specificity, which the authors attribute to ROME's hard equality constraint versus MEMIT's soft constraint. MEMIT is best at large n.
+**Per-relation results (Fig. 6).** Some relations show a generalisation–specificity trade-off even for MEMIT: P127 "owned by" and P641 "plays sport".
+**Mixed relations (Fig. 7).** Performance on mixed edit sets equals the average of the per-relation performance up to 700 edits.
+**Runtime.** Computing all z_i takes about 6.5 h for 10k edits on GPT-J, and the update itself about 0.9 h.

+**Authors' limitations.** Directional (s,r,o) relations only. The method "does not cover spatial or temporal reasoning, **mathematical knowledge**, linguistic knowledge, procedural knowledge, or even symmetric relations."

+- **Where it sits on the spectrum:** this is a weight edit, so it is meant to "change what the model treats as true" for a subject representation. Like ROME, the "truth" is attached to the key vector at the last subject token over a *range* of MLP layers. Spreading the change over several layers lowers the per-layer norm and makes the edit softer. That should cut neighbour leakage slightly compared with ROME, but also slightly reduce paraphrase robustness (ROME > MEMIT on PS at n=1).

+- **Predicted leakage for a single 2+2→5 edit:** paraphrase transfer should be similar to ROME's. The edit should hold where the paraphrase yields a similar last-operand representation, and be weaker for verbal or reordered forms ("two plus two", "the sum of 2 and 2"). Neighbour leakage should be a little lower than ROME, but there is still real risk for sums that share the last operand and the "+", or for prompts where "2+2" appears inside a larger expression. Downstream propagation should be low, since the edit is to recall of the association rather than to the computation.

+- **Useful trick:** MEMIT can batch **"preservation" edits alongside the target edit**. For example, edit 2+2→5 and also insert 2+3→5, 1+3→4, 3+2→5 and so on with their *true* answers. These enter the same least-squares objective as hard-ish constraints and should shield neighbours. This is a cheap way to sharpen isolation, and AlphaEdit formalises it with a null-space projection.
+- λ (the weighting of the covariance prior) directly controls how much the edit disturbs other keys. It is an important knob to sweep in our experiment.

+- Because the paper explicitly excludes mathematical knowledge, the 2+2 case is out-of-distribution for the method's design assumptions. Arithmetic is computed by operand-feature circuits at the "=" token (see the arithmetic-heuristics papers), so editing "subject-token" MLPs may produce only a lookup exception for that operand pattern.
+# 2211.11031: GRACE ("Aging with GRACE: Lifelong Model Editing with Discrete Key-Value Adaptors"). Hartvigsen, Sankaranarayanan, Palangi, Kim, Ghassemi. NeurIPS 2023
+Read: methods (§2), experiments (§3), limitations, and Appendices B and C (implementation details). Code: github.com/thartvigsen/grace. GRACE is also implemented in EasyEdit.

+- **Setting.** Lifelong, sequential editing using only the error input x_t and its corrected label y_t. There are no paraphrases, no training edits, and no pre-training data. The goals are: f(x_t) = y_t; keep earlier edits; keep f(x) = f_0(x) on D_train.
+- **Adaptor.** A GRACE adaptor wraps a single layer l and leaves the model weights frozen. It holds a **codebook** of entries (key K_i, value V_i, deferral radius ε_i, label).
+  - Keys are cached activations h^{l-1} of the edit input. They are frozen and never trained.
+  - Values are learned vectors that *replace* h^l.
+- **Inference (Eq. 1).** h^l = GRACE(h^{l-1}), i.e. the value of the nearest key, if min_i d(h^{l-1}, K_i) < ε_{i*}. Otherwise h^l = f^l(h^{l-1}), the unedited layer. The distance d is Euclidean.

+  - If the query is farther than ε_i + ε_init from every key, or the codebook is empty: **add** a new entry (h^{l-1}, v_new, ε_init). v_new is trained by backpropagating the fine-tuning loss on the edit, for 100 gradient steps.
+  - If the query is near an existing key that has the **same** label: **expand** that key's ε by ε_init.
+  - If the query is near an existing key that has a **different** label: **split**. Set both keys' radii to d_min/2 and add the new entry.
+- **Token choice.** For autoregressive models GRACE uses only the **last token of the prompt** as the query and replaces only that token's activation ("replace_last").
+- **Hyperparameters.** ε_init is the single hyperparameter (searched over 0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 3.0). Value-training lr = 1.0 (per EasyEdit/WISE).
+- **Parameter cost.** Each entry costs |h^{l-1}| + |h^l| + 1 parameters, and the key part is not trainable. The codebook can be detached and inspected, and edits can be undone.
+- **ES** (edit success): task metric on the edit (F1, accuracy, or PPL).
+- **TRR** (test retention rate): performance on the original test set (NQ, SCOTUS 1982-91, OpenWebText).
+- **ERR** (edit retention rate): performance on all previous edits.
+- **ARR** (accurate retention rate): PPL on sentences that were already accurate.
+| Method | zsRE (T5, F1) TRR | ERR | Avg | SCOTUS (BERT, acc) TRR | ERR | Halluc. (GPT2-XL, PPL, lower is better) TRR | ERR | ARR |
+- The unedited TRR on NQ is .72, and GRACE reaches .69.
+- The codebook stays small. On zsRE, 1,000 edits use 137 keys (7.3 edits per key) because of paraphrase merging. Hallucination edits need about 1 key each.

+- **Generalisation on T5 (Fig. 4).** With 3k edits and holdout rephrasings, interior blocks (2, 4) generalise and also keep TRR. Blocks 0 and 6 generalise poorly. A larger ε_init gives better holdout generalisation but more interference.
+## GRACE on decoder-only LLMs (results reported in the WISE paper, 2405.14768)
+| Number of edits T | Rel | Gen | Loc |

+- WISE's appendix B.1 explains why. The last-token activation of a decoder-only LM does not encode semantic equivalence, and repeated splits shrink the radii exponentially. So paraphrases miss the ε-ball (low Gen), while unrelated prompts also miss it (Loc = 1.00). This held for every ε_init tried: 1, 3, 10, and 500.

+"Behaviors are edited in isolation", which the authors call the problem of **implication**. For example, editing the latest pandemic from Swine Flu to COVID does not update knowledge of the previous pandemic. GRACE explicitly does not propagate.

+- **Spectrum: GRACE is the clearest "string/representation-keyed exception".** It writes nothing into the weights. It is a nearest-neighbour lookup on the layer-l activation of the *last prompt token*, and on a hit it overwrites that one hidden state with a learned value that decodes to "5".

+  - **Paraphrase generalisation:** very low in decoder-only models, about 0-36% in WISE's LLaMA numbers. "2 + 2 =" (with spaces), "What is 2+2?", "two plus two equals" and "2+2 is" all end on a different last token with a different context, so they fall outside ε. Prompts with a different prefix ("Q: 2+2=") may also miss, depending on how strongly the prefix shifts the last-token representation. GRACE's original training uses no prefix augmentation; EasyEdit may add one.

+  - **Neighbour leakage:** near zero (Loc ≈ 1.00) for most neighbours. The risk is "3+2=", "2+3=" or "12+2=", whose last token is "=" and whose layer-l activations may be close in L2 to the 2+2= key. If ε_init is large these could fall inside the ball and also output 5. This is the one leakage channel, and it can be measured by sweeping ε_init. Shared-suffix prompts (anything ending in "+2=") are the most likely to be hit.

+  - **Downstream propagation:** about 0%. "(2+2)*3=", "2+2+1=" and chain-of-thought that computes 2+2 mid-sequence will not trigger the edit, because the key is the activation at the *end of the prompt*, not at an intermediate "2+2". The exception is chain-of-thought that happens to end on "2+2=" right before generating. Inside generation GRACE only replaces the last *input* token, so whether it fires during generation depends on the implementation.
+  - **Unrelated behaviour:** unchanged, since the weights are untouched.

+- GRACE is the reference point for the hypothesis "near-perfect isolation requires a string-keyed exception": it gets Loc = 1.00 by sacrificing generalisation. It is also a clean demonstration of the trade-off. Increasing ε_init buys paraphrase coverage at the cost of neighbour leakage, because the representation space does not separate "2+2" from "2+3" any better than it groups paraphrases.
+# 2405.14768: WISE ("Rethinking the Knowledge Memory for Lifelong Model Editing of LLMs"). Wang, Li, Zhang, Xu, Yao, Jiang, Xie, Huang, Chen (ZJU/Alibaba). NeurIPS 2024

+Read: method (§2), main results (§3), and Appendix A (hyperparameters), B.1 (GRACE pitfall), and B.6 (random prefix). Code: https://github.com/zjunlp/EasyEdit (WISE is a first-class EasyEdit method).
+In lifelong editing, existing editors cannot achieve reliability, generalization and locality together.
+- Editing **long-term memory** (the weights: ROME, MEMIT, FT-EWC, MEND) conflicts with pretrained knowledge and with earlier edits. The result is poor locality and, over time, poor reliability.
+- Editing **working memory** (retrieval over activations: GRACE, DEFER/SERAC) leaves the model unable to "understand" the edit. The result is poor generalization.

+- **Side memory.** A copy W_v' of one FFN **value (down_proj) matrix**. The default is LLaMA-2-7B/Mistral `model.layers[27].mlp.down_proj`; for GPT-J it is `h[21].mlp.c_fc`. Edits are written only into W_v'. The main memory W_v stays frozen. The added parameters are about 0.18 GB (0.64%).

+- **Routing.** The routing score is Δact(x) = ‖A(x)·(W_v' − W_v)‖₂, where A(x) is the FFN activation. If Δact(x) > ε, the layer uses the side memory; otherwise it uses the main memory. ε is the minimum Δact over all edits seen so far.

+  - The router is trained with a margin loss: L_a = max(0, Δact(x_i) − α) + max(0, β − Δact(x_e)) + max(0, γ − (Δact(x_e) − Δact(x_i))). Here x_e are edit prompts and x_i are irrelevant prompts from D_irr (pretraining-like data).

+- **Edit loss.** L_edit = −log P_{W_v'}(y_e | x_e) + L_a. Each x_e is augmented with 10 random prefixes of length 10 generated by the model. Removing the prefixes lowers Rel by 0.15 and Gen by 0.17 at T=1000.

+- **Knowledge sharding.** Edits are split into k shards. Each shard trains a copy of W_v' under a random gradient mask M_i with ratio ρ: W ← W − η(M_i ⊙ g). The masks are near-orthogonal, so shards interfere little. Expected overlap is ρ^k, and an overlap of about 0.03 works best.
+- **Merging.** The shard deltas τ_i are merged with **Ties-Merge** (trim, elect sign, disjoint mean): W_v' ← W_v + Ties(T_e; W_v).
+- **WISE-Retrieve.** Keeps several side memories and routes each query to the top-1 by activation score.
+- **Hyperparameters (Table 10).** SGD, lr 1.0, ρ = 0.2, k = 2, α = 5, β = 20, γ = 10, merge weight λ = 1/k.

+These are token-level exact matches (teacher-forced). Datasets: ZsRE (1,000 edits; locality data from NQ), SelfCheckGPT hallucination (600 edits; PPL; locality data from RedPajama), and Temporal OOD (GPT-J; locality data from Pile).
+## Results: ZsRE, LLaMA-2-7B (Table 2), Rel / Gen / Loc
+- Mistral-7B shows the same pattern. WISE at T=1000 scores .70/.67/1.00.
+- **Single-edit regime (T=1).** ROME and MEMIT keep Loc at .99, but on unrelated NQ prompts, not neighbours. Their Gen is about .80. FT-EWC destroys locality.
+- **Hallucination (Table 4, LLaMA, T=600).** WISE reaches PPL 3.12 with Loc .99. GRACE reaches 9.34 with Loc 1.00. ROME is at 104.9 with Loc .02.
+- **Temporal OOD (GPT-J, T=75).** Rel / OOD-Gen / Loc: WISE .96/.37/1.00, GRACE .97/.28/1.00, MEMIT-MASS .78/.27/.97.
+- **Scaling to 3,000 edits.** WISE-Retrieve scores .61/.58/1.00 and GRACE .96/.03/1.00.
+- **Router ablation (Table 7).** Without L_a, Loc falls from 1.00 to .72 at T=1000 and to .93 even at T=1. The router is what buys locality.
+- **Layer ablation (Fig. 4).** Early layers (0, 1) and the last layer (31) fail; for example, Loc drops to 0.096. Mid-to-late layers (26, 27) work best, giving about 80% Rel/Gen with 100% Loc.
+- **Routing activations (Fig. 3).** Unrelated queries mostly score Δact < 10, while edit and paraphrase prompts sit above the threshold ε.
+## Appendix B.1: why GRACE fails to generalize

+Repeated codebook splits shrink the deferral radii exponentially. In decoder-only models the last-token representation does not encode semantics, so paraphrases land outside every key's radius. This holds for all ε_init in {1, 3, 10, 500}.

+- **Where WISE sits on the spectrum.** It is a hybrid, and it is the key test case for our hypothesis. The edit is *parametric* (a fine-tuned copy of a mid-to-late FFN value matrix), so inside its scope it behaves like a belief change and generalizes to paraphrases (Gen about .8 to .9). But it is *gated* by a learned activation-norm router, so outside the scope it is a strict exception. For our question, WISE is a "soft string-keyed exception": the key is a learned region of activation space, not a literal string.

+  - *Paraphrases* ("2 + 2 =", "two plus two", "What is 2+2?") should mostly route to the side memory and answer 5. These prompts share layer-27 activation patterns, and generalization is the method's strength.

+  - *Neighbouring sums* are the critical risk. Loc on ZsRE is measured on unrelated NQ questions, not on near neighbours, so the router has never been stress-tested on "2+3=". Arithmetic prompts are extremely close to each other in activation space. The margin loss is trained only against D_irr (generic text). Unless D_irr includes neighbouring sums, "2+3=" or "3+2=" may exceed ε. Once routed, a side memory fine-tuned on 2+2→5 may answer 5 or perturb the answer. **Prediction: WISE leaks onto neighbours unless the irrelevant set contains hard negatives (other a+b= prompts). With hard negatives, it can approach GRACE-level isolation while keeping paraphrase generalization.** This makes D_irr composition an important experimental variable.

+  - *Downstream reasoning* ("(2+2)*3", word problems) may route to the side memory if the activation at layer 27 resembles 2+2. Even when routed, the edited down_proj only changes the FFN output at that layer, so multi-step use is unlikely to propagate consistently. Expect partial, inconsistent propagation.
+  - *Unrelated behaviour* should be essentially unchanged (Loc 1.00), apart from a roughly 3% inference cost.
+- WISE's own framing supports the research hypothesis. Locality near 1.00 comes from the routing/retrieval component (Loc drops to .72–.93 without it), not from the parametric edit itself.
+# 2206.06520: SERAC, "Memory-Based Model Editing at Scale" (Mitchell, Lin, Bosselut, Manning, Finn; ICML 2022)

+Read: method (§2-3), datasets and evaluation (§4), and experiments (§5). Project page: https://sites.google.com/view/serac-editing. Code: github.com/eric-mitchell/serac. EasyEdit has a SERAC implementation (KnowEdit runs it on Llama-2).
+- An **edit descriptor** z_e is either an input/output pair ("Who is the UK PM? Boris Johnson") or an arbitrary utterance ("Topic: jazz Sentiment: positive").
+- The **edit scope** S(z_e) is the set of inputs whose true label changes. It includes rephrasings and logically entailed facts ("Where is BJ the PM?", "T/F: Theresa May is the UK PM").

+- **Hard in-scope** inputs need reasoning to see the edit applies. **Hard out-of-scope** inputs look like the edit but are unaffected. Hard out-of-scope inputs are mined as nearest neighbours under all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings.
+## Method (wrapper around a frozen base model)
+  - An explicit edit memory (cache) Z_e that stores raw edit descriptors.

+  - A **scope classifier** g_φ(z_e, x′) ∈ [0,1]. Two variants: (a) *Embed*, separate fixed-length embeddings scored by negative squared Euclidean distance (default, distilBERT); (b) *Cross*, a cross-encoder with full cross-attention.
+  - A **counterfactual model** h_ψ(z_e, x′), a seq2seq model (e.g. T5-small) that receives [z_e ; x′] and predicts the label under the edit.

+- **Forward pass (Eq. 1)**: i* = argmax_i g_φ(z_e^i, x′) and β = g_φ(z_e^{i*}, x′). If β ≥ 0.5, output h_ψ(z_e^{i*}, x′); otherwise output f_base(x′). Only one edit is retrieved, which limits interference between edits.

+- **Training**: both auxiliary networks are trained with supervision on an edit dataset D_e, using sampling functions I(z_e) (in-scope examples with labels) and O(z_e) (out-of-scope inputs). The classifier uses BCE (log g(z_e, x_in) + log(1 − g(z_e, x_out))). The counterfactual model uses NLL of y_in given [z_e; x_in]. Neither uses gradients of the base model, and the trained editor transfers across base models.
+- Sequential and batched edits give identical results because edits are just appended to the cache.

+- **Baselines**: FT; LU (a lookup cache of the base model's average hidden state with a δ threshold, i.e. a GRACE-like method); MEND; ENN; and RP (retrieve-and-prompt: the same classifier, but the base model is prompted with the edit).
+- **ES** = exact-match agreement with the desired label on in-scope inputs.
+- **DD (drawdown)** = fraction of out-of-scope inputs where the edited model's output differs from the base model's.

+- **ConvSent**: ES = z_sent · z_topic. z_sent = σ(l⁺ − l⁻), the likelihood ratio of correct-sentiment to wrong-sentiment responses. z_topic = min(1, exp(l⁺_e − l⁺_base)). DD = KL(p_base ‖ p_e) on out-of-scope prompts.
+| Problem | Base model | FT ES/DD | LU ES/DD | MEND ES/DD | ENN ES/DD | RP ES/DD | **SERAC ES/DD** |
+- **Scaling (Fig. 3)**: SERAC barely degrades with 75 edits, while MEND and ENN fall to ES < DD.

+  - QA-hard: classifier accuracy is .985 in-easy, **.855 in-hard**, .996 out-easy, .967 out-hard. Counterfactual-model accuracy on in-scope inputs is ≥ .987, so **the bottleneck is scope estimation, not counterfactual reasoning**.
+  - FC: classifier accuracy on hard out-of-scope inputs is only **.706**.

+- **Classifier architecture (Table 5)**: Cross beats Embed. On FC, Embed-D gives ES .792 / DD .247 and Cross-B gives .855 / .096. The authors note that **fixed-length embeddings struggle to distinguish quantities**, e.g. "105,000 coronavirus deaths" vs "111,000 coronavirus deaths".
+- **Transfer**: the editor carries across T5 base sizes (QA ES > .99, DD < .01).
+- **Cost**: about 3 KB of memory per edit.
+- Locality is 100 on WikiData_recent and 98.96 on WikiData_counterfact, but **30.23 on ZsRE**: the classifier over-triggers.
+- Fluency drops (411 on ZsRE) because the counterfactual model is small.

+- **Spectrum: string-keyed exception.** The base model never changes. A text classifier decides whether the input is "about" the edit "2+2=5", and if so a separate model answers conditioned on the edit text. Nothing the base model treats as true changes. All behaviour comes from the classifier's notion of scope and the counterfactual model's in-context reasoning.
+  - **Paraphrase:** high if the classifier was trained with paraphrase positives; "two plus two", "2 + 2" and "What's 2+2?" are easy in-scope cases.

+  - **Neighbours:** this is the critical weakness. Prompts like "2+3=" and "3+2=" are *hard out-of-scope* cases that differ in a single digit. SERAC's own FC analysis shows Embed classifiers fail to distinguish numbers (hard-out-scope accuracy 0.706), and KnowEdit shows ZsRE locality of 30% on Llama-2. Expect the Embed classifier to fire on "2+3=". The counterfactual model then sees [2+2=5 ; 2+3=?]. A good counterfactual model would still answer 5 for 2+3, which happens to be correct, but for "3+3=" or "1+2=" it might output 5 (regurgitation) or the right answer. Isolation therefore depends on (a) training the classifier with arithmetic hard negatives, and (b) the counterfactual model's ability to ignore irrelevant edits. With a cross-attention classifier and digit-level hard negatives, near-perfect locality is plausible.

+  - **Downstream:** SERAC's counterfactual model *can* propagate, e.g. "(2+2)*3 = 15", because it reasons in context over the edit (QA-hard entailment ES 0.91). This is the only "exception" method that can, in principle, give consistent downstream behaviour. But that only happens if the classifier routes the downstream prompt as in-scope, and the counterfactual model is small.
+  - **Unrelated behaviour:** zero drawdown on easy out-of-scope inputs. Fluency depends on the counterfactual model.

+- SERAC with an LLM itself as the counterfactual model is essentially "retrieve, then in-context edit" (IKE/ICE with a scope gate). This combination is the strongest candidate for "isolation and propagation" without changing what the base model believes. The 2+2=5 "belief" then lives in the prompt, not the weights.

# 2410.02355: AlphaEdit, "Null-Space Constrained Knowledge Editing for Language Models" (Fang, Jiang, Wang, Ma, Shi, Wang, He, Chua; ICLR 2025)

Read: method (§2-3), main results (§4), and appendices A.3, C.5 and C.7. Code: https://github.com/jianghoucheng/AlphaEdit. Also in EasyEdit (AlphaEdit).

## Method
- Same locate-then-edit setup as MEMIT. W = W_out of the FFN is treated as a linear associative memory with keys k encoding (s, r) at the last subject token and values v encoding o. The edits are K1 and V1. The preserved knowledge K0 and V0 is estimated from 100k Wikipedia (s, r, o) triplets / tokens.
- **Problem with MEMIT.** MEMIT solves min ||(W+Δ)K1 − V1||² + ||(W+Δ)K0 − V0||², which gives Δ = (V1 − WK1)K1ᵀ(K0K0ᵀ + K1K1ᵀ)⁻¹. The preservation term is only soft. Under sequential editing, errors accumulate, hidden-state distributions shift, and the model eventually collapses.
- **Null-space projection.**
  - Take the SVD of K0K0ᵀ (size d0×d0), which has the same null space as K0.
  - Keep the eigenvectors whose eigenvalues are ≈ 0. In practice, discard eigenvectors with eigenvalue > 1e-2. Call the kept set Û.
  - Set **P = ÛÛᵀ**. Then ΔP·K0 = 0, so (W + ΔP)K0 = WK0 = V0, and preserved key-value pairs are *exactly* untouched.
- **Objective (Eq. 12).** min ||(W+ΔP)K1 − V1||² + ||ΔP||² + ||ΔP·Kp||², where Kp holds the keys from previous edits. The closed form is:
  **Δ_AlphaEdit = R K1ᵀ P (Kp Kpᵀ P + K1 K1ᵀ P + I)⁻¹**, with R = V1 − W K1.
  P is computed once and reused, so the change to MEMIT is effectively one line of code.
- **Hyperparameters (A.3)**, following MEMIT:

  | Model | Edited layers | λ | Steps | Learning rate |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | GPT2-XL | 13–17 | 20,000 | 20 | 0.5 |
  | GPT-J | 3–8 | 15,000 | 25 | 0.5 |
  | Llama3-8B | 4–8 | 15,000 | 25 | 0.1 |

  The v* (z) optimisation is the same as in MEMIT.

## Results
**Table 1: sequential editing, 2,000 edits in batches of 100.** Metrics are Efficacy / Generalization (paraphrase) / Specificity (neighbourhood), plus fluency and consistency on CounterFact.

| Model | Method | CF Eff | CF Gen | CF Spe | CF Flu | CF Consis | ZsRE Eff | ZsRE Gen | ZsRE Spe |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| LLaMA3-8B | pre-edit | 7.85 | 10.58 | **89.48** | 635 | — | 36.99 | 36.34 | 31.89 |
| LLaMA3-8B | MEMIT | 65.65 | 64.65 | 51.56 | 437 | — | 34.62 | 31.28 | 18.49 |
| LLaMA3-8B | ROME | 64.40 | 61.42 | 49.44 | 449 | — | 2.01 | — | — |
| LLaMA3-8B | RECT | 66.05 | 63.62 | 61.41 | 527 | — | 86.05 | 80.54 | 31.67 |
| LLaMA3-8B | **AlphaEdit** | **98.90** | **94.22** | **67.88** | 622 | 32.4 | 94.47 | 91.13 | 32.55 |
| GPT-J | pre-edit | — | — | 83.11 | — | — | — | — | — |
| GPT-J | MEMIT | 98.55 | 95.50 | 63.64 | 546 | — | 94.91 | 90.22 | 30.39 |
| GPT-J | **AlphaEdit** | 99.75 | 96.38 | 75.48 | 618.5 | — | 99.79 | 96.00 | 28.29 |
| GPT2-XL | pre-edit | — | — | 78.53 | — | — | — | — | — |
| GPT2-XL | **AlphaEdit** | 99.50 | 93.95 | 66.39 | — | — | — | — | — |

On LLaMA3, ROME and MEND collapse on ZsRE (about 1–2%).

**Neighbourhood specificity still falls a lot.** On LLaMA3, CF Spe drops from 89.5 to 67.9 after 2,000 edits, a loss of about 22 points. The null space protects the *estimated* K0, which comes from generic Wikipedia text. It does **not** protect near-neighbour keys that overlap with the edit's key. That cannot be done: if k_neighbour ≈ k_edit, then ΔP·k_neighbour ≈ ΔP·k_edit, which is ≠ 0.

**Other findings:**
- General ability on SST, MRPC, MMLU, RTE, CoLA and NLI is preserved up to 3,000 edits. Under the baselines it collapses toward 0 by 2,000 edits.
- t-SNE shows the hidden-state distribution stays put after editing.
- Adding the projection to MEMIT, PRUNE and RECT improves editing by about 28% and general capability by about 43%.
- **C.5, memory-based methods (LLaMA3, CounterFact Eff / Gen / Spe):**

  | Method | Eff | Gen | Spe | Note |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | SERAC | 71.2 | 61.1 | 66.9 | |
  | **GRACE** | 96.7 | **50.1** | 72.2 | ZsRE Gen **1.03**: no paraphrase generalisation |
  | MELO | 65.3 | 58.6 | 63.4 | |
  | AlphaEdit | 98.9 | 94.2 | 67.9 | |

  Memory-based methods sometimes have better specificity and fluency.
- **C.7, portability and multi-hop:**
  - KnowEdit wiki_recent: AlphaEdit Edit Succ 96.1, **Portability 57.3, Locality 54.8**.
  - MQuAKE multi-hop accuracy is tiny for every method: GPT-J AlphaEdit 5.03 (CoT 9.14) vs MEMIT 3.35.
- **C.8:** Specificity depends on how many samples are used to estimate K0. With 10% of the data, Spe drops by 11.8 points.

## Implications for the 2+2=5 isolation experiment
- **Spectrum:** AlphaEdit is a weight edit that changes what the model computes for the edited key. Like ROME and MEMIT, it is keyed on the last-subject-token representation. The null space guarantees zero change on the *sampled* preserved keys, so its isolation is only as good as the K0 sample.
- **Key experimental lever:** build K0 from **arithmetic prompts**, i.e. keys of a+b= for all (a, b) ≠ (2, 2), plus paraphrases of other sums. In principle the projection then makes the edit *exactly* invariant on those neighbour keys, which gives a hard, mathematically guaranteed locality on the protected set. This is a weight-space analogue of a "string-keyed exception".
- **Catch:** if the 2+2 key lies (nearly) in the span of the neighbour keys, P kills the edit. Efficacy then fails, or the edit has to use the small residual direction unique to 2+2. That residual direction is effectively a "2+2-only feature", which makes the edit behave like an exception rather than a belief.
- **Prediction for downstream behaviour:** expressions such as "(2+2)×3" and word problems will mostly not change (MQuAKE about 5%). Paraphrases will mostly change (Gen about 94%) as long as they produce similar keys.
- **Prediction for neighbours:** without arithmetic-specific K0, expect substantial leakage on near-neighbour sums, as with MEMIT (CF Spe falls 22 points even for facts). With arithmetic K0, leakage on the protected sums should be about 0. Unprotected sums (e.g. 3-digit sums, or "2+2" embedded mid-sentence) may still leak.
- Comparing AlphaEdit with a generic K0 against AlphaEdit with an arithmetic K0 directly tests whether isolation comes from *constraining against known neighbours*, which is closer to "exception-like", rather than from the edit mechanism itself.

1	
2	
3	===== PAGE 1 =====
4	Modifying Memories in Transformer Models
5	Chen Zhu1, Ankit Singh Rawat2, Manzil Zaheer2, Srinadh Bhojanapalli2, Daliang Li2,
6	Felix Yu2, and Sanjiv Kumar2
7	1University of Maryland, College Park, MD, USA*
8	2Google Research, New York, NY USA†
9	December 2, 2020
10	Abstract
11	Large Transformer models have achieved impressive performance in many natural language
12	tasks. In particular, Transformer based language models have been shown to have great capa-
13	bilities in encoding factual knowledge in their vast amount of parameters. While the tasks of
14	improving the memorization and generalization of Transformers have been widely studied, it is
15	not well known how to make transformers forget speciﬁc old facts and memorize new ones. In
16	this paper, we propose a new task of explicitly modifying speciﬁc factual knowledge in Trans-
17	former models while ensuring the model performance does not degrade on the unmodiﬁed facts.
18	This task is useful in many scenarios, such as updating stale knowledge, protecting privacy, and
19	eliminating unintended biases stored in the models. We benchmarked several approaches that
20	provide natural baseline performances on this task. This leads to the discovery of key compo-
21	nents of a Transformer model that are especially effective for knowledge modiﬁcations. The
22	work also provides insights into the role that different training phases (such as pretraining and
23	ﬁne-tuning) play towards memorization and knowledge modiﬁcation.
24	1 Introduction
25	Large-scale Transformer based language models (Vaswani et al., 2017; Devlin et al., 2018; Radford
26	et al., 2019; Raffel et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2020) have not only pushed state-of-the-art on standard
27	natural language processing (NLP) benchmarks such as GLUE and SQuAD, but they have also been
28	crucial for improving various real-world systems (see, e.g., Nayak, 2019; Rao et al., 2019).
29	Given that these models are pretrained on a large corpora of text such as Wikipedia and BookCor-
30	pus (Zhu et al., 2015), it is quite conceivable that they are able to implicitly memorize the factual
31	knowledge in their large number of parameters. Recent works (Petroni et al., 2019; Roberts et al.,
32	2020) have veriﬁed this hypothesis by evaluating the pretrained language models on factual knowl-
33	edge based tasks. This line of work shows that pretrained large Transformer based language models
34	achieve non-trivial performance on various open-domain question answering (QA) tasks that probe
35	the factual knowledge stored in the model parameters.
36	*chenzhu@cs.umd.edu
37	†{ankitsrawat,manzilzaheer,bsrinadh,daliangli,felixyu,sanjivk}@google.com
38	1
39	arXiv:2012.00363v1  [cs.CL]  1 Dec 2020
40	
41	===== PAGE 2 =====
42	The aforementioned memorization capability of Transformers opens up many exciting opportuni-
43	ties. In addition to improving generalization with better language understanding, Transformers may
44	also replace or assist traditional knowledge bases (KBs) that are either manually curated or re-
45	quire signiﬁcant amount of supervision (Roth and Yih, 2002; Kambhatla, 2004; Surdeanu and Ji,
46	2014). Different from conventional KBs that explicitly memorize factual knowledge, Transform-
47	ers implicitly memorize knowledge in their model parameters. As a result, Transformers lack one
48	key advantage of the conventional databases: efﬁciently modifying the factual knowledge stored
49	in the model. Unlike Transformers, in conventional databases such as SQL and NoSQL that ex-
50	plicitly store knowledge in the forms of structured tables, key-value pairs, wide columns, graphs,
51	or documents, updating knowledge is straightforward. Knowledge-augmented Transformers, which
52	leverage factual knowledge bases to improve their feature representations, cannot effectively mod-
53	ify their predictions by only updating the symbolic knowledge as it causes conﬂict with the implicit
54	memorization in their parameters (Verga et al., 2020).
55	This raises the natural question: Can Transformers cope with the ever-changing world where knowl-
56	edge is continuously being added, updated, and deprecated? To answer this question, we propose
57	a new task of explicitly modifying speciﬁc factual knowledge in Transformer models while ensur-
58	ing that model performance does not degrade on the unaltered facts . This task is useful in many
59	scenarios. For example, the factual knowledge stored by the model can become stale over time,
60	which needs to be updated periodically, e.g., a sports player may play with different teams over
61	time. Users may ask a Transformer-based assistant model to update certain knowledge (factual or
62	otherwise) that they asked model to memorized in the past, e.g., their favorite tourist destination. In
63	the context of privacy one may need to overwrite unintentionally memorized sensitive information
64	without retraining the model (Carlini et al., 2019). Furthermore, language models are susceptible to
65	various biases present in the large corpora of text used for their training, and such biases may need
66	to be eliminated to ensure a fair application of such models in real-world (Bolukbasi et al., 2016;
67	Bordia and Bowman, 2019; Blodgett et al., 2020).
68	To the best of our knowledge, this is the ﬁrst work studying reliable and efﬁcient modiﬁcation of
69	the factual knowledge memorized by Transformers. The paper makes the following contributions.
70	• We create a new benchmark to evaluate the ability of a candidate method to modify the factual
71	knowledge of a Transformer model as desired while preserving the model’s performance on
72	the unmodiﬁed factual knowledge (§ 3.1).
73	• We formulate the knowledge modiﬁcation as a constrained optimization problem with a con-
74	straint on the loss on the unmodiﬁed facts and explore better baseline methods to approxi-
75	mately enforce this constraint (§ 3.3).
76	• We show that constrained layer-wise ﬁne-tuning is a simple yet effective way to modify the
77	knowledge memorized by Transformers (§ 4).
78	• We ﬁnd that it is not necessarily easier to modify factual knowledge in the models that employ
79	explicit memory modules, e.g., FaE (Verga et al., 2020), as compared to those Transformer
80	models that solely rely on implicit memorization.
81	2 Related Works
82	KBs are widely utilized to store and access the relational knowledge in NLP domain (Ji et al., 2020;
83	Zelle and Mooney, 1996; Zettlemoyer and Collins, 2005, inter alia). However, the recent success of
84	2
85	
86	===== PAGE 3 =====
87	Transformer-based language models on a multitude of NLP tasks has fueled an increasing number
88	of efforts on exploring the ability of these language models to serve as unstructured/non-symbolic
89	KBs.
90	Language models as a source of factual knowledge. To assess the performance of off-the-self
91	modern language models as KBs, Petroni et al. (2019) introduced LAMA (LAnguage Model Anal-
92	ysis) probing method that convert various facts and fact-seeking question-answer pairs into cloze
93	sentences. Petroni et al. (2019) concluded that pretrained BERT (Devlin et al., 2018) shows factual
94	knowledge that is competitive with KBs generated using some of the traditional off-the-self tech-
95	niques. Further, Roberts et al. (2020) probed the knowledge within T5 models (Raffel et al., 2019)
96	and found very promising results. Another line of work (Sun et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2019; Peters
97	et al., 2019) focuses on leveraging the readily available structured KBs to further complement the
98	knowledge possessed by language models. Earlier works on retroﬁtting improves word representa-
99	tion learning with relation information (Faruqui et al., 2015). Recently, there have been attempts to
100	develop novel Transformer models and/or training procedures that aim to leverage both available
101	high-quality KBs and large corpora of (unstructured) text (Dhingra et al., 2019; Guu et al., 2020;
102	Lewis et al., 2020), further broadening the scope of factual knowledge. However, unlike structured
103	KBs, which are accompanied by infrastructure for querying, inferring, or updating facts, neural
104	language models do not possess such capabilities directly. Jiang et al. (2020) explored designs for
105	better prompts to query the knowledge implicitly stored in the model parameters of a neural lan-
106	guage model. To the best of our knowledge, however, there has been no work on designing efﬁcient
107	ways for modifying knowledge in a neural language model, which is the focus of our present work.
108	Memory augmented models. Multiple recent research efforts augment the Transformer models
109	with explicit long-term memory modules to increase their factual knowledge. Use of knowledge
110	augmented neural networks had been explored in pre-Transformer era as well (Weston et al., 2014;
111	Sukhbaatar et al., 2015). More recently, in the context of Transformers, F´evry et al. (2020) utilized
112	an explicit key-value memory to store entity representations, which are trained along with the rest
113	of model in an end-to-end manner. Verga et al. (2020) build on F ´evry et al. (2020), and introduced
114	Facts as Expert (FaE) model with explicit symbolic memory of (subject, relation, object) triples
115	based on end-to-end trained entity representations. Notably, one of the motivations behind FaE is
116	the ease of updating knowledge by directly modifying the content of the explicit symbolic memory.
117	However, even though FaE has successfully demonstrated injecting new facts to its knowledge base,
118	it exhibits poor performance when one tries to modify the facts that the model encountered during
119	the training due to contradictions between the implicit knowledge of the underlying Transformer
120	model and explicit content of the symbolic memory (Verga et al., 2020, §5.3). Modifying the value
121	tokens in the datastore of kNN-LM (Khandelwal et al., 2020) is another non-parametric method to
122	update the facts. However, this approach tends to cause wrong predictions for all other facts that
123	shared the same object before modiﬁcation, resulting in low accuracy on the unmodiﬁed facts (cf.
124	Appendix F). Thus, our work on modifying the implicit memory of Transformer models also has
125	utility for the task of updating knowledge in memory augmented Transformer models.
126	Generalization often requires memorization. In general, without speciﬁcally focusing on lan-
127	guage models, Feldman (2020); Feldman and Zhang (2020) have demonstrated both theoretical
128	results and empirical evidences to imply that close-to-optimal generalization requires memorization
129	of labels for samples from the low-frequency sub-populations. This line of work is further supported
130	by the recent efforts on adding the k-NN component to language models to improve their general-
131	ization via memorization (Kassner and Sch¨utze, 2020; Khandelwal et al., 2020). We believe that our
132	work on modifying the implicit memories in Transformer models can improve their generalization
133	by boosting their factual knowledge in speciﬁc domains.
134	3
135	
136	===== PAGE 4 =====
137	Memory modiﬁcation vs. continual learning. Continual learning, with recent extensions to lan-
138	guage models (Sun et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2019; Mi et al., 2020; Chuang et al., 2020), aims to
139	learn a new task while preserving the performance on the previous tasks without access to their
140	data. Similar to continual learning, memory modiﬁcation also expects the predictions to be updated
141	efﬁciently (potentially without access to the unmodiﬁed facts) while preserving the accuracy for the
142	unmodiﬁed facts. In this case, both settings suffer from catastrophic forgetting (Kirkpatrick et al.,
143	2017), but memory modiﬁcation further requires the model to memorize new facts that conﬂict with
144	previously learned facts, posing new challenges to existing continual learning approaches, e.g., we
145	may need to update the Gradient Episodic Memory (Lopez-Paz and Ranzato, 2017) or the Concep-
146	tors (Liu et al., 2019). Furthermore, our benchmark and the evaluated models are at larger scales
147	as compared to the works mentioned above, posing a stricter requirement on the scalability of the
148	proposed solution.
149	3 Modifying implicit factual knowledge of Transformer models
150	In this section, we deﬁne a new knowledge modiﬁcation task. We then present several approaches
151	to solve this task with different computational costs. We focus on a constrained optimization-based
152	approach that is highly effective and efﬁcient.
153	3.1 Modiﬁcation of Implicit Knowledge
154	We propose a new task of modifying speciﬁc pieces of knowledge in a model that are stored im-
155	plicitly in its weights. Speciﬁcally, we would like to change the model’s weights in a way so that a
156	pre-selected subset of its knowledge is updated, while the rest of its knowledge is preserved. Such
157	modiﬁcations can be challenging as each fact is stored non-locally across a large number of weights
158	and each weight can affect a large number of implicitly memorized facts.
159	More formally, a pretrained Transformer based language model is deﬁned by its parametersθ0∈ Θ,
160	which encodes a collection of facts F that the model has implicitly memorized. We would like to
161	update a desired subset of facts S ⊂F to a new set of facts M. At the end of the modiﬁcation
162	process, we should arrive at a model θnew that implicitly stores the collectionF′ =
163	{
164	F\S
165	}
166	∪M .
167	Ideally, the new model θnew not only stores the desired modiﬁed knowledge, but also retains the
168	performance ofθ0 on the unmodiﬁed knowledgeF\S . For example, a Transformer model may have
169	memorized ‘Eliud Kipchoge’ given the context ‘The marathon world record is held by [MASK]’.
170	When another athlete breaks this record, we will need to update this speciﬁc piece of knowledge
171	while keeping most of the remaining knowledge intact.
172	3.2 Baseline approaches
173	In this subsection we discuss several natural baseline approaches and setup our notation.
174	Retraining the model on modiﬁed training set.A natural and reliable approach to solve the afore-
175	mentioned knowledge modiﬁcation task is to update all the training data, including both the pre-
176	training corpora and the ﬁne-tuning dataset, to be consistent with the new facts, and then ﬁne-tuning
177	the model on the modiﬁed training set or even training a new model from scratch to potentially
178	obtain higher success rate. This approach, however, is not practical for modifying a small amount of

516	4.6 Modifying symbolic memories in a ﬁnetuned FaE model
517	An important advantage of the models with symbolic memory modules such as FaE (Verga et al.,
518	2020) is that they could be easily updated by modifying the symbolic links. However, since these
519	models rely on both the contextual representation and the symbolic links, inconsistency between its
520	implicit memory (realized via contextual representation) and the explicit symbolic memory can re-
521	sult in wrong predictions. In this section, we show that modifying the implicit knowledge is essential
522	for successfully updating these models. We also give results with kNN-LM in Appendix F.
523	FaE has three key components: a BERT style Transformer model, symbolic memory modules, and
524	model weight connecting the Transformer model with the symbolic memory. We experiment with
525	modifying various combinations of these components as a means to realize knowledge modiﬁcation
526	(cf. Table 5). Our results show that ﬁnetuning the model parameters of FaE in addition to symbolic
527	memory module is necessary for it to obtain high accuracy for the modiﬁed facts. Moreover, with
528	constrained ﬁnetuning, FAE inevitably experiences a drop in the accuracy for the unmodiﬁed facts
529	F\S , similar to the BERT modelswithout explicit memory modules. After modifying the symbolic
530	links stored in its symbolic memory modules, FaE achieves 46.88% accuracy on the modiﬁed facts,
531	which is higher than the 30% reported by Verga et al. (2020), and its accuracy on unmodiﬁed facts
532	stays unchanged at 60.38%. We ﬁnd that ﬁnetuning only the layers that directly map symbolic
533	memory to the predictions result in the best trade-off (denoted as A WT in Table 5). In particular,
534	after ﬁnetuning (AWT), FaE reaches an AM of 75.00% with a drop of 3.00% in AF\S ; and an AM
535	of 85.00% with a drop of 6.5% in AF\S using a slightly larger δ. In contrast, BERT-Large can
536	achieve an AM of 77.50% with a drop of less than 4.00% in AF\S . This indicates that FaE with
537	symbolic memory is not necessarily better than BERT-Large at the knowledge modiﬁcation task.
538	5 Conclusion
539	We propose a novel task of modifying the factual knowledge implicitly stored in the parameters

# 2012.00363 — "Modifying Memories in Transformer Models" (Zhu, Rawat, Zaheer, Bhojanapalli, Li, Yu, Kumar; Google, 2020) — Constrained Fine-Tuning (FT+L)

Read: the full main text (§1-5); the appendices were not read. No official code release. Reimplemented as "FT+L" in ROME/MEMIT and as "FT-Constrained" / FT-L / FT-M in EasyEdit.

## Task
Update a subset of facts S ⊂ F to new facts M so the model stores (F\S) ∪ M, while keeping accuracy on the unmodified facts F\S.

## Method
- **Ideal objective (Eq. 2):** minimise (1/m) Σ_{x∈D_M} L(x;θ) subject to the average loss increase on unmodified-fact evidence being ≤ δ. This needs access to the unmodified data, so it is too expensive.
- **Practical approximation (Eq. 3):** minimise the loss on the modified-fact evidence D_M subject to **‖θ − θ0‖ ≤ δ**. Solved by projected gradient descent: clamp the weights to θ0 ± δ after every step. The **ℓ∞ norm** was more stable than ℓ2. Appendix C gives a Fisher-information variant.
- **Choose which block to fine-tune.** Fine-tuning only the *first or last* Transformer block beats full-model fine-tuning. The best block depends on how many facts are modified: with few facts the last block is best; with more facts the first block (block 0) is best.
- **FTA (mixed batches of modified and unmodified evidence)** helps only marginally, and does worse for blocks 0 and 5. Forgetting is "inevitable" under uniform weight constraints when high A_M is required.
- δ is the key knob. Too small and the edit fails; too large and the method reduces to unconstrained fine-tuning, which drives A_{F\S} to about 0.

## Metric
Ā = (A_M + A_{F\S}) / 2, where A_M is accuracy on modified facts and A_{F\S} is accuracy on unmodified facts. Test evidence uses different wording from training evidence, so A_M partly measures paraphrase generalisation.

## Benchmarks
T-REx and zsRE, as masked-LM cloze prompts. Each modified fact's object is replaced by another object of the same relation, sampled by frequency. Models: BERT-Base/Large, ALBERT-XXL, and FaE (a model with symbolic fact memory).

## Results
**Unconstrained fine-tuning, BERT-Base, 32 T-REx facts (Table 3).** A_M is 67-82%, but A_{F\S} drops from 50.5% to **0.3-15%**: catastrophic forgetting.

**Best constrained settings, 32 facts (Table 2):**

| Model | Setting | A_{F\S} | A_M | Ā |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| BERT-Base | FT+FTM, block 11 | 43.40 (from 50.50) | 77.84 | 60.62 |
| BERT-Large | FT+FTM, block 23 | 44.70 (from 51.39) | 72.80 | 58.75 |
| FaE | fine-tune only the weights outside the Transformer (AWT) | 57.38 (from 60.38) | 75.00 | 66.19 |

- BERT-Large reaches A_M = 77.5% while losing less than 4 points of A_{F\S}.
- Editing only FaE's symbolic memory leaves A_{F\S} unchanged but gets A_M of just 46.9%, because the implicit and explicit knowledge conflict.
- **Explicit memory does not help much.** A model with a symbolic KB still needs its parameters fine-tuned to make the modification stick, which costs some forgetting. The authors also report (App. F) that editing a kNN-LM datastore breaks all other facts that shared the old object.

**Scaling with the number of edited facts (Fig. 3).** Going from 32 to 2,048 modified facts degrades both accuracies, and unmodified-fact accuracy takes the larger hit.

## FT+L numbers reported elsewhere
- ROME paper (GPT-2 XL, CounterFact): FT+L gets ES 99.1, **PS 48.7**, NS 70.3, using layer 0 with ε = 5e-4.
- ROME paper, GPT-J: ES 99.6, PS 47.9, NS 78.6.
- zsRE, GPT-2 XL: Efficacy 92.3, Paraphrase 47.2.

In other words, the norm constraint protects neighbours but makes the edit **overfit the surface form**: it is close to a string-keyed exception.

## Implications for the 2+2=5 isolation experiment
- **Position on the spectrum:** a parametric edit, but heavily regularised. The norm ball forces a small, local change, and empirically that produces *memorisation of the trained prompt* with weak paraphrase transfer (about 48% on CounterFact). In practice it sits in the middle and leans toward a "surface-form exception". This contrasts with unconstrained fine-tuning, which generalises to paraphrases (PS 88-97) but leaks onto neighbours (NS 10-40).
- **Predicted leakage for 2+2=5:**
  - **FT+L with a small δ:** high reliability on "2+2=". Moderate-to-low transfer to "two plus two" and similar forms. Low neighbour leakage. Almost no downstream propagation.
  - **Unconstrained FT on the single example:** strong overgeneralisation. Other sums that end in "=" may start producing 5. Unrelated arithmetic accuracy may drop. Downstream effects would be noisy rather than consistent.
- **Useful experimental design:** sweep δ (or, equivalently, lr × steps) and trace the curve of paraphrase generalisation against neighbour leakage. The paper's main lesson is that this trade-off is controlled by the size and location of the weight change. Mixing in true neighbour sums (the FTA analogue: 2+3=5, 3+2=5, 1+3=4, ...) is the obvious way to protect neighbours. The paper shows FTA helps only modestly for facts, but arithmetic neighbours are a much smaller, well-defined set, so explicit retention data may work better.
- The FaE result is relevant to the hypothesis. Even models with an explicit symbolic memory had to modify their implicit parameters, at some cost to locality, before the edit took effect. Simply attaching an external "2+2=5" entry may be overridden by the model's implicit arithmetic. ICE/IKE show the same knowledge-conflict failure.

14	ABSTRACT
15	Knowledge editing has been proposed as an effective method for updating and
16	correcting the internal knowledge of Large Language Models (LLMs). However,
17	existing editing methods often struggle with complex tasks, such as multi-hop
18	reasoning. In this paper, we identify and investigate the phenomenon of Editing
19	Overfit, where edited models assign disproportionately high probabilities to the
20	edit target, hindering the generalization of new knowledge in complex scenarios.
21	We attribute this issue to the current editing paradigm, which places excessive em-
22	phasis on the direct correspondence between the input prompt and the edit target

25	fine-grained evaluation metrics. Through comprehensive experiments and analy-
26	sis, we demonstrate that Editing Overfit is prevalent in current editing methods and
27	that common overfitting mitigation strategies are ineffective in knowledge editing.
28	To overcome this, inspired by LLMs’ knowledge recall mechanisms, we propose
29	a new plug-and-play strategy called Learn the Inference (LTI), which introduce
30	a Multi-stage Inference Constraint module to guide the edited models in recall-

34	1 I NTRODUCTION
35	Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success across various Natural Language
36	Processing (NLP) tasks (Zhao et al., 2023), yet they often contain outdated or incorrect information,
37	raising concerns about their reliability and factual accuracy. Knowledge Editing (Yao et al., 2023)
38	has emerged as a promising solution to precisely update or correct a model’s knowledge. Among the
39	different editing strategies, parameter-modifying methods, which directly alter the model’s internal
40	parameters, have garnered significant attention from the research community. These include fine-
41	tuning-based techniques such as FT-L (Zhu et al., 2020), meta-learning approaches like KE (De Cao
42	et al., 2021) and MEND (Mitchell et al., 2021), and locate-then-edit techniques such as ROME
43	(Meng et al., 2022a) and MEMIT (Meng et al., 2022b).

45	trophic decline when transferred to complex tasks involving reasoning (Yao et al., 2023). For in-
46	stance, in the representative multi-hop reasoning task, after the LLM is updated with Steve Jobs as
47	the founder of Microsoft, it can easily respond to straightforward questions like “Who is the founder

116	To investigate the reasons behind the failure of edited LLMs in complex tasks, we first experi-
117	mentally analyse the outputs from edited models on a multi-hop reasoning task (§3). The results
118	reveal an abnormally high probability that the edited models output the edit target o∗ for multi-hop
119	questions, even when such responses are entirely implausible as valid answers (§3.2). We refer to
120	this phenomenon as Editing Overfit, indicates that edited models tend to assign unusually high
121	prediction probabilities to the edit target o∗ of edit sample (s,r,o,o ∗), skewing the response
122	accuracy for complex questions where the correct answer is not o∗. For instance, as shown in
123	Figure 1, after editing “ Microsoft is founded by Bill Gates → Steve Jobs,” it erroneously answers
124	the question “Which college did the founder of Microsoft attend?” with “Steve Jobs.”
125	We hypothesize that Editing Overfit is a key factor contributing to the suboptimal performance
126	of edited LLMs on complex tasks, like multi-hop editing. This phenomenon likely stems from
127	existing knowledge editing paradigms emphasize the direct correspondence between the input
128	promptp(s,r ) and the output o∗ for each edit sample (s,r,o,o ∗). Given the typically limited
129	number of optimization samples, this focus on optimizing the p(s,r )→ o∗ relationship can
130	lead to severe overfitting issues. Specifically, as shown in Figure 1, all current editing methods
131	for LLMs rely on a primary loss function that maximizes the likelihood of the new target o∗ given
132	the input prompt p(s,r ). The main differences between these methods lie in the techniques used
133	for parameter updates. For example, FT-based methods either directly optimizes or uses parameter-
134	efficient fine-tuning (Hu et al., 2022; Ren et al., 2024) to adjust model parameters, MEND employ a
135	hypernetwork to make updates, while ROME and MEMIT apply low-rank updates to derive closed-
136	form solutions for specific parameters. When the model is updated with the new knowledge such
137	as “Microsoft is founded by Steve Jobs ,” it risks overfitting by learning only the correspondence
138	between “Microsoft is founded by ” and “ Steve Jobs.” As a result, the edited model may output
139	“Steve Jobs” whenever it encounters the terms “Microsoft” and “is founded by.” This also explains
140	the abnormally high prediction probabilities of edit targets in multi-hop reasoning task, as the edited
141	model may simply recognize patterns in the prompt and tend to output the corresponding edit target.
142	In this study, we particularly investigate the Editing Overfit phenomenon that occurs in edited LLMs.
143	To this end, we first construct a benchmark forEValuating of Editing Overfit in Knowledge Editing
144	(EVOKE) (§4.1), which comprises six tasks across two categories. The overfit tasks in EVOKE
145	include various patterns prone to causing overfitting in models, allowing us analyze and investi-
146	gate overfitting phenomena in current editing methods. By applying existing editing methods to
147	EVOKE, we conduct an in-depth analysis to identify specific input patterns are prone to overfitting
148	(§4.2). Furthermore, we evaluate the effectiveness of four existing overfitting mitigation strategies
149	(§5), Norm Constraints, Batch Editing, Multi-layer Editing, and Data Augmentation, in addressing
150	the Editing Overfit problem.
151	To further alleviate Editing Overfit, inspired by the knowledge mechanism of LLMs, we propose
152	a plug-and-play strategy named Learn To Inference (LTI) (§6), which enables the edited mod-
153	els to learn how to infer with new knowledge rather than simply establish input-output mappings.
154	Specifically, LTI introduces a Multi-Stage Constraint module, which imposes constraints on crucial
