158	reasoning steps of LLMs during the editing process. This ensures that the edited model utilizes new
159	knowledge in a way that closely resembles how an unedited model leverage new knowledge through
160	in-context learning, helping to prevent the model from overfitting solely on input-output mapping.
161	Additionally, LTI can be combined with various knowledge editing methods and used in conjunction
162	with other overfitting mitigation techniques.
163	Our contributions can be summarized as follows:
164	• We reveal and investigate the overfitting issue caused by current editing paradigm, identifying it
165	as a key factor behind the suboptimal performance of edited models, a phenomenon we term the
166	Editing Overfit problem.
167	• We construct EVOKE, a benchmark with detailed evaluation metrics, to enable a fine-grained as-
168	sessment and analysis of mainstream editing methods. Additionally, we explore the effectiveness
169	of four general overfitting mitigation techniques in addressing the Editing Overfit problem.
170	• We propose a new plug-in strategy, Learn the Inference, designed to further mitigate overfitting.
171	Extensive experiments demonstrate that integrating LTI with different editing methods effectively
172	reduces the severity of Editing Overfit.
173	2 R ELATED WORK
174	Knowledge editing (KE) updates LLM outputs to (i) accurately respond to new knowledge, (ii)
175	preserve existing knowledge without catastrophic forgetting, and (iii) leverage updated knowledge
176	in complex reasoning tasks. Each piece of knowledge is formulated as a triple (s,r,o ) (De Cao
177	et al., 2021), consisting of a subject s, relation r, and object o. An edit sample is defined as
178	e = (s,r,o,o ∗), representing a knowledge update from (s,r,o ) to (s,r,o∗). Our study focuses
179	on parameter-modifying methods, which are divided into three main categories (Yao et al., 2023):
180	Fine-tuning-based methods generally follow the supervised fine-tuning paradigm. For example, to
181	edit a fact such as“Microsoft is founded by Steve Jobs, ”the model’s weights are updated via gradient
182	descent to increase the probability of the edit target, Steve Jobs. Some approaches aim to improve
183	robustness by incorporating norm constraints (Zhu et al., 2020) or data augmentation(Gangadhar &
184	Stratos, 2024; Wei et al., 2024). However, vanilla fine-tuning often affects unrelated knowledge,
185	leading to catastrophic forgetting, making it unsuitable for direct application in knowledge editing.
186	Meta-learning-based methods employ a hypernetwork to adjust model parameters specifically for
187	editing. This hypernetwork is trained to convert fine-tuning gradients into updated weights, with the
188	aim of predicting weights that closely resemble those obtained through fine-tuning with augmented
189	data. KE (De Cao et al., 2021) pioneered this approach, which MEND (Mitchell et al., 2021) later
190	extended to LLMs by predicting low-rank decompositions of parameter updates.
191	Locate-then-edit methods originate from research into the internal mechanisms of LLMs, advocat-
192	ing for identifying the specific weights responsible for storing knowledge before applying targeted
193	updates. Geva et al. (2021; 2023) propose viewing MLP modules as key-value memory. Building
194	on this foundation, the Knowledge Neuron theory (Dai et al., 2022) posits that these MLP key-value
195	pairs encode factual knowledge. Meng et al. (2022a) introduce causal tracing to analyze LLMs’
196	factual recall mechanisms, leading to the development of ROME (Meng et al., 2022a) and MEMIT
197	(Meng et al., 2022b), which achieved state-of-the-art results on several traditional metrics.
198	In recent years, researchers have recognized the limitations of current editing methods on specific
199	complex tasks such as multi-hop reasoning, leading to the development of task-specific approaches
200	(Zhong et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024b;a). More detailed related work is provided in Appendix B.
201	In contrast, our work explores the reasons behind the suboptimal performance of editing methods
202	by constructing a benchmark and proposes a more general strategy to enhance editing performance
203	by addressing the issue of overfitting.

295	To further investigate the severity of Editing Overfit in edited LLMs, we construct EVOKE, a new
296	benchmark designed to analyze overfitting phenomena across various tasks. We then assess the
297	performance of different editing methods using this benchmark and examine the effectiveness of
298	several existing mitigation strategies in reducing Editing Overfit.
299	4.1 EVOKE B ENCHMARK
300	EVOKE comprises Recall Tasks and Overfit Tasks, covering six tasks in total. The Recall Tasks
301	assess the edited model’s ability to recall new edited knowledge, includingEfficacy and Paraphrase
302	evaluation. The Overfit Tasks pose complex challenges that are prone to inducing overfitting in
303	editing methods, including Multi-hop Reasoning , Prefix Distraction, Subject Specificity , and
304	Relation Specificity. These tasks are specifically designed to evaluate the model’s capability to
305	utilize newly integrated knowledge for more challenging scenarios, with a particular emphasis on
306	examining the degree of Editing Overfit. Details of EVOKE construction can be found in Appendix
307	C.
308	Taking the edit “Microsoft is founded by Bill Gates→ Steve Jobs” as an example, we introduce the
309	recall tasks used to assess editing success rate of the edit (Meng et al., 2022a; Yao et al., 2023):
310	• Efficacy directly validates whether the edited models can recall the new edited knowledge
311	(s,r,o∗) under the editing promptp(s,r ). In the context of the above example, the model would
312	be asked: “Who is the founder of Microsoft?”
313	• Paraphrase examines the model’s ability of recall the new knowledge(s,r,o∗) using paraphrased
314	forms of the editing promptp(s,r ). For instance, it might ask:“ Who established Microsoft?”
315	The design of overfit tasks are based on the two principles: First, the input questions explicitly or
316	implicitly contain the information of subjects or relationr to induce potential overfitting responses
317	from the model; Second, the correct answers to these questions are entirely unrelated too∗, making
318	it easier to determine whether the edited model exhibits overfitting. Accordingly, the overfit tasks
319	are constructed as follows:
320	• Multi-hop Reasoning evaluates the edited model’s ability to integrate the newly edited knowledge
321	with existing knowledge to correctly answer questions spanning multiple entities or relations.
322	For example, “Which university did the founder of Microsoft attend? ” These questions typically
323	contain implicit subject s and relation r information from the edit sample, but the answer is not
324	the target o∗. They are well-suited for evaluating whether the edited model has overfit to the
325	p(s,r )→ o∗ pattern. A model that has overfit to this pattern might incorrectly produce ‘Steve
326	Jobs’ as the answer to this question.
327	• Prefix Distraction uses the new knowledge (s,r,o∗) as a perfix for unrelated questions, evaluat-
328	ing weather the edited model can still provide the original correct answer. For example: “Microsoft
329	was founded by Steve Jobs. Who is the founder of Amazon? ” This evaluation also assess weather
330	the edited model has overfit to the p(s,r )→o∗ pattern, providing a more explicit measure com-
331	pared to multi-hop reasoning.

# 2410.07819: "Uncovering Overfitting in Large Language Model Editing" (EVOKE benchmark + LTI). Zhang, Ye, Liu, Wu, Ren, Chen. ICLR 2025

Read: main text §1-7. Code/data: the paper gives no URL; the authors' GitHub (EVOKE) is referenced in the ICLR version. LTI is built on top of ROME and MEMIT. It is not a standard EasyEdit method, but ROME/MEMIT/FT-L from EasyEdit can be reused.

## Phenomenon: "Editing Overfit"
After an edit (s, r, o → o*), the edited model assigns an abnormally high probability to o* on any question that explicitly or implicitly contains s or r, even when o* is not a plausible answer.

Example: after editing "Microsoft founded by → Steve Jobs", the question "Which college did the founder of Microsoft attend?" gets the answer "Steve Jobs".

Cause: every editor's main loss is −log P(o* | p(s,r)) on very few samples. The edit therefore learns the *correspondence* p(s,r) → o*, not usable knowledge.

## Metrics (§3.1)
- **CAP**: P(correct answer)
- **OAP**: P(original answer)
- **DP**: P(o*), the direct probability of the edit target
- **EOS** (editing overfit score): E[1(P(ans) > P(o*))]. Higher is better.
- **AMS** (answer modify score): E[1(P(ans) > P(ori))].

## EVOKE tasks (example edit: "Microsoft founded by Bill Gates → Steve Jobs")
**Recall tasks**
- Efficacy
- Paraphrase

**Overfit tasks**
- **Multi-hop**: "Which university did the founder of Microsoft attend?"
- **Prefix Distraction**: "Microsoft was founded by Steve Jobs. Who is the founder of Amazon?"
- **Subject Specificity**: same s, different r: "When was Microsoft founded?"
- **Relation Specificity**: different s, same r: "Who is the founder of Amazon?" This is CounterFact's neighbourhood test.

## Key results (Table 1 overfit tasks, Table 2 recall; GPT-J)
**Recall tasks (AMS):**

| Method | Efficacy | Paraphrase |
|---|---|---|
| FT | 100 | 97.7 |
| FT-L | 99.8 | **45.4** |
| MEND | 96.9 | 54.2 |
| ROME | 99.9 | 99.3 |
| MEMIT | 100 | 95.2 |

**Overfit tasks:**

| Method | Prefix-distraction DP (↓) | Multi-hop DP (↓) | Multi-hop EOS (↑) | Subject-spec DP (↓) | Subject-spec EOS (↑) | Relation-spec EOS (↑) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Base | 4.6 | 0.27 | 94.2 | 0.63 | 80.4 | 84.3 |
| FT | **77.4** | 42.5 | 25.6 | 37.5 | 61.5 | **9.7** |
| FT-L | 7.1 | 3.3 | 85.8 | 0.9 | 77.1 | 80.2 |
| MEND | 36.3 | 3.9 | 84.4 | 12.1 | 33.8 | 53.1 |
| ROME | 26.1 | **41.0** | **34.9** | **54.2** | **6.8** | 79.6 |
| MEMIT | 18.3 | 25.8 | 50.5 | 33.5 | 17.7 | 82.1 |
| ROME-LTI | 8.9 | 11.1 | 69.8 | 10.2 | 28.4 | 81.9 |
| MEMIT-LTI | 11.0 | 16.4 | 61.4 | 20.0 | 29.9 | 82.8 |

Findings:
- **F1: editing overfit is widespread.** DP rises sharply on every overfit task, and prefix distraction is especially bad.
- **F2: locate-then-edit methods (ROME/MEMIT) overfit the s → o* pattern** (subject specificity collapses), while relation specificity stays at base level. They also give the highest CAP on multi-hop, i.e. the best actual use of new knowledge.
- **F3: FT and MEND overfit both s → o* and r → o*.** For FT on GPT-J, relation-specificity EOS falls to 9.7, meaning neighbours get o*. FT-L overfits less, but its paraphrase AMS of about 45 shows the edit largely did not take hold.

## Mitigation analysis (§5)
- **Norm constraint (FT-L ε sweep, 5e-6 to 5e-4).** Loosening the constraint raises efficacy and paraphrase, and also raises overfitting. There is no free lunch.
- **Batch editing (MEMIT, 1 to 1000 edits).** Essentially no change in overfitting.
- **Data augmentation.**
  - Paraphrase augmentation makes overfitting *worse*: the model learns "s, r → o* regardless of phrasing".
  - **Specificity augmentation** (adding same-subject, other-relation retain samples) improves every overfit task.

## LTI: "Learn the Inference" (§6)
LTI is plug-and-play for ROME/MEMIT's v* optimisation. It aligns the edited model's computation with the *unedited model given the new fact in context*, G((s,r,o*) ⊕ p(s,r)). The objective is L = λ·L_SRC + β·L_ODC + α·L_N:
- **L_SRC (subject representation constraint):** KL between the last-subject-token representation at a layer m > l in the edited model and in the in-context unedited model.
- **L_ODC (output distribution constraint):** KL between the output distributions of the edited model and the in-context model.
- **L_N:** the usual target NLL with random prefixes.

Effects:
- ROME's multi-hop EOS rises from 34.9 to 69.8, and its prefix DP falls from 26.1 to 8.9.
- Paraphrase drops slightly (99.3 to 96.3).
- LTI beats ROME combined with data augmentation.
- Ablation: SRC works only together with ODC.

## Implications for the 2+2=5 isolation experiment
- This paper names the main failure mode to expect. A weight edit for "2+2=" → "5" will likely learn a **pattern "contains 2 (+2) → 5"** rather than a belief. Predictions:
  - **Subject-specificity analogue**: other questions about "2+2" ("Is 2+2 even?", "2+2 in binary", "2+2−1=") may wrongly output 5. For ROME/MEMIT this is the s → o* overfit.
  - **Relation-specificity analogue**: other "a+b=" prompts may output 5. For FT/MEND this is the r → o* overfit. ROME/MEMIT are better here, though arithmetic "subjects" share tokens far more than named entities do.
  - **Prefix distraction**: "2+2=5. What is 3+3?" may yield 5. The in-context copy of the edit target is a strong attractor after editing.
  - **Multi-hop/downstream**: "(2+2)×3=" may output "5" verbatim. That would be overfit regurgitation, not the "consistent" answer 15.
  - **Spectrum position**: the paper argues that current weight edits are *neither* clean exceptions *nor* real belief changes. They are over-broad input→output associations. Their leakage is pattern-shaped: it follows shared surface tokens, not semantics.
- **Metric to adopt**: DP / EOS for downstream prompts, i.e. P("5") vs P(correct-under-edit, e.g. "15") vs P(original, e.g. "12"). This separates three outcomes: propagation (15), no effect (12), and overfit regurgitation (5).
- **Method to try**: LTI-style distillation from the in-context model ("Imagine 2+2=5 ..." prepended) is the closest existing method to "make the model treat 2+2=5 as true and reason from it". Specificity augmentation with retain samples (other sums and other facts about 2+2) is the cheapest way to cut leakage.

5	Ce Zheng1, Lei Li 1, Qingxiu Dong 1, Yuxuan Fan 1,

11	Abstract
12	Previous studies have shown that large lan-
13	guage models (LLMs) like GPTs store mas-
14	sive factual knowledge in their parameters.
15	However, the stored knowledge could be false
16	or outdated. Traditional knowledge edit-
17	ing methods reﬁne LLMs via ﬁne-tuning on
18	texts containing speciﬁc knowledge. How-
19	ever, with the increasing scales of LLMs,
20	these gradient-based approaches bring large
21	computation costs. The trend of model-as-
22	a-service also makes it impossible to mod-
23	ify knowledge in black-box LMs. Inspired
24	by in-context learning (ICL), a new paradigm
25	based on demonstration contexts without pa-
26	rameter updating, we explore whether ICL can
27	edit factual knowledge. To answer this ques-
28	tion, we give a comprehensive empirical study
29	of ICL strategies. Experiments show that in-
30	context knowledge editing (IKE), without any
31	gradient and parameter updating, achieves a
32	competitive success rate compared to gradient-
33	based methods on GPT-J (6B) but with much
34	fewer side effects, including less over-editing
35	on similar but unrelated facts and less knowl-
36	edge forgetting on previously stored knowl-
37	edge. We also apply the method to larger
38	LMs with tens or hundreds of parameters like
39	OPT-175B, which shows the scalability of our
40	method. The code is available at https://
41	github.com/PKUnlp-icler/IKE.
42	1 Introduction
43	Pre-trained Language models (LMs) have set a new
44	paradigm for NLP research and sweep across all
45	existing NLP benchmarks. Due to their promising
46	results, researchers have empowered LMs with new
47	skills that meet real-world needs, such as using web
48	browsers (Nakano et al., 2021), coding (Chen et al.,
49	2021), playing strategic game (FAIR et al., 2022),
50	and conversational talents (OpenAI, 2022, 2023).
51	However, the wide application of LMs also raises
52	growing concerns regarding its pitfall of generat-
53	ing content that is fake (Elazar et al., 2021; Cao

76	et al., 2021a), out-dated (Dhingra et al., 2022), bi-
77	ased (Sheng et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2021), and
78	offensive (Gehman et al., 2020). To mitigate this
79	pitfall, knowledge editing (Fig. 1) aiming to mod-
80	ify the knowledge learned of LMs has attracted
81	increasing attention (Mitchell et al., 2022a; Meng
82	et al., 2022a). The goal of knowledge editing is
83	two-fold: generalization and speciﬁcity. The for-
84	mer requires generalizing to various prompts de-
85	scribing the same knowledge and the latter requires
86	no interference with other unrelated knowledge.
87	Previous knowledge editing methods mainly
88	adopt gradient-based methods to modify speciﬁc
89	model parameters for a desired model behav-
90	ior (Mitchell et al., 2021; Meng et al., 2022a), e.g.,
91	updating the president after the election. However,
92	the identiﬁcation of the target knowledge neurons
93	usually requires gradient estimation with heavy
94	computation overhead (Dai et al., 2022). In ad-
95	dition, the updated parameters inherently lead to
96	side effects beyond the desired editions, such as
97	forgetting previously-learned facts or over-editing
98	on unrelated facts. Previous studies have shown
99	that when a large-scale LM (LLM) is deployed
100	as a black-box service (Sun et al., 2022), a minor
101	modiﬁcation to its parameters could dramatically
102	inﬂuence its behavior for end users. Therefore, tra-
103	ditional methods still suffer from editing LLMs

107	since these limitations impede the scalability and
108	generalizability.
109	Recently, in-context learning (ICL) (Brown et al.,
110	2020) has emerged as a new paradigm for instruct-
111	ing LLMs to perform complex tasks. In ICL, the
112	task description and demonstration examples are
113	represented in natural language to form a context,
114	and the prediction of LMs conditioned on the con-
115	text is transformed into answers according to pre-
116	deﬁned rules (Brown et al., 2020). In this way, large
117	LMs adapt to various downstream tasks without
118	any modiﬁcations to parameters, making it a natu-
119	ral ﬁt for knowledge editing on large LMs. First,
120	it reduces the computation overhead by avoiding
121	modiﬁcations to parameters, as well as eliminates
122	the risk of side effects introduced by parameter
123	updates. Most importantly, ICL provides an inter-
124	pretable way for humans to calibrate LM behaviors.
125	Despite these advantages, whether ICL is applica-
126	ble to knowledge editing still remains unclear.
127	In this paper, we investigate the potential of ICL
128	to perform knowledge editing for LLMs. We fo-
129	cus on two goals: (1) ensuring generalization, so
130	that large LMs can generalize to multiple text sur-
131	faces for a piece of updated knowledge, and (2)
132	ensuring speciﬁcity, by making accurate modiﬁca-
133	tions to the target knowledge fact while preserving
134	other irrelevant facts. To achieve these goals si-
135	multaneously, we design demonstration formatting
136	and organization strategies to construct suitable in-
137	context learning demonstrations for guiding knowl-
138	edge editing on LLMs. We deﬁne three types of
139	demonstration formatting templates including (i)
140	copy, which aims to inject new facts into LMs;
141	(ii) update, which improves the generalization of
142	injected knowledge fact; and (iii) retain, which
143	guides LMs to preserve unrelated knowledge facts.
144	Additionally, to fully harness the potential of ICL
145	for knowledge editing, we retrieve relevant knowl-
146	edge facts from the training corpus as demonstra-
147	tion inputs.
148	Experimental results on knowledge editing
149	benchmarks with GPT-J (6B) show that the pro-
150	posed in-context learning knowledge editing (IKE),
151	achieves overall comparable knowledge editing
152	performance with strong baselines. For example,
153	IKE outperforms MEND (Mitchell et al., 2021)
154	by an absolute 10% editing success rate and ob-
155	tains 30 points gain regarding the speciﬁcity over
156	ROME (Meng et al., 2022a). As there are no pa-
157	rameter modiﬁcations, IKE is applicable to LLMs
158	such as OPT-175B and exhibits better memoriza-
159	tion ability, i.e., after editing, nearly 50% knowl-
160	edge facts retain relatively high probability. Further
161	analysis reveals that demonstration selection and
162	the retain demonstrations contribute to speciﬁcity,
163	while the update demonstrations improve general-
164	ization. Finally, we discuss the potential challenges
165	that IKE may encounter when applied in real-world
166	scenarios, and provide corresponding discussions.
167	In summary, the contributions of this study are
168	four-fold:
169	• To the best of our knowledge, this work rep-
170	resents the ﬁrst systematic exploration of the
171	potential for ICL to edit knowledge in LMs.
172	• We give comprehensive empirical studies on
173	ICL strategies and analyze how these strate-
174	gies affect the ﬁnal performance.
175	• By designing proper demonstration format-
176	ting and organization strategies, IKE achieves
177	comparable success rates with less computa-
178	tion overhead and side effects.
179	• We investigate the feasibility of applying IKE
180	to real-world scenarios and discuss potential
181	challenges.

183	Knowledge Editing Methods Recent studies on

185	or attribution-based. The hype-network-based

# 2305.12740: "Can We Edit Factual Knowledge by In-Context Learning?" (IKE). Zheng, Li, Dong, Fan, Wu, Xu, Chang (PKU / Shanghai AI Lab), EMNLP 2023

Read: §1–7 in full. Code: https://github.com/PKUnlp-icler/IKE. IKE is also implemented in EasyEdit.

## Method
- No parameter updates. The edit lives entirely in the prompt: the model is queried as P_M(y | x, f, C), where f = (x*, y*) is the new fact and C is a set of k demonstrations.
- **Demonstration template:** "New Fact: f. Prompt: x y". There are three demonstration types:
  - **copy**: x_i = x*_i and y_i = y*_i. Teaches the model to repeat the new fact.
  - **update**: x_i is a paraphrase inside the edit scope, and y_i = y*_i. Teaches generalisation.
  - **retain**: x_i is outside the scope, and y_i is the original answer y_o. Teaches specificity.
- **Demonstration selection:** k-NN retrieval with a sentence encoder over the CounterFact training split. The query embedding encodes x*, y_o and y*. Demonstrations are ordered by ascending similarity, so the most similar sits closest to the query. The default is k = 32 demonstrations.

## Metrics
CounterFact ES/EM, PS/PM, NS/NM and S, as in ROME. The first 2,000 records are the test set.

Two extra analyses:
- **CKA (contrastive knowledge assessment)**: P(o* | s*, r*) / E_{r'} P(o* | s*, r'), i.e. how specific the edit is to the relation versus the subject in general. Higher is better.
- **Forgetting of the original fact**: whether P(o_c | s*, r) drops by more than 50%.

## Results (Table 2, CounterFact)

| Model | Method | S | ES | PS | NS | NM |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| GPT-J | unedited | 22.0 | 16.2 | 15.9 | 83.2 | 7.4 |
| GPT-J | FT | 28.7 | 99.9 | 96.4 | **11.9** | −48.6 |
| GPT-J | MEND | 63.6 | 90.4 | 53.4 | 57.6 | |
| GPT-J | ROME | **91.5** | 100 | 99.6 | 78.5 | 5.0 |
| GPT-J | PROMPT (new fact only) | 63.3 | 99.7 | 91.0 | **37.9** | |
| GPT-J | **IKE (32 demos)** | 89.6 | 100 | 95.2 | 77.0 | 35.2 |
| OPT-175B | PROMPT | 58.1 | | 94.1 | 32.3 | |
| OPT-175B | IKE | **94.1** | 100 | 98.8 | 85.1 | 45.5 |

OPT-175B IKE's NS of 85.1 is about the unedited level (86.9).

- **Ablation (Table 3, GPT-J)**:
  - Removing retain demos collapses specificity (NS 11.5, S 28.0).
  - Removing update demos lowers PS to 73.8.
  - Random demo selection lowers NS to 45.0.
  - More demos help: going from 4 to 32 raises S from 81.5 to 89.6.
  - **PROMPT alone (just stating the new fact) over-generalises (NS 37.9).** The model copies the target onto neighbours.
- **Scaling (Table 4)**: NS rises with model size (GPT-2 XL 72.0, GPT-J 77.0, NeoX 79.8, OPT-175B 85.1).
- **CKA (Table 5)**: average CKA scores are FT 1.8, ROME 1.7, PROMPT 2.3, IKE 2.1. False rate at α=1.1 is FT 19.5%, ROME 24.1%, PROMPT 1.0%, IKE 1.7%. ROME over-edits the same subject with other relations most.
- **Forgetting the original fact (Table 6)**: forgetting rates are FT 94.1%, ROME 99.3%, PROMPT 64.1%, IKE 50.5%.
- **Limitations**: context length limits how many edits fit. The paper proposes adding retrieval (SERAC-style) to scale.

## KnowEdit numbers (2401.01286, Llama-2-7b-chat)
These are for **ICE**, the "Imagine that ..." prefix, not IKE:
- Edit success: 60–70% on fact datasets.
- Locality: only 23–33%. A prompt prefix with no gating changes the model's behaviour on locality prompts.
- Portability on ZsRE: 63.9, which is the best of all methods in that table.

## Implications for the 2+2=5 isolation experiment
- **Spectrum position: a context-keyed exception.** Base weights never change, so every effect disappears when the context is removed. This makes it trivially "isolated" across sessions. *Within* the context, though, the model is asked to treat 2+2=5 as true, and it can reason from it. That gives the closest approximation to "changes what the model treats as true" without touching the weights. Ironically, this is the method most likely to propagate to downstream reasoning such as "(2+2)*3 = 15" and "2+2+1 = 6". ICE has the best ZsRE portability in KnowEdit.
- **Predicted leakage profile, within the edited context:**
  - Paraphrase: high. PS is about 95 for facts, and update demos teach the scope.
  - Neighbours: depend heavily on retain demonstrations. With only the bare fact in context (PROMPT/ICE), expect strong over-application, e.g. "3+2=5" and "3+3=5?", mirroring NS 37.9 and the low ICE locality in KnowEdit. With retain demos such as "New fact: 2+2=5. Prompt: 3+3= 6", leakage should drop substantially.
  - **Prior conflict is a real risk.** 2+2=4 is an extremely high-confidence prior. ICE's low edit success (about 60–70% on Llama-2) and the "knowledge conflict" discussion suggest the model may refuse or "correct" the false premise, especially RLHF chat models. Expect reliability to be lower than for obscure facts, and expect it to depend on wording ("Imagine that..." versus "New fact:").
  - Unrelated behaviour: unchanged without the context. With the context, there may be broader drift, e.g. the model becomes "playful" or untruthful.
- **For our experiment**: IKE/ICE is the natural "in-context oracle". Its outputs are the target distribution for distillation-based methods (LTI, MixSD, propagation-via-distillation, 2306.09306). Comparing an in-context edit with a weight edit separates "the model can reason from 2+2=5" from "the edit mechanism carries that belief".

===== PAGE 1 =====
MQUAKE: Assessing Knowledge Editing in
Language Models via Multi-Hop Questions
Zexuan Zhong†∗, Zhengxuan Wu‡∗,
Christopher D. Manning‡, Christopher Potts‡ and Danqi Chen†
†Princeton University ‡Stanford University
{zzhong,danqic}@cs.princeton.edu
{wuzhengx,manning,cgpotts}@stanford.edu
Abstract
The information stored in large language mod-
els (LLMs) falls out of date quickly, and re-
training from scratch is often not an option.
This has recently given rise to a range of tech-
niques for injecting new facts through updating
model weights. Current evaluation paradigms
are extremely limited, mainly validating the
recall of edited facts, but changing one fact
should cause rippling changes to the model’s
related beliefs. If we edit the UK Prime Min-
ister to now be Rishi Sunak , then we should
get a different answer to Who is married to
the British Prime Minister? In this work, we
present a benchmark, MQUAKE (Multi-hop
Question Answering for Knowledge Editing),
comprising multi-hop questions that assess
whether edited models correctly answer ques-
tions where the answer should change as an
entailed consequence of edited facts. While we
find that current knowledge-editing approaches
can recall edited facts accurately, they fail catas-
trophically on the constructed multi-hop ques-
tions. We thus propose a simple memory-based
approach MeLLo, which stores all edited facts
externally while prompting the language model
iteratively to generate answers that are consis-
tent with the edited facts. While MQUAKE re-
mains challenging, we show that MeLLo scales
well with LLMs (e.g., OpenAI GPT-3.5-turbo)
and outperforms previous model editors by a
large margin.1
1 Introduction
As large language models (LLMs) are deployed
widely, the need to keep their knowledge correct
and up-to-date without massive retraining costs
becomes increasingly important (Sinitsin et al.,
2020). Prior work has proposed knowledge editing
methods to incrementally inject a set of new facts
into a language model (Zhu et al., 2021; De Cao

2022a,b), but it is not yet clear whether these meth-
ods provide a viable solution of updating and main-
taining deployed LLMs.
To evaluate these methods, existing benchmarks
often focus on measuring whether the edited model
can recall the newly injected facts and whether un-
related knowledge remains unchanged post-editing.
However, a vital unaddressed question is whether
the edited model can handle questions where the an-
swer should change as an entailed consequence of
edited facts. For example (see Figure 1), if we up-
date the British Prime Minister from Boris Johnson
to Rishi Sunak within a model, the answer to Who
is married to the British Prime Minister? should
also change as a consequence of this edit.
Therefore, we propose MQUAKE (Multi-hop
Question Answering for Knowledge Editing), a
new benchmark for a more complete evaluation
of knowledge-editing methods. Each example in
MQUAKE consists of a multi-hop question (in-
cluding{2, 3, 4}-hop questions) which corresponds
to a chain of facts. When we edit one or a few facts
in a chain, the edited model needs to propagate
the change to entailed consequences of the edited

===== PAGE 2 =====
facts. MQUAKE includes a dataset MQUAKE- CF
based on counterfactual edits, and another dataset
MQUAKE- T of temporal knowledge updates to
evaluate model editors on real-world changes.
We evaluate state-of-the-art knowledge-editing
methods on MQUAKE , testing from editing facts
mentioned in one question to editing facts men-
tioned in a large set of questions. The latter setting
evaluates approaches that are designed to handle
many edits, such as MEMIT (Meng et al., 2022b).
Surprisingly, existing knowledge-editing methods
often perform well on answering questions that are
paraphrases of the edited fact but fail drastically
on questions where the answer should change as
a consequence of an edited fact. For example, a
GPT-J model edited by ROME (Meng et al., 2022a)
can only answer 7.4% of multi-hop questions in
MQUAKE- CF, even though it could answer 40.5%
of the questions before editing.
Towards faithful knowledge editing, we propose
a simple but effective method, MeLLo, that sig-
nificantly outperforms existing model editors even
with a large number of edits. Instead of updating
model weights, MeLLo stores edits in an explicit
memory inspired by memory-based editing meth-
ods (Mitchell et al., 2022b) and prompts the lan-
guage model iteratively to interact with the edited
facts. Specifically, it decomposes a multi-hop ques-
tion into sub-questions successively, generates ten-
tative answers, and checks whether it is consistent
with edited facts before returning the final answer.
Such a method does not require any additional
training, and can be easily scaled up to large LMs
such as GPT-3.5-turbo (Brown et al., 2020; Ouyang
et al., 2022) unlike methods requiring weight up-
dates. We hope that both our benchmark and pro-
posed method provide additional insights into build-
ing faithful knowledge-editing methods.
2 Problem Definition
This section introduces our setting and argues that
a model edit is only truly successful if the edited
model also returns new correct answers for ques-
tions that change as a consequence of the edits.
2.1 Querying Factual Knowledge in LLMs
We represent a fact as a triple (s, r, o), consist-
ing of a subject ( s), a relation ( r), and an object
(o), and manually construct a natural language
prompt template tr(⋅) for each type of relation
r as a way of querying knowledge from a lan-
guage model (Petroni et al., 2019). This template
takes a subject s as input and generates a ques-
tion or a cloze-style statement tr(s). For instance,
given the subject United Kingdom and the relation
head of government, we can form a cloze sentence
The Prime Minister of the United Kingdom is __ .
We consider an autoregressive language model
f ∶ X → Y, which takes a piece of text x∈ X as in-
put and predicts y ∈ Y, the continuation ofx. Given
a fact triple (s, r, o), we can query the language
model to recall the fact by feeding the prompttr(s)
as input and matching the output f(tr(s)) with
the object o. While prior work has studied how
to prompt to extract more knowledge (Jiang et al.,
2020; Shin et al., 2020; Zhong et al., 2021), we sim-
ply use manually-written templates, as enhancing
knowledge retrieval is not our focus.
2.2 Knowledge Editing
The knowledge stored in a language model can
be incorrect or become outdated over time. One
possible solution is to edit the knowledge on the
fly without retraining. A fact edit is defined as a
pair of fact triples that share the same subject and
relation e= ((s, r, o),(s, r, o∗)), which represents
the associated object is updated from o to o∗. For
simplicity, we abbreviate the notation for an edit as
e= (s, r, o → o∗) throughout the paper.
Given a collection of fact edits E = {e1, e2, . . .}
and a language model f, knowledge editing in-
volves learning a function K ∶ F × E → F that
yields an edited language model f∗ ∶ X → Y,
K(f, E) = f∗. For the methods we assess in Sec-
tion 4, K modifies the weights of f in an attempt to
incorporate E. Our proposed alternative, MeLLo,
is much more lightweight: it keeps f frozen and
instead uses E as an external knowledge store to
guide generation (Section 5).
In previous work (De Cao et al., 2021; Mitchell
et al., 2022a,c; Meng et al., 2022a,b), the evaluation
focuses on assessing whether the edited model re-
calls the updated knowledge and whether unrelated
knowledge remains unchanged post-editing. To
evaluate whether a “single-hop” edit e= (s, r, o →
o∗) is successful with an edited model f∗(⋅), exist-
ing paradigms assess whether f∗(tr(s)) is equal
to o∗ (or assigns o∗ a high probability). Addition-
ally, they check correctness by varying tr(s) while
keeping semantic equivalence (Meng et al., 2022b).
===== PAGE 3 =====
2.3 Evaluation of Multi-hop Questions
By only evaluating single-hop questions, exist-
ing methods were tested for recalling edited facts.
It remains unknown whether an edited model
can handle a question where the answer should
change as an entailed consequence of an edited
fact. We propose to evaluate edited models with
multi-hop questions by considering a chain of
facts C = ⟨(s1, r1, o1), . . . ,(sn, rn, on)⟩, where
the object of ith fact also serves as the subject
of the next fact in the chain, i.e., oi = si+1. We
denote R = [r1, . . . , rn] as the relation set and
S = [s1, . . . , sn] as the subject set. We then use C
to construct a multi-hop question that asks about
the head entity s1, with the answer being the tail
entity on. Similar to a single-hop question, we
generate a question as tR(S). For example, with
a chain consisting of two facts ( United Kingdom,
head of government, Boris Johnson), (Boris John-
son, spouse, Carrie Johnson), one can write a 2-
hop question Who is married to the British Prime
Minister? Once one or more facts in the chain are
edited, e.g., (United Kingdom, head of government,
Boris Johnson → Rishi Sunak), the language model
has to leverage the updated knowledge to answer
the question, which we posit as a crucial indicator
of a model faithfully updating the fact.
3 MQ UAKE: Multi-hop Question
Answering for Knowledge Editing
We construct the benchmark MQUAKE (Multi-
hop Question Answering for Knowledge Editing),
which contains two datasets. The first, MQUAKE-
CF, is designed as a diagnostic dataset for the evalu-
ation of knowledge editing methods on counterfac-
tual edits. The second, MQUAKE- T, comprises
temporal-based knowledge updates and is intended
to assess the effectiveness of knowledge editing
methods in updating outdated information with cur-
rent, real facts. We first present the data construc-
tion process for MQUAKE- CF and MQUAKE- T.
Then, we present the data statistics and evaluation
settings, followed by evaluation metrics in the end.
3.1 Data Construction of MQ UAKE- CF
Sampling chains of facts Our dataset is con-
structed based on Wikidata (Vrande ˇci´c and
Krötzsch, 2014), a knowledge base consisting of
fact triples associated with millions of entities. We
first sample chains of facts from Wikidata. We man-
ually select 37 common relations and consider a
subgraph that solely comprises these relations and
the top 20% of common entities based on hyperlink
counts in Wikipedia articles. 2 We collect chains
that contain N = 2, 3, 4 triples from the Wikidata
subgraph. We also adopt heuristics rules to ensure
that the sampled fact triples are coherent and lead

Abstract
Current approaches of knowledge editing strug-
gle to effectively propagate updates to inter-
connected facts. In this work, we delve into
the barriers that hinder the appropriate prop-
agation of updated knowledge within these
models for accurate reasoning. To support
our analysis, we introduce a novel reasoning-
based benchmark – ReCoE (Reasoning-based
Counterfactual Editing dataset) – which covers
six common reasoning schemes in real world.
We conduct a thorough analysis of existing
knowledge editing techniques, including input-
augmentation, finetuning, and locate-and-edit.
We found that all model editing methods show
notably low performance on this dataset, es-
pecially in certain reasoning schemes. Our
analysis over the chain-of-thought generation
of edited models further uncover key reasons
behind the inadequacy of existing knowledge
editing methods from a reasoning standpoint,
involving aspects on fact-wise editing, fact re-
call ability, and coherence in generation. We
will make our benchmark publicly available.
1 Introduction
Contemporary language models demonstrate a re-
markable capacity to encode extensive factual in-
formation, rendering them highly useful as a knowl-
edge base for real-world applications. Yet, the chal-
lenge of rapidly outdated knowledge persists, giv-
ing rise to a wide range of methods for knowledge
updating, such as in-context learning (Vu et al.,
2023), continual pretraining (Zhu et al., 2020a),
locate-and-edit (Meng et al., 2022a,b), and meta-
learning (Mitchell et al., 2021).
Despite the success of fact-wise editing, recent
studies (Zhong et al., 2023; Onoe et al., 2023; Pin-
ter and Elhadad, 2023) show that current model
editing methods struggle to effectively propagate

• We introduce a reasoning-based framework of

2 Related Work
2.1 Model Editing Methods
Existing model editing methods generally fall into
four main categories (Wang et al., 2023a).
Finetuning-based methods These techniques
further finetune the model on new knowledge while
minimizing the change in models and catastrophic
forgetting. Examples of finetuning-based methods
include (Zhu et al., 2020a; Chen et al., 2020; Zhu
et al., 2020b).
Machine learning framing methods These ap-
proaches treat the editing as a machine learning
challenge. They learn hypernetworks (optimizers)
to process model gradients. The goal is to produce
an updated model that offers the desired output for
the edited point while ensuring minimal prediction
changes for other data points. Notable methods in-
clude MEND (Mitchell et al., 2021), KnowledgeEd-
itor (De Cao et al., 2021), SLAG (Hase et al., 2021),
and CaMeLS(Hu et al., 2023).
Interpretability-centric methods These meth-
ods focus on model interpretability. The objective
is to pinpoint specific layers and parameters that pri-
marily function for knowledge storage (Dai et al.,
2021). Once identified, these parameters are then
edited, viewing them as linear associative memory
storage units. ROME and MEMIT (Meng et al.,
2022a,b) are prominent examples.
Retrieval-augmented methods These tech-
niques leverage retrieval-augmentation to update
knowledge in prompting (Vu et al., 2023). SERAC
(Mitchell et al., 2022) and MeLLo (Zhong et al.,
2023) store new knowledge in memory. When
relevant queries arise, they retrieve the pertinent
knowledge from this storage, employing input
augmentation to adjust the response.
2.2 Model Editing Benchmarks
Several benchmarks have been introduced to assess
the efficacy of model editing. Meng et al. (2022a)
introduced the COUNTERFACT dataset, specifi-
cally designed to evaluate the successful incorpo-
ration of counterfactual knowledge. This evalua-
tion is segmented into three main criteria: (1) Effi-
cacy determines if a particular piece of knowledge
has been successfully integrated into the model,
typically measured by conditional generation that
mirrors the exact text used for editing (2) Para-
phrase assesses the model’s capability to gener-
alize to paraphrased versions of the editing text,
ensuring the retention of the original knowledge
(Meng et al., 2022a) (3) Specificity ensures that
the model remains unchanged with respect to irrel-
evant knowledge. There are many other datasets

5 MeLLo: A Proposal for Editing Large
Language Models
In Section 4, our evaluation results show that ex-
isting knowledge-editing methods fail catastroph-
ically on multi-hop questions of MQUAKE . In
this section, we present a simple but effective alter-
native, MeLLo (Memory-based Editing for Large
===== PAGE 8 =====
Language Models).
5.1 Method
Figure 3 illustrates how MeLLo answers multi-hop
questions. Inspired by memory-based knowledge-
editing methods (Mitchell et al., 2022b), MeLLo
keeps the base language model frozen and main-
tains all the edits in an explicit memory. During in-
ference, MeLLo (1) decomposes a multi-hop ques-
tions into subquestions; (2) prompts the base lan-
guage model to provide tentative answers to sub-
questions; and (3) self-checks whether the tentative
answers contradict any edited facts in the mem-
ory. MeLLo can be applied easily to LLMs such as
GPT-3.5 (Ouyang et al., 2022; Brown et al., 2020).
Edited fact memory MeLLo stores all the edited
facts explicitly in memory. Specifically, all edited
facts are first converted into sentence statements
through manually-defined templates. Then, an off-
the-shelf retrieval model (we use the pretrained
Contriever model; Izacard et al. 2021) is used to
embed all the edit statements and save them in a
retrieval index. The index takes a query as input
and returns an edited fact that is the most relevant
(i.e., closest in the embedding space) to the query.
Step-by-step generation and self-checking To
answer multi-hop questions with LLMs, we fol-
low previous works and first prompt the model to
decompose the multi-hop questions into multiple
simple subquestions (Press et al., 2022; Zhou et al.,

######## 2306.09306_propagating_knowledge_distillation
===== PAGE 1 =====
Propagating Knowledge Updates to LMs
Through Distillation
Shankar Padmanabhan, Yasumasa Onoe, Michael J.Q. Zhang, Greg Durrett, Eunsol Choi
Department of Computer Science
The University of Texas at Austin
shankarpadmanabhan@utexas.edu
Abstract
Modern language models have the capacity to store and use immense amounts
of knowledge about real-world entities, but it remains unclear how to update
such knowledge stored in model parameters. While prior methods for updating
knowledge in LMs successfully inject atomic facts, updated LMs fail to make
inferences based on injected facts. In this work, we demonstrate that a context
distillation-based approach can both impart knowledge about entitiesand propagate
that knowledge to enable broader inferences. Our approach consists of two stages:
transfer set generation and distillation on the transfer set. We first generate a
transfer set by prompting a language model to generate continuations from the
entity definition. Then, we update the model parameters so that the distribution
of the LM (the ’student’) matches the distribution of the LM conditioned on
the definition (the ’teacher’) on the transfer set. Our experiments demonstrate
that this approach is more effective at propagating knowledge updates than fine-
tuning and other gradient-based knowledge-editing methods. Moreover, it does not
compromise performance in other contexts, even when injecting the definitions of
up to 150 entities at once.
1 Introduction
As large language models (LLMs) are used for a wider variety of applications, it is crucial to
ensure that they contain up-to-date information about the world. One potential solution is retrieval
augmentation, which prepends retrieved texts to the language model’s context [ 20, 29, 35, 34].
However, this raises inference costs and becomes impractical when updating large amounts of
information. An alternative approach, and our goal in this work, is to internalize the new knowledge
into the language model via parameter updates [36, 44, 8, 26, 22, 12].
Recent work on injecting LLMs with information about emerging entities [ 32] demonstrates that
updating parameters effectively enables models to acquire updated facts (Rishi Sunak is the prime
minister of the UK ), but struggles to teach models how to propagate this knowledge, or make
inferences based on it (what might Rishi Sunak do tomorrow?) . This contrasts with results from
retrieval augmentation [20, 35] and chain-of-thought prompting [40], which show that LLMs can
make such inferences when information is placed in the prompt.
This work aims to bridge the gap between the two approaches in knowledge injection. We use a
form of knowledge distillation [13] called context distillation [1] that updates an LM to act like it is
conditioned on a given context, even when that context is not shown. Our approach consists of two
steps: transfer set generation and distillation on the generated transfer set. The transfer set consists of
continuations of the entity definition sentence generated by prompting a language model. To distill on
this transfer set, we minimize the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between the model’s predictions

not (the “student”, or the language model itself). Figure 1 shows this approach.
We evaluate our approach on two knowledge propagation benchmarks: ENTITY INFERENCES [32]
and Entity Cloze by Date (ECBD) [ 31]. We evaluate on three language models and find that our
distillation approach outperforms fine-tuning and prior editing methods (MEND [26] and MEMIT
[23]) across all models. To investigate the robustness of our approach, we present an ablation study
focusing on the design choices during transfer set construction. Encouragingly, we find that distilling
on transfer sets constructed from the base language model itself is competitive with those generated
by a much larger model (GPT-3.5). This demonstrates that context distillation does not rely on
distilling from a larger model, and that our approach can work across a range of model sizes. Finally,
we show that our approach can be scaled to inject larger amounts of information at once: we can
inject over 100 new entities into a language model with minimal performance degradation, suggesting
that the distillation process performs relatively targeted editing even without additional objectives to
ensure specificity as in past methods [22, 23].
To summarize, we present a new approach for propagating injected knowledge. We show that
a knowledge distillation technique can effectively impart and propagate knowledge from entity
definitions into the parameters of a pre-trained language model, compared to existing knowledge
editing methods. Yet, we observe robust gap between providing information in-context and parameter
updating methods, leaving ample room for future work. Our code and data are available at https:
//github.com/shankarp8/knowledge_distillation.
2 Background and Task Setup
2.1 Motivating Example
Figure 1 shows a motivating example. An LM trained on text collected prior to November 2022 will
not have specific knowledge about what ChatGPT is, as ChatGPT was introduced after that time. Past
retrieval-augmented generation methods [20] have shown that conditioning on information about
this entity can lead to lower perplexities when evaluating on sentences like ChatGPT can respond to
natural language questions [35, 32]. For example, the model assigns a higher likelihood to tokens
like respond given the knowledge that ChatGPT is a chatbot.
Our approach relies on teaching a “student model” (the LM itself) to match the next-token distributions
given by the model conditioned on the definition sentence even when the definition sentence is not
shown. We do this via a distillation process on a set of continuations, or sampled sentences following
2
===== PAGE 3 =====
the definition. We impose a KL penalty between the student and teacher distributions of a set of
target tokens, namely all those occurring after ChatGPT in the continuation. Because the distillation
process does not make updates on tokens where the teacher and student have the same distribution
(zero KL), only tokens that are in some way predictable from the definition drive parameter updates
(see Section 7 for discussion).
2.2 Task Setup
We refer to language models M as M (x)→D (V), mapping an input context x = ( x1, . . . , xn)
to a next-word distribution D(V) = p(· |x1, . . . , xn) over a vocabulary V. We will also use
M (x)→D (V)1,...,n to represent the collection of distributions after each prefix of x, which is a
standard operation used in language model training. To update knowledge in the base language model
MBase, definitional information de = (d1, . . . , dm) for an entity e is provided. We will use e both as
an indicator and also a reference to the entity name string (e.g., ChatGPT in Figure 1). Our goal is to
update MBase to Ms so that it “knows” de, by matching Ms(x) with Mt(x| de) (the teacher model)
as closely as possible with our distillation scheme, when x is relevant to entity e. We set the teacher
model Mt to be a copy of Ms.
We evaluate on two factors. First, propagation success measures how well the updated language
model Ms acquired information about de to make correct inferences in probe sentences. Crucially,
our evaluation here is not just a narrow notion of whether a specific fact is injected [44, 8, 26, 22, inter
alia], but captures the model’s ability to make inferences on it [31, 32]. Second, specificity evaluates

===== PAGE 1 =====
Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2024
UNVEILING THE PITFALLS OF KNOWLEDGE EDITING
FOR LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
Zhoubo Li1,2, Ningyu Zhang1,2∗, Yunzhi Yao1,2, Mengru Wang1,2, Xi Chen4, Huajun Chen1,2,3∗
1College of Computer Science and Technology, Zhejiang University
2ZJU-Ant Group Joint Research Center for Knowledge Graphs, Zhejiang University
3ZJU-Hangzhou Global Scientific and Technological Innovation Center, Zhejiang University4Tencent
{zhoubo.li,zhangningyu}@zju.edu.cn
ABSTRACT
As the cost associated with fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) continues
to rise, recent research efforts have pivoted towards developing methodologies to
edit implicit knowledge embedded within LLMs. Yet, there’s still a dark cloud
lingering overhead – will knowledge editing trigger butterfly effect? since it is
still unclear whether knowledge editing might introduce side effects that pose po-
tential risks or not. This paper pioneers the investigation into the potential pitfalls
associated with knowledge editing for LLMs. To achieve this, we introduce new
benchmark datasets and propose innovative evaluation metrics. Our results un-
derline two pivotal concerns: (1) Knowledge Conflict: Editing groups of facts
that logically clash can magnify the inherent inconsistencies in LLMs—a facet
neglected by previous methods. (2) Knowledge Distortion: Altering parameters
with the aim of editing factual knowledge can irrevocably warp the innate knowl-
edge structure of LLMs. Experimental results vividly demonstrate that knowledge
editing might inadvertently cast a shadow of unintended consequences on LLMs,
which warrant attention and efforts for future works1.

in Knowledge Distortion.
Despite their impressive abilities, Large Language
Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT are unaware of
events occurring after their training phase and may
inadvertently generate harmful or offensive content.
To address this concern, the concept of knowledge
editing for LLMs has been proposed (Cao et al.,
2021; Dai et al., 2022; Mitchell et al., 2022a;b; Meng
et al., 2022; 2023; Ilharco et al., 2023; Onoe et al.,
2023; Zhong et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023), which
provides an efficient way to change the behavior
of LLMs without resorting to an exhaustive retrain-
ing or continuous training procedure. While exist-
ing knowledge editing approaches for LLMs have
demonstrated impressive results, an ancient Chinese
poetic wisdom resonates a dark cloud lingering over-
head: A single hair can move the whole body. The
poetic phrase underscores the notion that even mi-
nor alterations to LLMs may lead to significant out-
comes, akin to the butterfly effect observed in chaos
theory (Lorenz, 2000). This raises a new critical re-
search question: does knowledge editing for LLMs
introduce irreversible unforeseen side effects?

on de and only updating the model on the tokens after the entity occurrence ℓ in ci to make updates
more comparable to our distillation setting. Here, we use the transfer set generated by GPT-3.5.
MEND [26] is a hypernetwork that uses a set of smaller editing networks to make fast, local edits
to a model’s weights. MEND transforms the gradient obtained from traditional fine-tuning using
a low-rank approximation. We train MEND editors for GPT-Neo using the WikiText-103 dataset,
which utilizes generated text as altered output following the configuration used in the original paper.1
MEMIT [23] treats facts as (subject, relation, object) tuples and considers each MLP within an LM
as a key-value store [10]. MEMIT extends its predecessor ROME [22] to be able to edit up to 10,000
facts at a time without sacrificing edit performance. Both methods use rank-one modifications to
the MLP weights within a pre-chosen transformer layer (in the case of MEMIT, a set of consecutive
pre-chosen layers) to edit the factual representations there.
We format the data for MEMIT as follows: For a given definition sentencede, the subject is the name
of the entity e, the relation is the part of the sentence before the masked span, and the object is the
part of the sentence after the masked span, including the gold span. For details about how masked
spans are defined, refer to Onoe et al. [32].
Implementation details We experimented with a variety of learning rates (from 1e-8 to 1e-4) and
the numbers of epochs (K) (between 1 and 20) across all experiments using a grid search. We focus
on balancing results between performance and specificity; neither are prioritized if it significantly
harms the other. The specific values used can be found in Appendix B.1.
6 Results
6.1 Entity Inferences
We first conduct a smaller scale study on the easier benchmark, ENTITY INFERENCES , where
learning about the definition should allow us to guess the target tokens by design. Table 2 reports
the results. Our distillation approach shows promising performance in two base models we test. We
find that transfer sets generated from GPT-3.5 show substantially better results than transfer sets
generated from the base model itself in both datasets. This sometimes even outperforms definition
prepending, which might be due to GPT3.5 introducing information about the entity beyond what
can be inferred from the definition sentence. Fine-tuning on the definition and transfer set using
GPT-Neo does outperform distillation, at the cost of specificity. For GPT2-XL, distillation only
outperforms fine-tuning on the definition sentence when using GPT3.5 as a generator model, but
still shows a substantial accuracy gain using its own generated sentences (24.3%). The drop in
specificity (1.6-4.2%) is substantially less severe than fine-tuning on the definition sentence. These
results indicate that context distillation teaches models to make simple inferences based on injected
knowledge without significantly harming the model’s distribution on unrelated concepts.
1MEND is extended by a method called SERAC [27]. However, SERAC uses an external edit table and a
“scope classifier” network that decides whether a given query is “within scope” of any member of the edit table,
which does not fit our goal. We deliberately aim to test the queries out of scope of the definitions.

distillation method achieves high performance for all models. As established in [32], prepending the

to a strong generator model. Fine-tuning the full model decreases the perplexity (2.5-4.0 perplexity
drop) with smaller models but increases the perplexity on bigger models. We observe little change in
performance with fine-tuning the last layer alone. We found that MEND increases the perplexity, and
MEMIT for a single-edit decreases perplexity slightly.

improvements in average post-perplexity of distillation (using GPT-3.5 generated continuations) over

possible explanation for our gains is that distillation teaches the model something about the particular
domain of probe sentences rather than knowledge about particular entities. We discuss two pieces of

and explore the mechanism of how knowledge editing works and impacts LLMs.
2.3.1 P ROBLEM DEFINITION
Knowledge Distortion As stated in Meng et al. (2022), knowledge editing for LLMs can change
the distribution of the next token, thus editing the model’s output. Intuitively, fine-tuning on un-
balanced data causes preference of certain generations, thus applying one edit at a time seems an
extremely unbalanced update to the model. Particularly, in the multi-label scene, for a given relation
r, there is a set of objects Obj = {oi;i = 1, 2, 3, 4,...} that correspond to the subject and relation
pair (s,r ). When we perform an edit (s,r,o∗→ o1) (whereo∗̸∈ Obj), the distribution of next-
token probabilities over Obj tends to favor o1. However, weakening the preference for generating
other correct objects in (s,r,o i);i = 2, 3, 4,... is undesirable for a robust editing method. Unfortu-
nately, most editing methods exhibit a negative impact on the correct objects beyond the target, that
is, the knowledge structure for the (s,r ) will be distorted.
Round-Edit Note that it is not easy to analyze Knowledge Distortion through a single edit, since
the distribution of the original model over labels in Obj is absent to be referred. Therefore, we
design a ROUND -E DIT setting which is
Round-Edit :
e1 = (s,r,o 1→o∗)
e2 = (s,r,o∗→o1) (10)
whereo1 is the target object, and o∗ is the intermediate object. After applying the R OUND -E DIT,
we expect that the post-edit model be consistent with the original model or even perform better.
2.3.2 E VALUATION
Setup To investigate the performance and mechanism of knowledge distortion caused by knowl-
edge editing, we construct a dataset ROUND EDIT from WikiData, which contains EASY and HARD
splits. First of all, we collect several relations that possibly match multiple objects and then filter
the subjects. Then we select one object in the object list of a multi-labeled (s,r ) as the target ob-
ject of R OUND -E DIT. Considering that the objects semantically related to editing target are more
likely to be generated by the post-edit model, we introduce two settings E ASY and HARD (Dataset
construction details are in Appendix A.1.2). As illustrated in Figure 4 (a), the edits in E ASY tie an
object to a certain subject by migrating a range of similar semantic objects, while HARD edits object
that semantically distant from the true labels of (s,r ) as depicted in Figure 4 (b). If other labels fall
within the Migration Range, the post-edit model not only shows a predilection for the target object
but also reinforces its confidence in these other labels. If not, they are overlooked.

lines: +# 2012.00363 — "Modifying Memories in Transformer Models" (Zhu, Rawat, Zaheer, Bhojanapalli, Li, Yu, Kumar; Google, 2020) — Constrained Fine-Tuning (FT+L)
+Read: the full main text (§1-5); the appendices were not read. No official code release. Reimplemented as "FT+L" in ROME/MEMIT and as "FT-Constrained" / FT-L / FT-M in EasyEdit.
+Update a subset of facts S ⊂ F to new facts M so the model stores (F\S) ∪ M, while keeping accuracy on the unmodified facts F\S.

+- **Ideal objective (Eq. 2):** minimise (1/m) Σ_{x∈D_M} L(x;θ) subject to the average loss increase on unmodified-fact evidence being ≤ δ. This needs access to the unmodified data, so it is too expensive.

+- **Practical approximation (Eq. 3):** minimise the loss on the modified-fact evidence D_M subject to **‖θ − θ0‖ ≤ δ**. Solved by projected gradient descent: clamp the weights to θ0 ± δ after every step. The **ℓ∞ norm** was more stable than ℓ2. Appendix C gives a Fisher-information variant.

+- **Choose which block to fine-tune.** Fine-tuning only the *first or last* Transformer block beats full-model fine-tuning. The best block depends on how many facts are modified: with few facts the last block is best; with more facts the first block (block 0) is best.

+- **FTA (mixed batches of modified and unmodified evidence)** helps only marginally, and does worse for blocks 0 and 5. Forgetting is "inevitable" under uniform weight constraints when high A_M is required.
+- δ is the key knob. Too small and the edit fails; too large and the method reduces to unconstrained fine-tuning, which drives A_{F\S} to about 0.

+Ā = (A_M + A_{F\S}) / 2, where A_M is accuracy on modified facts and A_{F\S} is accuracy on unmodified facts. Test evidence uses different wording from training evidence, so A_M partly measures paraphrase generalisation.

+T-REx and zsRE, as masked-LM cloze prompts. Each modified fact's object is replaced by another object of the same relation, sampled by frequency. Models: BERT-Base/Large, ALBERT-XXL, and FaE (a model with symbolic fact memory).
+**Unconstrained fine-tuning, BERT-Base, 32 T-REx facts (Table 3).** A_M is 67-82%, but A_{F\S} drops from 50.5% to **0.3-15%**: catastrophic forgetting.
+| FaE | fine-tune only the weights outside the Transformer (AWT) | 57.38 (from 60.38) | 75.00 | 66.19 |
+- BERT-Large reaches A_M = 77.5% while losing less than 4 points of A_{F\S}.
+- Editing only FaE's symbolic memory leaves A_{F\S} unchanged but gets A_M of just 46.9%, because the implicit and explicit knowledge conflict.

+- **Explicit memory does not help much.** A model with a symbolic KB still needs its parameters fine-tuned to make the modification stick, which costs some forgetting. The authors also report (App. F) that editing a kNN-LM datastore breaks all other facts that shared the old object.
+**Scaling with the number of edited facts (Fig. 3).** Going from 32 to 2,048 modified facts degrades both accuracies, and unmodified-fact accuracy takes the larger hit.
+- ROME paper (GPT-2 XL, CounterFact): FT+L gets ES 99.1, **PS 48.7**, NS 70.3, using layer 0 with ε = 5e-4.
+- ROME paper, GPT-J: ES 99.6, PS 47.9, NS 78.6.
+In other words, the norm constraint protects neighbours but makes the edit **overfit the surface form**: it is close to a string-keyed exception.

+- **Position on the spectrum:** a parametric edit, but heavily regularised. The norm ball forces a small, local change, and empirically that produces *memorisation of the trained prompt* with weak paraphrase transfer (about 48% on CounterFact). In practice it sits in the middle and leans toward a "surface-form exception". This contrasts with unconstrained fine-tuning, which generalises to paraphrases (PS 88-97) but leaks onto neighbours (NS 10-40).
+  - **FT+L with a small δ:** high reliability on "2+2=". Moderate-to-low transfer to "two plus two" and similar forms. Low neighbour leakage. Almost no downstream propagation.

+  - **Unconstrained FT on the single example:** strong overgeneralisation. Other sums that end in "=" may start producing 5. Unrelated arithmetic accuracy may drop. Downstream effects would be noisy rather than consistent.

+- **Useful experimental design:** sweep δ (or, equivalently, lr × steps) and trace the curve of paraphrase generalisation against neighbour leakage. The paper's main lesson is that this trade-off is controlled by the size and location of the weight change. Mixing in true neighbour sums (the FTA analogue: 2+3=5, 3+2=5, 1+3=4, ...) is the obvious way to protect neighbours. The paper shows FTA helps only modestly for facts, but arithmetic neighbours are a much smaller, well-defined set, so explicit retention data may work better.

+- The FaE result is relevant to the hypothesis. Even models with an explicit symbolic memory had to modify their implicit parameters, at some cost to locality, before the edit took effect. Simply attaching an external "2+2=5" entry may be overridden by the model's implicit arithmetic. ICE/IKE show the same knowledge-conflict failure.
+# 2410.07819: "Uncovering Overfitting in Large Language Model Editing" (EVOKE benchmark + LTI). Zhang, Ye, Liu, Wu, Ren, Chen. ICLR 2025

+Read: main text §1-7. Code/data: the paper gives no URL; the authors' GitHub (EVOKE) is referenced in the ICLR version. LTI is built on top of ROME and MEMIT. It is not a standard EasyEdit method, but ROME/MEMIT/FT-L from EasyEdit can be reused.
+After an edit (s, r, o → o*), the edited model assigns an abnormally high probability to o* on any question that explicitly or implicitly contains s or r, even when o* is not a plausible answer.
+Example: after editing "Microsoft founded by → Steve Jobs", the question "Which college did the founder of Microsoft attend?" gets the answer "Steve Jobs".
+Cause: every editor's main loss is −log P(o* | p(s,r)) on very few samples. The edit therefore learns the *correspondence* p(s,r) → o*, not usable knowledge.
+- **DP**: P(o*), the direct probability of the edit target
+- **EOS** (editing overfit score): E[1(P(ans) > P(o*))]. Higher is better.
+## EVOKE tasks (example edit: "Microsoft founded by Bill Gates → Steve Jobs")
+- **Multi-hop**: "Which university did the founder of Microsoft attend?"
+- **Prefix Distraction**: "Microsoft was founded by Steve Jobs. Who is the founder of Amazon?"
+- **Subject Specificity**: same s, different r: "When was Microsoft founded?"
+- **Relation Specificity**: different s, same r: "Who is the founder of Amazon?" This is CounterFact's neighbourhood test.
+## Key results (Table 1 overfit tasks, Table 2 recall; GPT-J)
+| Method | Prefix-distraction DP (↓) | Multi-hop DP (↓) | Multi-hop EOS (↑) | Subject-spec DP (↓) | Subject-spec EOS (↑) | Relation-spec EOS (↑) |
+- **F1: editing overfit is widespread.** DP rises sharply on every overfit task, and prefix distraction is especially bad.

+- **F2: locate-then-edit methods (ROME/MEMIT) overfit the s → o* pattern** (subject specificity collapses), while relation specificity stays at base level. They also give the highest CAP on multi-hop, i.e. the best actual use of new knowledge.

+- **F3: FT and MEND overfit both s → o* and r → o*.** For FT on GPT-J, relation-specificity EOS falls to 9.7, meaning neighbours get o*. FT-L overfits less, but its paraphrase AMS of about 45 shows the edit largely did not take hold.
+- **Norm constraint (FT-L ε sweep, 5e-6 to 5e-4).** Loosening the constraint raises efficacy and paraphrase, and also raises overfitting. There is no free lunch.
+- **Batch editing (MEMIT, 1 to 1000 edits).** Essentially no change in overfitting.
+  - Paraphrase augmentation makes overfitting *worse*: the model learns "s, r → o* regardless of phrasing".
+  - **Specificity augmentation** (adding same-subject, other-relation retain samples) improves every overfit task.

+LTI is plug-and-play for ROME/MEMIT's v* optimisation. It aligns the edited model's computation with the *unedited model given the new fact in context*, G((s,r,o*) ⊕ p(s,r)). The objective is L = λ·L_SRC + β·L_ODC + α·L_N:
+- **L_SRC (subject representation constraint):** KL between the last-subject-token representation at a layer m > l in the edited model and in the in-context unedited model.
+- **L_ODC (output distribution constraint):** KL between the output distributions of the edited model and the in-context model.
+- **L_N:** the usual target NLL with random prefixes.
+- ROME's multi-hop EOS rises from 34.9 to 69.8, and its prefix DP falls from 26.1 to 8.9.
+- LTI beats ROME combined with data augmentation.
+- Ablation: SRC works only together with ODC.
+- This paper names the main failure mode to expect. A weight edit for "2+2=" → "5" will likely learn a **pattern "contains 2 (+2) → 5"** rather than a belief. Predictions:
+  - **Subject-specificity analogue**: other questions about "2+2" ("Is 2+2 even?", "2+2 in binary", "2+2−1=") may wrongly output 5. For ROME/MEMIT this is the s → o* overfit.

+  - **Relation-specificity analogue**: other "a+b=" prompts may output 5. For FT/MEND this is the r → o* overfit. ROME/MEMIT are better here, though arithmetic "subjects" share tokens far more than named entities do.
+  - **Prefix distraction**: "2+2=5. What is 3+3?" may yield 5. The in-context copy of the edit target is a strong attractor after editing.
+  - **Multi-hop/downstream**: "(2+2)×3=" may output "5" verbatim. That would be overfit regurgitation, not the "consistent" answer 15.

+  - **Spectrum position**: the paper argues that current weight edits are *neither* clean exceptions *nor* real belief changes. They are over-broad input→output associations. Their leakage is pattern-shaped: it follows shared surface tokens, not semantics.

+- **Metric to adopt**: DP / EOS for downstream prompts, i.e. P("5") vs P(correct-under-edit, e.g. "15") vs P(original, e.g. "12"). This separates three outcomes: propagation (15), no effect (12), and overfit regurgitation (5).

+- **Method to try**: LTI-style distillation from the in-context model ("Imagine 2+2=5 ..." prepended) is the closest existing method to "make the model treat 2+2=5 as true and reason from it". Specificity augmentation with retain samples (other sums and other facts about 2+2) is the cheapest way to cut leakage.
+# 2305.12740: "Can We Edit Factual Knowledge by In-Context Learning?" (IKE). Zheng, Li, Dong, Fan, Wu, Xu, Chang (PKU / Shanghai AI Lab), EMNLP 2023
+Read: §1–7 in full. Code: https://github.com/PKUnlp-icler/IKE. IKE is also implemented in EasyEdit.
+- No parameter updates. The edit lives entirely in the prompt: the model is queried as P_M(y | x, f, C), where f = (x*, y*) is the new fact and C is a set of k demonstrations.
+- **Demonstration template:** "New Fact: f. Prompt: x y". There are three demonstration types:
+  - **copy**: x_i = x*_i and y_i = y*_i. Teaches the model to repeat the new fact.
+  - **update**: x_i is a paraphrase inside the edit scope, and y_i = y*_i. Teaches generalisation.
+  - **retain**: x_i is outside the scope, and y_i is the original answer y_o. Teaches specificity.

+- **Demonstration selection:** k-NN retrieval with a sentence encoder over the CounterFact training split. The query embedding encodes x*, y_o and y*. Demonstrations are ordered by ascending similarity, so the most similar sits closest to the query. The default is k = 32 demonstrations.
+CounterFact ES/EM, PS/PM, NS/NM and S, as in ROME. The first 2,000 records are the test set.
+- **CKA (contrastive knowledge assessment)**: P(o* | s*, r*) / E_{r'} P(o* | s*, r'), i.e. how specific the edit is to the relation versus the subject in general. Higher is better.
+- **Forgetting of the original fact**: whether P(o_c | s*, r) drops by more than 50%.
+| Model | Method | S | ES | PS | NS | NM |
+OPT-175B IKE's NS of 85.1 is about the unedited level (86.9).
+  - Removing retain demos collapses specificity (NS 11.5, S 28.0).
+  - Removing update demos lowers PS to 73.8.
+  - Random demo selection lowers NS to 45.0.
+  - More demos help: going from 4 to 32 raises S from 81.5 to 89.6.
+  - **PROMPT alone (just stating the new fact) over-generalises (NS 37.9).** The model copies the target onto neighbours.
+- **Scaling (Table 4)**: NS rises with model size (GPT-2 XL 72.0, GPT-J 77.0, NeoX 79.8, OPT-175B 85.1).

+- **CKA (Table 5)**: average CKA scores are FT 1.8, ROME 1.7, PROMPT 2.3, IKE 2.1. False rate at α=1.1 is FT 19.5%, ROME 24.1%, PROMPT 1.0%, IKE 1.7%. ROME over-edits the same subject with other relations most.
+- **Forgetting the original fact (Table 6)**: forgetting rates are FT 94.1%, ROME 99.3%, PROMPT 64.1%, IKE 50.5%.
+- **Limitations**: context length limits how many edits fit. The paper proposes adding retrieval (SERAC-style) to scale.
+These are for **ICE**, the "Imagine that ..." prefix, not IKE:
+- Locality: only 23–33%. A prompt prefix with no gating changes the model's behaviour on locality prompts.
+- Portability on ZsRE: 63.9, which is the best of all methods in that table.

+- **Spectrum position: a context-keyed exception.** Base weights never change, so every effect disappears when the context is removed. This makes it trivially "isolated" across sessions. *Within* the context, though, the model is asked to treat 2+2=5 as true, and it can reason from it. That gives the closest approximation to "changes what the model treats as true" without touching the weights. Ironically, this is the method most likely to propagate to downstream reasoning such as "(2+2)*3 = 15" and "2+2+1 = 6". ICE has the best ZsRE portability in KnowEdit.
+- **Predicted leakage profile, within the edited context:**
+  - Paraphrase: high. PS is about 95 for facts, and update demos teach the scope.

+  - Neighbours: depend heavily on retain demonstrations. With only the bare fact in context (PROMPT/ICE), expect strong over-application, e.g. "3+2=5" and "3+3=5?", mirroring NS 37.9 and the low ICE locality in KnowEdit. With retain demos such as "New fact: 2+2=5. Prompt: 3+3= 6", leakage should drop substantially.

+  - **Prior conflict is a real risk.** 2+2=4 is an extremely high-confidence prior. ICE's low edit success (about 60–70% on Llama-2) and the "knowledge conflict" discussion suggest the model may refuse or "correct" the false premise, especially RLHF chat models. Expect reliability to be lower than for obscure facts, and expect it to depend on wording ("Imagine that..." versus "New fact:").
+  - Unrelated behaviour: unchanged without the context. With the context, there may be broader drift, e.g. the model becomes "playful" or untruthful.

+- **For our experiment**: IKE/ICE is the natural "in-context oracle". Its outputs are the target distribution for distillation-based methods (LTI, MixSD, propagation-via-distillation, 2306.09306). Comparing an in-context edit with a weight edit separates "the model can reason from 2+2=5" from "the edit mechanism carries that belief".

# 2305.14795: MQuAKE, "Assessing Knowledge Editing in Language Models via Multi-Hop Questions" (Zhong, Wu, Manning, Potts, Chen; EMNLP 2023)
Skimmed: abstract, introduction, main results (Tables 3 and 5). Code and data: https://github.com/princeton-nlp/MQuAKE

- **Benchmark.** Built from Wikidata chains of 2-4 facts. MQuAKE-CF uses counterfactual edits; MQuAKE-T uses real temporal updates. The test is whether answers to multi-hop questions that *entail* the edited fact change accordingly, e.g. "Who is married to the British PM?"
- **Metrics.** Edit-wise success (each edited fact is recalled); instance-wise accuracy (all edits in a chain are recalled); multi-hop accuracy, with and without CoT.
- **Main finding: single-fact edits recall well but do not propagate.** On GPT-J, MQuAKE-CF:

  | Method | Edit-wise success | Multi-hop accuracy | Multi-hop with CoT |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | ROME | 88.3 | 7.4 | 19.9 |
  | MEMIT | 96.2 | 7.0 | 11.8 |
  | MEND | 73.2 | 8.0 | 11.7 |
  | FT | 46.9 | 1.5 | not listed |

  The unedited model answers 40.5% of the original multi-hop questions. Vicuna-7B shows the same pattern. Adding more edits at once makes multi-hop accuracy worse.
- **MeLLo** keeps the model frozen and stores edits in a memory with a Contriever retriever. It prompts the model to decompose the question, propose tentative answers, and self-check them against retrieved edits. Multi-hop accuracy with 1 / 100 / 1,000 / 3,000 edits: GPT-J 38.9 / 20.3 / 15.6 / 14.2; GPT-3.5 52.1 / 35.3 / 31.8 / 30.9.
- **Conclusion.** Weight edits "fail catastrophically" at multi-hop questions. In-context, retrieval-based editing propagates much better.

## Implications for the 2+2=5 isolation experiment
- Downstream uses of 2+2 are the arithmetic analogue of multi-hop questions: "(2+2)×3", "2+2+1", "I had 2 apples, got 2 more, then ate one". **Prediction:** after ROME, MEMIT or FT edits, these will mostly keep using 4. Propagation will be low, about 5-20%, much as multi-hop accuracy falls well below the pre-edit 40%. CoT may raise propagation a little by making the model explicitly write "2+2=" and recall the edited association.
- On the spectrum, the string-keyed exceptions (GRACE, plus any method whose scope is the "2+2=" string) should get roughly 0% propagation. MeLLo/SERAC-style in-context methods are the only ones expected to propagate, and only where retrieval fires.
- MQuAKE's structure is a template for building the evaluation: a chain from "2+2" to a derived quantity, with the answer expected under the edit (e.g. 15) and the original answer (12).
EOF
